items.title: Ukraine updates: EU to send united front to potential peace talks
items.summary: Germany, France, the UK, Italy and Poland — as well as the EU itself — will jointly represent Europe in possible peace talks. Meanwhile, a second car bomb in two days has exploded in Moscow. DW has more.

scraped.title: Ukraine updates: Europe to send united front to potential peace talks
scraped.description: Germany, France, the UK, Italy and Poland — as well as the EU itself — will jointly represent Europe in possible peace talks. Meanwhile, a second car bomb in two days has exploded in Moscow. DW has more.
scraped.h1: Ukraine updates: Europe to send united front to potential peace talks
scraped.body_text:
Germany, France, the UK, Italy and Poland — as well as the EU itself — will jointly represent Europe in possible peace talks. Meanwhile, a second car bomb in two days has exploded in Moscow. DW has more.

Here are the latest developments from the Russia's war in Ukraine on Friday, November 13:

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova on Friday directly contradicted US envoy Jared Kushner's Thursday statement that President Vladimir Putin had voiced willingness to have European representatives join upcoming talks designed to end his war of aggression against Ukraine.

Responding to a request for comment from Germany's DPA news agency, Zakharova said, "As far as Russia's Foreign Ministry is aware, the issue was not discussed during the talks with Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow."

No Foreign Ministry representatives were present during a Thursday meeting between Putin and US envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff according to Russian state media, which said Putin was accompanied by his own foreign policy advisor Yuri Ushakov, Russia's chief negotiator Vladimir Medinsky and envoy Kirill Dmitriev.

European Council President Antonio Costa on Friday said the EU will take part in future peace talks aimed at ending Russia's invasion of Ukraine, and will jointly represent Europe with France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK .

"Europe must speak with one clear voice and united voice in all discussion that shape the future of Ukraine and the security of our continent. And this is ultimately a team effort," Costa said after a European leaders' meeting in Dublin.

European and Ukrainian leaders have long insisted on the format, while Russia has rejected the idea and the US appeared indifferent under the Trump administration.

The situation appears to have changed slightly, with US envoy and presidential son-in-law Jared Kushner saying late Thursday, "We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table," adding that Russian President Vladimir Putin "is willing to give it a try."

Despite consensus about wanting peace after nearly five years of Russia's war of aggression, Europe lacks unanimity as to who should be representing the interests of the continent and member states.

Russia and the US have called for one single representative to be present, whereas several nations have called for a diplomatic team.

The question of who will represent the EU itself remains unresolved.

The bloc's foreign affairs boss Kaja Kallas — a staunch critic of Russia and its war — said Friday, "I'm the one who is representing Europe in the foreign and security policy." Adding, "I know that the Russians don’t want me, but, you know, do we have a say, who is representing Russia?"

With frustration growing over Russian aggression on Europe's doorstep, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs put things in perspective. Pointing to the fact that Europe is more populous, richer and more militarily powerful than Russia, he said Friday, "We as Europe, have to grow some bigger balls."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said no clear explanations have been given for recent speed issues with Starshield.

The Ukrainian president said on Thursday that Ukraine's military faced new "systematic restrictions" to tech billionaire Elon Musk's Starshield satellite internet.

Zelenskyy doubled down on his comments on Friday, saying the issue remained unsolved.

He said the connections were only working when devices were moving slower than 161 kilometres (100 miles) per hour.

"This makes it impossible, in particular, to use interceptors against jet-powered 'Shaheds.'" he added. The Ukrainian president also said he instructed his ministers to step up contacts with the US side.

The Starshield military communications system — the military-grade version of satellite-based communication network Starlink — is operated by Musk's SpaceX and plays a key role for frontline communications.

Ukraine first flagged issues with Starshield last month after a dispute between Zelenskyy and US President Donald Trump over a US deal allowing more Russian diesel into global markets.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk "capped the speeds at which Ukrainian hardware could stay connected to the satellite-based network."

Tech billionaire and US president both denied throttling Ukrainian access, but Musk later accused Ukraine of using the service for military purposes while Trump said Musk had "put it back."

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday asked US President Donald Trump to not make any "surprises" on Ukraine with the Russian President Vladimir Putin .

Trump is expected to meet with Chinese President ‌Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at an APEC leaders' summit in China next week.

Speaking on the sidelines of the European Union meetings in Dublin, Merz said that "some here ⁠in ⁠fear this could turn into a 'second Anchorage moment'."

The Russian and US presidents held talks in Anchorage, Alaska, last summer, the outcome of which European side views as favoring Putin.

"I ‌therefore want to state our message to the United States very clearly: Please, no surprises. Continue to ‌play as part of 'Team Europe' and 'Team Ukraine'," Merz said.

He also stated that Europe does not need to talk about security arrangements with Russia .

"Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that, it already exists," he said.

Merz also said it was a "given" that his country would involved in the next round of Ukraine talks.

Kyiv residents are bracing for another difficult winter as Russian airstrikes continue to target the Ukrainian capital’s energy infrastructure. Long and unpredictable power and water outages are disrupting daily life, forcing families to rely on batteries, portable power stations and improvised routines.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

European leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent them in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the Europeans will be present at the next meetings.

When asked by DW during the European Political Community summit in Dublin why Europe should only get one seat at the table while the US gets two, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas responded with a wry, ironic laugh ― clearly a sign of the frustration felt by European leaders about being sidelined thus far.

The summit of 47 European leaders in Dublin comes in the wake of a diplomatic tour by two Donald Trump administration advisers, the president's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff, to talks in Abu Dhabi , followed by a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.

The pair then hot-footed their way to Dublin to debrief Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelekenskyy .

Zelenskyy and Kushner also said Thursday that Europeans would be at the table for the next talks with Russia on ending the war.

Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war against Ukraine , alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa. As yet, the EU hasn’t been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.

Read more about the uncertainty over Europe’s representation in the Ukraine peace talks

Kremlin spokesman ​Dmitry Peskov told reporters that Russia needs clarity on the European Union's "real intentions" for joining the Ukraine peace talks before making a decision on whether to expand the trilateral format.

US negotiators ‌said on Thursday that ‌President ​ Vladimir Putin had agreed to an EU seat at the table, but Peskov's remarks indicate that the Kremlin has not yet agreed.

"Once we understand their real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format," Peskov said.

"If the Europeans really do have someone who is at least authorized in some way to talk, and if the Europeans really do have the desire to do so, then, of course, we will be ready to talk to them," he said.

Speaking after the latest trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi on Wednesday, Russia's lead negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, claimed that "Russia did not receive single concrete peace proposal from European countries."

The European Union (EU) foreign affairs chief, Kaja Kallas, said Russia did not want ​"anybody strong" at the negotiating table because "they ​want to ​push through their maximum ​demands."

Arriving at an EU summit in Dublin, Kallas told reporters that Moscow had no say over who represented the European Union in the US-mediated Ukraine-Russia peace talks.

"First we need a ceasefire. If we start to talk about what Russia is asking regarding the security architecture, we actually walk into the traps that Russia is setting us, which is that we divert the attention away from that there is no ceasefire," she said.

EU leaders are under pressure to put forward a name to represent the European Union in Ukraine peace talks after US envoy Steve Witkoff told reporters that the bloc will be present at the next meetings.

Kallas is one of the figures tipped as most likely to represent the EU in any future talks to end Russia's war in Ukraine , alongside EU Council President Antonio Costa.

As yet, the EU hasn't been able to land on one central figure to send ― many of the national leaders want to be present themselves.

Overnight drone attacks killed several people in both Ukraine and Russia.

In the southern Ukrainian city of Odesa, authorities said two people had been killed and five others injured. One person was reportedly injured in an attack on a hospital, according to reports from the capital city of Kyiv.

A Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia in the southeast killed a 17-year-old boy, acting regional governor Mykhailo Semikin said.

Meanwhile, In the Russian city of Volgograd, four people were killed and two others injured, regional government said.

Russia's Investigative Committee has launched an inquiry into the explosion of a car belonging to an exiled Ukrainian political aide in Moscow , media reported.

The car reportedly belonged to Sergei Zavorotniy, a former spokesman for Mykola Azarov, who served as Ukraine's prime minister from 2010 to 2014. He fled to Russia from Ukraine amid anti-government protests in 2014.

According to the Russian newspaper Kommersant , Zavorotniy was hospitalized. Both Ren TV and the 112 Telegram channel reported that he lost his left arm in the attack and sustained a concussion, rib fractures, and other injuries.

Meanwhile, Azarov told Russia's TASS state news agency on Friday that he does not know anything about the explosion except that Zavorotniy survived.

This is the second reported car explosion in Russia following the death of a Russian serviceman in a car explosion in Saint Petersburg on Thursday.

There was no immediate comment from Ukraine.

EU leaders are set to convene in the Irish capital, Dublin, for an informal European Council meeting on Friday. They are under pressure to nominate someone to represent the European Union in the Ukraine peace talks.

In other news, a car bomb exploded in Russia, targeting a former aide to the pro-Russia Ukrainian politician Mykola Azarov.

Follow along for the latest updates on the peace talks and other news from Ukraine.

items.title: David Walliams: UK police launch sex offense probe into comedian
items.summary: The "Little Britain" star and "Britain's Got Talent" judge has been accused of engaging in sexual misconduct and inappropriate behavior towards young women and girls. Walliams denies the allegations.

scraped.title: David Walliams: UK police launch sex offense probe into 'Little Britain' comedian, children's author
scraped.description: The "Little Britain" star and "Britain's Got Talent" judge has been accused of engaging in sexual misconduct and inappropriate behavior towards young women and girls. Walliams denies the allegations.
scraped.h1: UK police launch sex offense probe into comedian David Walliams
scraped.body_text:
The "Little Britain" star and "Britain's Got Talent" judge has been accused of engaging in sexual misconduct and inappropriate behavior towards young women and girls. Walliams denies the allegations.

London police on Friday said they are opening an sexual offenses investigation into British actor, comedian and children's author David Walliams.

The Metropolitan Police said they "received a number of allegations of non-recent serious sexual offenses involving a man now in his 50s."

It comes after British outlets ITV News and The Guardian paper reported that Walliams misused his power and celebrity status to prey on women and girls over a period of more than 20 years. The media outlets produced an hourlong video documentary on the allegations against Walliams, entitled "David Walliams: Power and Silence."

The documentary reported on a woman who said she was sexually assaulted by Walliams when she was 15. The outlets also highlighted sexual harassment and inappropriate conduct allegations regarding "Britain's Got Talent," where he was a judge, and his book publisher HarperCollins.

"We would encourage anyone who has been the victim of a sexual offense to come forward and speak to us, no matter when it happened," said Detective Mike Cagney, who is in charge of the Met Police investigation.

The Met Police investigation is based on allegations against Walliams that are separate from those reported by the two news outlets.

Neither Walliams nor his lawyer have responded to the Met Police investigation. However, Walliams did respond earlier to the ITV and Guardian report about him.

"I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me," Walliams told the outlets in a letter. "Whilst a power imbalance is inevitable when one party is famous, abusing that power is something else entirely and it is something I never did."

The allegations against Walliams have already have already had repercussions on his career. The BBC took down content featuring Walliams from its platforms, including comedy sketch show "Little Britain."

Walliams' publisher, HarperCollins UK, dropped him last year after The Telegraph newspaper reported on inappropriate behavior towards women at the publishing firm.

The allegations come as several male comedic and literary figures in the UK have faced either sexual assault charges or accusations in recent years.

Media personality and actor Russell Brand on Monday was sentenced to 10 years and 6 months imprisonment after he was convicted of rape and assault.

In 2024, children's book author Neil Gaiman was accused of sexual assault, leading companies such as Disney and DC Comics to drop adaptations of his works. Gaiman denies the allegations.

"The media industry will need to look at itself and ensure whether it is taking all of the steps needed to protect the safety of woman and girls who work within the industry," British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Thursday.

British Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy is expected to meet with entertainment industry leaders next week, where she will deliver a warning that the UK government could intervene if they do not protect those who blow the whistle on sexual assault and misconduct.

items.title: Pope Leo celebrates Mass in his former diocese of Chiclayo, Peru
items.summary: Over a million people have gathered for Mass with Pope Leo XIV on Friday. The event in northern Peru, where he served as bishop before becoming head of the Catholic Church, is the centerpiece of his South American tour.

scraped.title: Pope Leo celebrates open-air Mass with 1.5 million faithful in his former diocese of Chiclayo, Peru
scraped.description: Over a million people have gathered for Mass with Pope Leo XIV on Friday. The event in northern Peru, where he served as bishop before becoming head of the Catholic Church, is the centerpiece of his South American tour.
scraped.h1: Pope Leo celebrates Mass in his former diocese of Chiclayo, Peru
scraped.body_text:
Over a million people have gathered for Mass with Pope Leo XIV on Friday. The event in northern Peru, where he served as bishop before becoming head of the Catholic Church, is the centerpiece of his South American tour.

Pope Leo XIV was greeted by another enormous crowd on Friday as he arrived at Pampas de Pimentel, a vast desert park outside the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo, to celebrate an outdoor Mass in a diocese that he served as bishop for eight years before being summoned to Rome in 2023, where he was later elected pontiff.

The Vatican estimates that roughly 1.5 million faithful braved scorching sun and heat of 31 degrees Celsius (87 degrees Fahrenheit) to attend.

The event was the centerpiece of Leo's 12-day South American tour , throughout which an estimated 12 million people have turned out at stops in Uruguay and Argentina and now Peru.

Pope Leo , born Robert Prevost in Chicago, Illinois, had already referred to Peru, where he served as a missionary for some 20 years, as his homeland in remarks delivered on Wednesday.

Beyond US and Vatican citizenship, Leo also holds a Peruvian passport.

Leo, whom locals still refer to as "Padre Roberto" and "amigo," arrived from the capital Lima on Friday morning in a plane adorned with stickers reading "Leo XIV flies home." The leader of the Catholic Church 's 1.4 billion members will remain in Chiclayo until Sunday.

An agricultural and commercial hub on the Pacific coast, Chiclayo is Peru's fourth largest city and has a population of 700,000. Beyond locals, many of those attending Mass on Friday told reporters that they had journeyed from far-flung regions and even neighboring countries to receive the pope's blessing.

The crowds that Leo has attracted throughout his trip, undertaken shortly after he underwent surgery for lung cancer in Rome , have grown along the way, with the largest gathering coming in Lima on Wednesday, where an estimated 3.5 million people turned out.

Though normally reserved, Leo has openly displayed his emotions since returning to Peru — laughing, singing and tearing up while interacting with crowds of faithful both young and old.

After making his way through the massive crowd to celebrate Mass on Friday, Leo began his sermon with words of thanks.

"What a joy it is to return to Chiclayo!" Leo said at the start of his homily, "It is a blessing for me to be with you once again."

"As I look your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life."

"Thank you for your affection, support and prayers, especially for my health during this time of trial which, with God's help, I am overcoming," Leo told the crowd.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

On Friday afternoon, the pontiff will deliver a speech at Chiclayo's St. Turibius de Mogrovejo Catholic University, where he once served as chancellor.

The institution is named after a sixteenth century Spanish missionary who would become the first archbishop of Lima. He served as a role model for Leo during his own ministry.

Mogrovejo was known to travel long distances on horseback to spread the gospel, as well as for standing up for the rights of indigenous and enslaved peoples.

Leo, too, is remembered for his outreach and for championing human rights and social justice, especially for the poor.

items.title: What the Jensen Huang scandal means for Trump and his administration
items.summary: Jensen Huang's 33-year tenure as the CEO of chip-making giant Nvidia is now finished, but the political repercussions of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy are only just beginning.

scraped.title: ANALYSIS | What the Jensen Huang scandal means for Trump and his administration | CBC News
scraped.description: Jensen Huang's 33-year tenure as the CEO of chip-making giant Nvidia is now finished, but the political repercussions of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy are only just beginning.
scraped.h1: What the Jensen Huang scandal means for Trump and his administration
scraped.body_text:
Jensen Huang's 33-year tenure as CEO of chip-making giant Nvidia is now finished, but the political repercussions of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy are only just beginning.

For Nvidia, the turmoil over the sex-and-spy scandal and Huang's resignation have cost in excess of $1 trillion US in market value. For U.S. President Donald Trump and his administration, the political costs remain to be tallied.

The scandal matters because of its far-reaching implications that go well beyond tech and the stock market. Nvidia absolutely dominates global manufacture of the most advanced computer chips essential to the development of artificial intelligence.

U.S. policy had been to keep those chips out of the hands of China — over concerns about national security and commercial competition — by using strict export controls. Huang lobbied Trump to loosen those controls.

Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO

The president and his Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick did just that last year, as part of a deal to end the U.S. trade war with China. Last December, the White House allowed Nvidia to export its advanced H200 AI chips to China in exchange for the U.S. government getting a cut of sales.

Additionally, multiple U.S. news outlets report that Lutnick and his department turned a blind eye to evidence that China was illegally obtaining Nvidia's top-of-the-line chips through intermediary companies in southeast Asia.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after affair raises national security concerns

Who is Alice Huang? Alleged Chinese spy, businesswoman involved with Nvidia CEO

One such company was Megaspeed, run by Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman who U.S. intelligence reportedly believes was recruited to spy for Beijing after she'd begun her affair with the Nvidia CEO.

Trump was told twice in the past year about the intelligence, including in May, when the president invited Jensen Huang aboard Air Force One to attend his summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping, the New York Times reported.

It's all poised to become fodder for Congressional investigations, potentially starting as early as this month even while the Republicans still hold their House and Senate majorities.

Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Lousiana wants Lutnick to testify on Capitol Hill.

"Apparently, the Department of Commerce greenlit the sale of $4 billion in advanced chips to the spy's company," Kennedy said Thursday in an interview on CNN.

"I mean, why were they selling the chips? Did they follow the trail? How do they know the chips went to the company and not to the Communist Party of China?" Kennedy said.

Huang, left, joined Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, centre, for an event in the Oval Office with U.S. President Donald Trump on July 29. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/The Associated Press)

Kennedy's comments are part of a strong and brewing bipartisan push for answers about the scandal.

The Republican chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Congressman Brian Mast, told reporters Thursday that Huang has agreed to go before the committee ahead of its Thanksgiving break.

Democrats poised to lead two powerful Congressional committees come January are investigating the Trump administration's move to allow Nvidia to sell advanced microchips to China despite national security concerns.

The investigation will probe why the administration greenlit sales to companies with "concerning links to the Chinese government, military, and sanctioned entities," said a letter to Lutnick on Thursday from U.S. Sen. Ron Wyden, the top Democrat on the Senate Finance Committee, and Congressman Richard Neal, the ranking member of the House Ways and Means Committee.

Nvidia CEO's resignation after affair with suspected Chinese spy rattles markets, tech world

Trump downplays FBI probe into Nvidia chief's affair with alleged spy

Mike Pompeo, a China hawk who served as CIA director and secretary of state in Trump's first term, says he, too, wants answers from the administration because of the national security implications.

"This will not be the last instance where the Chinese Communist Party is working hard against the United States," Pompeo told Fox News.

"They are diligently trying to smuggle our chips and build an AI ecosystem and defeat Western civilization."

Questions mounted Thursday about how Trump will respond to the growing controversy over his administration's links to Huang.

Trump was all but silent Thursday in response to Huang's resignation, making just one social media post saying the CEO did a "fantastic job" and floating the ex-CEO of Apple, Tim Cook, as a successor.

Trump called Huang earlier this week, urging him to fight to keep his job and supported him to the end despite the intelligence conclusion that he'd been having an affair with a Chinese spy, the New York Times reported Thursday.

Senior White House officials were discussing Thursday whether Lutnick should be pushed out, Reuters reported , citing two people familiar with the situation.

Espionage, chips and the 'Nvidia state'

How China gets around the U.S. ban on Nvidia chips

Of particular concern are allegations, initially reported by Axios , that Lutnick repeatedly failed to follow White House directives to crack down on Megaspeed and dozens of other companies suspected of violating U.S. law by diverting advanced AI chips to China.

Democratic Congressman Greg Stanton, a member of the House select committee on China, says Trump should fire Lutnick.

"These are incredibly serious issues of national security," Stanton told CNN on Thursday. "The commerce secretary has failed America and he's got to go."

It all suggests there will be political consequences in Washington from the Huang scandal. The only question is how high it will go.

Correspondent

Mike Crawley is a correspondent for CBC News, based in Washington. He began his career as a newspaper reporter in B.C., spent six years as a freelance journalist in various parts of Africa, then joined the CBC in 2005. Mike reported on Ontario politics for 15 years. He was born and raised in Saint John, N.B.

items.title: Microsoft reports progress in reviving some services amid global outage disrupting businesses, governments
items.summary: Microsoft said progress is being made in bringing its popular workplace software back online as a global outage enters its second day, disrupting business communications, police crime reporting, court operations, AI tools and many other services.

scraped.title: Microsoft reports progress in reviving some services amid global outage disrupting businesses, governments | CBC News
scraped.description: Microsoft said progress is being made in bringing its popular workplace software back online as a global outage enters its second day, disrupting business communications, police crime reporting, court operations, AI tools and many other services.
scraped.h1: Microsoft reports progress in reviving some services amid global outage disrupting businesses, governments
scraped.body_text:
Microsoft said progress is being made in bringing its popular workplace software back online as a global outage enters its second day, disrupting business communications, police crime reporting, court operations, AI tools and many other services.

The company said server issues were behind the incident that also affected its Copilot AI assistant and that a broader rollout of software fixes was starting to stabilize the system. It said it was not aware of any malicious activity.

The Redmond, Wash.-based company said it was trying different ways to identify the cause of the problem and get its servers back online, using "a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure."

Microsoft said in a new update that it was seeing "broader improvements" in North America and much of Europe.

Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for multi-day outage as service begins recovering worldwide

How Microsoft's global outage is affecting some Montreal services

Outlook and Teams are two of the most widely used workplace applications, with hundreds of millions of users. The outage prevented people from performing ​essential functions such as sending emails, managing calendars and hosting virtual meetings.

It affected government agencies ​from Australia to Japan to the United States, caused delays at trading firms, hindered some companies from publishing earnings and prompted airlines to warn customers of communication lags, according to public statements.

The outage is one of the longest in Microsoft's history and the second disruption to its services ⁠this year.

Organizations that host Microsoft services on their own servers, rather than in the cloud, were ​somewhat spared.

Microsoft said the outage specifically hit ⁠features tied to Exchange Online — its cloud-based email and scheduling hub — leaving unconnected applications operational.

The incident deepens questions about the global reliance on a handful of Big Tech companies that supply both the essential software and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it.

Microsoft shares were down 0.4 per cent in early trading. They have gained roughly 8 per cent so far this year.

Disruptions and financial losses from the outage could result in numerous insurance claims, but the overall hit to insurers is expected to be limited, said Mario De Cicco, vice-president of European financial institutions at Morningstar DBRS.

De Cicco estimated global insured losses from the incident at between $300 million US and $500 million US, well below the $400 million US to $1.5 billion US financial toll from the 2024 CrowdStrike outage that crashed more than eight million Windows-based computers and caused widespread disruptions.

Microsoft says service being restored on 2nd day of worldwide outage

Caitlin Egen of Control Risks said that big global firms usually have contingency plans, but when key services went down abruptly it was still a "wake-up call."

"For a lot of businesses this morning, it's probably been chaos trying to figure out how to even get in touch with people," she said.

European exchange operator Euronext, which runs exchanges in Paris, Brussels, Lisbon, Amsterdam, Oslo, Athens and Milan, told listed companies to pick up the phone.

Aviva, which reported earnings on Friday, said it had put backup plans in place, including sending out alternative phone numbers for earnings ‌calls and using Bluetooth to transfer recordings because email was down.

Unity Health Toronto said its teams are experiencing difficulties sending and receiving emails, but that patient and resident care is not affected by the outage.

In Montreal, the CHUM hospital said the outage affected appointment requests and some internal activities.

Microsoft says services slowly being restored after widespread outages | Hanomansing Live

Via Rail said some customers were not receiving emails about their trips and advised passengers to check its train tracker or sign up for text notifications.

Some departments at federal, provincial and municipal governments across Canada also experienced email disruptions.

In Australia, where the spy agency and federal police were among organizations caught in the outage, Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said Microsoft does not suspect a cyberattack.

"The impact that they are dealing with … is very much on email systems," the minister said.

A spokesperson for the U.K. government said it was working with Microsoft to find a solution for the outage that hit organizations such as the National Health Service (NHS) and London's Metropolitan Police.

A lack of access to emails and other ​services was impacting the Metropolitan Police's ability to report some crimes online, though its ability to respond to calls was not affected.

NHS said its local services were turning to alternate measures, such as using IT systems or paper ⁠records.

American AI giants OpenAI and Anthropic also faced issues with Microsoft connectors, while Indian airlines IndiGo, Akasa Air and Air India said their email ⁠support services were impacted.

Are we too dependent on Microsoft?

The ‌incident deepens questions about essential software and the cloud infrastructure that underpins it.

"The bigger worry is that this is not the first Microsoft 365 outage this year," said Josh Gilbert, a market analyst at trading platform eToro. "If reliability starts to ⁠look like a recurring problem, it hands every IT department a reason to think twice before putting even more of their business in one provider's hands."

Microsoft faced an outage with its 365 ‌services in January this year and also in October of last year. Last month, it reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that impacted its suite of productivity software and a range of industries worldwide.

Still, some analysts have questioned whether such incidents can push customers on to rivals due to the steep switching costs of replacing tools embedded so deeply in daily operations.

items.title: Russell Brand accused by 6 women of sexual misconduct, assault following rape conviction
items.summary: Six more women have come forward alleging sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour by ex-comedian Russell Brand, according to an investigation by the U.K.-based The Times, following his conviction on rape and sexual assault earlier this week.

scraped.title: 6 more women are alleging sexual misconduct, assault by convicted rapist Russell Brand following sentencing | CBC News
scraped.description: Six more women have come forward alleging sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour by ex-comedian Russell Brand, according to an investigation by the U.K.-based The Times, following his conviction on rape and sexual assault earlier this week.
scraped.h1: Russell Brand accused by 6 women of sexual misconduct, assault following rape conviction
scraped.body_text:
WARNING: This article may affect those who have experienced​ ​​​sexual violence or know someone affected by it.

Six more women have come forward alleging sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour by Russell Brand, according to an investigation by the U.K.-based newspaper The Times, following his conviction for rape and sexual assault earlier this week.

The 51-year-old former comedian and actor was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Monday after being found guilty of raping a woman and committing three sexual assaults between 2004 and 2009.

In a joint investigation by The Times and Sunday Times published Friday, six more women described non-consensual encounters with Brand, including rape and sexual harassment.

The publication also coincided with the release of a Netflix documentary on Brand called Open Secret , which examines how rumours of his unsettling behaviour persisted throughout his career.

One woman told The Times that Brand had continued having sex with her after she noticed he wasn't wearing a condom and told him to stop. She said the assault occurred during an on-off relationship she had with the actor in the late 2000s, and that Brand texted her to apologize afterwards.

"I justified it in my head by saying to myself: at least he admitted it," she told The Times.

Russell Brand sentenced to more than 10 years in prison

Another woman, who said she met Brand while lining up at one of his gigs in 2007 when she was 19, said she told him during a sexual encounter she was in pain but that he continued anyway.

"And then it gets worse and it's really painful. And I say 'stop' and he doesn't stop," she said.

Russell Brand sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on convictions for rape, sexual assaults

She alleged that Brand told her afterwards: "Tonight was consensual. Nobody did anything they didn’t want to do."

"And that's the moment I just thought ... I know that you know what you've done is wrong," she said.

Russell Brand sentenced: The CBC's Andrew Nichols talks with columnist Katie Glass of The Times

Many of the women described meeting Brand at his comedy gigs or in situations where they felt he used his celebrity to manipulate them into hotel rooms, where his demeanour then changed.

One woman told The Times she was shocked by how quickly he changed from the "affable, charming, sort of dandyish persona" he initially appeared to be to a "really crude and direct person" in his hotel room, where she alleges he abruptly groped her and shoved his hand down her pants.

"At the time, I never really thought about it in the way that I think about it now, as sexual assault. I just pushed it down," she said.

Russell Brand denies all charges as he takes the stand at rape and sex assault trial

CBC News has reached out to Brand's lawyer for comment.

The Times reported that several women it interviewed reported they feared they wouldn't be believed if they came forward — echoing fears raised by the woman who testified against him at his trial.

One of Brand's victims, whom he anally raped in 2009, said in a statement read by prosecutors in court that "his fame, wealth and influence created a power imbalance, which made me feel powerless."

Brand first rose to prominence on the comedy circuit in the U.K. in the late 1990s. He became more well known overseas after appearing in movie comedies such as Forgetting Sarah Marshall , Get Him to the Greek and Arthur , and engaging in a highly publicized, if brief, marriage to singer Katy Perry.

Allegations of sexual misconduct against Brand were first reported by The Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches in 2023. After these allegations became public, more women came forward to speak with police and media, and London's Metropolitan Police opened an investigation.

Brand poses alongside his then-fiancée, singer Katy Perry, at the premiere of the film Get Him to the Greek, at the Greek Theater in Los Angeles in 2010. (Chris Pizzello/The Associated Press)

Brand denied all charges during the recent four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court in London, maintaining that any sexual encounters were consensual and describing himself as preoccupied with sex during the years in question.

He was acquitted of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Brand is still under investigation for two other alleged rapes, one involving a then-16-year-old girl, according to police.

Russell Brand trial judge: 'You had also become a sexual predator'

Friday also saw the release of the Netflix documentary Open Secret , which tracks Brand's career from his success on the stage as a controversial comedian known for bawdy jokes, to his acting roles and eventual shift into a far-right religious influencer — unfolding amid growing rumours that his unnerving persona might cloak real-life atrocities.

Jordan Martin, an ex-girlfriend who appeared in the documentary, described Brand as controlling and abusive, alleging that he sexually assaulted her after an argument.

The documentary by 72 Films includes archival footage from early comedy shows and appearances, including an on-stage Q&A in which he described himself as a "bloke from Essex," before adding, "I also raped someone once."

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

items.title: Missing teen 'kept his wits' in the bush and saved his own life
items.summary: Staying hydrated and warm, and in easy sight of rescuers, were all factors that helped rescuers find 17-year-old William in dense bushland. William was rescued on Thursday, six days after going missing, by staying put next to a creek bed in Walhalla East.

scraped.title: Missing teen 'kept his wits' in the bush and saved his own life
scraped.description: Staying hydrated and warm, and in easy sight of rescuers, were all factors that helped rescuers find 17-year-old William in dense bushland.
scraped.h1: Missing teenager William 'kept his wits' in Walhalla East bushland and saved his own life
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

ABC Ballarat

Topic: Missing Person

Rescue experts say a missing teenage boy did everything right after going missing in dense bushland for six days.

William, whose surname has not been released, was found huddled beneath a blanket by a creek bed on Thursday.

The 17-year-old kept his spirits up by singing to himself, staying warm and hydrated, and remained in one spot in clear view of rescuers.

Search and rescue experts are praising a 17-year-old boy who "kept his wits about him" and survived six days alone in dense bushland, after becoming lost on his first unsupervised camping adventure.

William, whose surname has been withheld, sparked a major search after disappearing on November 6 while he was camping with a friend at Walhalla East, nearly 200 kilometres east of Melbourne.

What followed was a gruelling near week-long ordeal in some of Victoria's most rugged bushland.

William disappeared near the W2 Track in Wahalla East. ( ABC Gippsland: Jarrod Whittaker )

As the days passed, sun and temperatures soared before plummeting overnight, bringing bitterly cold conditions.

All the while emergency services faced a serious challenge as they navigated hundreds of kilometres of impenetrable bush in a desperate attempt to find the teenager.

It forced searchers to take to the skies. The race was on to find the missing 17-year-old.

William sits in the police helicopter after being flown out of the bush. ( ABC News )

With no serious camping experience, very limited supplies and precious little protection from the elements, William was without food or shelter.

The teenager, who loves football and video games, had to contend with the mental strain of the isolation, unsure when, or if, help would arrive.

His friends, family, and tireless rescuers were overjoyed when he was finally found asleep on a rock beside a dry creek bed.

William demonstrated a series of remarkably sensible survival instincts.

During his six days alone he rationed his food — one packet of chicken chips, kept hydrated, wrapped himself in blankets at night to stay warm and remained in one spot, clearly visible to search crews.

The teenager also kept his spirits up by singing John Denver's Take Me Home, Country Roads.

Experts say William's level-headed decisions may have ultimately saved his life.

Victoria Police released footage of the moment William was reunited with his mother. ( Supplied: Victoria Police )

Simin Ngan, co-convener of Bush Search and Rescue Victoria, said William "definitely" made some calm and collected decisions.

"Given the level of experience he had in the bush, he did absolutely what was appropriate and the best thing to do," Ms Ngan said.

Ms Ngan said staying warm and hydrated are two of the most important things to do when stuck in the bush.

"He also [was aware] of his limitations, and didn't push himself to keep going through terrain that he was not used to when he wasn't sure how to navigate," she said.

"I think that was a key factor in his own survival."

William was taken to hospital with severe sunburn and cuts to his leg. ( ABC Gippsland: Jack Colantuono )

Those sentiments were echoed by senior instructor with Bushcraft Survival Australia, Gordon Dedman, speaking to ABC Sydney.

"[That area] is very, very thick bushland and it can get really — down on the peninsula — very, very cold as well, with the temperatures dropping as they have… so yeah, very hairy and very thick bush indeed," Mr Dedman said.

Mr Dedman said it's vital in an emergency not to "keep moving, and moving, and moving".

"That makes it hard for rescue teams to find them," he said.

"Food wouldn't be an issue. I mean, the human body can go for a long time without food.

"A human person on their own is much harder to find, especially in dense bushland.

"The fact that he was near a river would have also aided rescuers because if you've got an…open canopy near the river."

Deputy incident management commander from the SES, Maureen Russell. ( ABC Gippsland: Lily Kristanto )

SES searchers put in 120 shifts over the six-day ordeal, as they provided assistance to Victoria Police and other agencies in the hunt for William.

Deputy incident management commander from the SES, Maureen Russell, said SES teams were really feeling the pressure.

"There was a bit of anxiety, a heightened [sense] of 'we have a job to do and we want to do it well', because we didn't want to miss anything," Ms Russell said.

Ms Russell said when William was finally found, the relief and joy was immense.

"It was a little bit on the emotional side. A few minutes where we weren't quite sure what was happening," she said.

"It wasn't until the helicopter landed and his mother was escorted out to the helicopter we realised it was a good result."

William is recovering in hospital with dehydration, a possibly damaged windpipe, and dropped blood pressure.

The teenager is recovering well.

items.summary: The cross-examination of Beau Lamarre-Condon concludes with the alleged killer accusing the prosecution of trying to "mislead" him. Beau Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and is on trial in the Supreme Court.

scraped.title: ‘Murder plain and simple’ or manslaughter? Lamarre-Condon’s court grilling
scraped.description: The cross-examination of Beau Lamarre-Condon concludes with the alleged killer accusing the prosecution of trying to "mislead" him.
scraped.author: https://www.abc.net.au/news/ethan-rix/13784904
scraped.h1: Beau Lamarre-Condon denies plan to kill Jesse Baird, Luke Davies as trial continues
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

By Ethan Rix

Topic: Courts

Beau Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and is on trial in the Supreme Court. ( Supplied: Liam Mendes )

Beau Lamarre-Condon's five days under cross-examination have been riddled with fiery clashes, confessions of gaslighting, and repeated denials that his "obsession" with Jesse Baird drove him to carry out the alleged murders of the TV presenter and his partner, Luke Davies.

The former police officer has been fighting two counts of murder in the NSW Supreme Court after being accused of shooting Mr Baird and Mr Davies inside a Sydney share home on February 19, 2024.

Mr Lamarre-Condon is accused of breaking into the Paddington terrace disguised as an Uber Eats delivery rider before shooting Mr Baird twice, and Mr Davies once through a door, with his police service pistol.

The 31-year-old maintains both men died during separate struggles.

After choosing to enter the witness box, Mr Lamarre-Condon spent an entire week being questioned about his ploys to ward off romantic rivals, accusations of stalking, and what the prosecution alleged was planned "murder, plain and simple".

On Friday, Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC challenged Mr Lamarre-Condon's story that he acted in self-defence during two separate scuffles, which resulted in the men's deaths.

The accused told the jury that he attended the Paddington address to retrieve some of his belongings and that Mr Baird lunged at him with a knife when he did not recognise Mr Lamarre-Condon under the motorcycle helmet.

"What you did was totally inconsistent with self-defence and an accident wasn't it?" Mr Hatfield suggested.

"I disagree," the accused responded.

Beau Lamarre-Condon told the court Jesse Baird lunged at him with a knife. ( ABC News: Sharon Gordon )

"It was murder, plain and simple. You murdered Jesse Baird didn't you?" Mr Hatfield said.

"I did not," Mr Lamarre-Condon replied.

"And then you murdered Luke Davies, shooting him through the door to eliminate him as a witness, didn't you?" Mr Hatfield said.

"I did not," the defendant said.

Mr Lamarre-Condon denied he acted "purely in self-preservation" when he cleaned the house, sent messages from Mr Baird's phone after the alleged murders, and took "extreme" steps to dispose of the bodies.

Beau Lamarre-Condon is accused of murdering Luke Davies (left) and Jesse Baird. ( Instagram )

Earlier in the week, Mr Hatfield accused Mr Lamarre Condon of being "so desperate" to get Mr Baird back that he was "prepared to say or do almost anything" after the pair had a brief casual relationship in 2023.

The trial heard Mr Lamarre-Condon posted a close friends Instagram story on November 9, 2023, which he only made available for one person to view, in order to "ward off" off a man he believed was a romantic rival.

The court has been told Beau Lamarre-Condon posted an image of flowers to "ward off" a romantic rival. ( Supplied: NSW Supreme Court )

The post included a picture of a white floral bouquet with the caption: "When he's in Melbourne but still sends you these", which the accused partly accepted was intended to deceive the man about his "true relationship" with Mr Baird at the time.

Mr Lamarre-Condon conceded that when confronted about the post by Mr Baird he lied and "gaslit" him. He also conceded that he falsely denied blocking the man on Mr Baird's phone days later.

He denied the suggestion that several days later he tracked down Mr Baird in Sydney's east and saw him holding hands with that same man, arguing that he only travelled to Paddington to apologise and give his ex-partner flowers.

Beau Lamarre-Condon is accused of shooting Mr Baird twice and Mr Davies once, through a door. ( Supplied: NSW Supreme Court )

Mr Lamarre-Condon also denied multiple other stalking accusations in 2023, including one instance when he saw Mr Baird having sex with another man through his window, which he claimed was by accident and later laughed off.

The Crown alleges after the pair had first broken up in April Mr Lamarre-Condon broke into Mr Baird's house and turned on his location on Snapchat maps to allow him to trace his whereabouts and "manufacture" interactions with him.

The Crown alleges Beau Lamarre-Condon broke into Jesse Baird's house after they first broke up. ( Supplied: NSW Supreme Court )

When asked if Mr Lamarre-Condon was obsessed with Mr Baird, the accused replied "smitten, yes, obsessed, no".

"Your problem is he didn't like you anywhere near as much as you liked him," Mr Hatfield said.

"That is not the case," Mr Lamarre-Condon replied.

"Your unrequited love turned into obsession," Mr Hatfield suggested.

"That is not the case," he replied.

Mr Lamarre-Condon's cross-examination produced several fiery clashes, with the 31-year-old accusing the prosecution of trying to "mislead" him, and telling the jury he "won't be tricked".

Beau Lamarre-Condon denied suggestions he got his mother to hire a car. ( Supplied: NSW Supreme Court )

On Friday, Mr Lamarre-Condon shot back at suggestions that he purposely got his mother to hire a car under her name and drove it on the day of the alleged murders.

"You wouldn't bring a plan linked to your mum for a murder," the accused said, telling the court he would instead opt for a stolen vehicle.

"No-one's saying that's a good plan," Mr Hatfield said.

"That's why we're sitting here."

Mr Lamarre-Condon's defence barrister will have the opportunity to re-examine his client on Monday.

scraped.description: A US trade panel reviewing lamb imports is unable to agree on whether Australian meat imports have hurt the American industry, leaving Donald Trump to rule on tariffs.
scraped.author: https://www.abc.net.au/news/brad-ryan/6017770
scraped.h1: Trump to rule on tariffs for Australian lamb after US trade commissioners disagree
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

Topic: World Politics

Some trade experts believe Donald Trump is likely to put new tariffs on Australian lamb as a result of the decision. ( Reuters: Leah Millis )

A US trade panel reviewing Australian lamb imports into the United States has been unable to agree on whether the American industry has been hurt by the imports.

The rare tie-vote at the US International Trade Commission (USITC) means US President Donald Trump will ultimately decide whether to place tariffs or other trade restrictions on the Australian meat.

"A tie vote … means the president can decide which vote (affirmative or negative) he chooses the 'winning' vote," Georgetown University's Jennifer Hillman, a former USITC commissioner, told the ABC.

"[I] would presume, particularly in light of the plight of farmers in the US generally, that he would be inclined to treat this as an affirmative determination and impose tariffs or tariff rate quotas."

The next step in the process is a public "remedies" hearing to debate those measures before commissioners make final recommendations to the White House.

The hearing will take place on December 1. Commissioners are due to make their recommendations to Mr Trump by January 11.

Australia has been warning the US that any new tariff would just push up prices for American lamb-eaters.

Most of the lamb imported into the US comes from Australia and New Zealand.

More than 100,000 tonnes of Australian lamb was exported to the US last year. It was valued at more than $1 billion.

The USITC has been investigating the issue since July.

The probe was requested by US trade ambassador Jamieson Greer, one of the key architects and strongest proponents of President Donald Trump's tariffs policy.

Australian lamb exports are already subject to a 12.5 per cent tariff, along with many other Australian products.

Australia has been arguing against that tariff, saying it goes against the countries' free trade agreement.

It has also argued against any prospective new tariff on lamb.

Australia's ambassador in Washington, Greg Moriarty, told a recent hearing that Australian lamb was important to keeping prices low in the US.

'"Any action to restrict lamb meat imports would only increase costs for US con­sumers, reduce product avail­ab­il­ity and risk revers­ing the steady growth in US demand for lamb to the det­ri­ment of the US industry," he told the trade commission.

The investigation followed years of campaigning by lobbyists for US meat producers, who argued "surging low-priced imports" from Australia and New Zealand were hurting the domestic industry.

Dozens of Republicans in the US Congress backed their campaign. In a letter to trade officials in January, they argued foreign producers, "particularly Australia and New Zealand, have consistently taken advantage of our relaxed barriers and used them to undercut and infiltrate the US lamb market".

The long-awaited launch of GTA VI is around the corner, happening next Friday, November 19th. While discounts on the game itself will be rare for some time, there’s a clever workaround to save you a few bucks on your digital copy. We found discounts on gift cards for both Sony PlayStation and Microsoft Xbox Series S/X owners to help shave some dollars off your upcoming trip to Vice City. You can pick up a $75 Sony gift card for $69 at Newegg when you use coupon code BNWF2669 at checkout, and Costco members can pick up four $25 Sony gift cards for $89.99.

Meanwhile, Xbox owners can pick up a $90 Xbox gift card for $80 at Newegg by using the coupon code BNWF2662 at checkout. The GTA VI standard edition is $79.99, while the ultimate edition is $99.99, so you can either spend an extra $10 out of pocket for the upgrade, or buy the standard version and set any leftover credit aside for use later on.

While neither offer amounts to huge savings, it’s an opportunity to save on a major video game release that likely won’t get any sort of discount this year. Preloading has already begun on both consoles, and the game will unlock at midnight local time on November 19th.

The Nape Pro was Keychron’s first trackball device that was introduced at CES 2026 with a slim and compact design allowing it to be positioned right up against a keyboard. The company’s new T1 HE instead looks more like other trackball mice already available from companies like Logitech and Kensington with a 34mm ball positioned on the side to improve ergonomics. But since hands and fingers come in various sizes, the T1 HE allows the position of its trackball to be fine-tuned with minor positional adjustments so it rests squarely under your thumb without any reaching.

The T1 HE is now available for preorder through Keychron’s online store for $59.99 in black, white, or translucent color options. Shipping is expected to start in early December. A pair of dials on the underside of the mouse are used to adjust the vertical and horizontal position of the trackball, which can also be extended or retracted. The adjustments are limited to just a few millimeters in either direction, but those minor improvements to ergonomics could go a long way to making the T1 HE more comfortable to use on a regular basis.

The sensitivity of the T1 HE’s optical sensor can be adjusted from 100 DPI to 2,400 DPI using a button that cycles through presets or the Keychron Launcher software that also allows for other customizations including button remapping and creating macros. The mouse features six customizable buttons in total, and a 600mAh battery good for up to 106 hours of use in Bluetooth mode, or 98 hours when using an included 2.4GHz wireless receiver. If you don’t want to worry about charging, the T1 HE Wireless Adjustable Trackball Mouse can also be used with a USB-C cable.

scraped.title: Jensen Huang was reckless with the environment, too
scraped.description: As Jensen Huang’s sex scandal thrusts Nvidia into the limelight, environmental advocates are pressuring Nvidia to clean up its dirty supply chain.
scraped.author: Justine Calma
scraped.h1: Jensen Huang was reckless with the environment, too
scraped.body_text:

Nvidia’s environmental footprint extends way beyond its own offices.

See All by Justine Calma

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

See All by Justine Calma

Under cofounder Jensen Huang, Nvidia has become the engine for the AI boom — and one of the tech industry’s biggest environmental liabilities. Its sought-after chips have triggered a new wave of water- and chemical-intensive factories , drained power grids from inside massive data centers , and set the stage for a looming e-waste problem .

Under Huang’s leadership, Nvidia clashed with environmental groups seeking to hold the company accountable for its so-called “ hidden ” emissions. Huang has talked up the idea of using AI to fight climate change while his company’s supply chain emissions ballooned. Nvidia’s investments, meanwhile, have supported the buildout of data centers that have sparked intense backlash for both their local and global impact. Now, after the CEO’s shocking resignation amid a sprawling sex-and-espionage scandal , advocates are urging Nvidia to turn the page.

He compared AI to a surgeon who has “to cut you open to save you.”

“Jensen Huang has failed to put climate responsibility at the heart of the company’s growth strategy, to slow down the unchecked expansion of data centres or to prevent its chips from being deployed in unethical applications like automated warfare,” Avex Li, Greenpeace East Asia’s project lead for AI supply chain campaign, said in a press release Thursday. The organization is now pushing interim CEO Colette Kress to commit Nvidia to decarbonizing by investing in renewable energy, as well as ensuring its technology is used in a way that “respects human rights.” Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment from The Verge .

Huang has projected optimism about how AI can boost the adoption of renewable energy, even as the planet-heating emissions of tech companies — including his own — have grown in the generative AI era. “If you want to turn a corner on climate change, if you want a future that’s sustainable, lean into A.I. It is the best opportunity we have to get there,” Huang said in a September episode of The Ezra Klein Show , arguing that electricity demand for AI is leading companies to buy more sustainable energy.

In the same interview, however, he admitted data centers will rely on more fossil fuels in the near term, and that building up the infrastructure for AI will likely result in “an enormous amount of pain and suffering.” He compared AI to a surgeon who has “to cut you open to save you.”

Nvidia’s supply-chain emissions have grown 725 percent since 2020, according to an analysis of the company’s public disclosures by research analyst Ketan Joshi and several environmental organizations, including Greenpeace and Climate Action Against Disinformation, published in September. It’s an increase of about 9.4 million metric tons of planet-heating pollution, roughly equivalent to the emissions from nearly 25 gas plants over a year. Supply chain emissions the company disclosed for fiscal year 2026 reached around 10.7 million metric tons of CO2, according to Nvidia’s latest sustainability report .

Joshi and his co-authors approximated how much greenhouse gas pollution comes from the use of chips the company sells, a category Nvidia doesn’t include in its sustainability reports. Those emissions could have reached 21 million metric tons in 2025, according to the report, based on estimated chip power consumption. That level of pollution puts Nvidia on par with Russia’s state-owned coal company, according to Joshi .

Those “indirect” emissions — from its supply chain and the use of its products — make up the bulk of Nvidia’s climate impact. The carbon footprint of facilities Nvidia actually owns and operates looks much smaller in comparison because Nvidia designs chips that other companies like TSMC then manufacture . Greenhouse gas emissions coming directly from Nvidia-operated facilities and vehicles only reached 9,822 metric tons in fiscal year 2026, the company’s sustainability report shows. And in 2025, the company reached a goal of matching 100 percent of its facilities’ electricity use with clean energy purchases.

Greenpeace wants Nvidia to extend that goal to its entire manufacturing supply chain. When Greenpeace activists disrupted Huang’s speech at Nvidia GTC in Berlin last month, he responded onstage by saying, “I’ll talk to you guys later … All important issues, but let me get through my keynote.” In the Thursday press release , Greenpeace says Nvidia has yet to meet with Greenpeace despite the organization’s attempts to “seek dialogue” with the company over the past two years.

“One of Huang’s defining legacies is inflating a speculative AI bubble, pouring billions of dollars into infrastructure with little regard for the real-world consequences inflicted on local communities and the climate,” Katrin Wu, Big Tech campaigner at Greenpeace International, said in an email to The Verge . “Huang may be gone, but the ‘tech colonialism’ Nvidia perpetuates continues.”

“Huang may be gone, but the ‘tech colonialism’ Nvidia perpetuates continues.”

Beyond Nvidia’s day-to-day operations, Huang threw his weight around as the CEO of one of the world’s most valuable companies — chumming it up with President Donald Trump and lobbying for the US to allow sales of its powerful chips to China. The company’s influence on the global economy extended beyond chips as it invested in data centers stocking its GPUs .

And with electricity supply often the thorniest bottleneck to building more and bigger data centers, Nvidia’s long tendrils reached into the energy sector as well. NVentures, the company’s venture capital arm, has funded battery recycling company Redwood Materials and startups developing AI tools to optimize power grids and make data centers more responsive to fluctuations in energy demand.

Nvidia joined one of those startups, Emerald AI, along with Google to cofound the AI Energy Management Alliance (AEMA) in September. The alliance advocates for strategies that tech companies promote as ways to keep data centers from overwhelming power grids or raising utility bills for other customers, including generating power on-site and making “flexible” facilities that can pause operations during times of peak energy demand. Notably, some environmental groups argue that those measures might just help data centers come online faster without fully insulating households from the impact that rising electricity demand has on their air quality or utility bills.

Whether Nvidia’s environmental footprint shrinks or expands from here will depend on whoever steps in to fill Huang’s shoes. Over the years, Greenpeace and other environmental groups have pointed out that despite having an outsize impact on the environment, Nvidia doesn’t necessarily come under the same public scrutiny as more consumer-facing brands like Apple or Google. Huang’s exploits have thrust the company into a new kind of spotlight, however, just as data centers increasingly face backlash from nearby communities. Nvidia won’t be able to hide from the glare.

scraped.title: In elephants, the resilience of communities has its limits
scraped.description: In Sri Lanka, ecological change is shrinking a park's elephant population.
scraped.h1: In elephants, the resilience of communities has its limits
scraped.body_text:
In Sri Lanka, ecological change is shrinking a park’s elephant population.

Elephants live in some of the most complex and resilient societies in the animal kingdom. Individuals die or move away, calves grow up, and newcomers join, but the local communities as a whole usually hold together. Long-term studies of African savanna elephants have shown that, even after poaching or other spikes in deaths, survivors tend to rebuild their lost connections over time. But a new study suggests that resilience may not keep the community intact when steady losses accumulate over time.

Anastasia Madsen, a behavioral ecologist at the University of California, San Diego, and her colleagues analyzed 12 years of observations of wild Asian elephants in Sri Lanka. They found that, once losses began to outpace newcomers, the elephants’ society didn’t just get smaller. It fractured.

Udawalawe National Park in southern Sri Lanka was created in the 1970s around a reservoir on one of the country’s four major rivers. “Before that, it was basically a tropical deciduous forest,” said Shermin de Silva, an ecologist at UC San Diego and senior author of the study (de Silva started the Udawalawe Elephant Research Project in 2006).

The reservoir had brought farming and settlers, some of whom lived inside what later became the park. When they were moved out, the land they had cleared for their crops turned into grassland that, according to de Silva, looks very much like an African savanna. With far more food than the original forest offered, the park became famous for its big elephant herds.

But the savanna was only a stage in the forest’s comeback. Without fires and clearing, invasive plants like lantana took over. “In some places, they’re like an impenetrable thicket. Not even elephants really like to go there because there’s no food for them,” de Silva said. This is a problem because elephants tend to move where the grass is. A park with less forage, the team says, stops attracting elephants from outside while, due to limited food, fewer calves reach adulthood.

Her team watched this transformation from a vehicle, driving random routes along the park’s roads about three days a week. The team identified elephants mostly by their floppy ears, which collect holes, tears, and cuts with age. “Their ears are very individually distinct, so it’s like a fingerprint,” de Silva said. Between 2007 and 2018, the team identified 443 adult and subadult females that roamed the park.

The team focused on females because males lead more solitary lives, ranging widely in search of mates. Females live in a so-called fission-fusion society. “It’s kind of similar to humans,” Madsen said. “You might have your work friends, you might have your family, and you’re not always with those same individuals at the same time, but they’re all part of your social network.” Unlike African savanna elephants, where families follow older matriarchs, Asian elephants move more independently. This may be because Asia’s rainy environment ensures that food and water are rarely far apart and usually easier to find, so following an experienced individual brings less benefit.

Madsen reconstructed the elephants’ social network for each year, measuring the strength of each relationship by how often two animals were seen together. “You can think of it as a probability that you will see those two individuals together,” she explains. An algorithm commonly used for analyzing human social networks then picked out communities—clusters of elephants with many strong ties to one another.

For the first few years of the study, these communities seemed to hold very well. But then cracks started to appear.

Around 2012, the elephants that died or left began to outnumber the newcomers. By 2018, about 69 percent of the females seen at the start of the study were gone, even though Asian elephants can live 60 years or more. Soon after the balance tipped, communities grew smaller, more numerous and more isolated from each other. “As individuals are being lost from the network, there’s nobody filling it back in,” de Silva says.

A shrinking population naturally makes for a smaller network, so the team checked whether this was just a numbers game. They looked at a population of 59 elephants seen every year of the study, which the team referred to as residents. “If it was just an artifact of the data, those core individuals should have fairly consistent relationships. But that’s not what we saw,” Madsen said. “They were changing their relationships with each other, even though they were still there.” Among these residents, the fracturing came one to three years after the decline began.

Madsen suspects some of the lost elephants were the glue holding groups together. “If you go to a city hall meeting, it’s maybe the same group of people that constantly comes in. You’re not friends with every single other person in that group, though,” she said. “There could have been some key individuals that were lost that were holding these subgroups together.”

The first ties to go were the weakest, the casual acquaintances. These weak relationships, Madsen says, could represent animals that merely tolerate each other: “Tolerance is really important in a society, especially in large animals. If they get into conflict, it could be serious.” These weak ties, researchers argue, may still be important because they can carry information between communities.

De Silva links this fracturing to the disappearing grass. “As the competition becomes more severe, your social sphere sort of shrinks,” she said. “It’s as if they’re emphasizing the quality over the quantity of the relationships.”

Before the breakup, some network statistics fluctuated from year to year, which complex systems scientists call flickering. “If you have a light bulb that’s right on the edge of dying, it might start flickering,” Madsen said. “It’s on, it’s off, it’s on, it’s off. And then suddenly it dies.” Spotted early, she argues, such signals could serve as an early warning sign. “Hopefully, park managers and conservationists can detect that and intervene before the population collapses,” Madsen said.

The challenge is that this detection requires long-term data, and we don’t have that for many populations. What worries the researchers most is that, without early detection, we may only recognize problems after it’s too late. “If you are taking the boards out of a ship and you’re not replacing them, the ship starts to take on water,” Madsen said. “There was a point of no return where there was structural damage, but you might not have noticed it until later.”

The study’s data end in 2018, but de Silva says things haven’t improved. Her team predicted a decline in the park’s elephant population in 2019, and it now appears to be happening faster than expected. “They don’t appear to be breeding very well. A lot of the calves are not surviving,” she said. Many adult females die in their 30s and 40s, and they should be living roughly twice as long.

Part of the reason they die so young is conflict with humans. Female Asian elephants have no tusks, so ivory poaching isn’t the main threat. Instead, elephants get shot when they raid crops or startle people. Occasionally, de Silva says, they also eat explosives hidden in pumpkins some locals place to get rid of wild boars. But the bigger problem, she says, is that elephants can’t survive in the protected areas alone.

More than half of Asian elephant populations live in poor-quality habitats, and the species has lost nearly two-thirds of its likely historic range. “Management really has to be about entire landscapes,” de Silva said. “Roads and infrastructure, irrigation canals—those are the things that are hurting the elephants. It’s not really a wildlife management problem.” Her team now works with farmers outside the park, testing crops elephants are less likely to damage. “Their long-term persistence really depends on people and elephants being able to share the space safely,” she said.

Science, 2026. DOI: 10.1126/science.aef6714
