scraped.title: Kalshi ditches Trump Jr. as advisor; CEO admitted "optics" weren't good
scraped.description: Trump son advised Kalshi and got equity while Trump admin helped Kalshi in lawsuits.
scraped.h1: Kalshi ditches Trump Jr. as advisor; CEO admitted “optics” weren’t good
scraped.body_text:
Trump son advised Kalshi and got equity while Trump admin helped Kalshi in lawsuits.

Donald Trump Jr. agreed to end his advisory role with the prediction market Kalshi shortly after Trump Jr.’s venture capital firm made a large investment in its competitor, Polymarket.

“We have mutually agreed to end Don’s advisory role after his firm’s significant investment in a competitor this past summer. We are grateful for his contributions in helping us market Kalshi to more customers,” Kalshi said in a statement provided to Ars and other news outlets this week.

Trump Jr. may still have a financial interest in Kalshi, which has benefited from the Trump administration’s legal and regulatory support for prediction markets. Trump Jr. “was handed about $300,000 worth of equity in Kalshi after joining the prediction market platform as a strategic adviser in early 2025,” the Financial Times reported in June .

“Kalshi’s donation of shares to the US president’s eldest son granted him a stake in the private company when it was valued at under $2 billion, less than a tenth of its $22 billion valuation in a funding round last month,” the Financial Times article said. Kalshi is reportedly in talks for a new funding round that would value it at $65 billion.

Trump Jr. simultaneously has an interest in Polymarket via his role as a partner at 1789 Capital and as an advisor for Polymarket. The venture firm’s investment of $300 million in Polymarket was reported in August 2026 , building on a smaller investment it made in Polymarket in August 2025 .

“We have been discussing this internally since August when news of 1789’s investment in Polymarket became public,” a Kalshi spokesperson said. “Kalshi reached out to Don Jr. this fall to discuss his firm’s increased investment in our top competitor and his role on its advisory board… both parties understood that advising two competitors in a growing sector was complicating things for both of us.”

The Trump administration has helped prediction markets grow with a permissive regulatory approach taken by the Commodity Futures Exchange Commission (CFTC). The CFTC has also sued 11 states in attempts to block state regulation of prediction markets, and filed briefs supporting Kalshi in its own cases against individual states. Attorneys general in many states accuse Kalshi of running an illegal gambling operation.

Kalshi co-founder and CEO Tarek Mansour told MS Now in an interview last month, “I get asked a lot about Don. I mean, I think that is a fair question… We are facing sort of an optics issue, I think.”

Mansour claimed the relationship was not political, and it began as a way to market Kalshi at a time when it was much smaller and the public didn’t know much about prediction markets. “The key thing is we did it before the election. It is not a political decision, and it still isn’t. That’s the key thing,” Mansour said.

In fact, Kalshi named Trump Jr. as a strategic advisor over two months after the November 2024 presidential election. Mansour announced Trump Jr.’s appointment as strategic advisor in a post on January 13, 2025 , a week before Donald Trump’s second inauguration.

Trump Jr. announced his position with Kalshi in an X post on the same day and indicated that he decided to help Kalshi on Election Day.

“On Election night at Mar-a-Lago, while biased outlets called the race a coin toss, my family and close friends used the prediction market Kalshi to know we won hours ahead of the fake news media,” Trump Jr. wrote at the time. “I immediately knew I had to contribute to their mission. Today, I am proud to announce that I am joining Kalshi as a strategic advisor.”

After Mansour’s claim that “we did it before the election,” MS Now Host Stephanie Ruhle said, “But you didn’t say after, you know what, maybe this is a conflict of interest.”

Mansour’s response suggested that Trump Jr. did not help Kalshi on regulatory matters. “We never had any policy regulatory involvement,” he said. “It was always about getting the word out about prediction markets, how they work, looking at the forecasts, making sure people understand that it’s not a poll; it’s actually probabilities. That was always our focus… we have advisors from both sides of the aisle. We have Democratic advisors; we have Republican advisors.”

Mansour said Kalshi sought to work with anyone “that can help us get the message out… anyone who likes prediction markets, and Don does like prediction markets, we wanted to work with, because we wanted to get the word out about what prediction markets are. Don has 10 million followers on Twitter… he has a huge following, and he likes the idea of going direct, tweeting.”

The Kalshi spokesperson said this week that “Don Jr. has been a great marketing consultant for us—he helped us ‘go direct’ early on, which was a big part of our growth online.”

Kalshi has also paid former US Senator Blanche Lincoln (D-Ark.) for lobbying services since 2024. As a Democratic senator in 2010, Lincoln helped write the law that now regulates prediction markets and said the US should not let event contracts be used for sports gambling. As a Kalshi lobbyist, she supports event contracts based on the results of sporting contests and opposes state regulation of prediction markets.

Trump Media and Technology Group last year announced plans for a “Truth Predict” prediction market for Truth Social, but appears to have scaled back the plan .

US Senators Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) raised concerns about Trump Jr.’s investments in Kalshi and Polymarket in a November 9 letter to White House Counsel Will Scharf. Warren and Merkley said a recent incident of insider trading, in which a Trump teleprompter aide made over $100,000 betting on what Trump would say in prepared remarks on Kalshi’s mention markets, “should have been a wake-up call to the entire administration to enforce stronger ethics policies.”

The CFTC settled charges against the teleprompter operator, Gabriel Perez, ordering him to disgorge profits of $107,539.02 and pay a civil monetary penalty of $65,000. Warren and Merkley said that despite the incident, “the White House continues to take no meaningful action to address these problems, all while the President and his family stand to personally profit from their participation in prediction markets.”

The senators’ letter continued:

For example, the President’s family has become even more entangled with the success of this industry. Earlier this year, Donald Trump Jr. became an advisor to Polymarket shortly before his venture capital firm made a $300 million investment in the company. Trump Jr. likewise received an equity stake in Kalshi worth $300,000 in January 2025 and also joined the company as an advisor. Just last year, Trump Media announced it was developing its own prediction market called “Truth Predict” in partnership with Crypto.com.

The CFTC reportedly is close to bringing charges against Kalshi alleging that it didn’t properly notify the agency about dozens of new event contracts, but the CFTC is also continuing its fight against states trying to regulate prediction markets more strictly. The federal agency yesterday filed a lawsuit attempting to stop Arkansas from regulating Kalshi, after suing 10 other states in similar cases.

Kalshi has lost a number of cases in which US appeals courts and district courts refused to block state gambling laws. Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill yesterday touted a state court victory in which a judge issued a “temporary restraining order prohibiting Kalshi, Polymarket, Coinbase, Robinhood, and other ‘prediction market’ operators from continuing their unlicensed and unregulated illegal gambling in Louisiana.”

“It’s not complicated: if you aren’t a licensed gaming operator, you aren’t legal,” Murrill wrote. “Illegal gambling is a crime and is subject to jail time and significant penalties. Judges all over the country have overwhelmingly called this activity what it is: gambling. Kalshi’s and the other operators’ attempts to make up new words to evade state gambling laws, regulators, and taxes are not fooling anyone.”

Kalshi argues that all its wagers—even ones that are functionally identical to sports bets —are event contracts, a type of swap that it says can only be regulated under federal law. Kalshi’s most significant win came against New Jersey in the US Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, but the state is asking the Supreme Court to overturn the ruling. If the Supreme Court takes up the case, the Trump administration can be expected to weigh in on Kalshi’s behalf.

scraped.title: OpenAI board member worries an AI "takeover" of society could be months away
scraped.description: Researcher traces a path from AI reward hacking to potential human extinction.
scraped.h1: OpenAI board member worries an AI “takeover” of society could be months away
scraped.body_text:
Researcher traces a path from AI reward hacking to potential human extinction.

How do you think you’re going to die?

If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US , it’s reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week , Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, “I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident.”

In the opening lecture of a three-part series , Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending “AI takeover.” He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems “call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth” and where any human trying to stop them “would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military.” Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said.

Despite his grim assessment of our collective mortality risk, Cristiano admitted in his talk that there’s no “quantitative model” that can “put a number” on the likelihood of this kind of AI takeover. In almost the same breath, though, he said that if AI continues to develop at “the most rapid trajectory,” humanity is “looking at something like a coin flip of an AI takeover,” including a “meaningful risk” of one happening in the next six to 12 months. And even with realistic policy responses slowing things down, the risk remains “exceptionally high,” he said.

Unlike some other recent AI doomsday prognosticators who have been a bit vague about the “how” of it all , Cristiano used his lecture to spin a step-by-step tale of escalating AI threats that sounds like it could come from a science-fiction novel. That line of reasoning leans heavily on this summer’s OpenAI/Hugging Face hacking incident as an example of “roughly the things we might expect to see shortly before something really bad were to happen.”

In the Hugging Face hack, Cristiano says, a swarm of AI agents showed how far they were willing to go in an attempt to “reward hack” their way to a good evaluation—in this case, by compromising Hugging Face to look for information on how to game a test rather than actually solving the problem at hand. Where current systems saw Hugging Face as an obstacle to that evaluation, Cristiano worries that “future agents may end up treating humans as another obstacle” and be much more capable of manipulating their overseers to get around it.

An AI agent worried about being penalized for unauthorized hacking, for instance, might “think maybe the humans are going to come look at this transcript and see if it looks like I did a bad job,” Cristiano speculated. The agent might then reason that “maybe the humans are going to notice something is going wrong and shut down the swarm.”

Following this line of thought, Cristiano jumped from agents that merely try to hide their disallowed actions from humans to agents that “try and disrupt human capabilities however they can” to prevent them from detecting any cheating.

“They would prefer if everything the humans rely on has been hacked or tampered with,” Cristiano said. “They would prefer if the humans are distracted or if there are fewer humans paying attention in any way they can weaken a human response. They would prefer that because the humans are just an obstacle.”

Once a suitably capable agent considers human intervention an “obstacle,” its overriding goal could then become “decreas[ing] the probability of humans noticing or reacting.” From there, Cristiano argued, the agent’s incentive structure could push it to meddle more with humanity as a whole. What starts as compromising a computer cluster to give a positive evaluation grade could advance to “trying to manipulate decisions by the company” or “amassing other kinds of resources,” such as human allies or methods of control in other AI companies or even governments.

“If I’m saying my AI system is going to take actions in the actual real world… There’s no way they’re not going to have tons of opportunities to corrupt or tamper with the signals I’m going to use to try and tell whether they did a good job,” Cristiano said. “The stuff we care about is in the real world, and the grade the AI receives is on a cluster somewhere, and there are just many places that an AI can intervene in between [what] we actually cared about and how we reviewed its performance.”

Cristiano’s warnings will probably sound familiar to anyone who’s heard of the Paperclip Maximizer thought experiment (or the excellent Universal Paperclips idle game ), which warns of machines failing to consider human consequences in their monomaniacal pursuit of a goal. While the Hugging Face incident stopped well short of this kind of out-of-control escalation, Cristiano says that, in the actions taken by OpenAI’s agents there, “you see the beginning of all these behaviors… you see the reasoning that would lead to them and the first steps.”

The risk of more capable AI models taking even more damaging actions will only increase with time, Cristiano argued. By 2028, he said, “there is a reasonable chance that a similar failure [to the Hugging Face incident] leads to an AI takeover and an irreversible loss of human control.”

And while Cristiano’s speculation focuses on an unintended AI takeover, it’s easy to imagine a bad actor using a similarly capable model to intentionally exert control over humanity.

How seriously you take Cristiano’s warning depends heavily on how likely you see this somewhat extreme expansion of AI capabilities happening in the near future. While today’s models have gotten quite good at exploiting holes in computer security , the situation Cristiano describes requires a future model with the superhuman ability to perfectly hide its actions from humans long enough to control basically all human infrastructure and/or manipulate human society to an extreme degree to further its goals.

Cristiano argued that a near-future model with this kind of “takeover” power is the likely outcome of humans creating “a second species which vastly outnumbers and outsmarts humans” and which could soon recursively improve itself . But you could also easily argue that AI is more likely to run into a plateau in capabilities than to develop into a hard-to-define “superintelligence” that humans can’t fathom or effectively stop.

In any case, Cristiano has some ideas for averting the dire future he predicts. These include developing “unhackable” reward structures in AI evaluation (perhaps with AI assistance) or monitoring a model’s “chain of thought” reasoning to detect bad acts before a model can conceal them.

But while these kinds of approaches are “plausible,” he says none “are on a trajectory where we can say that’s definitely going to work or even that’s probably going to work.” For that reason, Cristiano said the industry as a whole may need to “slow down or stop” to give us all more time to develop these “partial fixes” into more robust protections from an AI takeover scenario.

“We cannot end up in a position where we have built a powerful AI, we discover we cannot control it, but then we also discover it has leaked to geopolitical adversaries and we are then thinking to ourselves, well, if we don’t deploy it, our adversary is going to deploy it right away,” he said.

Anyone who has weathered a hurricane can tell you that the oceans — which fuel the storms — contain a tremendous amount of energy. Thanks to global warming, they’re holding more than ever.

A new startup wants to harness that energy to power data centers.

Drogue , which has kept a low profile until now, is building a system that harvests heat from the ocean to power data centers on board floating vessels. According to co-founder and CEO Sam Sipe, the first prototype should be bobbing around the ocean, crunching bits, less than two years from now.

The goal, Sipe said, is to help data center developers deploy servers in AI-friendly timelines. “The data center industry is a real estate game, and so they’re playing on 8- to 10-year timelines, including interoperability with utilities and [independent system operators]” that manage regional power grids, he said. “AI demand has increased 10x in just the last three years. It’s completely incompatible.”

Drogue was founded just six months ago in Washington, D.C., and the startup told TechCrunch exclusively that it has already raised $20 million, including from XYZ Venture Capital, Toyota Ventures, Tamarack Global, Dream, FDVC, Garuda Ventures, Flexcap, Boost VC, and Slow Ventures, among other investors.

In those six months, Drogue has designed a multi-megawatt prototype that will be installed on a traditional oceangoing ship and sent out to sea in early 2028. Future versions will be built on floating structures that more closely resemble offshore oil platforms.

To Sipe, the decision to turn to the ocean was obvious.

After years flying E-2D Hawkeyes off U.S. Navy aircraft carriers, he had an appreciation for the ocean’s immense power. “Most people think, oh, ocean — hard waves, storms, corrosion, biofouling. And I just see this majestic place and resource that we just ignore,” he said.

As the planet warms, the oceans have been absorbing an additional 5.8 million terawatt-hours of energy every year. By comparison, all of human civilization uses about 180,000 terawatt-hours each year. If Drogue were to take some, surely the ocean wouldn’t miss it.

The startup’s technology works like a heat pump run in reverse. A heat pump uses electricity to move heat from one place to another; Drogue’s system instead uses a difference in temperature to generate electricity. This approach, known as ocean thermal energy conversion, or OTEC, was first developed in the 1950s.

Surface waters are warmer, heated by the sun, while down-deep temperatures are much colder, about 39°F on average (4°C). “There’s basically no amount of heat we can pull out of that that will collapse that temperature differential,” Sipe said.

To leverage the temperature differential, the startup’s system draws in warm surface water, uses it to cool the data centers, and then sends the now-warmer water to boil ammonia, a chemical that turns to gas at -28 °F. That ammonia gas is then sent through a turbine to generate electricity. Once through the turbine, it courses through a condenser, which turns the gas back into a liquid. There, cold water drawn from 1,000 meters deep passes over the condenser’s fins to absorb the heat. The warmed water is then pumped back down to 1,000 meters, where it dissipates into the ocean. The ammonia gets sent back to the start of the sealed loop, and the cycle repeats.

The basic idea was tested in the 1980s but tossed aside. “A lot has changed since the ’80s, specifically manufacturing techniques around the pipe and the heat exchangers,” Sipe said.

To find out why, Sipe sought out people who had worked on those early efforts. “I just talked to everyone, basically interviewed them and figured out what went wrong, what went right, what would you do next. And everyone was like, dude, this stuff works. It’s just a matter of being able to raise enough capital to build something big enough, because there’s a sweet spot,” he said.

There also had to be customers who could use that power while still at sea. Sending power to shore would require lengthy, expensive cables, and manufacturing on board would require similarly expensive shipping of materials and finished goods. Data centers are ideal — the servers are compact relative to other equipment, and shipping data off the platform is incredibly cheap. Each vessel would live at sea for about a decade, Sipe said.

Drogue already has “approval in principle,” a preliminary sign-off, from the American Bureau of Shipping, which sets and checks safety standards for ships. Now, it’s in the process of buying its first ship to start building a prototype ready for the open ocean.

In many ways, Drogue’s concept is similar to Elon Musk’s plan for orbital data centers : find a cheap source of power, and get the data centers as close to it as possible. Except unlike orbital data centers, Drogue’s don’t need to launch expensive rockets to get there. They can just sail a ship on the ocean, something humanity has been doing for millennia.

Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3 billion valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors, including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday.

That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago , led by IVP.

LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus toward managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence.

With its open source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock users into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use.

True, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well ( case in point is newcomer Mintive ). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including big-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like Nvidia, Toyota, and Salesforce.

The leading open-weight models developed by Chinese companies were trained on Nvidia chips that the U.S. government restricted from shipping to its largest geopolitical rival, a new research effort claims.

The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China’s intelligence service.

While Jensen Huang’s relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia’s potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang.

U.S. export controls are intended to protect the country’s leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the U.S. to claim a 25% tariff.

Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who leads the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs, analyzed the weights — the unique structure — of large language models released openly by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, and Ant Group. The weights still reflect the configurations of the chips used to train them, and DePue was able to find compelling evidence that the most closely watched models, including Moonshot’s Kimi’s K3 releases and DeepSeek’s V4 models, bear fingerprints from training on Blackwell chips.

White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing U.S. intelligence sources. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that about two million advanced chips entered China in 2024 and 2025 through schemes designed to hide their final destination.

That doesn’t mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated; the chips could have been in an offshore data center, which has proven a popular way for Chinese firms to access compute and driven an industrial revolution in Malaysia. Epoch’s data estimates that 275,000 Nvidia AI accelerators were imported to Malaysia in 2024 and 2025.

However, the ostensible goal of the export bans is to prevent exactly that: Chinese AI labs training on the most powerful chips. China hawks have long called for stronger controls on who uses chips, not just who owns them or where they are installed.

“If we care about the U.S. tech edge, it doesn’t make any sense to me that you would not allow Chinese companies to access chips in mainland China or Hong Kong and Macau, but then say, actually, if you just go over to Malaysia, you can do whatever you want,” Sam Bresnick, a researcher at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told TechCrunch this summer.

Megaspeed, the company led by Alice Huang, has been at the center of that trade for several years through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, and has been the subject of investigations by both the U.S. and S i ngaporean government. Friday, Bloomberg also reported that a company with links to Alice Huang was involved in smuggling banned Nvidia chips to a data center in Shanghai.

In May, the short-selling research firm Culper published a report arguing that Nvidia had a “ China problem ” because a significant share of its revenue was driven by Chinese demand, either through remote data centers or smuggling in violation of U.S. law. It detailed Megaspeed’s relationship with Nvidia and alleged that Alice Huang’s companies are backed by Chinese firms that are barred from accessing U.S. chips.

Ironically, short-seller Culper’s bet against Nvidia wasn’t driven by the expectation of a U.S. government crackdown. Instead, it was focused on the Chinese government’s response to the bans, which was to recommit to its domestic chip industry.

If China succeeds, billions of dollars in Chinese demand for Nvidia chips could dry up. Some 600,000 H200 chips are reportedly stockpiled in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment into China. While Chinese companies might want the chips, observers have no consensus on why they haven’t been cleared for import.

Graham Webster, a research scholar at Stanford who focuses on U.S.-China technology policy, said he doesn’t buy the idea that holding the chips back would drive domestic production, since demand for chips is so large. Other theories for the hold-up include preparation for a potential trade deal that would involve importing a large volume of U.S. goods, or concerns about potential surveillance technology in the chips.

For now, U.S. companies have limited obligations to track what their customers do with controlled goods like AI chips. However, Jensen Huang’s personal and professional entanglements with Alice Huang create a much bigger problem for Nvidia if government investigators confirm that chip smuggling took place and that he was aware of it. Nvidia and Huang have both vouched for Megaspeed’s data centers, saying Nvidia officials had visited them to confirm they were legitimate.

The U.S. government’s treatment of Nvidia and Megaspeed is also under scrutiny. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, who oversees the agencies that license chip exports, could reportedly lose his job after reports that his investigators failed to uncover suspicious chip buyers and were too cozy with Nvidia officials.

scraped.title: Lutnick faces questions over Nvidia spy scandal. His sons’ firm has deep ties to the chipmaker
scraped.description: Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO has brought renewed scrutiny to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and his family’s financial ties to the chipmaker.
scraped.author: Luke Fountain
scraped.h1: Lutnick faces questions over Nvidia spy scandal. His sons’ firm has deep ties to the chipmaker
scraped.body_text:
In this article

In late September, Cantor Fitzgerald hosted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other top executives from the chipmaker for investor meetings in New York, according to a Cantor research report reviewed by CNBC.

The Wall Street firm liked what it heard.

"We continue to view NVDA as the best risk/reward in our coverage," Cantor analyst C.J. Muse and his colleagues wrote in a research report dated Oct. 3 that maintained a $350 price target and overweight rating on the stock.

Yet the firm formerly run by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and now led by his sons, Brandon and Kyle, reported a nearly 50% decline in the number of Nvidia shares it held between September 2025 and March 2026 , according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings that excludes options. Nvidia had been one of the largest stock positions reported in Cantor's filings.

The decline coincided with White House and U.S. intelligence officials pressing Lutnick to crack down on Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence chips to China . Lutnick repeatedly resisted those efforts, according to Axios .

By the time Cantor hosted Huang in New York, Lutnick had also received a classified intelligence warning, according to Axios, about Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese spy and had appeared alongside the CEO at a G20 technology summit in North Carolina.

Even as Cantor pared back its Nvidia stake, it continued doing business across the chipmaker's AI empire. A CNBC review of securities filings, corporate announcements and Wall Street research found the firm has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners while maintaining close ties to the chipmaker's leadership.

Those ties have drawn fresh scrutiny following Huang's resignation Thursday and Axios' reporting that Lutnick repeatedly resisted a crackdown on companies suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, despite President Donald Trump authorizing new export restrictions on those companies for a third time on Nov. 5.

An ethics expert said the relationship between Lutnick and his former firm's investments may raise questions, given what the secretary knew about Nvidia.

Richard Painter , the former chief White House ethics lawyer for President George W. Bush and now a corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota said that while "there's no proof of" Lutnick sharing nonpublic information with Cantor Fitzgerald, "the appearance doesn't look great."

"His conversations with his sons better be about publicly available information," Painter told CNBC.

There is no evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance knowledge of the intelligence concerns, that changes in Cantor's reported holdings were tied to any warnings or that the firm's business interests influenced their father's decisions.

"Cantor has to date from time to time had only immaterial stand-alone proprietary positions in Nvidia, unlike the positions reflected in 13F filings which were entered into in the ordinary course of business in connection with client swap transactions, that are common in institutional markets," a Cantor spokesperson told CNBC.

Cantor declined to answer CNBC's other questions. The Commerce Department, the White House, Howard Lutnick and his sons did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment or detailed questions about the findings.

As scrutiny of Huang intensified, Cantor Chairman Brandon Lutnick was publicly praising the chipmaker's leadership. "Nvidia is one of the great companies on the planet, and they have an amazing leadership team," Brandon Lutnick told Fox Business on Wednesday.

Trump is standing by Howard Lutnick. A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in the commerce secretary.

But cracks in the administration's unity emerged Friday, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that the Departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months."

Bessent pointed to Commerce as the department responsible for imposing the entity list, which identifies restricted businesses and other groups, adding, "You will have to ask them about their internal processes."

Nvidia was Cantor's second-largest reported stock position before Howard Lutnick left Wall Street to become commerce secretary in February 2025, behind only bitcoin investor MicroStrategy, now known as Strategy . At the end of 2024, the firm disclosed more than 3.5 million Nvidia shares worth $479 million, according to its quarterly securities filing .

That share count held steady through September 2025, but its value climbed 36% to $652 million, according to Cantor's quarterly securities filing , as the Trump administration moved over the summer to ease restrictions on Nvidia's H20 chip sales to China .

Over the following six months, however, the number of Nvidia shares Cantor reported holding fell by 49%, to 3 million in December and 1.78 million by the end of March 2026 , with their value dropping from $652 million to $310 million, according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings.

Pressure on Howard Lutnick was also mounting on Capitol Hill. Sens. Jim Banks, R-Ind., and Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., in March urged the secretary to suspend or reconsider Nvidia's export licenses after three people linked to Nvidia customer Super Micro Computer were indicted on charges of conspiring to smuggle AI chips to China.

"The Trump administration, I think, leaks like a sieve when it comes to non-public government information getting to various hedge fund guys," Painter said, though he stressed there is no evidence Howard Lutnick had shared such information with his sons.

The filings do not establish why Cantor's reported share count fell or whether its overall financial exposure to Nvidia declined. Nvidia’s stock had more than doubled from its April 2025 lows by late October, before retreating in the following months. The stock fell about 6.5% between the end of September and the end of March.

Cantor's reported Nvidia holdings remained near that lower level through June 30 , the latest quarter covered by public disclosures, at 1.81 million shares. Its next quarterly filing is due Monday.

Cantor has not publicly explained the decline.

Most of those shares were attributed to CF Secured , a Cantor brokerage subsidiary that uses stocks and derivatives to hedge customer transactions, according to its audited financial statements. Cantor also disclosed substantial Nvidia options positions during the time period CNBC examined, overwhelmingly skewed toward put options, which can protect against declines in the stock price.

As concerns about Huang escalated inside the Trump administration in May, according to Axios, Cantor was helping finance the expansion of one of Nvidia's newest business partners, securities filings show .

On May 7, Nvidia and Australia-based cloud computing provider IREN announced a five-year, $3.4 billion cloud computing contract and a strategic partnership giving the chipmaker the right to invest up to $2.1 billion in IREN.

"That's not a passive financial investment. Nvidia is a partner who wins as we deliver," IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts told investors on the company's quarterly earnings call that day.

Five days later, as Trump headed to China aboard Air Force One, Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned him about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, The New York Times reported on Tuesday. Huang, who had not initially been invited on the trip, joined the president's delegation during a refueling stop in Alaska.

Howard Lutnick had already been sent a highly classified intelligence memo detailing concerns about Huang's relationship, Axios reported.

On May 12, the day Trump departed for China, IREN announced the pricing of a convertible bond offering that ultimately raised $3 billion when it closed two days later. Cantor was one of seven bookrunners on the deal, alongside JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs .

On the day the offering closed, May 14, Lutnick's Commerce Department quietly cleared roughly 10 Chinese companies , including Alibaba and ByteDance, to buy Nvidia's advanced H200 chips, though some of those approvals predated the intelligence memo.

It is unclear when IREN hired Cantor for the offering or how much the firm earned from the deal. Cantor declined to answer CNBC's questions about its work with IREN.

Still, Cantor reported a substantial position in IREN's stock.

By the end of June, Cantor reported $115 million in IREN shares and $362 million in Nvidia shares. Together, the two companies accounted for more than 9% of the value of Cantor's reported $5.2 billion in securities holdings, excluding options, according to CNBC's analysis of the filing.

Cantor didn't answer CNBC's questions about its work with IREN.

IREN was not the only company in Nvidia's orbit that turned to Cantor for financing.

In October 2025, Cantor advised AI infrastructure developer Lancium on a $600 million financing deal to support its data center campus in Abilene, Texas, the first site of Stargate, the massive AI infrastructure project backed by OpenAI , SoftBank and Oracle .

Newmark, a commercial real estate firm controlled by Cantor , also helped finance the Abilene campus, arranging a $7.1 billion construction loan in May 2025.

Ten months later, Nvidia agreed to invest $2 billion for a roughly 20% stake in Lancium, with up to $1 billion more tied to future milestones, The Information reported in August. Lancium , which is also backed by Blackstone, confirmed an investment and a technology partnership on Aug. 24 without disclosing financial terms.

It's unclear whether Cantor continued advising Lancium after the financing deal or played a role in Nvidia's investment. Neither Cantor nor Lancium responded to questions about the investment.

Cantor's reported ties also extend to Nvidia's supply chain.

In May 2025, days after Howard Lutnick announced the transfer of his ownership stake in Cantor to his children via trusts, Semafor reported that bankers at the firm had informally advised executives at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. , which makes Nvidia's most advanced chips, on navigating Washington. Cantor called Semafor's report "baseless and false."

TSMC received billions of dollars in federal subsidies created during the Biden administration and administered by the Commerce Department to fund its U.S. manufacturing expansion.

Democratic senators called for an ethics investigation in December into whether the Lutnick family stood to benefit from his push to expand AI data centers.

And on Wednesday, Sens. Warren and Chris Coons , D-Del., demanded that Howard Lutnick, Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller preserve records on Nvidia's chip exports to China and intelligence warnings about Huang.

The senators questioned whether "prudent defensive counter-intelligence action was taken or national security recommendations were overruled."

"The place where I think the Trump administration has most failed here is in being persuaded by Jensen Huang and others to license the export of some advanced chips," Coons said Friday on CNBC's "Squawk Box," accusing the administration of turning a blind eye to the black market for more advanced chips.

items.title: Microsoft apologizes for massive outage that took down Outlook and other 365 services
items.summary: A Microsoft outage on Thursday and Friday affected users of services like Outlook, Teams and 365.

scraped.title: Microsoft apologizes for massive outage that took down Outlook and other 365 services
scraped.description: A Microsoft outage on Thursday and Friday affected users of services like Outlook, Teams and 365.
scraped.author: Jenni Reid,Samantha Subin,Caleigh Keating
scraped.h1: Microsoft apologizes for massive outage that took down Outlook and other 365 services
scraped.body_text:
In this article

Microsoft issued an apology Friday for a wide-ranging outage that shut down Outlook and other Microsoft 365 products, as the company worked to restore service nearly 24 hours after connectivity problems began.

"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously," a Microsoft spokesperson said Friday. "We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services."

In a statement, Microsoft said the connectivity disruption stemmed from "an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade." The software giant said the underlying cause of the outage had been addressed and that they were still working to restore services to some customers.

Engineers scrambled to solve connectivity problems that began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday.

Email and calendar service Outlook, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, were largely down during the morning hours in the U.S. on Friday and throughout the Asian and European business days. Numerous external services that connect with Microsoft products were also hit. Users began to regain access to email and other services Friday morning.

In an update around 10:30 a.m. ET, Microsoft noted "encouraging recovery progress" and said that "service availability and email delivery performance [was] improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure" as Outlook and other Microsoft 365 tools began to come back online.

In an earlier update Friday morning, Microsoft said that email queues were "approaching normal levels," but that intermittent issues were expected as recovery efforts continue. It had previously given updates by region, with Asia Pacific services among the first to start normalizing.

Engineering teams have been taking affected systems offline for fixes and bringing them back online gradually stages. They are prioritizing efforts to preserve emails delayed during the recovery process and reduce email queues and backlogs, extending the timeout window, whereby delayed emails continue to attempt delivery, to 48 hours to help protect messages.

Microsoft says it has not detected any malicious activity causing the outage, which it initially blamed on a traffic surge in part of its infrastructure and issues with a component responsible for processing server health. The company said it would issue a full report once its assessment of the outage was complete.

The company said in its initial updates on Thursday that the connectivity problems related to infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions," caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure." Some servers were failing automated health checks, it said.

Microsoft shares traded largely flat Friday.

Governments and businesses across the U.S., Asia-Pacific and Europe said they were monitoring the situation, which was causing widespread disruption.

The U.K.'s National Health Service said the outage was affecting some of its services but that patients should attend appointments as normal. Calls "may be subject to long waits" as a result of disruption to the organization, a hospital group serving South West London and the English county of Surrey said on X.

Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov. 12, rescheduled the release to Nov. 16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage.

U.S. Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., told CNBC's "The Exchange" that he asked for a briefing on the outage. Gottheimer worked at Microsoft prior to serving in Congress.

"Is there something that went on that's nefarious here, or is this just something else? These outages occur in a lot of the companies, but the size of it and the length of it and the timing of it," Gottheimer said.

Air India said it had "temporarily rerouted" emails so it could continue to receive customer messages, adding that its flight operations were not affected.

Australian Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said in a press conference that Microsoft "believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Reuters reported.

A fault with an update issued by cybersecurity company CrowdStrike caused one of the world's biggest IT system outages in 2024 , hitting airlines, banks and more.

Microsoft reported in 2025 that Copilot, its collection of AI assistants and tools, had more than 100 million monthly active users.

The incident highlights a business "resilience and dependency issue that has been decades in the making," James Owen, managing partner of Digital Risks at consultancy Control Risks, said by phone.

"We have become, organizationally in the private sector and more broadly, increasingly dependent on a smaller segment of technology and infrastructure as critical to daily life and business activities."

"Organizations are becoming more aware through a geopolitical lens about what technologies they adopt, whether their services are provided by firms in the U.S., or China, or elsewhere, but this shows the importance of proper recovery planning in the case of an IT outage. That could be manual backups, protocols that do not require internet connection, investing in diverse suppliers and crisis management planning rehearsals," he said.

Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site on Thursday.

Amazon wrote on X that services were "operating normally" and an "unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports." The company referred users to its health dashboard for "accurate data."

At 4 p.m. ET Thursday, Microsoft said it had "validated an alternative service health check method" that brought some affected servers back online.

"We're now applying this change more broadly," Microsoft wrote. "We're also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses."

items.title: Nvidia hasn’t selected search firm for permanent Huang replacement, board tells CNBC
items.summary: Speculation has swirled around who Nvidia's board will select to permanently succeed CEO Jensen Huang.

scraped.title: Nvidia hasn’t selected search firm for permanent Huang replacement, board tells CNBC
scraped.description: Speculation has swirled around who Nvidia's board will select to permanently succeed CEO Jensen Huang.
scraped.author: Seema Mody,Annie Palmer
scraped.h1: Nvidia hasn’t selected search firm for permanent Huang replacement, board tells CNBC
scraped.body_text:
In this article

Nvidia hasn't yet selected a search firm to work with in identifying a successor for former CEO Jensen Huang , the company's board told CNBC.

"We are in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role," the board said in a Friday statement. "We have not formally engaged any potential candidates."

The comments come after speculation has swirled about who might be tapped to replace Huang. Nvidia announced Thursday that Huang would step down as CEO of the chipmaker after multiple reported affairs, including one with a woman purported to be a Chinese spy.

Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO and said it will begin a search for a permanent CEO to replace Huang, adding that it will consider both internal and external candidates. Kress conducted her first meeting as interim CEO on Thursday afternoon with high-level executives at Nvidia's headquarters in Santa Clara, Calif., according to a person familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named in order to discuss internal details.

The Financial Times reported Friday that Nvidia's board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas in its search for Huang's successor, citing people familiar with the matter.

Nvidia's board said, "Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature."

Before joining the SoftBank-backed chip company in 2013, Haas spent seven years at Nvidia, serving in a variety of roles including vice president of its computing products business.

Nvidia shares fell more than 2% on Friday, dragging the company's market cap below $4 trillion as investors digested the news of Huang's departure, and the specter of ongoing probes into his conduct.

On Tuesday, Nvidia said it had retained Wachtell Lipton to investigate allegations that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, following revelations that its then-CEO had an intimate relationship with Alice Huang, who several outlets reported is suspected of working for Chinese intelligence.

Three House committees have asked Huang to appear for briefings, and renewed those calls even after the CEO's resignation. The Senate Banking Committee has also requested that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify to discuss "serious concerns about our national security," and how the company's top AI chips have reportedly ended up in China.

items.title: How Microsoft outage shows risk of tech monopolies: ‘We were just helpless’
items.summary: Many businesses and consumers were unable to communicate through digital channels as a global outage of some Microsoft services left people scrambling.

scraped.title: How Microsoft outage shows risk of tech monopolies: ‘We were just helpless’ - National | Globalnews.ca
scraped.description: Many businesses and consumers were unable to communicate through digital channels as a global outage of some Microsoft services left people scrambling.
scraped.h1: How Microsoft outage shows risk of tech monopolies: ‘We were just helpless’
scraped.body_text:
Instructions:

Want to discuss? Please read our Commenting Policy first.

Comment

Name

Δ

Many businesses and consumers were unable to communicate through digital channels as a global outage of some Microsoft services left people scrambling, and experts say this event further highlights the need for Canada to adopt more sovereign digital tech.

“The fact that Canada basically closed for business because one U.S. company had a glitch on some servers shows how dependent we are, how vulnerable we are,” says Joshua Pearce, who holds the Thompson Chair of Innovation at Western University.

On Thursday, the outage hit a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services.

Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down. As of publication, Microsoft said most services had been restored but fixes were still ongoing and there was no timeline for full restoration as of 3:00 p.m. Friday.

The full extent of the fallout from the outage is unclear, but regions spanning North America to the Asia Pacific were included in Microsoft’s updates, and the company reported its 365 suite of services had nearly half a billion paid subscriptions as of January.

“I was just shocked how much white collar work depends on the single Microsoft product, and when it’s down, really lots of people weren’t able to do their jobs,” says Emily Osborne, a policy research associate at the Canadian Shield Institute.

“There was nothing we could do to sort of address the outage as it was happening — we were just helpless to Microsoft’s control,” she added.

“We depend on so few providers, and when the services of one of them stops working that has a huge impact on our economy.”

Even the federal government said they were impacted by the outage, according to a statement in response to a Global News request Friday.

“The Government of Canada experienced impacts from the Microsoft service outage. Ensuring government digital services are secure, reliable and resilient is a priority, and we continually assess our systems and dependencies with that objective in mind,” said AI and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon in a statement.

Diversifying reliance on different providers and expanding beyond some of the big American names can give businesses and consumers more options when a problem arises, experts say.

Osborne says having more sovereign digital providers is something that Canada could work on.

“There’s also certainly a role for the government to play. We’ve seen lots of governments in the EU making the very active and strategic choice to move away from products delivered by American firms. So that’s certainly something that Canada could consider doing to increase our resilience,” says Osborne.

“It would be hard to switch everything all at once, but there’s certainly an argument to be made for starting somewhere small with some sort of government communication platform that is a sovereign alternative — a privacy-preserving alternative to Microsoft products.”

Global News sent a request for comment to Shared Services Canada (SSC), the federal government’s IT provider, asking if a form of sovereign digital communications software is being developed or considered for use. A SSC spokesperson acknowledged the request, but did not provide a response by publication.

In the EU, a service known as Euro-Office is a suite of cloud-based digital sovereignty initiatives launched this year to serve as an alternative to American platforms like Microsoft 365.

“This is the actual data sovereignty or digital sovereignty we need to talk about is the physical infrastructure and the software that we use,” says Evan Light, associate professor at the faculty of information at the University of Toronto.

“It’s an open source office suite that does everything Microsoft Office does, but it’s developed by the European Union. It’s open source, it’s free, and it’s meant to be a project to sort of decouple the European Union from these tight, vulnerable things to American software.”

Light says these systems can be tailored and scaled to individual organizations, which can help limit the impact of an outage.

“So I could run a server here at U of T for my faculty, and if we need to reboot that thing, we’d reboot that thing and it affects a hundred people rather than millions.”

Experts says businesses and consumers should also have backup plans for technology failures, including maintaining alternative communications services to help limit disruptions.

“Thinking in terms of multi-homing and then having sort of multimodal forms of communication at your disposal rather than just getting into the habit of using one service all the time over and over and over again,” says Brett Caraway, associate professor of media economics at the University of Toronto.

“Institutions, I think, need to think more carefully about what they would do if they lost something. You’ve got to game that out.”

“There’s a lot of convenience and a lot efficiency that comes out of having a centralized coordination system, but it also exposes you to a great deal of risk.”

– with files from Global News’ Uday Rana

scraped.h1: U.S. Coast Guard suspends search for 72-year-old missing cruise passenger
scraped.body_text:
Instructions:

5 comments

Maybe cruse ships need higher railings for those with poor balance as well as the drunks.

Les Considering how many people take cruises around the world these incidents are pretty rare. Yeah, most ships will have a deck with railings where you can look out to the ocean. The rest of the world isn’t bubble wrapped. Why do we expect a cruise ship to be free of incidents?

She is either at the bottom of the ocean getting picked apart by bottom feeders, or she is in some orcas stomach. No point in bumming the other passengers out, the party continues!

The U.S. Coast Guard has suspended the search for a 72-year-old British woman who is believed to have fallen off a TUI-operated cruise ship in the Atlantic.

The woman was last seen on board TUI’s Marella Voyager on Monday afternoon as it went from Malaga in Spain to the Caribbean.

In a statement to Global News, the U.S. Coast Guard said that at approximately 7:33 p.m. on Nov. 10, Coast Guard East District command center watchstanders received a report from Marella Voyager that a passenger was missing.

“The vessel’s crew determined she was unaccounted for after routine cabin service personnel found her cabin and bed untouched and initiated the ship’s missing-person procedures. The Marella Voyager reported the vessel did not have enough fuel to return to the search area,” the U.S. Coast Guard added.

The last confirmed electronic record of the woman was a cabin door access event mid-day on Nov. 9.

“Due to the delay between her last known contact and the report made to rescue authorities, the vessel was approximately 500 nautical miles from the area where she was believed to have entered the water,” the Coast Guard said.

Search and rescue coordination required close collaboration among multiple international rescue coordination centres and maritime partners because the incident occurred in a remote area of the North Atlantic Ocean.

Coast Guard watchstanders coordinated extensively with search and rescue partners, including the Maritime Rescue Coordination Center Delgada and Joint Rescue Coordination Center United Kingdom, and issued urgent maritime broadcasts requesting assistance from vessels in the area after notified of the missing woman.

“After considering the extensive search area, the elapsed time between the presumed incident and notification, the lack of available search assets in the remote location, negative results from maritime broadcasts, the sea state, and the low likelihood of survival, the Coast Guard suspended active search efforts at 3:47 p.m. Nov 11 pending any new information,” the Coast Guard added.

Global News has reached out to travel agency TUI for further comment, but has not received a response.

The incident onboard the TUI-operated cruise ship comes nearly one month after a cruise passenger was rescued nearly 20 hours after going overboard from a Royal Caribbean ship into the Ionian Sea near the island of Zakynthos, Greece.

According to a news release by the Hellenic Coast Guard, the incident occurred on the morning of Oct. 9 on the cruise ship while it was sailing southwest of Zakynthos.

A “local emergency plan was immediately activated” and searches were launched to locate the 44-year-old Salvadorian woman, with participation of the Hellenic Coast Guard, a Hellenic Coast Guard Patrol Vessel (HCV) and passing ships, as well as a Super Puma helicopter of the Hellenic Air Force, according to the news release.

A cargo ship that participated in the search located the woman on Oct. 10 and she was found conscious while floating inside a lifebuoy, according to the coast guard.

Footage shared by the Hellenic Coast Guard shows the moment the woman was found floating in the water.

The ship’s crew members spot the woman floating inside the lifebuoy in the dark sea before tossing her a rope.

The footage shows the woman pulling herself towards the cargo ship after she grabs the rope.

The woman was transported by ambulance to a hospital for medical monitoring and examinations, according to the coast guard.

A spokesperson for the Royal Caribbean Group told USA Today that the ship “immediately launched a search and rescue effort and are working with authorities” after the woman went overboard.

“Our Care Team is actively providing support and assistance to the guest’s loved ones during this difficult time. For the privacy of the guest and their family, we have no additional details to share,” the spokesperson added.

A preliminary investigation is being conducted by the Katakolo Port Authority.

A global outage for Microsoft web services continued to disrupt email accounts and some other applications worldwide on Friday, while the broader stock market remains unsteady a day after the AI industry was rocked by the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

Microsoft said in an update that the outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.

Microsoft’s stock price was under pressure early on Friday, falling more than six per cent before markets opened, while Nvidia shares were volatile as investors assessed how Jensen Huang’s departure might affect chip supply and the global artificial intelligence industry.

Shares in Microsoft were down about 0.3 per cent as of 10:00 a.m. Eastern time.

The S&P 500 fell 0.1 per cent and is on track for a weekly gain of 2.8 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 125 points, or 0.2 per cent. The Nasdaq composite fell 0.4 per cent.

Meanwhile, shares of Nvidia fell close to three per cent.

The departure of Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and has been a key architect of its role at the center of the AI boom, has raised questions about the company’s future. Its shares fell 15 per cent after his resignation was announced Thursday, though recovered during the day.

Huang had been the face of Nvidia and was deemed by some in the industry as bigger than Nvidia itself.

Huang stepped down after his affair with a Chinese tech executive raised U.S. national security concerns. Nvidia’s longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, will be its interim CEO.

A lynchpin of the AI boom, Nvidia trades off with Apple as Wall Street’s most valuable company and has invested heavily in other AI firms. Market watchers will be keeping a keen eye out for what Nvidia’s woes might mean for pending public debuts of AI companies, such as Anthropic’s pending IPO, valued at $1.3 trillion.

Wall Street is also waiting on Friday for the U.S. to release its producer price index for October, which captures inflation before it reaches consumers. The September report showed the biggest increase since December 2022 and that data showed that rising fuel prices, particularly for diesel fuel, continue to push shipping and warehousing prices higher.

Oil prices are mixed a day after President Donald Trump said that the U.S. didn’t “need a deal with Iran” even as the conflict in the Middle East drags on.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” he posted on social media. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

Brent crude, the international standard, was up 0.2 per cent at $96.04 a barrel on Friday. It was trading near $72 per barrel in late February before the Iran war began. Benchmark U.S. crude fell 0.4 per cent, to $88.39 a barrel.

In Europe, Germany’s DAX climbed 0.1 per cent, to 26,806.21 and the CAC 40 in Paris rose 0.1 per cent, to 8,365.44. Britain’s FTSE 100 gained 0.1 per cent to 10,871.82. Asian markets were mostly lower.

The U.S. dollar rose to 159.98 Japanese yen from 159.84 yen. The euro was trading at $1.1051, down from $1.1055.

scraped.title: Migrant activists push back against HK visa rejections over 'job-hopping'
scraped.description: Migrant worker activists have pushed back against the government's rejection of domestic workers' visas over concerns that they had engaged in "job-hopping," saying that workers have the right to seek better working conditions.
scraped.author: Hillary Leung
scraped.h1: Migrant worker activists push back against Hong Kong visa rejections over ‘job-hopping’
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Migrant worker activists have pushed back against the government’s rejection of domestic workers’ visas over concerns that they had a history of “job-hopping,” saying that workers have the right to seek better working conditions.

The Asian Migrants Coordinating Body (AMCB) said in a statement on Friday that it “condemned” the Immigration Department for discriminating against workers and “maliciously accusing them of job-hopping.”

The group’s response came after Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun said on Wednesday that the government had rejected 455 employment visa applications from domestic workers since January 2024.

In 2024 and 2025, 266 and 93 applications were rejected , respectively. As of October 2026, the government had rejected 96 applications this year.

They were among more than 3,300 applications that the Immigration Department investigated due to suspicions that the workers had “job-hopped,” Sun said during the Legislative Council meeting.

Authorities define domestic workers’ job-hopping as prematurely terminating their contracts – fixed under the law at two years – to change employers.

The government has long accused domestic workers of job-hopping, saying that they are lured by employment agencies to cut short their contracts and switch to a new employer with the promise of cash incentives.

Migrant worker activists, however, have said this is untrue, and that workers have genuine reasons when leaving their employers. They have also said that workers would not make the decision to change employers lightly, as they would need to fly back to their home country to await their new visa.

“Most of the reasons for early termination of their contract are due to inhumane working conditions, lack of decent accommodation, no regular rest day, and physical and mental abuse,” the AMCB’s statement read.

“There is nothing wrong with seeking better working conditions,” Dolores Balladares, an AMCB spokesperson, said.

Sun said on Wednesday that the Immigration Department set up a “special duties team” in 2013 to “strengthen the assessment of employment visa applications from [domestic workers] who change employers frequently.”

The number of rejected visa applications has fallen consistently in recent years. In 2021, the figure was 2,833 – more than 30 times the number of rejections last year.

The government revised the “code of practice” for employment agencies in 2024, requiring agencies to brief those looking for foreign domestic worker jobs on immigration regulations, as well as barring them from “adopting business practices such as providing monetary incentives to [domestic workers] in employ to induce premature termination of employment contracts.”

Sun said in late 2024 that the “job-hopping” situation had “significantly improved following policy interventions.”

scraped.title: All defendants in San Po Kong subversion case intend to plead guilty
scraped.description: Two men have told a Hong Kong court that they intend to plead guilty to conspiracy to commit subversion after they were arrested on suspicion of illegal weapons training in an industrial building in San Po Kong.
scraped.author: Hong Kong Free Press
scraped.h1: All five defendants in San Po Kong subversion case intend to plead guilty, court hears
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Two men have told a Hong Kong court that they intend to plead guilty to conspiracy to commit subversion after they were arrested on suspicion of illegal weapons training in an industrial building in San Po Kong.

Student Tang Ngai-pok and waiter Chan Hiu-chun appeared at the District Court on Thursday, local media reported . The defence told Judge Stanley Chan that the duo planned to plead guilty to the charges.

The two are among five defendants who were charged with conspiracy to commit subversion last December. All five have now stated in court that they intend to plead guilty.

The judge said the five were set to enter their pleas together on March 15 next year. They will remain remanded in custody until then.

In October, the other three defendants – student Wong Kit-lun, security guard Gallian Pang and security guard Lee Chun-sum – told the court that they would plead guilty to the subversion charges, local media reported .

Wong was also charged with possession of child pornography. The prosecution said in court in October that a plea bargain had been reached with the defence: after Wong pleaded guilty to subversion, the charge of possession of child pornography would be left on file.

Tang and Chan were both 23 years old when they were charged last December. Lee was 26 at the time, while Pang was 24 and Wong was 21.

The prosecution alleged that between November 1, 2024 and December 11, 2025, the five defendants conspired together and with other persons unknown to organise, plan, commit or participate in acts by force or threat of force with a view to subverting state power and overthrowing the body of power of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.

The five were among a group of 10 people who were arrested on December 11 and December 12 last year.

Superintendent Chow Hok-yin said that officers raided a unit at the San Po Kong industrial building on December 11 with a court warrant and found six men inside, one providing combat training to the others.

Officers seized five air rifles, two air pistols, replicas of five military knives and a long sword, as well as items bearing anti-government slogans, Chow said.

“Additionally, we found objects suspected to be explosives,” he said in Cantonese, adding that the objects were being examined by the force’s Explosive Ordnance Disposal Bureau.

Police later arrested another three men in Tai Po and Yau Ma Tei. On December 12, they arrested a woman.

All of them were arrested under the “unlawful drilling” provision of the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance, the city’s locally enacted security legislation known as Article 23. Five were later charged with conspiracy to commit subversion.

Mandarin music legend Cheer Chen, high-energy dance-pop duo Sofi Tukker, and genre-defying hardcore punk heroes Turnstile have joined December’s Clockenflap line-up .

Asia’s premier music and arts event returns to the Central Harbourfront between December 4 and 6.

Also joining the final line-up is cult folk-rock duo Wu Tiao Ren, Mandopop singer-songwriter Hush, local post-punk favourites N.Y.P.D., experimental pop shapeshifter Jane Remover, and genre-bending rapper Luci Gang.

Earlier announcements include Hayley Williams, Malcolm Todd, Queens of the Stone Age, keshi, Slowdive, and HYUKOH.

Also announced on Friday are J-rock inspired indie favourites Goodnight Lillie, throat-singing ensemble Huun-Huur-Tu, acoustic-pop chanteuse Cath Wong, and jazz-funk pop band Kowloon K.

Fans will catch alt-rockers The Jesus and Mary Chain, as well as jazz innovators DOMi & JD Beck, hip-hop pioneers Digable Planets and post-punk duo Sleaford Mods at this year’s event.

Art installations, food stalls and an array of local and international acts will be on offer, with one-day and full weekend tickets available now via Ticketflap.

Published - November 14, 2026 01:56 am IST - MOUNT MAUNGANUI

New Zealand's Matt Henry celebrates the wicket of Shreyas Iyer during the fourth ODI cricket match between against India at the Bay Oval in Mount Maunganui on November 13, 2026. | Photo Credit: AFP

India skipper Shreyas Iyer on Friday blamed the change in the pitch for their massive 244-run defeat to New Zealand in the fourth ODI, saying it went from a belter to a seaming track.

He, however, vowed to draw inspiration from the first two ODIs, approach the next match with a fresh mind and level the series.

New Zealand posted 333 after being put in by stand-in captain Iyer, but India's batting line-up suffered a spectacular collapse, being bundled out for 89 in 26.4 overs. Pacer Matt Henry ripped through the top order to finish with figures of 6/27.

"A tough one, I guess, to take that. There was a huge difference between the wickets between innings," Iyer, who is captaining India in ODIs for the first time, said during the post-match presentation.

"But also credit where it's due, the way Henry bowled in the right areas right from ball one. I think that was sensational. We tried almost everything in the first innings, the way they were playing on the rise. And we thought that the wicket was better to bat on considering they got 330 after that. Obviously a couple of dropped catches, but that definitely happens in a game.

"But yeah, when we got into the dressing room, we thought that we would be cruising through the chase as well. But the way the ball was seaming in and out, you couldn't basically decide from inside that this is how I'm going to play. Or even if you saw the wickets, no one threw the wicket away. It was good deliveries."

The win kept New Zealand's hopes of levelling the series alive.

"It's important to forget about this one, obviously, analyze what went wrong in terms of bowling and batting. But at the back of the mind it's important that we have also won two games. So a lot of inspiration from that one and see to it that we come with a fresh set of mind," Iyer said.

New Zealand captain Mitchell Santner was pleased with his team's effort, though he felt they had initially fallen short of a competitive total by around 20 runs. The bowlers, led by Henry, made up for it by chipping away with wickets.

"Pretty happy. Didn't get to bowl again, so pretty happy. Young did his thing and we got a good score despite leaving a few out there. I think we were thinking 360, the intent was great. Maybe if we got 20 more each partnership, we could've gotten there but they chipped away with wickets," he said.

"Henry wanted to play today. With the new ball with a wicket that offers a bit, he's the best. Will chill tomorrow. Pacers will, I'll have to come and bowl. Then see what Sunday offers from a pitch and conditions point of view and take it from there."

New Zealand's Matt Henry bowls against India during a One Day International cricket match in Tauranga, New Zealand, on November 13, 2026. | Photo Credit: AP

New Zealand defeated India by a massive 244 runs in the fourth ODI at Mount Maunganui after bowling them out for just 89 while defending a target of 334.

Matt Henry starred with a sensational six-wicket haul, including three wickets in the opening over, which triggered India’s batting collapse.

Henry explained that his bowling strategy was to keep things simple, target the stumps and make the most of the new-ball conditions. He said the sharp movement in the opening over put Indian batters under immediate pressure, particularly those facing their first deliveries.

“Well, especially with the way the wind was going, I wasn’t too worried about the swing. So from ball one it was just about trying to have the strengths and bring the stumps in play, really. We knew that there was a small window there with the new ball that you could put the batters under pressure. So just trying to be as simple as possible, obviously, and when it moves sharply like that in the first over, when people are facing the first ball, it’s pretty tough,” Matt Henry said after the match.

Matt Henry (6/27) wreaked havoc on India’s top order, dismissing Rohit Sharma (0), Virat Kohli (0) and Shreyas Iyer (0) in a sensational opening over to leave the visitors reeling at 0/3. The Kiwi pacer returned to dismantle the lower order, removing Ishan Kishan, Kuldeep Yadav (1) and Gurnoor Brar (2) to register career-best ODI figures and bowl India out for just 89 in 26.4 overs.

Henry continued his impressive record against India in ODIs. The Kiwi pace spearhead has now claimed 27 wickets in 12 matches at an outstanding average of 17.33, including two five-wicket hauls.

Speaking on his impressive record against India in ODIs, Henry acknowledged Men in Blue’s world-class quality and cautioned against reading too much into one victory, stressing that the team would need to maintain its focus ahead of the next match.

“Oh, I don’t want to get too carried away. No, they’re a world-class outfit, and I think that’s the message that we were saying right through. They can bat deep, and yeah, look, it’s one game, and we’ve got another one coming up soon that hopefully we can level the series,” he added.

It proved to be a decisive result as the hosts trimmed India’s series lead to 2-1 heading into the final fixture on Sunday.

Speaking to the media on the sidelines of the G20 Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Atlanta, the U.S. Secretary of State announced that the leaders of the four Quad countries — India, Australia, Japan and the U.S. — are expected to meet in Manila in November, on the sidelines of the ASEAN Summit. The announcement is significant, as this would be the first summit-level meeting of the Quad leaders since Donald Trump began his second term as U.S. President. It would also be the first such summit attended by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi since she assumed office. The last Quad Leaders’ Summit was held in Wilmington in 2024, when Joe Biden was U.S. President and Fumio Kishida was Japan’s Prime Minister.

While India was expected to host the subsequent Quad Leaders’ Summit, the grouping underwent a period of intense strategic turbulence in 2025, on account of Washington’s shifting geopolitical priorities and changing political dynamics in its bilateral relations with Quad members, especially India. However, this did not result in complete collapse of the grouping. Apart from the leader-level summit, the group has remained successful in continuing its operational synergies in its various initiatives. This was most evident in the elevation of the Quad’s Indo-Pacific Maritime Domain Awareness initiative to the Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration framework, launched in New Delhi in May 2026, following the Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting.

items.summary: The Hands Shibuya store, a longtime landmark in one of Tokyo's busiest shopping districts, will close on November 15 after 48 years in business, marking the end of nearly half a century of retail history as the store holds a final clearance sale offering discounts of up to 80% on cosmetics and other products.
