scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Hands Shibuya Store to Close November 15 After 48 Years
scraped.body_text:
TOKYO - The Hands Shibuya store, a longtime landmark in one of Tokyo's busiest shopping districts, will close on November 15 after 48 years in business, marking the end of nearly half a century of retail history as the store holds a final clearance sale offering discounts of up to 80% on cosmetics and other products.

The store's familiar green sign has been replaced with a message reading "Thanks," expressing gratitude to customers who have supported the business over the decades. Posters carrying farewell messages have also been displayed throughout the premises as the closing date approaches. A special clearance sale is underway, with cosmetics and other merchandise discounted by as much as 80%. The store has also set up a space where visitors can write personal messages on cards, allowing longtime customers to share memories and express their appreciation. One customer in their 30s said they had taken paid leave from work to revisit the store before its closure. Recalling their university days, the customer described visiting Hands when they first began living alone, using money from their mother to buy as many household items as they could fit into a suitcase before taking everything home. Expressions of gratitude have also spread to neighboring businesses, reflecting the store's longstanding presence in the Shibuya shopping district and its importance to generations of customers. With just two days remaining before the November 15 closure, Shibuya is preparing to say goodbye to another familiar landmark that has been part of the area's commercial and cultural landscape for almost five decades.

items.title: Art Installation Vandalized at Kyoto's Takase River Festival
items.summary: An artwork installed in Kyoto's historic Takase River has been broken in half during an autumn art festival, with organizers expressing anger after discovering that the sculpture had suffered further damage despite already being found broken two days earlier. (News On Japan)

scraped.title: Art Installation Vandalized at Kyoto
scraped.description: An artwork installed in Kyoto
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Art Installation Vandalized at Kyoto's Takase River Festival
scraped.body_text:
KYOTO - An artwork installed in Kyoto's historic Takase River has been broken in half during an autumn art festival, with organizers expressing anger after discovering that the sculpture had suffered further damage despite already being found broken two days earlier.

The damaged work, titled "Moon World Floating on the Water," is one of approximately 30 installations displayed in the river as part of the Kyoto Takase River Art Festival, which began on November 7. Designed to capture the beauty of the moon reflected on the water's surface, the circular sculpture was intended to convey a sense of traditional Japanese aesthetics. However, by November 13, the once-flat, disc-shaped installation had been split down the middle and bent inward, exposing sections of its wooden framework. Fallen leaves had accumulated inside the damaged structure, while parts of its base appeared to have been forced upward. Tetsuro Fujimori, chairman of the festival's organizing committee, said he first discovered the damage on November 11 but was shocked to find that the artwork had deteriorated further when he inspected it again on November 13. "It's heartbreaking. It really is heartbreaking," Fujimori said. "When I looked at it again today, it had been damaged even more. It's a truly shameful situation." Organizers suspect that someone entered the shallow river and climbed or stood on the sculpture, causing its structure to collapse. Although the person responsible has not been identified, Fujimori believes the damage may have resulted from reckless behavior involving alcohol. "I've already consulted the police, and I suspect it was probably someone fooling around after drinking. It's something I simply cannot forgive," he said. The incident occurred in one of Kyoto's busiest entertainment districts. The installation is located along the Takase River in the heart of the city, surrounded by major commercial streets and close to the restaurants and nightlife establishments of Pontocho. The Takase River is one of Kyoto's historic waterways and is known as the setting for "Takasebune," a novel by celebrated Japanese author Mori Ogai. The river is also a popular cherry blossom viewing destination in spring, when rows of trees along its banks burst into bloom. The festival, which features approximately 30 works installed directly in the water, was intended to bring art into the everyday urban landscape and encourage visitors to experience the river in a new way. Visitors continued to gather along the river on November 13 to view the installations, but some expressed disappointment at the destruction. "It's sad that someone would do this when an artist has gone to the trouble of creating something for everyone to enjoy," one visitor said. "As a Japanese person, I find it disappointing." The artist responsible for the damaged sculpture acknowledged that the installation might have needed a stronger structure to withstand unexpected interference, while expressing disbelief that someone would actually climb onto an artwork. "I don't have much experience exhibiting works outdoors, so I suppose I could have anticipated the possibility of someone climbing onto it," the artist said. "But I'm still surprised that someone would actually do such a thing. It's very disappointing." Despite the extensive damage, organizers have decided to leave the sculpture in its current condition for the remainder of the exhibition rather than remove or immediately repair it. The festival's organizing committee also plans to file a formal damage report with police as it seeks to identify those responsible.

A 26-year-old woman from Nagoya has been arrested on suspicion of defrauding men by encouraging them to develop romantic feelings for her before repeatedly requesting money, with 13 men reporting losses totaling approximately 30 million yen in a scheme resembling the notorious "Itadaki Joshi" romance fraud case.

A rare red Coca-Cola bench was stolen from outside a prepared-food shop in Nagareyama, Chiba Prefecture, in the early hours of October 24th, with the owner suspecting the thieves intended to resell the collectible item to enthusiasts after similar benches were found listed online for as much as 180,000 yen.

Emperor Naruhito presented prestigious Grand Cordon decorations to Toyota Motor Chairman Akio Toyoda and other recipients of Japan's autumn honors at a ceremony held at the Imperial Palace on November 10th, recognizing their longstanding contributions to the country and society.

items.title: Japan Startup Targets Brain Implant Trials in 2027
items.summary: A Japanese startup founded at Osaka University is preparing to begin clinical trials of a brain-computer interface in 2027, aiming to enable patients with severe physical disabilities to communicate and operate electronic devices using only their thoughts, with commercialization targeted for around 2030. (News On Japan)

scraped.title: Japan Startup Targets Brain Implant Trials in 2027
scraped.description: A Japanese startup founded at Osaka University is preparing to begin clinical trials of a brain-computer interface in 2027, aiming to enable patients with severe physical disabilities to communicate and operate electronic devices using only their thoughts, with commercialization targeted for around 2030.
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Japan Startup Targets Brain Implant Trials in 2027
scraped.body_text:
OSAKA - A Japanese startup founded at Osaka University is preparing to begin clinical trials of a brain-computer interface in 2027, aiming to enable patients with severe physical disabilities to communicate and operate electronic devices using only their thoughts, with commercialization targeted for around 2030.

The technology, known as a brain-computer interface (BCI), detects electrical signals generated by the brain and converts them into commands that can control computers and other equipment without physical movement. The development is among the major technological advances highlighted in Nikkei BP's predictions for 2027, which examine how artificial intelligence, emerging technologies and economic changes could reshape Japan and the wider world. A demonstration of the technology showed two men playing rock-paper-scissors, with a computer determining its response based on the thoughts of one participant rather than through conventional controls. The demonstration illustrated how brain signals could be interpreted and translated into computer commands. In the United States, Neuralink, the brain technology company led by Elon Musk, is already conducting human clinical trials of implanted brain-computer interfaces. Japan is also entering the field through G-Med, a startup originating from Osaka University that is developing a sheet-shaped device designed to measure electrical activity directly from the brain. The device is implanted inside the skull, where it detects brain signals that are subsequently analyzed and converted into instructions for external equipment. For example, when a patient thinks about closing their hand, the system can recognize the corresponding brain signal and convert it into a mouse-click command. By combining this function with a cursor that moves sequentially through a Japanese character selection grid, the technology could allow patients to select characters and communicate without physically operating a computer. The company hopes the system will provide a new means of communication for patients who remain conscious and retain their senses but cannot move their bodies or communicate through conventional methods. Its developers also envision applications that could help patients operate equipment to support their daily lives, potentially providing greater independence for people with severe mobility impairments. G-Med is preparing to begin clinical trials as early as 2027, marking an important step toward bringing the technology into medical practice. The company currently expects its product to become available around 2030, although commercialization will depend on the results of clinical testing and subsequent development. The brain-computer interface is one of 10 major developments identified by Nikkei BP in its outlook for 2027, which draws on expertise from its publishing, research and technology divisions to assess changes likely to affect business and society. Among its broader predictions is a shift in the relationship between humans and artificial intelligence, as increasingly capable AI systems raise questions about the future role of human intelligence and the meaning of human work. The report suggests that AI could fundamentally change how companies operate and how people understand their place in society. Another major concern is the sustainability of economic growth driven by borrowing and financial leverage. The report points to more than 200 trillion yen in hidden liabilities, including lease obligations and other commitments that may not be fully reflected on corporate balance sheets, warning that economic expansion supported by increasingly complex financial arrangements could be approaching its limits. Companies that have concentrated investment heavily in artificial intelligence may also face pressure to reconsider their strategies as financial constraints and the enormous electricity requirements of AI infrastructure become more apparent. Nikkei BP predicts that access to electricity will become an increasingly important factor in determining global economic and technological leadership. In consumer markets, the report highlights longevity as a major growth opportunity, with scientific advances making it increasingly possible to measure biological age rather than relying solely on chronological age. The ability to monitor and potentially influence the aging process is expected to create new markets for healthcare products, technologies and services. While many of the predictions concern major economic and technological shifts, brain-computer interfaces offer a particularly direct example of how emerging technology could improve everyday life. For patients unable to speak or move, the ability to communicate through brain signals could provide a new connection to the outside world, making 2027 a potentially significant year in the development of technology that allows people to control devices simply by thinking.

Japan launched a new national disaster management agency on November 2nd to strengthen its response to major emergencies, just days before a powerful earthquake struck Aichi Prefecture, injuring 24 people and renewing concerns over the possibility of a catastrophic Nankai Trough earthquake.

Russia's Foreign Ministry on November 11 defended the government's unilateral decision to place the local subsidiary of Japan Tobacco (JT) under the management of a Russian company, describing the move as a countermeasure against what it called Japan's "blatantly hostile actions."

East Japan Railway (JR East) announced on November 10th that it will introduce touch-free ticket gates at 40 stations, including every station on Tokyo's Yamanote Line, from spring 2028, allowing passengers using Mobile Suica to pass through without taking their smartphones out of their pockets or bags.

Japan's Children and Families Agency unveiled its first national guidelines on November 10th for parental involvement in children's internet use, dividing those aged 0 to 18 into six developmental stages as the government considers tighter regulations on social media platforms to protect young people from online bullying, exploitation, and other growing risks.

The Hands Shibuya store, a longtime landmark in one of Tokyo's busiest shopping districts, will close on November 15 after 48 years in business, marking the end of nearly half a century of retail history as the store holds a final clearance sale offering discounts of up to 80% on cosmetics and other products.

A Japanese startup founded at Osaka University is preparing to begin clinical trials of a brain-computer interface in 2027, aiming to enable patients with severe physical disabilities to communicate and operate electronic devices using only their thoughts, with commercialization targeted for around 2030.

Japan's recent stock market recovery has prompted warnings against excessive optimism, with investors urged to remain disciplined and avoid chasing short-term gains before there is clearer evidence that the market has established a sustainable upward trend.

Japan's Nikkei 225 Stock Average closed 322.99 points higher, or 0.53%, at 61,142.35 at 3:30 p.m. on Friday, November 13, recovering from the previous day's decline but surrendering most of its early gains as investors weighed renewed pressure on the yen, rising government bond yields, corporate earnings and uncertainty surrounding the global technology industry.

Kobe is undergoing a sweeping transformation, with major redevelopment projects around Sannomiya Station, the planned closure and renovation of the Mosaic shopping complex at Harborland, and the international expansion of Kobe Airport raising hopes that the port city can attract more overseas visitors while improving everyday life for residents.

Paid acquisition has become harder for small retailers. Apple’s App Tracking Transparency, introduced with iOS 14.5 in April 2021, cut the data that social ad platforms used for targeting, and many small shops saw their cost per sale rise in the following months.

Japan's Nikkei 225 Stock Average fell about 429 points, or 0.7%, to close near 60,819 on Thursday, November 12, ending a three-day winning streak as reports concerning Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang triggered heavy selling in semiconductor-related shares, while the broader TOPIX index edged 0.2% higher to around 3,937.

SoftBank Group raised a record 1 trillion yen through bonds aimed at individual investors in September, offering an annual interest rate of 4.75% on seven-year securities as the Japanese technology investment giant seeks to finance massive investments in artificial intelligence and strengthen its cash reserves.

items.title: Members of Georgia’s Election Board Have Been Coordinating With Cleta Mitchell’s Network
items.summary: The post Members of Georgia’s Election Board Have Been Coordinating With Cleta Mitchell’s Network appeared first on ProPublica. The Georgia State Election Board meets in Marietta in March. Mauricio Rodriguez Pons/ProPublica In the run-up to the midterms, members of Georgia’s State Election Board and much of its professional staff were coordinating with an activist group led by Cleta Mitchell, the conservative attorney who worked with President Donald Trump to try to overturn his defeat in the...

scraped.title: Members of Georgia’s Election Board Have Been Coordinating With Cleta Mitchell’s Network
scraped.description: For much of the past year, members have worked with the Election Integrity Network on shared priorities, including a controversial, error-prone software tool used to search voter rolls for purportedly suspicious voters.
scraped.author: Doug Bock Clark
scraped.h1: Members of Georgia’s Election Board Have Been Coordinating With Cleta Mitchell’s Network
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up to receive our biggest stories as soon as they’re published.

In the run-up to the midterms, members of Georgia’s State Election Board and much of its professional staff were coordinating with an activist group led by Cleta Mitchell, the conservative attorney who worked with President Donald Trump to try to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election.

The board sets the swing state’s election rules , oversees the conduct of its election officials and investigates allegations of fraud.

Recordings of private calls and events reviewed by ProPublica show current and former state board members working with the Election Integrity Network and allied organizations on shared priorities. Among them: advancing the use of a controversial, error-prone software tool known as ELLY to search voter rolls for purportedly suspicious voters.

The state board’s current vice chair, Janelle King, and her predecessor, Janice Johnston, have both attended meetings of EIN or VoterGA, an aligned organization whose membership and goals significantly overlap with EIN. Johnston retired in June but still plays an active role in state election matters behind the scenes.

At an August 2025 fundraiser for VoterGA , Mitchell declared she loved Johnston and King, who were both present. “You know, we’ve worked so hard together,” Mitchell said.

At least three members of the state board’s eight-person professional staff have participated in EIN meetings, including people who handle allegations of voter fraud and misconduct by election officials.

The board’s executive director, James Mills, likewise has worked closely with members of the EIN, according to five sources with knowledge of these interactions, board documents and EIN communications shared with ProPublica.

EIN’s close ties to the board and its staff have given it extraordinary influence over how elections are run in Georgia, experts said. In particular, the group has been able to enlist the board’s help in getting counties to remove voters from their rolls based on information from ELLY.

“Trump allies captured the State Election Board to keep claims of a stolen 2020 election going and tilt Georgia elections toward Republicans,” said Max Flugrath, a director at Fair Fight Action, a voting advocacy nonprofit that has closely tracked the board’s and the network’s actions. “EIN was the behind-the-scenes driver spearheading these changes.”

The board’s chair, John Fervier, told ProPublica he had not known about EIN’s sway over the board or its staff, but said he’d long sensed that an outside force was shaping the board’s actions.

“The more I look into this, the more I’m realizing that the Election Integrity Network has been having an undue influence on the State Election Board, and that needs to cease,” he said in an interview, though he declined to go into specifics about personnel matters. “I’m looking forward to changes in how the election board operates.”

Fervier has called a special meeting for Friday , in part to discuss personnel matters .

In response, Garland Favorito, an EIN leader and head of VoterGA, called on social media for his followers to inundate state board members with messages defending Mills and other staffers associated with the group.

“There is a significant possibility that these members will vote to terminate the Executive Director, investigators or possibly even staff members, any of which would destroy the SEB as we now know it,” Favorito wrote on Wednesday, referring to the State Election Board. “As most of you know, the SEB staff has made remarkable historical progress this year in … accountability for election corruption and much more. The Executive Director and staff deserve raises for amazing performances, not threats of termination.”

In interviews in late September, Johnston did not directly answer questions about her relationship to EIN. “I’m all about election integrity, wherever it comes from,” she said. She acknowledged she had remained involved with board affairs after her retirement. “It gets in your blood,” she said. Two days later, she posted on social media that “Cleta Mitchell, Election Integrity expert has the right ideas” about how elections should be run.

Johnston did not answer detailed questions about her relationship with EIN and affiliated groups.

King acknowledged she spoke about election matters with activists from EIN and VoterGA, but said they did not influence her decisions. She also said she saw no problem with EIN activists working for the board, though the staff is supposed to be independent and nonpartisan.

“As long as they are representing the SEB well, fine,” she said in an interview. “If they choose to become members of an organization in their private time, that is their choice.”

When a reporter recounted instances in which staffers had worked to advance EIN goals in their official capacity, she said she was unaware of this. “That is the first I’ve heard about it,” she responded.

Mills declined to answer questions from ProPublica about his relationship to EIN.

Mitchell did not respond directly to ProPublica but, after receiving detailed questions, put a post on X celebrating EIN’s work with the election board. “An election integrity group is working with election officials to oversee elections,” she wrote. “Wow! What a discovery!!! Pulitzer anyone?”

Favorito called the idea that the board and its staff had been working secretly with the EIN and VoterGA a “patently false conspiracy theory.”

EIN has been deeply entwined with conservatives’ efforts to reshape Georgia elections since at least 2024.

That year, ProPublica’s reporting revealed, EIN members secretly pushed a rule through the State Election Board allowing local officials to potentially delay certifying the state’s vote count. A court subsequently struck down the change, which experts had warned could enable county election boards to disrupt certifying the election if Trump had lost .

In late 2025, the board played a role in instigating the Trump administration’s unprecedented effort to reinvestigate alleged 2020 voting irregularities , formally asking the Justice Department to obtain Fulton County election records subsequently seized by the FBI. It was a move pushed by the EIN. The affidavit authorizing the raid cited Johnston and King as witnesses. The affidavit also cited a report put together by an EIN researcher compiling activists’ debunked allegations of fraud.

In recent months, EIN’s allies and participants at the state board pushed counties to use ELLY, a tool developed by an EIN member, to search voter rolls for signs of fraud and purge suspect registrants.

ELLY aggregates public data from state voter files, federal change-of-address records, tax documents, obituaries, property websites like Zillow and other sources, but doesn’t have access to personal identifiers such as Social Security numbers or full dates of birth. As a result, voting rights groups have said, ELLY often erroneously flags legitimate voters.

Nonetheless, before the midterms, the State Election Board’s investigative staff pressured Chatham County, a Democratic stronghold, to purge more than 200 registered voters that the tool identified as questionable, the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reported .

After the election, a Forsyth County election board member who is also a member of EIN submitted ELLY data questioning the validity of over 60 ballots, including four cast by people who were supposedly dead. ProPublica found that all four were, in fact, alive. The board rejected the challenges.

EIN members and state board officials have defended ELLY’s accuracy .

The EIN’s connections to the board carry additional importance in light of last week’s election results, in which Democrats wrested control of all statewide offices and the state House from Republicans. The House appoints a member to the State Election Board , opening the door to change.

Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms ran on a platform that promised a new approach to the election board.

“The State Election Board has become mired in political games, conspiracy theories, and partisan interference,” the platform stated . Bottoms’ platform pledged that she would “work with the General Assembly to eliminate the current State Election Board and replace it with a stronger, more independent election oversight structure that is insulated from partisan manipulation.”

Fervier is part of the board’s four-member Republican majority, but he has clashed repeatedly with Johnston, King and Mills and has effectively been relegated to a member of the minority at times.

Emails and communications between board members and staff obtained by ProPublica via public records requests show that Fervier and other board members who oppose steps supported by the EIN have been excluded from some board hiring decisions.

Earlier this year, Fervier publicly accused Mills of going beyond what the board had authorized in calling for the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security to intervene to assess the security of the state’s voting machines.

“Activists should not control the board,” he told ProPublica. “I’m really looking forward to this meeting because I think that we’re going to address some issues that should have been addressed awhile ago.”

Lisa Riordan Seville and Mauricio Rodríguez Pons contributed reporting. Misty Harris contributed research.

I’m a ProPublica reporter covering threats to democracy, elections and voting rights.

I welcome tips about how politicians, activists, and others are trying to transform American elections for partisan advantage. I am also interested in tips about North Carolina’s legislature, court system, and state government.

scraped.description: Marshall and Jennifer Phillips had to choose between their church and their son’s life. That choice later put them at the center of another family’s tragedy.
scraped.author: Teresa Mahoney, Noelle Crombie, Beth Nakamura, and Samantha Swindler
scraped.h1: His Church or His Child? A Sixth-Generation Member of a Faith-Healing Sect Had to Choose.
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

By Faith Alone

Co-published with The Oregonian

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up for Dispatches , a newsletter that spotlights wrongdoing around the country, to receive our stories in your inbox every week.

What if you had to pick between your deeply held faith and the life of your child? That’s the gutting choice that faced Marshall Phillips, an Oregon dad who was born into the Followers of Christ, a sect whose creed bars medical treatment. When his 11-year-old son was stricken with a dire health crisis, Phillips became caught between his faith, his family and the state of Oregon, which had begun cracking down on faith-healing parents who don’t seek medical help for their minor children. A decade later, Phillips was pulled into another one of his church’s life-or-death dramas when he was asked to care for a newborn whose twin had died because her parents had refused to seek medical attention.

To examine the power of faith-healing churches and the toll of their teachings, The Oregonian investigative reporter Noelle Crombie, senior staff photojournalist Beth Nakamura and videographer Samantha Swindler spent months with Phillips and his family, piecing together rare accounts from inside the deeply shuttered world of the Followers of Christ and of the state officials who fought to protect children who need medical treatment. The documentary, produced by The Oregonian’s managing producer of video, Teresa Mahoney, not only lays out in visceral detail the agonizing choices that families like the Phillips have to make, it also chronicles how they overcame the clash with their religious beliefs.

Go inside the secretive Followers of Christ sect and watch the extraordinary journey . Read more in this riveting print narrative , and meet the man who dominated and shaped the sect .

Mauricio Rodríguez Pons of ProPublica contributed graphics. Karly Imus of The Oregonian and Almudena Toral of ProPublica executive produced.

Standing where ships once delivered coal for combustion, he said the same dock would soon launch components fo...

scraped.title: The Offshore Wind Industry Gave Him the Well-Paying Work He Needed. Then Trump Gutted It.
scraped.description: Massachusetts and Connecticut invested millions into offshore wind in the hopes the once-blossoming industry would jump-start local economies. But amid Trump’s multifront war on the industry, workers say they’re watching opportunity dry up.
scraped.author: Ben Berke, John Moritz, and Anastasia Lennon
scraped.h1: How Trump’s War on Offshore Wind Upended a “Limitless” Future for Thousands of New England Workers
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

Co-published with Ocean State Media , The Connecticut Mirror , and The New Bedford Light

This article was produced for ProPublica’s Sustainability Desk, a project of the Local Reporting Network, in partnership with The New Bedford Light, The Connecticut Mirror and Ocean State Media. Sign up for Dispatches to get our stories in your inbox every week.

On a hot July day in 2022, then-President Joe Biden gave a speech from the ruins of a coal-fired power plant on the southern coast of Massachusetts.

Standing where ships once delivered coal for combustion, he said the same dock would soon launch components for wind power out to sea.

He praised an Italian company’s plans to build a new factory there, set to create 250 jobs and supply American-made undersea power cables to what was then a line of offshore wind projects waiting to be built along the coast.

Four years later, weeds and tall grass have reclaimed the dirt lot on which Biden spoke.

The company never came.

A 20-minute drive east, in New Bedford, hundreds of workers who helped assemble wind turbine parts from Canada and Europe over the last three years have given way to seagulls and geese. The birds shuffle along the now-empty pier the state of Massachusetts spent $140 million to build for offshore wind development.

In nearby Providence, Rhode Island, a newly built factory that manufactured offshore wind turbine foundation platforms has emptied out.

Amid the Trump administration’s multifront war against offshore wind, the cost on the ground in New England, the launchpad of the country’s offshore wind industry, can be seen in empty warehouses, silent marine terminals and ledgers recording hundreds of millions of dollars of state investment that may not be recouped.

ProPublica partnered with Ocean State Media, The Connecticut Mirror and the New Bedford Light to document the consequences of the administration’s efforts.

Many offshore wind projects faced a precarious future before President Donald Trump retook office. Rising construction costs driven by inflation and supply chain shortages forced some developers to back out of contracts to build wind farms and supply electricity to states. Various groups have also fought construction of projects saying they disrupt marine ecosystems and mar coastal views.

But last year, the administration temporarily forced five projects to stop construction , further clouding the horizon. Courts allowed the developers to proceed, but that has not eliminated the threat. Last month, the U.S. Department of the Interior asked a court for permission to reconsider a key permit for one of those five projects, Revolution Wind, which is already up and running and can power more than 350,000 New England homes at maximum capacity.

The administration also has frozen future development on all offshore wind farms, including a cluster of projects that haven’t been built but proposed to power up to 1.7 million New England homes. It has blocked or is seeking review of the permits that would allow these to be built. Meanwhile, the administration is paying other wind developers billions of dollars to sell back their leases and walk away.

At a press conference Monday, Trump said he supports a bipartisan bill that would accelerate U.S. energy development. When a reporter pointed out that the bill includes wind energy, Trump said he would not approve “wind turbines ’cause wind turbines are a major loser.”

The upheaval has had ripple effects. The cable company Biden touted decided not to build its factory, citing “long-term trends in the U.S. market.”

Port cities like New Bedford, Massachusetts, and New London, Connecticut, are left trying to hold onto the economic gains they have made building wind farms.

The Connecticut Mirror: Offshore wind offered a ‘limitless’ future for Connecticut. Trump scuttled the plan.

The New Bedford Light: Fishermen’s offshore wind work drying up

Ocean State Media: Offshore wind saved a struggling New Bedford union. Now its future is uncertain.

As recently as last winter, New Bedford, a historic whaling and textile manufacturing center, had hotels, offices and piers buzzing with offshore wind workers. Local businesses from caterers to cleaners to fuel suppliers landed new contracts servicing the wind industry.

In New London — another port once central to the whaling industry — officials worked with one of the world’s largest wind developers to pump more than $300 million of public and private funds into a state-owned pier. Despite significant cost overruns and some early construction challenges, the effort transformed the pier into a staging area for the wind industry.

Over the last four years, the pier has been a hive of activity. Hundreds of workers were employed loading and offloading turbine parts — with blades the length of a football field — from specially designed ships, some with names drawn from Greek mythology. Local companies also found work supporting the industry, including one that offered water rescue training for people working on construction sites offshore.

“I think the future just looked limitless, ” said New London Mayor Michael Passero.

Before wind, Passero said that officials tried for years to attract different industries to the pier, which is overshadowed by larger port facilities in New York and Boston. It was often used to import and store large piles of road salt.

The most recent wind project based at the pier is scheduled to finish work next year. Port officials have yet to find a tenant to occupy the space.

“They’ll be back to the old days of trying to lure cargo here,” Passero said.

Amid Trump’s war on wind, a frontline of union and nonunion workers watches opportunity disappear. One project alone, Vineyard Wind, directly employed a total of more than 3,700 full- and part-time workers — most of them from Massachusetts — over eight years of development and construction, according to the developer.

During peak construction activity, as many as 300 union members worked onshore in southeastern Massachusetts for the project, the first large offshore wind farm fully permitted by the federal government. The wind farm was completed this year.

Longshoreman Onix Vazquez, 34, worked full-time tying up barges and moving turbine components on and off New Bedford’s wind pier. He grew up a few blocks away and said he had struggled to find lucrative work until Vineyard Wind began hiring from his union.

Vazquez’s hourly wage of $50 was nearly double what he previously earned unloading occasional shipments of tangerines and juice concentrate. It allowed him and other members of his historically Black union to make down payments on houses, pay off medical bills and for the first time take their families on out-of-state vacations.

“Most of us have to get other jobs for now or collect unemployment,” said Kevin Rose, president of New Bedford’s longshoremen union, which put about two dozen members to work on the project.

The union had been planning to rebuild its nearby meeting hall, which was demolished a decade earlier when work grew scarce. But the next developer to lease New Bedford’s wind pier has delayed its project indefinitely. The union members have put the plans for their new hall on hold.

Vazquez said he now works a seasonal job in the cranberry industry for much lower pay.

“They don’t see that it affects us, the ones that work the projects,” he said.

In response to questions about the impact of the administration’s actions on American offshore wind workers, a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of the Interior repeated criticisms of offshore wind as an expensive and unreliable source of energy.

“The reality is that the Biden administration lured companies into these projects with the promise of millions of taxpayer dollars in subsidies to make these offshore wind projects viable,” the spokesperson said in an email.

The view is more nuanced on the ground. New Bedford’s fishing industry is generally critical of wind farm development because fishermen worry about disruption to fishing grounds.

But fishing catch limits keep boats tied to docks for much of the year. Work for wind farms gets them out to sea and helps pay the bills.

Over the past few years of construction, Vineyard Wind paid about $11 million to 55 fishing vessels from New England and an estimated 60 to 70 fishermen, according to the developer. (The figure also covers fuel.) The fishermen look out for protected species, guard exposed underwater cable as it’s being laid and log information for the developer.

Some fishermen say they will work in offshore wind for as long as they can.

“The scallop boats need the extra revenue,” said Patrick Walsh, 37, a fifth-generation fisherman who plans to rejoin his father’s fishing business when wind work wraps up. “The worst thing for a boat is to sit. Those boats are made to work.”

Wind farm work made it possible for him to buy his first house, he said.

“Fishing would pay bills, and wind was going in the bank.”

items.title: Why the Microsoft 365 outage is different and why it takes so long to restore email services

Microsoft was a source of frustration for computer users when it stopped working on Nov. 12, 2026. AP Photo/Michel EulerThe Microsoft services outage that began on Nov. 12, 2026, is not like other internet outages. The failure affected the Microsoft 365 suite of productivity services, including the video conferencing and collabo...

scraped.title: Why the Microsoft 365 outage is different and why it takes so long to restore email services
scraped.description: When one email service goes down, others don’t stop trying to send emails to users of the affected service. The result is snarled traffic that takes time to clear up.
scraped.author: Doug Jacobson
scraped.h1: Why the Microsoft 365 outage is different and why it takes so long to restore email services
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

The Microsoft services outage that began on Nov. 12, 2026, is not like other internet outages. The failure affected the Microsoft 365 suite of productivity services, including the video conferencing and collaboration platform Teams, AI assistant Copilot and, significantly, the Outlook email service.

Microsoft reported on Nov. 13 that the company is “continuing to see improvements in service availability” but that “some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery.”

Despite decades of predictions about its decline , email remains a central pillar of how organizations function. Password resets, invoices, legal notices and cybersecurity incident response coordination all depend on it. The Microsoft 365 outage affected businesses, governments and schools around the world.

When most people think about cloud outages , they picture a broken website or a stalled app. When the service going down includes email, however, the mechanics of the failure and how to recover from it are different from those of almost every other cloud service.

Unlike modern web apps or authentication gatekeepers, email wasn’t designed to fail fast, meaning to immediately halt when a problem arises.

When a typical cloud service breaks , it acts like a closed door. If an authentication provider or a cloud application goes down, users are immediately locked out and see an error message. Access stops. When people cannot get into the system, they are not actively generating new work or adding heavy processing loads to the broken servers. Once engineers fix the underlying bug and unlock the door, traffic can resume and the service often recovers fairly quickly.

Email does not have a closed door. It is built on an older, decentralized “store-and-forward” architecture designed to never lose a message, even when the destination is unreachable.

Because email is a network of thousands of independent systems, an outage at one major provider does not stop users on other platforms from hitting “send.” During major email disruptions like the one that hit Microsoft, millions of outside users on Gmail, corporate servers or other platforms could still compose and send emails to affected accounts without seeing an immediate error message.

From the sender’s perspective, everything works normally. Their email provider accepts the message, attempts to hand it off to the downed provider, realizes the destination isn’t answering, and quietly holds onto the message in an outbound queue to try again later.

One way to think about email traffic in outages is to imagine a multilane interstate highway where an accident blocks two lanes of traffic. Drivers miles away don’t stop leaving their driveways just because there is a wreck up ahead; they keep entering the highway system. Soon, traffic backs up so severely that metered on-ramps have to stop letting new cars merge onto the interstate. Before long, that gridlock spills backward onto local feeder roads and city streets, choking traffic miles away from the actual crash site.

In this analogy, a downed email provider is the crash. Every other email server around the world is an on-ramp or a feeder road. While the outage lasts, millions of messages continue to pile up in queues across the internet, with unaffected servers repeatedly resending email to see whether traffic is moving yet.

When engineers finally fix the root cause of an email outage, it is the equivalent of tow trucks clearing the wreckage from the highway. The road is technically open again, but traffic does not instantly return to normal speed.

First, the massive backlog of vehicles already stuck on the main highway has to start moving. Only after that congestion clears can the on-ramps start letting queued-up cars merge back in, which in turn slowly relieves the gridlock on the surrounding local roads.

Similarly, when a major email provider comes back online, it is immediately hit with a tidal wave of pent-up messages and retry attempts from every other mail server on the internet. Processing those queues without overwhelming the newly restored servers takes time – typically hours to days.

Because organizations have largely outsourced their email to a small number of global providers, an outage doesn’t just disrupt one company; it can stall entire sectors at once, cutting off the communication tool teams rely on to coordinate their emergency response.

And for everyday users, this unique architecture explains why email failures feel so drawn out: Even hours after a provider officially announces a problem is fixed, messages can still arrive out of order or trickle in slowly as the digital traffic jam finally clears.

University Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Iowa State University

scraped.title: Oceans and forests have absorbed roughly half our carbon emissions for decades, slowing climate change – but can they keep it up?
scraped.description: A method for measuring the world’s crucial carbon sinks finds that the ocean’s so-far-increasing ability to help might taper off in the future.
scraped.author: Andrew C. Manning
scraped.h1: Oceans and forests have absorbed roughly half our carbon emissions for decades, slowing climate change – but can they keep it up?
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

Over the past two centuries, humans have pumped billions of tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere by burning fossil fuels , raising global temperatures in the process.

Luckily for humanity, Earth has done what it could to soften the impact.

The world’s oceans have absorbed 35% of carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels since 1990, our new research shows, and the forests and other plants of the world have absorbed another 13%.

The importance of these two enormous natural carbon sinks cannot be overstated as global temperatures rise, fueling heat waves, fires, storms, floods and droughts around the world. Yet there is much that scientists do not understand about these carbon sinks – most importantly, how exactly they’ll behave in the future.

If the oceans and forests keep absorbing the same amount of carbon dioxide, scientists will have a sense of what to expect in the future and what can be done to slow climate change. And governments will know their remaining carbon budgets – that is, how much carbon dioxide can still be emitted into the atmosphere while keeping global temperatures below agreed-to levels.

But what if those carbon sinks change?

We have been working on greenhouse gas measurements for decades. In a new study, published Nov. 12, 2026, in the journal Science, we describe an alternative method for measuring these crucial carbon sinks, and what it shows.

We found that while the ocean sink has been expanding, meaning the oceans are taking in more carbon dioxide, that expansion might begin to slow down , leaving the oceans less effective at absorbing carbon in the coming decades. We found that the land sink has not been expanding, which was something of a surprise.

Measuring how much carbon is being taken up by the world’s oceans and forests is devilishly difficult and prohibitively expensive.

This is because many parts of the land and ocean don’t behave in the same ways. What occurs in one ocean region or forest can be very different from another; and the behavior in one year can be very different in the next, often for reasons scientists do not fully understand.

Computer models can help overcome some of these complexities, but they too have limitations. Satellites can also help, but they cannot see through clouds, nor can they see what is happening in the soil or mid-to-deep ocean.

As carbon cycle scientists, we set out to find a different way to measure these carbon sinks.

Our new study approaches the problem from another angle. We used high-precision measurements of atmospheric oxygen (O₂), combined with atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) measurements , to quantify how the ocean and land carbon sinks takeing up carbon dioxide.

This works because land, oceans and burning fossil fuels have different effects on oxygen: When fossil fuels are burned, they not only produce CO₂, they consume O₂. On land, when plants take up CO₂ to grow, they simultaneously release O₂. When the oceans take up atmospheric CO₂, there is no corresponding release of O₂.

This means that if we measure both CO₂ and O₂ in the atmosphere, then we can quantify the ocean and land carbon sinks. It is a straightforward mathematical approach of solving two equations with two unknowns, combined with our knowledge and measurements of the global budgets of CO₂ and O₂.

When we looked at the ocean and land carbon sinks over the past three decades, the results were surprising and sobering.

In contrast to most computer model simulations , we did not find the land carbon sink increasing over time to keep pace with increasing fossil fuel emissions. We did, however, find a larger ocean carbon sink than predicted by most models , and we found that it has been increasing as emissions grow.

If these trends in carbon sinks continue, then in the coming decades, humans will be relying more heavily on the oceans to slow down climate change. But in the next few decades, there are reasons to believe the oceans could become less effective at absorbing carbon.

For example, warmer waters are not able to hold as much gas , such as carbon dioxide. Warmer surface waters are also less efficient at mixing into the deep ocean , which has the beneficial effect of locking carbon dioxide away from the atmosphere for many hundreds of years.

The data for the past decade hints at the possibility that while the ocean carbon sink is increasing now, its rate of increase may be slowing down.

For the oceans, most computer models agree with each other, but, for the historical period, they do not match our oxygen-based results. For the land, models vary widely from each other, and most do not match our oxygen-based results.

Computer models are essential to provide governments with feasible scenarios to avoid dangerous climate change, but to be effective they need to be better grounded in what real-world observations are showing. Nature is difficult to represent with a series of equations, and observations are few considering the size of the planet.

We believe our study improves understanding of global carbon sinks and can help lead to more reliable projections of what might happen with climate change in the coming decades. But like any scientific approach, our oxygen method also has drawbacks.

The measurements themselves are challenging, such that only about 10 research laboratories in the world are routinely doing them. Calibrating the measurements is an ongoing challenge. Earth is not helping: Warmer waters hold less gas, meaning that as oceans warm in response to climate change, they expel some oxygen into the atmosphere . We must account for this in our carbon sink calculations. And to take into account variability in ocean circulation and other ocean processes, we have to average our results over 10-year time frames.

Policymakers and the public need answers faster . We believe the solution involves both improving the atmospheric oxygen approach and using other independent approaches: measurements of carbon and oxygen in the oceans, computer models and satellites are all essential. Combining these approaches will lead to more robust understanding of the carbon cycle and climate change, and better knowledge of where these valuable carbon sinks and the global climate are headed.

Visiting Professor of Carbon Cycle Science, Rochester Institute of Technology

Professor of Marine and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Exeter

Project Scientist in Geosciences, University of California, San Diego

scraped.title: To get Americans to care about climate change, just call it climate change
scraped.description: Phrases like ‘climate crisis,’ ‘climate emergency’ or ‘climate justice’ used at COP31 might seem to escalate urgency, but a large survey shows they don’t help and may actually hurt.
scraped.author: Gale Sinatra
scraped.h1: To get Americans to care about climate change, just call it climate change
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

You may be hearing phrases like “climate crisis,” “climate emergency” and “climate justice” a lot as the 2026 United Nations climate summit is underway. Political leaders, including U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres , are using them to try to get across the urgent risks and consequences of climate change. The danger is real , but is using this language actually persuasive?

It turns out that Americans are more familiar with – and more concerned about – climate change and global warming than they are about climate crisis, climate emergency or climate justice, according to a survey we conducted with a nationally representative sample of 5,137 Americans.

Moreover, we found no evidence that the alternative terms increased people’s sense of urgency, willingness to support climate-friendly policies or willingness to act.

The familiar terms – climate change and global warming – did at least as well, and sometimes better, than climate crisis and climate emergency in eliciting concern, perceived urgency and willingness to act. The phrase climate justice consistently tended to do worse, likely in part because it was the least familiar. These response patterns were similar among Republicans, Democrats and independents.

In our work as research psychologists , we have explored how Americans respond to the ways climate change is communicated and have uncovered a need to use straightforward language.

For example, people we interviewed for a study published in 2021 felt that climate experts were talking over their heads with terms like “adaptation,” “mitigation,” “sustainability” and “carbon-dioxide removal.” They wanted experts to use more familiar terms instead.

This inspired us to write a quick guide to climate jargon , published in The Conversation. Using everyday language makes information easier to understand, and even highly educated people tend to prefer it.

Jargon like “ biodiversity loss ” has similar problems. That refers to the shrinking variety of life on Earth, which is exacerbated by climate change. A survey of 7,338 U.S. adults led by one of us found people were much more familiar with and more concerned about “extinction of plants and animals” – or, if an explanation was provided, “nature loss”.

Even with an explanation, “biodiversity loss” was the least familiar and of least concern for people among several terms. Most people didn’t find “biodiversity crisis” or “extinction crisis” familiar either.

Yet, experts often use complex jargon because it is familiar to them, and they may not realize it is unfamiliar to others.

It has become common to talk about climate change and global warming as if they have the same meaning, but there are differences . Climate change refers to changes in the overall climate, while global warming refers specifically to rising temperatures.

A historical review found that, in the past, people were less likely to associate the term climate change with the idea that humans are actively warming the planet than they were with the term global warming. Perhaps this is why Democrats used to like the term global warming, while the popularization of the term climate change has been credited to Frank Luntz , an adviser to the George W. Bush administration.

Past surveys also found that Democrats used to think of global warming as being more serious than climate change, while Republicans thought of climate change as more serious than global warming. But according to a recent review , these partisan differences have now faded.

Alternative terms such as climate crisis, climate emergency and climate justice have been used to emphasize other aspects of climate change and to try to raise concern. In 2019, the British newspaper The Guardian switched to using climate crisis and climate emergency because it wanted to convey urgency.

Activists use the term climate justice to draw attention to climate change as a human rights challenge: Low-income people around the world suffer the most from the effects of climate change, despite being the least responsible for causing it.

Right now, the terms climate crisis, climate emergency or climate justice are less familiar and elicit less concern than climate change or global warming.

Even if these terms become more commonplace, there is no guarantee that they will heighten concern or inspire action. In fact, studies have suggested that phrases like climate crisis could backfire if they don’t resonate with people.

Our advice: Don’t make the mistake of using overheated language. Just stick with familiar terms that people understand – use global warming when referring to rising temperatures and climate change for overall changes in the climate.

This updates an article originally published Aug. 12, 2024 , with a new study and discussions at the 2026 U.N. climate conference, COP31.

scraped.description: New voluntary water conservation programs in the Upper Colorado River Basin appear on track after the 320th meeting of the Upper Colorado River Commission concluded this week. But Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, Wyoming and the federal government have yet to agree on how any conserved water would be credited and stored. These questions, experts say, […]
scraped.author: By Jake Bolster
scraped.h1: Conservation Programs in the Colorado River’s Upper Basin Inch Forward, Despite Thorny Questions
scraped.body_text:
New voluntary water conservation programs in the Upper Colorado River Basin appear on track after the 320th meeting of the Upper Colorado River Commission concluded this week. But Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, Wyoming and the federal government have yet to agree on how any conserved water would be credited and stored.

These questions, experts say, may not come with easy answers.

This June, the federal Bureau of Reclamation put $100 million on the table for the four states in the Upper Basin to fund their own voluntary water conservation programs, which usually entails paying ranchers and farmers to use less water. Overuse and drought-diminished flows on the Colorado River threaten the water supply of roughly 40 million people, 30 tribes, seven states and Mexico.

Most Upper Basin states are planning to implement programs in 2027 (Utah already has one running), and their success could be crucial to the states’ assertion that they should only have to ease the pressure on the Colorado River through voluntary measures. This fall, the federal government implemented new mandatory reductions on the Lower Basin, and Nevada , later joined by Arizona , sued over the potential for even deeper cuts.

“It’s … important to recognize, and I say this in a positive way, a complimentary way, the audacious ambition of attempting to put this together in the time frame that we have,” Wayne Pullan, the Bureau of Reclamation’s Upper Colorado Basin regional director, told negotiators from the Upper Basin states at the virtual meeting.

Colorado made it clear that its program can only move forward with an agreement from Reclamation that conserved water would remain under the state’s jurisdiction.

“We really need to get some credit for the upper division states through a program like this,” said Amy Ostdiek of the Colorado Water Conservation Board, who presented the state’s conservation program. “What that means in Colorado is seeing that that water is treated as operationally neutral, and not simply passed downstream.”

“Operationally neutral” water is conserved by one state and stored in federal reservoirs for future use by that state. Arizona, California and Nevada, the Lower Basin states, have banked water in Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States, with the option to withdraw it for future use. But the Interior secretary is the legal water master in the Lower Basin and has the ability to allocate surplus water there. The secretary does not play the same role in the Upper Basin.

Pullan said that Reclamation is “able and willing” to keep working on how the government would credit and handle water conserved by the Upper Basin. Some observers wondered how the Upper Basin’s condition would sit with the federal government, which built and financed the dams that store the water.

“They don’t like to turn over the keys of the car to the states,” said James Eklund, a partner at Taft Law and Colorado’s Colorado River negotiator from 2013 to 2019.

The Lower Basin would also need to agree that water conserved in the Upper Basin could be stored for the upstream states’ use, something Kathryn Sorensen, director of research for Arizona State University’s Kyl Center for Water Policy, had a hard time envisioning.

The Lower Basin states “would expect some sort of quid pro quo for that type of arrangement,” she said.

The Upper and Lower basin negotiators from each of the seven Colorado River states had years to agree on new guidelines for the federal government to implement. After they missed several deadlines, Reclamation implemented its own new operating plan this year, and the states appear no closer to an agreement.

The possibility of one of the seven basin states suing another before the Supreme Court looms over the basin.

Various conservation programs in the Upper Basin are in different phases of development. Utah’s program saved about 5,500 acre feet of water in 2025, Amy Haas, executive director of the Colorado River Authority in Utah, announced at the meeting.

One acre foot of water can supply anywhere from three to six homes for a year, depending on the region’s climate and urban density.

New Mexico and Wyoming made their programs compatible with other funding sources, like state appropriations or grants from nonprofits, should they become available, state representatives said.

The Upper Basin uses less water than the Lower Basin, which recently reined in its consumption after years of drawing more water than it was allocated, though it has plans to divert yet more water from the river. In its operating guidelines released this summer, Reclamation modeled up to 200,000 acre feet of voluntary conservation annually in the Upper Basin—if hydrology allows.

Eklund, who attended the virtual meeting, said it’s disappointing the seven basin states still can’t agree on a solution to the problems plaguing the Colorado River. “If this system collapses, it doesn’t really matter what we’re legally entitled to,” he said.

“If Phoenix sneezes, the Upper Basin catches a cold,” he added. “We’re very, very connected economically to each other, and if we don’t start governing the system like we’re all part of one country and not seven different sovereign countries, then we’re A: only going to have ourselves to blame, and B: we’re not going to like the results.”

Perhaps you noticed: This story, like all the news we publish, is free to read. That’s because Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization. We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.

That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. We’ve built bureaus from coast to coast to report local stories, collaborate with local newsrooms and co-publish articles so that this vital work is shared as widely as possible.

Two of us launched ICN in 2007. Six years later we earned a Pulitzer Prize for National Reporting, and now we run the oldest and largest dedicated climate newsroom in the nation. We tell the story in all its complexity. We hold polluters accountable. We expose environmental injustice. We debunk misinformation. We scrutinize solutions and inspire action.

Donations from readers like you fund every aspect of what we do. If you don’t already, will you support our ongoing work, our reporting on the biggest crisis facing our planet, and help us reach even more readers in more places?

Please take a moment to make a tax-deductible donation. Every one of them makes a difference.

Thank you,

David Sassoon Founder and Publisher

Vernon Loeb Executive Editor

scraped.author: By Bob Berwyn
scraped.h1: U.N. Leader Says People Power Is the Secret Weapon Against Global Warming
scraped.body_text:
ANTALYA, Turkey—Despite the lack of progress toward the goal of curbing global warming, outgoing U.N. Secretary General António Guterres urged climate activists and environmental justice advocates at the United Nations COP31 climate change conference here not to give up hope.

“You pushed governments to face up to the role of fossil fuels,” he said during his speech Friday to about 800 representatives of civil society groups from around the world. “You fought for finance for communities facing the worst impacts of a crisis they did little to cause. But let’s be clear. We face powerful lobbies that are pressuring governments. So civil society must put the needed counter-pressure against that.”

Guterres, former prime minister of Portugal, said a big part of the effort is to protect future generations who can’t influence today’s decisions. He said it’s essential to “do everything to make sure that those responsible for essential decisions create the conditions for a rapid, drastic reduction of emissions.”

While cutting carbon dioxide emissions is the only proven way to stop warming, this year’s Conference of the Parties, as the meeting is formally known, once again is far from addressing the issue of fossil fuels.

Our #1 newsletter delivers the week’s climate and energy news – our original stories and top headlines from around the web.

Dan Gearino’s habit-forming weekly take on how to understand the energy transformation reshaping our world.

A once-a-week digest of the most pressing climate-related news, written by Kate Waxman and released every Tuesday.

Don’t miss a beat. Get a daily email of our original, groundbreaking stories written by our national network of award-winning reporters.

An inside look at top climate news, delivered every two weeks.

A digest of stories on the inequalities that worsen the impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities.

A voluntary global pledge to increase electrification holds the most promise for reducing emissions, but even that has become contentious, as some countries are resisting using the term “clean electrification,” which means producing electricity from renewables, rather than fossil fuels. Converting systems to run on electricity doesn’t reduce emissions if the electricity is produced by burning coal, oil or gas.

And there is a danger the U.N. process could backslide. Observers at some of the closed-door sessions this week said several countries, mainly Russia and Saudi Arabia, may be trying to block adoption of a final conference decision document—an outcome that could lead to the summit being widely perceived as a failure, even if such a text is not procedurally required.

All decisions and documents at the conference must be adopted by consensus, and Saudi Arabia’s 30-year history of obstructing efforts to address fossil fuels is well documented .

Guterres’s 10-year term as U.N. secretary-general ends Dec. 31. He has been outspoken about global warming and environmental justice. Even though international cooperation on climate and other issues has deteriorated recently, he has an abiding faith that collective action can overcome seemingly intractable social and political circumstances.

That belief, he has said , is rooted in part from his experiences during Portugal’s 1974 Carnation Revolution, when citizens arose against the country’s military dictatorship to establish what has become one of Europe’s most stable democracies.

“We are losing ground to climate change because we are not doing enough,” Guterres said. “We must turn the promise to transition away from fossil fuels into clear commitments … with clear timelines and real support for the workers and impacted communities.”

Shamini Selvaratnam , director of international climate and clean energy at the Ocean Conservancy, applauded Guterres’ leadership on climate change.

“Secretary-General Guterres has been a tireless champion for climate action and a powerful voice for protecting our ocean and the communities that depend on it,” she said. “His unwavering belief that cooperation is possible, even in a deeply divided world, was the message many of us needed to hear.”

Selvaratnam said his promise to keep up the fight after leaving office affirms that ”none of us can give up on protecting our oceans and our planet.”

scraped.title: Trump’s ‘Reckless And Shortsighted’ Plan To Fish Protected Pacific Waters - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: After falling short the first time, the Trump administration is again trying to roll back protections on culturally significant and ecologically vital Pacific waters.
scraped.author: By Johnny Sturgeon
scraped.h1: Trump’s ‘Reckless And Shortsighted’ Plan To Fish Protected Pacific Waters
scraped.body_text:
In 1935 , a group of Hawaiian school boys embarked on a secret military operation to colonize remote Pacific islands for the United States.

Inhabiting one of America’s most distant outposts in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, they built the runway Amelia Earhart never arrived at, endured fatal Japanese bombing and forged a Native Hawaiian cultural presence more than 6,600 miles from Washington. Decades later, and with bipartisan support, the legacy of the Hui Panalā‘au was enshrined with one of the largest marine protected areas in the world to safeguard the vibrant waters surrounding several of the islands.

This week, the Trump administration proposed reintroducing commercial fishing to parts of the Pacific Islands Heritage Marine National Monument.

Following the public comment period, if the National Marine Fisheries Service enacts the proposal, longline fishing boats and purse seiners that encircle dense schools of fish with vertical walls of netting would be allowed to return to more than 400,000 square miles of pristine, ecologically rich and culturally-valued waters.

“You take people and their lives, and now you want to come back and take the resources,” said Sol Kahoʻohalahala, a Native Hawaiian elder and knowledge holder, questioning the administration’s move. “We need to stop this idea of extraction and taking for profit and not being concerned with the children yet unborn,” said Kahoʻohalahala, whose uncle from the island of Lānaʻi died during Japanese raids on one of the island settlements.

“This is one of the last wild, healthy ocean ecosystems on the planet. It’s truly a gem,” said Sheila Sarhangi, founder and executive director of the Pacific Islands Heritage and Papahānaumokuākea Coalitions. “It’s completely reckless and shortsighted to allow industrial fishing, with its heavy amount of bycatch, to come back into the area.”

It’s not the administration’s first time pushing to fish these waters.

In April 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order dismantling Obama-era protections around Johnston Atoll, Jarvis Island and Wake Island, temporarily allowing commercial fishing to return between 50 and 200 miles offshore. Three days later, the National Marine Fisheries Service notified permit holders that they could fish the waters.

Following a lawsuit filed by Earthjustice , the federal district court in Honolulu halted commercial fishing operations in the area in August 2025, citing the fisheries service’s failure to adhere to due process and incorrect invoking of the Antiquities Act, a legal precedent which allows the president to establish marine protected areas but not shrink boundaries or strip protections.

A historically bipartisan conservation issue—President George W. Bush originally established the monument in 2009 —the latest proposal reverses course.

With a 5,000-year-old coral system and at least 165 seamounts, the monument functions as a biodiversity hotspot for blue whales, leatherback sea turtles and seabirds. Conservationists consider it to be one of the most important habitats for threatened and endangered wildlife in the world.

The administration has suggested the potential ecological harm would be “negligible” because the proposed fishing gear would “not come into contact with the ocean floor.” Yet the harmful impact of industrial fishing in the area, whose ecological health has beneficial spill-over effects for the wider Pacific Ocean, is evident from historic data.

In 2013, the last year industrial fishing was allowed within the expanded range, the Hawaiian longline fleet ensnared over 2,300 sharks. Keeping just 10, the vast majority were discarded dead or injured, including the threatened silky shark and the globally critically endangered oceanic whitetip shark.

“The proposed rule threatens to reverse decades of progress in protecting one of the planet’s last wild, healthy ocean ecosystems,” said the Pacific Islands Heritage Coalition in a press release . “[It’s] a place of profound cultural significance for Indigenous Pacific Islanders.”

Framed as part of President Trump’s efforts to “unleash American commercial fishing” in the region, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration contends re-opening the area would mean American boats “do not have to compete with foreign fleets” nor pay other nations to fish in their waters.

However, the economic benefit would likely be limited. The fisheries service concedes the change would only offer a “minor, beneficial impact” by “reducing transit times” and fuel use.

This June , Trump signed a proclamation seeking to undo protections in three other Pacific areas: the Islands Unit of the Mariana Trench Marine National Monument in the Northern Mariana Islands, the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument in Hawaiʻi and the Rose Atoll Marine National Monument in American Samoa.

“This is driven by politics. It’s more show than go,” said David Henkin, an Earthjustice attorney who helped defeat the administration the first time around. “Sending the bull into the china shop messes up important scientific research, affects pristine ecosystems and for what?”

Indeed, even when fleets were briefly granted access to the area in 2025, activity was limited . Just over 1,700 fish were caught—a testament to the geographic impracticality of fishing in the monument’s remote protected waters.

“They know that ‘unleashing American fishing’ in the monument will not result in any more fish being caught because these fisheries operate under international quotas. They can’t catch any more fish,” Henkin added. “The whole thing is a charade.”

The fisheries service has now opened a 30-day comment period, open until Dec. 9, 2026. “I think this is one of those moments where people need to realize that their voice carries power, and they need to speak up for one of the last wild, healthy, remote ocean ecosystems in the world,” said Sarhangi.

A spokesperson for NOAA told Inside Climate News that the agency “remains dedicated to providing factual, timely information, research and resources that serve the American public and ensure our nation’s economic and environmental resilience.” They did not respond to questions about ecological harms, cultural critiques or the motivations behind the move.

For Kahoʻohalahala, retaining marine protections is about more than just conservation and cultural preservation, it’s also about setting a precedent for America’s relationship with nature.

“We have a thinking in our Hawaiian culture that if we create the resources on the earth to be fattened or abundant, then we can ensure this abundance is going to be carried on into generations yet unborn,” said Kahoʻohalahala, who felt the administration’s announcement was a betrayal of both history and the ocean itself.

“If we look at fishing as an extractive industry just for profit, and pay no attention to how we reciprocate that, it would be our demise,” added Kahoʻohalahala.
