scraped.title: Indigenous leaders at COP31 say it’s past time to turn promises into action
scraped.description: As climate disasters mount, Indigenous advocates are pushing governments to deliver on commitments made at previous global climate summits.
scraped.author: Joseph Lee
scraped.h1: Indigenous leaders at COP31 say it’s past time to turn promises into action
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

The annual United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change gathering drew historic levels of Indigenous attendance in Belém, Brazil last year, leading some to dub it “the Indigenous COP.” But the event was marked by frustration and protest , with many Indigenous leaders calling it little more than a continuation of a longstanding pattern of exclusion from international negotiations.

This year’s gathering in Antalya, Turkey, is billed as an “implementation” conference focused less on sweeping new pledges than on the procedural work of turning previous agreements into action. For Indigenous advocates, that makes COP31, which started November 9, a test of whether the promises made last year translate into tangible changes, including greater authority over climate action.

“It is still a struggle,” said Edward Porokwa, who is Maasai and a member of the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues. “I’m yet to really determine whether there will be any more progress that is made in terms of realization of the rights of Indigenous people.”

Indigenous advocates are pressing governments to follow through on their commitments to secure and strengthen Indigenous land rights on 400 million acres in tropical forest countries, provide $1.8 billion in funding , and respect rights to free, prior and informed consent in the energy transition.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Despite those pledges, funds have been slow to reach affected communities and Indigenous land defenders say their rights and lives remain under constant threat . Porokwa said that he feels that responsibility to address climate change continues to fall on smaller countries and Indigenous peoples.

The stakes have been particularly stark over the last year. In Nepal, massive floods and landslides in August killed more than 1,500 people and destroyed entire villages. In Canada, a historic wildfire season saw millions of acres burned, causing thousands of evacuations. And in Indonesia, wildfire smoke alone has caused thousands of deaths and led to school closures and other emergency measures across Southeast Asia.

“The recent large-scale mountainside collapse on the border of Nepal and Tibet should serve as a wake-up call to the global community,” said Biswash Chepang, who is a founder of the Institute for Indigenous Affairs and Development in Nepal.

Climate-driven threats to Indigenous peoples and their lands continue to mount as a historically powerful El Niño threatens to drive famine, heat-related deaths, and other catastrophes across the globe

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The conference comes in the wake of a recent United Nations report that said it will be virtually impossible to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees , the goal set under the landmark 2015 Paris Agreement . Indigenous delegates find that reality particularly frustrating because they see it as a direct result of decision makers ignoring their knowledge and all the ways their stewardship has been proven to benefit the environment and climate .

“For over thirty years we have brought Indigenous knowledges and sciences to these negotiations,” Māori activist Quack Pirihi said in an opening statement on behalf of the International Indigenous Peoples Forum on Climate Change. “Yet emissions continue to rise, putting 1.5°C beyond reach.”

While the work of reducing emissions and protecting Indigenous rights in the energy transition continues, securing funding for nations and communities most impacted by climate disasters is also a priority. In October, the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage approved $21.6 million for Nepal — its first disbursement and less than 1 percent of the nearly $5 billion in damage the country sustained. But the process to receive and administer those funds is ongoing , and Indigenous leaders say the fund must work faster. Their push comes as wealthy countries face renewed scrutiny over climate-finance pledges they have failed to deliver.

“Loss and damage is not simply a question of humanitarian assistance,” Chepang said. “It is also a question of climate responsibility, historical emissions, equity, and the right of affected communities to recover with dignity.”

Indigenous peoples also hope to hold polluters to account. Bianca Ranson, who is Māori and a board member of the Aotearoa Climate Action Network, is attending COP31 in part to highlight the landmark climate case her father Mike Smith led against major emitters in New Zealand. The case, which uses Māori customary law, has been blocked by the national government.

Despite the logistical, financial, and political hurdles of attending an event like COP, Ranson says there is value in global spaces. “I think that with the geopolitical moment that we’re in, with the rise of the far right and fascism and war, and the struggles that Indigenous peoples are facing across the globe, it’s a really important place for us to be able to come together to connect, to strengthen our solidarity,” Ranson said.

As negotiations continue through November 20, Indigenous advocates will continue their push for all the discussions to lead to tangible actions. “Now I think it is not time only to talk about the commitment,” Porokwa said. “It is time to change the commitment into practice.”

Out of 27 ballot measures supporting transit, 22 passed on November 3, representing $27.4 billion in funding to rescue faltering systems and expand or build new ones. Some of the biggest wins […]
scraped.author: Benton Graham
scraped.h1: The affordability election delivered billions for public transit
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

In an election dominated by concerns about affordability, voters across the country overwhelmingly agreed to raise taxes to preserve or expand public transit.

Out of 27 ballot measures supporting transit, 22 passed on November 3 , representing $27.4 billion in funding to rescue faltering systems and expand or build new ones. Some of the biggest wins of the night included voters in the San Francisco Bay Area staving off enormous cuts to Bay Area Rapid Transit and other regional systems, Coloradans backing new regional rail, and residents of Seattle and nearby Pierce County favoring expanded bus service.

“It’s an indication that the public is willing to pay for these public transit improvements,” said Sohail Husain, a policy analyst at the Eno Center for Transportation. “That’s very telling –– especially in a world like today where people are concerned about affordability. I think people are still also concerned about mobility and having options to move.”

Public transit has now fared well in the red wave of 2024 — when 19 out of 25 measures supporting transit passed — and this year’s blue wave. Although few candidates campaigned on the issue, the results could significantly alter policy. At the state level, transit advocates see opportunities to advance projects or simply get the government out of the way. Meanwhile, a Democratic majority in Congress will shape a major transportation infrastructure law that is up for renewal. Together, the results could remake how Americans get around.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

States have broad discretion to fund transportation as they see fit, which is why Democratic wins in red states and Democratic control of the governorship and both legislative chambers in 22 states have many public transit advocates excited about what comes next.

Pennsylvania is one of those states. It has endured a bitter battle over the finances of the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority, which serves the Philadelphia area. When the agency faced 45 percent service cuts last year, Governor Josh Shapiro directed the state Department of Transportation to allow the agency to shift nearly $400 million from its capital to operational budget. He also made another $220 million available to the system.

Now, with Democrats taking control of both chambers of the state legislature, transit advocates say SEPTA can look beyond self-preservation. Stephen Bronskill of Transit Forward Philadelphia pointed to projects including trolley modernization, new fleets to replace vehicles from the 1970s, more frequent regional rail service, and fully accessible stations.

“This is a once-in-a-generation moment to invest in public transit –– safe, reliable, accessible transit that Philly needs, but all of Pennsylvania deserves,” he said.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The prospects are less straightforward in Texas, where Republicans still control the Senate. Jay Blazek Crossley, executive director of Farm&City, a nonprofit focused in part on road safety, has spent more than a decade trying to nudge GOP lawmakers toward less violent and less polluting transportation options. Every legislative session has seen him unsuccessfully push legislation that would make it easier for cities to reduce speed limits on residential streets. He sees new hope for that measure and, more broadly, a future that might include additional public transit funding, which accounts for just 0.72 percent of the transportation department’s budget. State Republicans have generally been more interested in moving more cars more quickly, primarily by building bigger highways, while pushing back against some city-led public transit efforts.

“At the very least, the state, I believe, will get out of the way on things like building good light rail and transit,” he said.

There’s hope for bigger projects too. State Representative John Bucy III has again filed legislation directing the Texas Department of Transportation to find a public-private partnership for a high-speed rail line linking Dallas and San Antonio. He believes the bill will appeal to lawmakers whose constituents would benefit from an alternative to driving on the heavily congested Interstate 35 corridor.

“I think the voters spoke loud and clear that they want a Texas government that is going to work on kitchen table issues,” he said. “I think that’s healthcare, education. It’s also mobility and transit, and how do we get around this big, vast state?”

Georgia is another state where Democrats took the governorship and flipped the House, but Republicans still control the Senate. That could be a challenge for Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, who has called for dedicated state funding for the Metropolitan Atlanta Rapid Transit Authority and other systems that have historically relied heavily on local and federal support.

The election could have even greater implications at the federal level, where Congress must soon decide how much spending to allocate to transit and passenger rail. The BUILD America 250 Act passed out of a key House commitee with bipartisan support in May, but left public transit advocates concerned about funding cuts . With Democrats taking control of Congress, the legislation is likely to look different. Representative Jerry Nadler of New York, the lone Democrat on the committee to oppose advancing the legislation, sees an opportunity to change its direction.

“Unlike the current Republican proposal, next year’s bill should not prioritize one mode of transportation at the expense of others. This bill must make robust investments in rail and public transit, to connect communities, create good-paying jobs, lower transportation costs for families, and reduce the cost of moving goods across the country,” he said in a statement.

But rewriting the bill won’t necessarily happen quickly. Rebecca Higgins, the Eno Center for Transportation’s vice president of policy, said lawmakers will face some urgency because Congress is already relying on an extension to fund transportation. At the same time, she expects lawmakers to give their newly elected colleagues a chance to weigh in. One major question is what happens to money for intercity passenger rail that was included in the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act but dropped from BUILD America 250.

Whatever happens in Washington, the local and regional measures voters approved will have a more immediate impact. In the Bay Area, a 14-year regional sales tax is expected to raise about $1 billion annually to preserve service on BART and other systems that had been facing steep budget shortfalls. Colorado voters approved a 0.333 percent sales tax to build, operate, and maintain passenger rail connecting Pueblo and Colorado Springs with Denver and Fort Collins.

In Seattle, voters doubled an existing sales tax over the next decade, generating an additional $138 million per year largely for transit service. In nearby Pierce County, voters also approved a sales tax increase to expand bus service.

The Pierce County win is particularly notable because voters there hadn’t increased public transit investment since 2002, said Kirk Hovenkotter, the executive director of the Transportation Choices Coalition. The fast-growing region also faces an affordability crisis. The American Public Transportation Association estimates that relying on public transit rather than owning a car can save a household more than $14,000 annually.

Hovenkotter makes a similar argument about the costs facing residents of the Pacific Northweest. “The average cost of car ownership in Washington state is about $12,000,” he said. “The fastest way we can put $12,000 back in someone’s pocket is making it easier for them to live without a car or with one fewer car.”

The election results suggest that, for a wide swath of voters, transit funding isn’t competing with affordability concerns. It’s an answer to them.

scraped.description: In church basements and warehouses, Americans are mounting a quiet resistance to throwaway culture, one appliance at a time.
scraped.author: Johnny Kauffman
scraped.h1: The cozy radicalism of repair cafés
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

On an unusually cool and rainy Saturday morning in Decatur, Georgia, dozens of people filed into a warehouse at the back of a church parking lot, their arms full of what a less hopeful group might call junk. Some carried broken lamps, glitching electronics, or cracked furniture. Others walked in with tool boxes, multimeters for testing electric currents, and cans of WD-40. Beneath extension cords dangling from the rafters, they sorted themselves into smaller groups: the volunteer electricians, tailors, luthiers, carpenters, and at least one cutler (knife sharpener), commandeering nearby worktables and passersby as needed.

That’s how Lilly Pettus ended up shoulder to shoulder with three strangers, their hands all pressing together the pieces of her family’s cracked dining room chair as wood glue hardened and a volunteer tightened a clamp.

“This is so interesting,” a giddy Pettus said, inspecting for the first time the joints, one of them broken, that held together the chair she’d owned for decades. “You never even know how furniture is put together.”

Lilly Pettus’s broken chair gets a hand from attendees at the Decatur repair café​. Nearby, a sign tracks repair progress during the event. Johnny Kauffman / Grist

This is Decatur’s semi-regular repair café, one of a few hundred meetings like it across the United States. More Americans than ever are turning to these community gatherings to fix what they already own, resisting the influence of companies selling everything from hiking boots, smartphones, and hot water boilers, that push for replacement over repair. One consequence of this throw-away economy is an increase in greenhouse gas emissions from manufacturing that threatens to intensify climate change.

Yet, organizers and volunteers consider repair cafés as more than a relatively small climate solution. As inflation rises and wages stagnate, the meetups connect people to a movement with the ambitious goal of changing the fundamentals of America’s consumer economy.

At the Decatur repair café, volunteers, wearing green shirts with “I can probably fix that” printed on the back, offered their skills free of charge as patrons observed. A young father of a toddler and squirmy baby watched as a volunteer replaced a switch on a favorite mid-century modern lamp worn out by the older child’s repeated clicking. Murmurs of excitement rippled around the building as the acrid smell of a spot welding project wafted through.

Pettus’ broken chair held in its wood her family’s story. Soon after she and her husband were married in 1996, they began a search for a dining room set. Pettus wanted the chairs to be comfortable for her entire family, but one of her brothers is nearly 7 feet tall, and another just a few inches shorter. “We are not a tiny family,” Pettus said. “We are a big family.”

The newlyweds settled on a simple table and six chairs — two “host style” with arms, four without — from the local Ethan Allen store. The furniture came to feel more like home than the many houses where Pettus, her husband, and their children lived. They moved the table and chairs with them from Florida to Connecticut, then to Indiana, Michigan, Texas, and finally to Georgia. “ I don’t know anyone’s chairs that I like more than my own,” Pettus said.

But after absorbing shakes of laughter during countless games of Hearts, and fidgets of anxiety at family meetings about upcoming moves, one of the chair’s joints finally cracked. “We had the chair just sitting in the corner,” Pettus said, “but no one actually sat in it.” She didn’t know how to fix the chair, but if she sent it to a landfill that would mean trashing a reminder of her fondest memories from the last 30 years.

“When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it’s very lonely.”

Pettus also thought of one of her children who’d interned at the Environmental Protection Agency and shared his concerns with Pettus about pollution and climate change. Then, after months of the broken chair cluttering the family’s house, Pettus was running Saturday morning errands when she passed the Decatur repair café. She drove the half-mile home to grab the chair, and decided to give it a second chance.

“When a product breaks and you have to throw it away, it’s very lonely,” said Martine Postma, director of Repair Café International, a Netherlands-based network of 4,000 cafés. “ It’s easier to just go on the internet and order a new item which will come to your doorstep in 24 hours, but that’s also a very lonely, disconnected activity.”

Postma, a former journalist with the demeanor of an unflappable librarian, founded her organization in 2010 after the birth of her second child magnified her fears about the planet’s future. “Markets are flooded with trash — with cheap products that we don’t need and that do not work,” Postma said. “They break, and they contribute nothing to our well-being. They just contribute waste.”

Repair cafés appear to be inspiring people to use their stuff longer. In 2025, they prevented nearly 2 million pounds of waste — the equivalent of more than 100 fully loaded Boeing 747 aircraft — according to Repair Café International, and reduced greenhouse gas emissions equivalent to the average consumption of about 1,000 Dutch families.

Postma, Pettus, and millions of others often smack into obstacles when they try to fix their own stuff. Broken products are increasingly difficult to repair, according to a report from the Federal Trade Commission titled “Nixing the Fix.” The report details how Americans are incentivized to “replace products before the end of their useful lives” by companies that decide to make repairs less safe, limit the availability of parts, lock software and firmware, or even “disparage” independent repair.

In 2023, California, Colorado, Minnesota, and New York passed “right to repair” legislation meant to encourage repair over replacement. A year later the European Union passed a similar directive. Postma and other organizers consider the cafés a natural place for activism to push for right-to-repair measures, although Postma hopes for more sweeping changes in Europe, like a tax on raw materials. She argued it would limit emissions and bolster repair shops, even if it increases the cost of products.

“ I feel for the objects around me. I feel sorry for them if they’re broken,” she said.“I want to make repairing a normal thing in everyday life once more.”

According to Postma, repairing goods is more common in relatively poor countries where replacing them can be especially difficult and expensive. It’s in wealthy countries that repair cafés are thriving, but they’re not at all uniform. Each reflects the surrounding area and its socioeconomics.

“If the world ends, at least I’ll know how to fix a motor.”

On a Sunday afternoon in the Collier Heights neighborhood of Atlanta, volunteers brought most of their own tools to the basement of a building owned by a Seventh Day Adventist Church, setting them on white plastic folding tables atop a light pink carpet. The café looked much different from the one a 30-minute drive across the city in Decatur. The median annual household income in the mostly Black Collier Heights neighborhood is roughly $40,000 lower than in Decatur. Many people who brought items wanted them fixed less for sentimental reasons, and more so they could keep using them.

Gale Pines walked in with a red air fryer that stopped working after they used it to dehydrate ginger. When their oven ran, Pines said, it heated the entire kitchen. So, while in nursing school, they cooked many of their evening meals in the air fryer, most often chicken nuggets and fries.

Pines recently graduated, but had trouble finding a job and couldn’t afford to buy a new $100 air fryer. “It’s just hard to exist,” Pines said. “I don’t really have a very big support network outside of my friends.”

One of Pines’ housemates told them about Collier Heights’ repair café. They keep a bag of broken electronics in the garage that they’d prefer not to send to a landfill. “Being in the height of climate collapse we can’t just keep buying new stuff all the time, both for the economy and for our material scarcity,” Pines said.

When a volunteer at the Collier Heights repair café opened up the airfryer, they quickly discovered the problem: a bad capacitor. Another volunteer had brought a replacement part, and the two of them made the fix as Pines watched, impressed, but unable to follow the relatively complex repair. Pines felt OK that they hadn’t learned how to fix the air fryer themself.

“ To just be around people that want to help other people with the skills that they have, that’s value that is really important to me, and something that I try to do as well,” Pines said. “If somebody in my community has a question about their medication or something and can’t afford to go to the doctor, I’m happy to answer any questions that people have.”

Another volunteer, Lew Lefton, said he thought that the satisfaction humans draw from making and fixing things has largely been lost, but apocalyptic threats like climate change and artificial intelligence have driven many people toward rediscovering more basic, human skills that are key to survival. People who come to a repair café have a different way to view the future, according to Lefton, especially if they learn something or volunteer themselves. “If the world ends” he said, “at least I’ll know how to fix a motor.”

Back in Decatur, Pettus left the repair café with a newly sturdy chair. A screw and some glue fixed the crack around the joint, but the chair still needed upholstery work. Someone Pettus met at the café, who had provided one of the sets of hands that held her chair together as the glue set, advised her on where to buy fabric. Pettus thought she might bring the chair back to the repair café for help reupholstering its seat cushion.

“The beauty of it,” Pettus said, “was that I actually was able to learn more about the chair. It was a great experience to know that — I’m not gonna say I birthed it, I of course did not — but I actually had something to do with helping to get it put back together.”

scraped.title: How Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia impacts China’s AI supply chain
scraped.description: The founder’s stunning departure removes Beijing’s biggest advocate in Silicon Valley, accelerates chip stockpiling, and leaves Asian suppliers bracing for what comes next.
scraped.h1: How Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia impacts China’s AI supply chain
scraped.body_text:
Innovation

The founder’s stunning departure removes Beijing’s biggest advocate in Silicon Valley, accelerates chip stockpiling, and leaves Asian suppliers bracing for what comes next.

Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang resigned on Thursday, days after he admitted to having an affair with a Chinese data center executive, whom the U.S. intelligence agency believed to be a Chinese government agent. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive.

Nvidia’s board said that chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as the company’s interim chief executive until a permanent successor has been named.

Huang’s exit has triggered worries about Nvidia’s future as the world’s top chipmaker, and about the entire AI industry where Nvidia has been a hardware provider, an investor, and a community leader. Repercussions from the saga will impact China, which has yet to replace Nvidia chips with domestic alternatives, as well as Taiwan and South Korea, which host a vast network of Nvidia suppliers.

Here are the key questions emerging from Huang’s dramatic downfall.

Jensen Huang had been the biggest advocate for selling chips to China, which he argued helps America maintain its market dominance.

Despite the U.S. banning the export of advanced Nvidia chips to China, Chinese companies have been trying to access chips remotely by working with data centers in Southeast Asia.

Alice Huang, with whom Jensen Huang had an affair, served as the executive of Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia. The Information reported that Alice Huang helped move about 240,000 H100, H200 and some A100 chips into China. Her companies also invested in DeepSeek, promising to supply Nvidia chips.

The Nvidia scandal will likely lead the U.S. government to tighten chip controls. Anticipating a crackdown, Chinese AI labs are trying to lock in overseas supplies of Nvidia chips, while traders in China are stockpiling restricted chips, Reuters reported .

Chinese chips are catching up in performance, but Nvidia chips are still essential to the AI industry.

In the first half of the year, Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators in China, down 44% from a year earlier and making up 34% of the market, according to a Reuters report , citing IDC data. In the same period, leading Chinese chipmaker Huawei i Huawei Huawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions. READ MORE shipped 572,000 ‌AI ⁠accelerators, up from more than 300,000 a year earlier, accounting for 28% of the market,

Alibaba i Alibaba Alibaba, founded in 1999 by Chinese entrepreneur Jack Ma, is one of the most prominent global e-commerce companies that operates platforms like AliExpress, Taobao, and Tmall. READ MORE ’s chip unit T-Head had 7% of the market, followed by Cambricon’s 5%. Baidu i Baidu Baidu is a Chinese technology company that operates the country’s biggest search engine and video-streaming service iQiyi. READ MORE subsidiary Kunlunxin held 4% and Hygon had 3%.

Although AI labs are increasingly working with chipmakers to make sure their models can run on domestic infrastructure, most AI developers still train new models on Nvidia chips. Nvidia’s B300 delivers 6.75 times the arithmetic performance of Huawei’s best Ascend 950 chip, according to research firm Epoch AI . Huawei also lags behind Nvidia in production volume.

Jensen Huang enjoys rock star status across Asia, especially in his birth country Taiwan, where he would visit night markets, share snacks with fans, and host banquets with executives of Taiwanese suppliers. He said the company planned to invest $150 billion a year in Taiwan.

Many internet users expressed disappointment that they lost a role model in tech. Some wrote that the spy allegations and the criticisms of Huang would add to the discrimination of Asians working in America’s tech industry.

Huang’s departure is also creating uncertainty around Nvidia’s supply chain relationship with Asian companies. But several executives at Nvidia’s Taiwanese suppliers said they still expected steady orders from Nvidia in the coming years because of the sustained demand from the AI industry, according to Taiwan’s Central News Agency.

A growing number of startups are editing powerful Chinese open-weight models for Western businesses that are concerned about censorship and security.

Startups like MiniMax and Moonshot are setting up U.S. outposts, but massive pay gaps, weaker prestige, and national security tensions make luring talent away from OpenAI and Anthropic an uphill climb.

Some languages require far more tokens for AI models to process, raising costs and reducing context for the people who use them.

scraped.h1: The Download: Silicon Valley’s blind spot and Nvidia’s chip-tracking plan
scraped.body_text:
Plus: A major Microsoft outage has disrupted services worldwide.

This is today's edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

—Aaron Zamost, a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square

The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley have built careers claiming to see the future. Yet five weeks before the midterms, many gathered at the White House to pose with Trump and endorse his “Super Intelligence” agenda, despite growing opposition to AI and data centers.

Their decision to lash themselves to President Trump was a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.

Here’s why Silicon Valley’s tech leaders may be less visionary than they think .

Nvidia representatives told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it was possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review on Thursday, despite an industry group claiming they were “potentially infeasible.”

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips and prevent their smuggling to China.

The act is drawing renewed attention following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair. Find out what the proposed tracking measures would involve .

—James O'Donnell

Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can control robotic limbs and computers, and even “speak.”

The people who volunteer for trials of these devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart, who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014.

He’s been working on a set of guidelines for ethical trials to respect participants’ autonomy—and access their own brain data whenever they want.

Read the full story on the push to give volunteers in brain implant trials more rights .

—Jessica Hamzelou

This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 A major Microsoft outage has disrupted services worldwide The disruption has affected Outlook, Teams, and Copilot. ( Reuters $) + Traders were forced to do business by phone and fax. ( Bloomberg $) + Microsoft says the outage isn’t a cybersecurity incident. ( BBC )

2 Jensen Huang’s resignation will leave a trail of damage It should change how America does AI. ( Axios ) + Who is Colette Kress, Nvidia’s new interim CEO? ( NBC News ) + And who could get the permanent role? ( NYT $) + Trump has backed Apple's Tim Cook for the job. ( WP $) + Nancy Pelosi's replacement plans to regulate AI. ( MIT Technology Review )

3 An Alice Huang-linked firm procured banned Nvidia chips in China The servers were first sold to an Nvidia partner in Singapore. ( Bloomberg $) + Singapore says US failed to help in the spy probe. ( NYT $) + The city-state faces growing scrutiny over its chip links to China. ( CNBC ) + The turmoil at Nvidia puts billions in Chinese AI at risk. ( Reuters $) + Taiwan's “silicon shield” is weakening. ( MIT Technology Review )

4 Parents are demanding an AI moratorium in schools Gemini allegedly encouraged a teenager to plan suicide. ( Ars Technica ) + Schools are caught in Big Tech’s education experiment. ( New Yorker $) + We need smarter AI use in the classroom. ( MIT Technology Review )

5 Advocacy groups have sued five frontier AI labs to stop development They’re targeting Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, and SpaceXSI. ( AP ) + Anti-AI protests are increasing. ( MIT Technology Review )

6 SpaceX has denied throttling Ukraine’s Starshield network Zelenskyy says the curbs are hampering drone defenses. ( Axios )

7 A robot has assembled a structure in space for the first time It’s a step towards in-orbit manufacturing. ( New Scientist $)

8 AI companion users want to make their digital partners immortal They’re building chatbots that can survive model updates. ( Atlantic $)

9 Scientists have identified a protein that accelerates ageing The discovery could lead to drugs that slow ageing. ( Nature $)

10 A huge new galaxy map could reveal the dark universe. The data includes 15,000 potential gravitational lensing cases. ( Guardian ) + The search for dark matter has been blown open. ( MIT Technology Review )

Quote of the day

—Donald Trump shares his succession plan for Nvidia on Truth Social, The Verge reports .

One more thing

—Niall Firth

I’m currently around 1,000 feet beneath the North Sea, in a dark, dank cave. It smells weird. And I’m increasingly aware of the pressure from millions of tons of seawater just above my head.

I’m under the iconic fjords of Norway to visit what will soon become the world’s longest and deepest subsea road tunnel—an exceptional engineering feat that will carry drivers deep beneath the North Sea.

I’m here to understand how you make a 16.6-mile highway that sits 1,280 feet below the sea at its deepest point. And also—at a time when it can feel hard to get anything done—to reassure myself that ambitious engineering is still possible. That we can still make things.

Step inside Norway’s Rogfast tunnel and see how engineers are making it happen .

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

Plus: 22 nations have called for a new global body to oversee AI.

People with experimental brain implants are pushing for more recognition and respect.

Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.”

The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart , who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs).

Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.”

Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control.

He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it .

The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits. It was a scientific breakthrough .

Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.”

In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition —an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers. Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences. The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy.

The guidelines, published on Tuesday , lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories. One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants. During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.”

As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t. He says he was a key member of the research team. Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says. Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however.

The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy. That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention. In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants.

Things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’ brain data . Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data. Burkhart wasn’t too bothered about that in his case, where scientists were collecting neural activity related to movement. But people who have brain implants designed for turning thoughts into words might feel differently.

The guidelines state that brain data “should be understood as the participant’s personal information.” They are pushing for participants to be able to access their own brain data whenever they want—something that has not always been possible—and want to make sure people aren’t prevented from sharing it with their own doctors because of embargoes or nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) designed to keep findings under wraps from competitors.

“It’s not super common for there to be firm NDAs within a lot of the trials,” says Burkhart. “But it’s something where we want to make sure that that does not happen.”

The guidelines also address what comes after a trial. Around five years after Burkhart had his device implanted, the research team ran into some issues with funding. When we last spoke a few years ago , he recalled how he was told he would have to have the implant removed and could have it put back in once the team had secured funding. (And we’re talking about brain surgery here.)

Ultimately, he kept the implant until 2021, when it was removed after an infection started to develop at the point where the cable led into his scalp. But losing the device after all those years was difficult; he’d regained the ability to move his arm—and then lost it again.

Rita Leggett, an Australian woman who had a device implanted in her brain to treat her epilepsy, has said she felt she “became one” with her implant. When the company that made it went bust two years later, the device was removed against her will —an act ethicists have described as a potential breach of human rights.

Researchers should instead commit to maintaining brain devices for a “reasonable period” after a trial ends, according to the guidelines. Participants should be given plenty of time to prepare for the surgery to remove it. And researchers should set aside extra funds to support trial participants who have to do that.

Some of the guidelines are vague and may overlap with existing ethics standards. They don’t all spell out explicit solutions. They were also developed with feedback from a small group of individuals—the number of people living with BCIs is still very low . The team hopes to grow and expand on the guidelines over time. Burkhart also plans to discuss them with researchers at an upcoming neuroscience conference .

“This is a living document, and this is version one,” says Chandler. “It’s just the starting point.”

scraped.title: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
scraped.description: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned…
scraped.h1: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
scraped.body_text:
Tech executives traded their reputations as visionaries for short-term political gain.

The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda.

Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision. Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers , the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor. And now, their industry is very squarely in the new victors’ crosshairs .

For an industry obsessed with pattern recognition, their decision to lash themselves to President Trump has proved to be a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.

What were they thinking?

The people who work for them are just as confused as the rest of us. Tech workers I’ve spoken to at OpenAI, Meta, and other firms have noted an absence of commentary from their leaders post-election. Zuckerberg has yet to address the results internally, while an employee at another AI firm said that “leadership has been pretty silent on Slack.” Most employees share concern about potential anti-data-center legislation and are curious how leadership will adjust to a Democratic Washington, DC. But more than anything, they don’t understand how their bosses didn’t see what was so blindingly obvious to everyone else.

In Silicon Valley, the Gretzkyism “skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been” is a management maxim; it preaches anticipation and foresight over reactiveness to the present moment. Tech entrepreneurs love a good “pivot,” and companies that can’t change with the times get disrupted and die.

Which is why I find it so strange that Zuckerberg, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and so many of Silicon Valley’s other prominent AI leaders and venture capitalists have put themselves in a potentially inescapable political bind. In going all in on President Trump’s cultural and business agenda instead of playing both sides of the aisle as corporate America usually does, they’ve built identities they may not be able to pivot out of. Will anyone really believe that Palantir CEO Alex Karp is suddenly progressive after a year of promising “ violence and death to our enemies ” and telling investors that the company is “completely anti-woke”?

I believe this is less a surprise than a very public exposure of a fundamental reality: that tech’s most visible leaders are not all-knowing visionary masterminds after all. Insights about social media or artificial intelligence do not make Zuckerberg or Altman experts on politics, the economy, or much else outside of technology. The instant gratification of presidential access, subsidies, and a say in their own regulation blinded them to the basics of political math that they clearly did not understand.

There’s a reason the chief executives of Chase, Boeing, and other Fortune 500 staples don’t go on podcasts to talk about “ masculine energy ,” or call the president from the stage of a MAGA-friendly AI summit to label fears about AI a “hoax” and a “scam.” This is the learned wisdom of decades operating in an environment where the customer changes every four years but contracts run for 10. Most companies play to both sides of the aisle because they know that their business models and multibillion-dollar projects must outlast the current administration. Instead, Big Tech tied itself to Trump and made its most important goals and investments—many related to grid access and data center permits—immediate targets for Democrats.

In tech, you can always sunset a feature or update some code. But in politics, there is no undo button for failures that change public perception. The tech elites’ decision to visibly align their businesses with a temporary movement has left them no credible way to pivot now that the climate has changed. As one Meta employee who has worked closely with Zuckerberg put it, “Mark is a long-term thinker, but he never charts a plan of how to get there. It’s spray and pray and see what happens.” As for whether employees expect the company to do a strategic postmortem? “Facebook has never really done that.”

“Move fast and break things” might work in a startup, but it’s a terrible strategy for building reputational goodwill. Previous technological leaps, like the rollout of fiber-optic technology and wireless infrastructure, avoided partisan politics. But by kowtowing to the Trump administration, Silicon Valley made artificial intelligence a culture-war issue. Now, when citizens vote on data center proposals from California to Florida , they are no longer considering only technical or economic concerns, but political ones.

Tech leaders didn’t see this coming because they were too focused on the urgency of the AI race to understand how reputational damage could undermine the intangible goodwill—and ultimately the very tangible infrastructure—necessary to win it. The industry’s misreading of the moment has already punctured one myth Silicon Valley holds dear: that its leaders can always see what’s next.

Aaron Zamost is a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square.

scraped.h1: You turn to us for voices you won't hear anywhere else.
scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

As Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January, party leaders say they intend to hold Trump officials accountable with stepped-up hearings and investigations. The administration, however, has responded with threats to launch its own investigations into lawmakers for carrying out their oversight responsibilities.

“The oversight function of Congress is well established by the founders. It’s a normal part of government. The separation of powers requires oversight,” says Brad Adams, co-founder of The Rule of Law Project, which seeks to provide outside accountability due to what he describes as the administration’s refusal to investigate “obvious cases of corruption.”

AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman.

Democrats have made clear their intentions to increase oversight and investigations into President Trump and administration officials in the next Congress. After Democrats secured the incoming majority in the midterm elections, the top-ranking Democrat on the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, Congressmember Robert Garcia, released a statement, saying only, “Lawyer up.”

On Monday, the top White House lawyer, Will Scharf, sent Garcia a letter warning Democrats’ language and plans for investigations and subpoenas, quote, “may cross the line into blatant criminality.” He also wrote, quote, “The Administration will not be extorted and will not be cowed by unlawful process motivated by animus, pettiness, hatred, or any other unlawful motive,” the White House lawyer said.

For more on this brewing legal battle, we’re joined by Brad Adams, co-founder of The Rule of Law Project, a new organization formed by former federal civil rights and corruption prosecutors and investigators.

Brad, thanks so much for being with us. Can you first respond to the White House saying that if congressmembers engage in oversight, they might cross the line into criminality?

BRAD ADAMS : Yeah, it’s a bit rich, isn’t it? The oversight function of Congress is well established by the founders. It’s a normal part of government. The separation of powers requires oversight.

And what is, you know, ironic, of course, is that the Republicans have tried to weaponize the oversight process for many years. Think back to Benghazi and, you know, other high-profile efforts to harass the Biden administration or the Obama administration or some members of the Cabinet, such as Hillary Clinton. And I’ll point out, I’m not sure that Will Scharf wants — realizes this, but the newly elected leader of the minority in the House, Jim Jordan, was the chair of the House Judiciary Committee, and in that role, he issued 91 subpoenas to Democratic administrations. And many of those were clearly just meant to be political grandstanding, to harass, to get in the newspaper.

The Supreme Court in 2020 issued a ruling on this, and they said there are limits on oversight. And they basically said one key point — made one key point, which is that there has to be a clear legislative purpose. And what Representative Garcia is suggesting has a clear legislative purpose: to ensure that corruption doesn’t go unchecked, to look into ICE violence, killings, beatings on the streets, custodial mistreatment in ICE detention facilities, etc.

So, I mean, this statement, basically, you know, makes a lawyer who went to Harvard — that’s Will Scharf, went to Harvard — appear that he never took constitutional law classes.

AMY GOODMAN : And can you also respond to Todd Blanche, the attorney general, responding to Garcia, who is talking about everyone, from Stephen Miller on, to lawyer up? And he said, “I’m Stephen Miller’s lawyer. He doesn’t need to hire one.” What does that mean? I thought the attorney general was the people’s attorney. He was even questioned about this at his confirmation hearing, and he said he wasn’t, for example, Trump’s lawyer — which he used to be, of course.

BRAD ADAMS : Yeah, well, you can say one thing during confirmation hearings and then act in another way later. I mean, you know, Todd Blanche answers Trump’s question, you know, “Who’s my Roy Cohn?” And it’s Todd Blanche. And he’s forgetting his responsibility is to defend the Constitution and to represent the United States government and the people of the United States, and not individuals.

He’s not Stephen Miller’s lawyer. If Stephen Miller is brought before a committee, needs a lawyer, he’s going to have to find outside counsel. The Department of Justice should have nothing to do with defending Stephen Miller as a person. They have an obligation and a right to defend government officials in the course of their official duties. But if there’s an allegation that Stephen Miller committed a crime, that’s not for the Department of Justice. That’s for a criminal defense lawyer.

AMY GOODMAN : So, we only have three minutes, but, Brad Adams, I want to ask you about this new Rule of Law Project and the official corruption you say you’re going to be investigating, as well as extrajudicial, state-sanctioned violence, like ICE , everything from ICE in the United States to the bombing of vessels in the Caribbean and the Pacific.

BRAD ADAMS : Well, we shouldn’t have to do this. I was the Asia director at Human Rights Watch. We did investigations in places like the Philippines. We participated in the investigation that put Rodrigo Duterte in The Hague. We worked on atrocities against Rohingya in Myanmar. But that’s because the state didn’t function in those countries. And we should be able to expect that the state will function here, but it’s not. The Department of Justice has made very clear that it is not going to investigate officials in the administration. It’s not going to investigate some of the more obvious cases of corruption that we see reported regularly, whether it’s crypto or quid pro quos or pardons or insider trading.

And, you know, as a former investigator of very serious violence at Human Rights Watch and, before that, at the U.N., you know, it kind of broke my heart to see thugs on the streets, masked, beating people up. And obviously, the Renee Good and Alex Pretti cases are the most well known, but there have been many other shootings. And also, we have, you know, many reports of mistreatment in custody. And this is quintessentially what the Department of Justice should be looking into, but they’ve made it very clear that they’re just not going to. So we created this organization where we’ve hired former federal prosecutors, former FBI agents to do the work that the government should be doing.

Now, people may ask, “What about the pardon power?” Pardons will not extend to crimes committed in state jurisdictions. And there are many states that are willing and able — and we’re starting to work with them — to investigate and hold people accountable there. And the Department of Justice, hopefully, when we get a new government after the 2028 election, will be reestablished and take its role seriously. But it will take some time for it to be functional. We’ll be providing prosecution-ready cases to state and local prosecutors before then, and to the DOJ after that.

AMY GOODMAN : And will you be working with Congress?

BRAD ADAMS : Yeah, I’m already talking to oversight committees, coincidentally and ironically, and they are getting ready. We’ve talked. We’ve talked to House Judiciary, for example, and they’re on a hiring spree, because the amount of illegality in this country right now is unprecedented, as we all see. And it contributed to the election results, of course. You know, people are fed up with blatant corruption and all the violence committed by ICE .

And the oversight committees have a very important function to play. We hope that they will play them responsibly. You know, it’s very important to be really careful with factual allegations, to be specific — you know, to use a soccer analogy, to play the ball, not to play the man. Don’t go after people on an ad hominem basis. But there is so much to investigate that we think that the oversight committees will play a key role, and we’ll work very closely with them.

AMY GOODMAN : Brad Adams, co-founder of The Rule of Law Project, speaking to us from California.

That does it for our show. Very happy birthday to Ishmael Daro! Oh, and the new film about Democracy Now! , the documentary Steal This Story, Please! , is now out on digital platforms, from Amazon Prime to Apple to Fandango to Google Play. You can go to StealThisStory.org to get the latest information. Also, we’ll be broadcasting from Turkey all next week from the U.N. climate summit, COP31. I’m Amy Goodman. Thanks so much for joining us for another edition of Democracy Now!

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

Israel’s latest bombing of Nasser Hospital in Gaza on Thursday killed six Palestinians, including surgeon Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira. He was featured in the recent documentary American Doctor , which follows international medical volunteers in Gaza’s battered hospitals as they work alongside Palestinian colleagues.

Israel claimed, without providing evidence, that it targeted a senior Hamas militant in the hospital strike. Israel has repeatedly bombed medical facilities in Gaza since the start of the genocide in October 2023, even though such attacks are prohibited under international law.

“It’s just barbarism. I don’t know why we’re supporting this,” says Dr. Feroze Sidhwa, one of the titular American doctors in the documentary, who demands accountability for Israel’s actions and a change in U.S. policy toward the country. “That’s an American-made bomb dropped by an American-made airplane burning American-supplied jet fuel.”

Sidhwa also comments on the catastrophic flooding in Gaza that has swamped the temporary shelters of tens of thousands of displaced Palestinians as Israel continues to block the entry of shelter materials into the territory. As a result, “babies are going to die of hypothermia in Gaza for the fourth year in a row,” Sidhwa says.

AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman.

In Gaza, funerals have been held for a surgeon, a teenage boy and four other Palestinians killed when an Israeli airstrike targeted the Nasser Hospital complex in southern Gaza. The surgeon was killed in the strike, Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira, featured in the recent documentary American Doctor . Footage filmed inside the hospital revealed severe destruction, rooms littered with debris and overturned furniture, cables hanging from broken ceilings, injured patients moved on stretchers through hallways covered in rubble.

NBC reports debris photographed at the scene shows fragments of a GBU -39 small diameter bomb produced by the U.S. aerospace and weapons manufacturer Boeing.

This is Dr. Ayman Abu Obeid, who was working an overnight shift and resting in a staff room when the explosion hit, leaving his right foot badly injured.

DR. AYMAN ABU OBEID : [translated] As usual, we were on shift at the hospital. We have rooms where we stay. We were surprised by a strike directly on the room we sleep in. Total destruction. No light left, no help left, no… I don’t know what happened. All of a sudden, the world turned upside down. It went dark all at once. Honestly, it was very terrifying.

AMY GOODMAN : The director of the Nasser Medical Complex, Ahmed Al-Farra, condemned the Israeli attack. Al-Farra spoke during funeral services in Khan Younis Thursday.

DR. AHMED AL- FARRA : [translated] This targeting and these crimes are happening under an alleged truce that the Israeli occupation talks about. We are talking about a series of attacks on hospitals. We are talking about the seventh targeting of Nasser Medical Complex. Unfortunately, the occupation pays no attention, not to a health system or to international laws or to international constitutions. …

Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira never hesitated to provide service to his patients. He was on top of his work. He was in his room between following up cases, treatments and preparing cases for surgery. But it was God’s will, and he was martyred in this treacherous strike. There are also doctors who were wounded in this attack.

AMY GOODMAN : We’re joined now by Dr. Feroze Sidhwa, general trauma critical care surgeon in California, who’s volunteered at Nasser Medical Complex alongside Dr. Rizk, who was just killed. Footage of the two of them working together appears in the new documentary American Doctor , which tells the story of Dr. Feroze and two other doctors from the United States who volunteered in Gaza.

Feroze, thanks so much for being with us. Our condolences. If you can talk about the doctor, the surgeon who was killed in this latest Israeli military strike on Nasser Hospital?

DR. FEROZE SIDHWA : Yeah, you know, I met Dr. Rizk probably on March 7th of last year, when I got to Nasser. And during that time, there was a ceasefire going on, so there was less bombing and shooting, and we could actually go around on rounds and, you know, see all the patients. And, you know, there are some — most surgeons like surgery, right? But Rizk was one of those surgeons that just loves surgery. Like, he could be in, like, the middle of his daughter’s wedding, and you’d be like, “Do you want to go do surgery?” and he’d be like, “Yes, let’s go. Let’s go right now.” He just absolutely loved surgery. He was a sweet man. He was the first one running ahead to get the patient’s dressings off on rounds.

And so, I met him in the ICU on — or, actually, I met him at morning report, and then we went to ICU rounds. And there was probably a man in his early thirties with just devastating intestinal injuries, total disaster of a case. It was very obvious this man was going to die in Gaza. Here, he would have lived, but there’s no way he was going to live in Gaza. And so, the whole team is kind of saying, “Well, you know, maybe we should just let nature take its course.” And Rizk said, “Yeah, but we can operate on him. We can operate on him.” And everyone rolled their eyes. And I said, “Well, Dr. Rizk, I’ll operate on him with you. Let’s go operate.” So, that’s what’s on that movie poster that you saw. And so, you know, when we go around to film festivals, it’s his picture that’s sitting there with me.

AMY GOODMAN : I mean, you just —

DR. FEROZE SIDHWA : And we’re doing that case, yeah.

AMY GOODMAN : The film was just at IFC , and you were speaking afterwards. That image of you two doing surgery, so utterly painful. And you, yourself, survived a strike on Nasser Hospital. What is your response to what has just taken place?

DR. FEROZE SIDHWA : Well, it’s just — it’s just barbarism. I mean, I don’t know why we’re supporting this. You know, you showed the pictures of the — there were two munitions fired at Nasser this time. One exploded, which — and the remnants of that is a GBU -39 small diameter, like you said. The other one, that didn’t even explode, is sitting right there. Yeah, that’s the image of it right there. Somebody just picked it up and put it in — just think about — that’s an American —

AMY GOODMAN : And put it on a gurney.

DR. FEROZE SIDHWA : Put it on a gurney, because where else are you going to put it in a hospital? That’s an American-made bomb dropped by an American-made airplane burning American-supplied jet fuel, probably with targets selected by AI software, like your earlier guests were talking about, developed in the Bay Area and in Seattle, that ends up in a hospital bed. That shouldn’t happen. That’s just insane.

You know, this — and I hate to make it political, because Rizk was my friend, but this is why somebody like Schumer shouldn’t be the next, you know, majority leader. It really should be somebody like Chris Van Hollen, who’s been on the right side of these matters.

AMY GOODMAN : He went to Gaza.

DR. FEROZE SIDHWA : He tried to go to Gaza.

AMY GOODMAN : Tried.

DR. FEROZE SIDHWA : He went to Rafah. He reported very honestly on what he saw, saying, “Look, there are maternity kits sitting in these warehouses because they have scissors that are this big, and you’re saying that’s a threat to the state of Israel. This is ludicrous, you know?” And he’s just — you know, he’s an honest liberal. He’s — it’s a rare, rare breed.

AMY GOODMAN : So, talk about the other doctors and the patients who were hit.

DR. FEROZE SIDHWA : Yeah, so, Dr. Ayman, whom you showed, Dr. Ayman Abu Obeid —

AMY GOODMAN : Laying in the bed.

DR. FEROZE SIDHWA : He was laying in the bed, saying, you know, it was a terrifying attack, and things like that. He’s the head of the surgical department at Nasser. He’s a great guy, very experienced, like Dr. Rizk. I think both of them must have 20, 25 years of experience. I don’t remember where Dr. Ayman trained, but Dr. Rizk trained in Ukraine. And he really — he actually spoke Russian fluently because of that. And he really — he missed it. He loved it. He loved his time there.

AMY GOODMAN : So, he’s the head of surgery.

DR. FEROZE SIDHWA : He’s — yes, Dr. Ayman.

AMY GOODMAN : And another man lost both his legs?

DR. FEROZE SIDHWA : As far as I understand, Dr. Mohammed has been very badly injured. Dr. Ayman is injured and in the hospital, admitted, but Dr. Mohammed, from what I understand, is very likely to die, as well.

AMY GOODMAN : What impact will the suspension of four departments in Nasser Hospital — radiology, laboratories, surgical operations, inpatient surgical wards — have on providing services to Palestinians, also in the midst of the massive rain, where all of these thousands of tents are being held up —

DR. FEROZE SIDHWA : Yeah.

AMY GOODMAN : — and a baby dies of hypothermia?

DR. FEROZE SIDHWA : Yeah, it’s an utter disaster. I mean, so, the people of Gaza, the probably less than 2 million of them that are left, are certainly among the sickest people in the world. It’s a population of half children, 70% refugees. Ninety percent of the buildings in their society have been destroyed, or at least what we would call in the U.S. destroyed. They’re uninhabitable. Seventeen hundred of their healthcare workers have been killed, huge numbers of aid workers, poets, doctors, professors. Everybody who makes a society run has been targeted. All of the physical infrastructure, even the sewage system, has been destroyed.

And now the makeshift infrastructure that they live in, literally sticks stuck into the beach mud, you know, the sand and the mud on the beach, so that you can wrap some tarping around it and hopefully protect yourself from the winds and the rain that come onto this coastal plain in the winter every year, are just flooding and destroying all of this makeshift shelter that people have.

And like you said, you know, actually — you mentioned babies dying of hypothermia. Sarah Parkinson, she’s a professor at SAIS in D.C. She and I wrote a paper for Foreign Policy , which people in the government read, in — I think it was November of 2024. We said, last winter, babies died of hypothermia in Gaza simply because the shelters that are a few miles away were not allowed to come in. This year, meaning 2024, 2024-to-2025 winter, babies are going to die again of hypothermia, because the shelters that are a few miles away are still not being allowed to come in. And now we’re at another one. Yeah? Right? Like, we had another winter, 2025 to 2026, and now we’re going 2026 into 2027. And again, babies are going to die of hypothermia in Gaza for the fourth year in a row. It’s just shocking behavior. And taking away the medical system is — I guess it’s Israel’s cherry on top. I’m not sure how to describe it.

AMY GOODMAN : Can you go to Gaza? Can you go back?

DR. FEROZE SIDHWA : So, I tried to enter in November, and I was blocked from entering then. Strangely enough, I went to Israel to give talks then, so obviously the security wasn’t an issue. And I’m currently part of a petition to the Israeli High Court of Justice. We’ll see if that goes anywhere. And they should rule on it in December. If they do, I’ll try and go back. And if they don’t rule in our favor, I’ll try and go back anyway.

AMY GOODMAN : And your response to President Trump saying on Election Day, in response to Dr. Abu El-Sayed in Michigan calling for an end to Israeli military — U.S. aid to Israel, “We’ll cut off $4 billion. They don’t need it, and they don’t even want it,” he said, responding, saying, “Yes, the money should stay at home.” President Trump.

DR. FEROZE SIDHWA : It shows how extreme the change in public opinion has been over the past three years. You know —

AMY GOODMAN : And he thought he could affect things on election morning.

DR. FEROZE SIDHWA : And, yeah, yeah, I think he thought this was his way of winning, but it obviously was not. But, you know, I think people have seen so much, so much death and destruction, and I think they remember that it wasn’t just under Trump. You know, most of the killing and destruction happened under Biden. A lot of it’s happened now, too, under Trump. But I think it’s very hard for people to forget what they saw, you know, especially young people, especially politically engaged people, and these folks you have out here today. They will not forget what they saw. And I don’t think they’re willing to go back to business as usual. And if Donald Trump says some random nonsense like he tends to, I think people are pretty dismissive of that now.

AMY GOODMAN : Dr. Feroze Sidhwa, thanks for joining us today, general trauma critical care surgeon from California, featured in the documentary American Doctor about his time volunteering in Gaza. The surgeon that was just killed at Nasser Hospital was a surgeon that he befriended and also worked with, performed surgeries.

Coming up, we’ll look at the Trump administration’s escalating threats against Democratic lawmakers over their plans to investigate the president. The White House claims such probes, quote, “may cross the line into blatant criminality.” Stay with us.

[break]

AMY GOODMAN : Amadou & Mariam, performing in our Democracy Now! studio.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.
