scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including with an employee and a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence officials accuse of spying for Beijing. The company says Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent replacement.

Nvidia’s computer chips are at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom, driving the company’s value above $4 trillion and making Huang one of the most influential business leaders in the world. His spectacular fall from the company he co-founded in 1993 comes as the U.S. stock market has become highly dependent on a handful of AI-related companies and amid intense competition between the United States and China over control of the technology, with access to Nvidia’s chips becoming a major point of contention between the two countries.

Tech critic Paris Marx notes that the AI industry’s “circular financing,” in which companies are both clients and investors for one another, has created systemic risk.

We also speak with Ramesh Srinivasan, director of the AI Futures Lab at UCLA , who says the “soap opera” of the Huang scandal has exposed “how precarious the governance of this AI truly is,” with only a handful of people and firms controlling “incredibly powerful technology that feeds off of all of us and the planet.”

AMY GOODMAN : We begin today’s show looking at the fallout from Jensen Huang’s resignation as the CEO of Nvidia, one of the world’s most powerful companies. Nvidia’s advanced AI computer chips have powered much of the artificial intelligence boom. Huang cultivated close ties to President Trump and is credited with helping to shape U.S. policies around artificial intelligence and rules around the export of advanced AI chips.

Huang’s resignation came days after reports emerged he had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman named Alice Huang — no relation — whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspected of spying for Beijing and helping China obtain advanced Nvidia chips, which are banned by U.S. export controls. The Information news outlet reports Alice Huang helped route at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips to China via a Singapore-based cloud computing company called Megaspeed International. Jensen Huang confirmed he had an affair with the woman. Later, published reports revealed he also had affairs with two employees at Nvidia, including with a senior executive who reported to him.

Nvidia has announced its longtime chief financial officer, Colette Kress, would serve as interim CEO as the board searches for a permanent replacement.

On Thursday, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche took questions about Nvidia.

REPORTER : When did the Justice Department learn, with regard to Nvidia, that Alice Huang might be a suspected Chinese asset? And there’s been concerns raised that the Commerce Department was giving favoritism to Nvidia and Megaspeed, which is Alice Huang’s company. Do you share the concerns that maybe the Commerce Department was impeding the ability to uncover the smuggling network that Alice Huang was involved in?

ATTORNEY GENERAL TODD BLANCHE : Well, your first question assumes something that I have never said and that I don’t know to be true. So, you assume that DOJ learns that she is, in fact, a spy. I’m not — nobody said that. I certainly haven’t said that. And I don’t — all I said a minute ago, and all that I think I will say, is that, of course, DOJ is investigating or looking at it. So, there’s no — there’s no conclusions reached by the Department of Justice or by me or by Director Patel around who she is or is not.

I don’t have concerns with the Commerce Department. I don’t. We have a good relationship with the Commerce Department. I’ve read some of the stories, which, you know, are sourced or not sourced, and so I don’t have any — but, no, I don’t have — the answer to your question is, no, I don’t have any — I don’t have any concerns.

AMY GOODMAN : On Capitol Hill, Republican and Democratic lawmakers are calling for probes into Nvidia’s actions and the Trump administration’s policies regarding chip exports to China. Republican Senator Tim Scott, the chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has requested Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify. Democratic lawmakers Ron Wyden of Oregon and Richard Neal of Massachusetts are investigating the Trump administration’s decision to allow Nvidia to sell advanced chips to China.

For more on Nvidia and questions about the concentration of power in the AI industry, we’re joined now by two guests. In Toronto, Canada, we’re joined by Paris Marx, a tech critic and host of the award-winning Tech Won’t Save Us podcast . He writes the Disconnect newsletter, author of the book Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires . And in Germany, we’re joined by Ramesh Srinivasan, professor of information studies, director of the AI Futures Lab at UCLA and host of the podcast Utopias .

Paris Marx and Ramesh Srinivasan, welcome back to Democracy Now! Professor Srinivasan, let’s begin with you. What should we understand about what has just taken place? And talk about the centrality of Nvidia to the whole AI bubble, to the whole AI industry.

RAMESH SRINIVASAN : Right. Thank you so much for having me, Amy.

AI is not magic. It comes from the planet, and the technologies that produce it often return to the planet as electronic waste. It’s powered by water, energy sources, labor and our data, and those come from us, from the planet itself. Right? So, what has occurred is this astonishing technology that reduces life to data and numbers, and reduces intelligence to pattern recognition, has been — has now been governed and run by just a few people on the planet, mainly men, and men that you’ve discussed, you know, commonly on Democracy Now! , who were there at the inauguration and so on.

So, now when we have soap opera sorts of moments, like Mr. Jensen Huang being connected to, you know, this Chinese — potential Chinese spy, various affairs and so on, you can see how precarious the governance of this AI truly is, because the administration has completely handed the keys to this incredibly powerful technology, that feeds off of all of us and the planet, to basically a few people, and they can do what they want — their vagaries, their mishaps, their corruption in certain cases, their gluttony. That is what is being accumulated more and more.

So, the story of AI is a story that’s tied to data centers — right? — which you cover all the time, which are, you know, computing and so on, much like server farms in the past. They’re tied to chips, and that’s very key to this story, the Nvidia chips, or superchips, that were originally used in the context of gaming and now were applied to artificial intelligence and large language models. But it also comes from all of our data, and then the screens and systems that determine and shape our lives.

So, this is a technology that is harvested, extracted from our planet and all of us to create potentially trillions of dollars of valuation, which might be a massive bubble — and we can talk about that — with returning almost next to nothing for the rest of us, other than anxiety, insecurity and deep concerns. The technology doesn’t have to go in that direction, but that’s the direction the Trump administration has taken it.

And I think it’s incredibly notable that it’s the China — it’s the China scare yet again, just like we saw with Huawei, just like we saw with COVID . It’s the China scare that’s forcing all of this action and this spectacle and this controversy, rather than the real conditions of AI, which are disenfranchising and robbing people of many aspects of their futures.

AMY GOODMAN : Paris Marx, if you could continue, talking about what is the role of Nvidia when it comes to, overall, fueling so much? And explain the issue of the ban on these — on these superchips, why they’re so significant, what kind of monopoly Nvidia has on this, and why you believe he is so close to President Trump, who didn’t want him to resign.

PARIS MARX : Absolutely. Great to join you this morning, Amy.

You know, Nvidia is key to this AI market. You know, it controls about 90% or so of the chips that go into, you know, all these data centers that are powering the AI boom that we have seen occurring now for the past few years, right? And as a result of that, Nvidia has become one of the most valued companies, and for a while has been, you know, the most valuable publicly traded company on the planet, which is just staggering to imagine, right? You know, it went from kind of just, you know, a regular old tech company, you know, not particularly notable — sure, it made some graphics cards for gamers — to being now one of the key companies that, as you say, you know, is so important for what so many other companies are doing.

And it’s not just the fact that it creates these chips — right? — these chips that are just essential to, you know, the generative AI workloads behind ChatGPT and the image generators and those sorts of things, but because Nvidia has made so much money for the past number of years, it has also become a major investor, plowing more than $120 billion into other AI companies across the economy, across the United States, around the world, which has meant that now there are all these companies that not just depend on Nvidia’s chips, but also depend on Nvidia’s financing. You know, I’m sure you’ve been talking on the show about the upcoming Anthropic IPO , you know, Anthropic looking to go public. It is expecting about $10 billion from Nvidia as part of its public offering. And so, Nvidia has been really key here.

And because of that, you know, because Nvidia was valued at something like more than $5 trillion until recently, it’s no surprise, then, that Jensen Huang has become very close with Donald Trump, right? It’s a very valuable company. It is a company that makes the technology that is very important to the broader AI boom that has been kind of lifting the U.S. economy and the U.S. stock market — right? — because of the investment, not just in all these AI products, but in all these data centers that, you know, have been being built across the country, as well. And so, Jensen Huang has become a major adviser to Donald Trump on AI policy and has certainly been pushing him to weaken the restrictions on, you know, basically, his ability to sell these chips to China.

And I think now in light of these revelations, there are questions as to whether, you know, that is kind of a firmly held belief that Jensen Huang had because there was obviously, you know, as someone who runs a major company, a big market opportunity in selling those chips to China, or whether there was influence on his thoughts, you know, from Alice Huang. And I think those are questions that we don’t have answered yet, but certainly is probably, you know, what some of these lawmakers are hoping to try to get more insight into by having Jensen Huang come speak to congresspeople.

AMY GOODMAN : Paris Marx, in your book, you quote one investor who describes Nvidia as “the central bank of AI.” And there are many descriptions of how Huang is really the conduit from the other tech billionaire bros to reaching President Trump and making the demands that they want.

PARIS MARX : Absolutely. You know, as I was mentioning, when we look at Nvidia, it is not just a company that is selling all these chips. It is a company that has gone to a lot of these other AI and data center companies and made sure that they had investment, sure, so that they could, you know, grow, expand their businesses, what have you, but also that they — so that they could then buy more Nvidia chips from Nvidia, right? So, it’s kind of like a circular financing scheme, where Nvidia gives it the money to operate, and then they buy the chips from Nvidia, and Nvidia makes more money in that way, right? So the money comes back to Nvidia all the time.

And then, of course, linked with that is it has also used that money to try to support companies that were in difficult situations. So, for example, a company called CoreWeave, that creates data centers to power AI and kind of sells that computing power to these AI companies, has been in trouble, on and off, for a number of years, and Nvidia has often been there to support that company when it has been in dire straits. And it’s not the only one like that.

And so, of course, you know, linked to that, Jensen Huang has developed this really close relationship with Donald Trump. You know, we saw this just the other day, just yesterday, after Jensen Huang resigned, and, you know, Donald Trump came out and said that he was talking to Jensen and, you know, that things are difficult, and, you know, basically, had this really kind of personal relationship to him, seems to be someone who he really trusts. And as a result of that, I’m sure that Donald Trump has been open when Jensen Huang has been discussing AI and tech policy with him.

And, of course, Jensen has been pushing to make sure that there is not regulation of AI products, in the way that your other guest has been talking about, you know, is really necessary, but then, on top of that, again, trying to weaken these restrictions on the ability to sell chips to China. And, of course, you know, the U.S. government’s concern and many lawmakers’ concern there is that by selling those chips, because they are some of the — because they are the most advanced chips that are out there, that if they get sold to China, you know, China will not just be able — Chinese companies will not just be able to use them to power their own AI products, but that there’s a concern that, you know, Chinese companies will be able to kind of reverse-engineer the technology and then have a big kind of leap in their — in their kind of chip-making capabilities, essentially.

AMY GOODMAN : In October of last year, Jensen Huang spoke to the media about whether China should have access to Nvidia’s most advanced chips.

JENSEN HUANG : The China market is large, and it’s a vibrant, vibrant market with a lot of developers. And those developers create AI technology that’s exported from China all over the world. And so, to the extent that American tech stack can run and operate those AI models, it’s good for the United States and around the world.

REPORTER : So, would you want the Blackwell to be sold in China?

JENSEN HUANG : I hope so. I hope so. But that’s a decision for President Trump to make.

AMY GOODMAN : So, Professor Ramesh Srinivasan, if you can explain what he is saying there? And also, this whole issue of the so-called Chinese spy, what evidence do we have of this? Is it other competing companies saying this? Is there a big division within the U.S. government in the intelligence community who had informed Trump of this months and months ago?

RAMESH SRINIVASAN : Right. It’s not clear what the evidence is as of this point. You could even see in the story, in the introduction to this story, that even the Attorney General Todd Blanche is, you know, very elusive and vague in his comments about, you know, what is — what exactly occurred here.

But I do think it’s very important to note a couple things that were already mentioned here. First of all, the AI industry, there’s incredible amount of concern that this is an overspeculated bubble. That’s because many of the revenues are occurring in the circular way that your other guest just described. So the revenues seem to be inflated here.

And talking about China, as we actually discussed before, Amy, back, you know, about almost two years ago, Chinese models around AI are performing nearly as well as the top American so-called frontier models. I mean, the question of what we’re building all these models for is a worthwhile question, I think a big elephant in the room. But they’re doing it at a fraction of the cost. So, we have to really consider what’s occurring here and what’s really occurring here, right?

So, the president’s response around all these concerns is often to say that the economy is super healthy. And when he says that, what he’s talking about — Trump, I’m saying — is he’s talking about the S&P 500. But the vast majority of people in America and around the world do not have large amounts of investment capital. Investment capital is how people make money, but there’s a deep amount of concern that these — this is not going to actually produce the type of revenues that even legitimate it for investors.

But what about the rest of us, as workers, as consumers? AI is being pushed out as a technology of replacement, not a technology to augment or expand or help us, you know, create together. It’s not a telescope. It’s not, you know, a microscope. It’s not what Steve Jobs once famously called a “bicycle for the mind.” It’s being — it’s using us. It’s surveilling us. It’s turning us into data. It’s turning life and intelligence into patterns to replace us, to read, write, speak for us. In fact, a CEO in Big Tech told me recently, because I’m from Silicon Valley and I have friends in that industry, “Hey, Ramesh, you don’t even have to do this interview with Democracy Now! Very soon, an AI can do that for you, and better than you.” What does that even mean? So, this is what’s at play here.

And so, this has been cast, as I alluded to earlier, as some sort of flat, you know, geopolitical battle between the U.S. and China, when, in reality, what we need is cooperation between the two nations, and, most importantly, outside of the elites in those two nations, governance by stakeholders, not just in the Global South and around the planet, where I’m part of a Global South AI alliance, but also from workers, consumers and so on, to ensure that a technology that uses patterns to predict the present and construct the future is a technology that’s applied to the right domains. And no one, at the end of the day, has been paid for their data. None of us have equity in any of these companies, but these companies are feeding off us to potentially replace us. And that’s what I would call a parasitic technology. But it doesn’t have to go in that direction.

AMY GOODMAN : Ramesh, can you show us your hands? AI models are notoriously bad at generating the correct number of fingers. I’m only kidding. OK, Paris Marx, Paris, this was from Bloomberg. You have Bloomberg in — let’s see, says, “Jefferies Financial Group Inc.’s Chris Wood said the most likely long-term outcome of the AI boom will be massive capital destruction in the U.S.” Do you see that coming now?

PARIS MARX : It’s hard to say when exactly that would come. You know, I think that there are multiple moments over the past few years where it looked like, you know, maybe — maybe the bubble is going to start bursting, and then, you know, it has continued. I think that it is facing a serious threat in this moment, and not just because of the resignation of Jensen Huang from Nvidia.

And to be clear, you know, Nvidia was a company that was really like Jensen Huang’s fiefdom. You know, it was not set up to have a lot of kind of people who could easily take over from him if he were to leave the company. You know, a number of his family members are also executives within the company. And so, you know, I think that there’s real concern about what this is going to mean for Nvidia’s future — right? — as such a key player in the AI market, you know, again, one of the most valuable companies in the world, supplying the key technology that these companies need, but also providing a lot of financing to other companies.

But we’ve also been seeing, through this year, a lot of major companies kind of pulling back on their generative AI spending, because they’re finding they’re not getting the return on investment from what they’re doing there. There was just a report at the end of October from an analyst at Apollo called Torsten Slok, and he basically looked at the S&P 500 to see, you know, whether companies had really been benefiting from this rollout of generative AI, and found that with the big seven tech companies, you could clearly see an increase in profit margins and in revenue per employee, you know, from rolling out generative AI products, but for those other 493 companies within the S&P 500, he did not see, you know, kind of like a notable difference or that generative AI had really benefited them.

So, there are growing questions there about the economic benefits of actually using this technology, not to mention, you know, kind of the many social harms that your other guest was talking about that need to be addressed and reined in. And so, you know, there are already — there’s already kind of skepticism and questions about all the money that has been put into these AI models, into these data centers in order to power them, whether they’re actually going to be as useful or whether the market for them is actually going to be as big as the companies are promising. And so, on top of those existing concerns, now these issues at Nvidia are kind of adding on top of that, which means that there is a potential kind of greater risk there, you know, of a collapse of some sort coming in the near future. But I certainly wouldn’t want to go as far as to call that this is the moment that it’s all going to happen.

AMY GOODMAN : And, Paris Marx, as you look down on us in the United States from Toronto, and across, of course, at Alaska, I wanted to get your comment on the midterms. You’ve written extensively about the anti-data center movement in the United States. It certainly fueled a lot of people, might have driven a lot of people to the polls. If you can also talk about the possibility of Democrats investigating tech CEOs? And, of course, right now we have the demand of Democrats and Republicans to investigate Jensen Huang.

PARIS MARX : Yeah, I would love to see it. Let’s bring on more investigations of the tech CEOs. Start with Jensen, and we can go from there.

But I do think that the midterms were not just a repudiation of the Republican Party and Donald Trump, but also of these tech CEOs that have been wielding so much power over, you know, our societies collectively for such a long period of time. And especially it feels like they really took this to a new level with what they’ve been doing the past few years — right? — not just the rollout of this generative AI technology that, as I was saying, is not as beneficial as they promised, but also had a lot of negative social and environmental consequences that came along with it, but then, paired with that, trying to push these massive hyperscale data centers into so many communities across the United States and around the world.

And so, what we saw is voters really push back against that. You know, so many races in the United States had a data center component to them. And if we look at key states like, say, Texas or Georgia or Ohio, we can see that data centers were really consequential in the battles that played out there, and that Democratic lawmakers recognized that, you know, going against data centers, promising moratoriums, was going to win the votes.

I think now the question is where this goes from here, right? Are we actually going to see those Democrats follow through on those promises? Is the pressure going to keep up? Or is the tech industry, which I’m sure it is, you know, about to pivot at this moment, hiring a ton of lobbyists to try to find a way to shape some of what Democrats are going to try to do, try to shape that kind of tech regulation, data center regulation agenda to make sure it’s not going to be as biting as it might otherwise appear? And so, I think that’s what I’ll be watching, you know, going forward, how this is going to play out.

AMY GOODMAN : Well, Paris Marks, I want to thank you for being with us, author of Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires , speaking to us from Toronto, and Ramesh Srinivasan, director of the AI Futures Lab at UCLA , today speaking to us from Germany. Thanks so much, both, for being with us.

Coming up, an Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital in Gaza has killed at least six people, including a surgeon. We’ll speak to Dr. Feroze Sidhwa, who volunteered at Nasser and worked with Dr. Abu Shaira. Stay with us.

scraped.h1: Israel Used a U.S.-Made Missile to Kill Six at Gaza’s Nasser Hospital
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

“That’s not complicity," said a U.S. doctor. "That's active participation in the murder of physicians and other healthcare workers.”

Throughout Israel’s war on Palestine, doctors Thaer Ahmad and Feroze Sidhwa spent months at Nasser Hospital in the southern Gaza city of Khan Younis, where they provided care as volunteers and survived a raid and an airstrike on the complex. On Wednesday evening, they were in an Uber in New York headed to a screening of their film about their time in Gaza when they realized Nasser was the target of another Israeli airstrike.

“They just hit Nasser again,” Ahmad said, turning from the front seat toward Sidhwa. “I think Rizk is dead.”

He was referring to Dr. Rizk Abu Shaaira, an experienced surgeon and fixture of the Palestinian medical community whom both had worked alongside at the hospital and who appears in their film “ American Doctor .” When Israel attacked Nasser Hospital on Wednesday — for at least the seventh time since the genocide escalated in 2023 — Abu Shaaira was one of the six people killed.

As the doctors arrived at a theater in Westchester for their screening, they received a flood of messages, photos, and video from their colleagues at Nasser, showing smoke-filled departments and wrecked operating rooms. The attack forced the closure of the hospital’s emergency, surgery, radiology and laboratory departments, hospital officials said.

Most Read OpenAI Fooled by Russian Pranksters Into Thinking They Were Speaking to Ukrainian Official Sam Biddle Hegseth Survives Impeachment Attempt Matt Sledge, Nick Turse Debunking Pete Hegseth’s Bullshit Impeachment Defense Nick Turse

Six people were killed in the airstrike, according to Gaza health officials, and 52 others were wounded, said Médecins Sans Frontières/Doctors Without Borders. Israel said it had used a precision-guided missile to target a Hamas commander.

One video showed a body bag holding Abu Shaaira, who had been working a night shift in the surgical ward, one of several floors severely damaged in the airstrike. Sidhwa, who worked directly with Abu Shaaira during his time volunteering at Nasser, described the 52-year-old father as a colleague who was “enthusiastic about everything” and “loved surgery.”

Another image showed unexploded ordnance launched at the hospital that medical workers had placed atop a stretcher, bearing the label “ GBU-39/B ” – a model of guided missiles manufactured by U.S. company Boeing. Israel purchases this precise missile model using funds from the U.S. State Department.

“That’s not complicity,” said Feroze when asked about the U.S.-made missiles used in the attack. “That’s active participation in the murder of physicians and other healthcare workers.”

Wednesday’s attack on Nasser Hospital, which serves a population of about 1.3 million people, is the fourth Israeli strike on a hospital since the so-called ceasefire agreement in October 2025. It is the seventh on the Nasser complex, including a double-tap strike in August 2025 when Israeli warplanes struck the hospital twice within minutes, killing first responders and journalists. Sidhwa had been volunteering at Nasser during an earlier airstrike on the complex in March 2025 violating an earlier ceasefire . That strike killed multiple people, including a 16-year-old boy.

“Under international humanitarian law, hospitals must be respected and protected.”

When Ahmad volunteered at Nasser in early 2024, a part of the hospital’s pediatric ward was still damaged from an Israeli tank shell that flew through a window, killing Donia Abu Mohsen, 12, while she received care from a previous airstrike that killed her family. During his stint, Israeli soldiers raided the complex and detained several doctors with whom he worked; they remain imprisoned without charge . Ahmad said his colleagues at Nasser told him that upon hearing the first booms on Wednesday, they knew immediately, due to familiarity, that they had been hit by an Israeli attack.

“Something that has troubled us so much is how normalized the targeting of these hospitals has become for Palestinians serving their communities,” Ahmad said. “They knew what was going on right away.”

Since returning from their time treating patients in Gaza, both Ahmad and Sidhwa have lobbied members of Congress to support the Block the Bombs Act , a House bill that seeks to prohibit the sale of certain arms to Israel that are tied to violations of U.S. and international human rights law. Among the weapons subject to the ban is Boeing’s 250-pound GBU-39. With a new Congress soon to be controlled by Democrats , many of whom ran campaigns touting support for the bill, both Ahmad and Sidhwa called on lawmakers to act.

“If our Congress upheld international humanitarian law, as well as U.S. domestic law, Dr. Rizik would still be alive,” Ahmad said, “and there wouldn’t be a surgeon who lost both of his legs in this bombing.”

The Israeli military claimed in a series of statements posted to social media that it had targeted a senior Hamas commander and other Hamas members who were “hiding” in the hospital and that the strike was meant to “eliminate the threat they posed.” The military did not specify the actual threat nor address the killing of Rizk, patients, and other civilians by “precision-guided missiles” it claims to have deployed to mitigate civilian harm. Israel alleged Hamas was operating out of the hospital’s second floor, but provided no evidence beyond a computer-rendered video . At least six Israelis have been killed in Gaza since the start of the so-called ceasefire, the Israeli military has said . Israel has killed more than 1,400 Palestinians in that time, according to Gaza health officials. The United Nations said that among those reported dead are at least 340 children.

In a statement to The Intercept, the Israeli military repeated its claim that Wednesday’s strike was targeting a Hamas commander, but it declined to confirm whether the alleged target of their strike was killed or comment on the civilians killed in the attack.

President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, tasked with rebuilding Gaza, called Wednesday’s attack a “tragic loss of life” but went on to repeat the Israeli allegation that Hamas carries out “continued exploitation of hospitals and other critical civilian infrastructure for military purposes.”

Sidhwa called the Board of Peace statement on Hamas’ alleged embedding in hospitals “bullshit,” adding that he has seen no evidence of Hamas embedding its fighters within any hospital in Gaza, a recurring observation by international doctors who volunteer in the strip.

“Show me one example,” Sidhwa said. “I would love to see a single photo, a single video, a single testimony from a Palestinian. Literally anything. It’s just completely absurd.”

Médecins Sans Frontières/Doctors Without Borders said in a statement that it was “appalled and outraged” by Israel’s attack, adding that its doctors had to operate on two of their colleagues and another patient injured in the strike. The group referred to its earlier decision in January to temporarily halt its teams’ operations at Nasser, citing reports of “armed men in different areas of the large compound of the hospital,” and said similar incidents have taken place more recently. Even so, the group said, this does not justify Israel’s attack.

“Under international humanitarian law, hospitals must be respected and protected,” the group said. “In no conceivable circumstances can attacks on functioning hospitals in Gaza be treated as normal or acceptable.”

The strike came days after the board issued a rare condemnation of the Israeli government for its blockade of humanitarian aid from entering Gaza in the aftermath of a storm that wiped out thousands of tents, killing four people. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu rebuffed the criticism and blamed Hamas for not disarming. Israel, meanwhile, continues to occupy about 70% of the Gaza strip, extending beyond the yellow line, a border drawn in the ceasefire agreement that is meant to mark where Israel can operate its military, and launches attacks on the strip on a weekly basis, all violations of the agreement.

“The same military who’s blocking the necessary supplies, as a middle finger to you, decides that they’re going to bomb a hospital,” Ahmad said. “I’m sure behind closed doors everybody is fuming and reeling, but unless people are ready to actually hold the Israelis accountable, actually use their leverage, nothing is going to change.”

IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

scraped.description: By failing to show discipline on the Pete Hegseth impeachment vote, Democrats seem poised to repeat the mistakes of the past.
scraped.author: Eoin Higgins
scraped.h1: The Hegseth Vote Was Jeffries’s First Big Test. He Failed.
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

By not showing discipline on the Pete Hegseth impeachment vote, Democrats seem poised to repeat the mistakes of the past.

Eoin Higgins is the author of “Owned: How Tech Billionaires on the Right Bought the Loudest Voice on the Left.”

Democrats rolled into Washington this week fresh off a generational sweep election on the promise of affordability for Americans and accountability for the Trump administration.

But on Tuesday night, Democrats in the House failed the first test of their incoming majority. An impeachment resolution introduced Monday by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., targeting Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, one of the main architects of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran, provided Republicans with a chance to score an early victory.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and the chamber’s Democratic leadership failed to take advantage, as 11 Democrats missed a critical vote that would have kept the resolution alive. The attempt failed by a slim margin, 211 to 204; Massie told The Intercept on Wednesday that even if the missing Democrats showed up he was sure House Speaker Mike Johnson could have rallied his members and made up the difference anyway. Until the new term begins, the chamber is still controlled by the GOP.

Nonetheless, the vote was a chance to send a message to the White House. One was sent: that of a disorganized, dysfunctional caucus. Other Democrats sought to take advantage of the misstep, noting that they were unwilling to miss the vote—Rep. Jasmine Crockett of Texas said she rerouted around traffic, and Rep. Pat Ryan of New York made it the day after back surgery.

“No matter what, I wasn’t going to allow traffic to keep me from that vote,” Crockett told MS NOW . “It was just that important to me.”

When asked about the absences, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who was present for the vote, offered only “someone may have had a health issue” as an explanation.

House members who missed the vote blamed a number of factors for their absence, including traffic. On Wednesday, all of those same House Democrats save Rep. Haley Stevens (Mich.) began to offer explanations. Rep. Jonathan Jackson (Ill.) told TMZ DC that his “traffic jam”-related absence was “inexcusable.” He wasn’t the only one to blame traffic — Reps. Marilyn Strickland (Wa.) and Laura Gillen (N.Y.) also cited D.C. gridlock as the reason they missed the vote; Rep. Julia Brownley (Calif.) said she was “rushing” to the vote but missed it. Reps. Nancy Pelosi (Calif.), Lou Corea (Calif.), and Frederica Wilson (Fla.) were all out of town.

Momentum lost can’t be regained. If Jeffries doesn’t understand that, he’s not the man for the job.

Rep. Melanie Stansbury (N.M.) offered a front-facing video apology to constituents . Rep. Steven Horsford (Nev.) took “full responsibility” in a floor speech. And Rep. Brittany Pettersen (Colo.) acknowledged that she was at a super PAC event and said there was “ no excuse ” for missing the vote.

Expressing regret is a good start. It shows these lawmakers are aware that their actions are antithetical to where their voters are at this moment and are adjusting accordingly. It’s not enough.

Leadership was asleep at the wheel. As whip, Rep. Katherine Clark should have kept the caucus in line. (It’s worth noting that Clark officially launched a bid for majority leader last week.) A number of reps who blamed traffic were previously at an event hosted by the group Elect Democratic Women, which receives some of its funding from AIPAC. The event overlapped with the impeachment resolution vote; Clark is a cofounder of the group .

“Republicans just blocked the House from impeaching Pete Hegseth,” Clark posted on X after the vote—failing to take responsibility for her party’s own lack of discipline.

Most Read OpenAI Fooled by Russian Pranksters Into Thinking They Were Speaking to Ukrainian Official Sam Biddle Hegseth Survives Impeachment Attempt Matt Sledge, Nick Turse Debunking Pete Hegseth’s Bullshit Impeachment Defense Nick Turse

Democrats missing a vote to hold one of the main figures in the war on Iran accountable so they could attend a fundraiser is so tailor-made for progressive complaints over the state of party leadership, it’s hard to believe.

Jeffries tried to spin the vote as only a temporary reprieve for Hegseth, but he didn’t telegraph much willingness about holding his caucus to account.

“I haven’t had a conversation with anyone on the floor team about what may or may not have happened in terms of the Hegseth resolution, but this is not the end of it. It’s just the beginning,” he told Politico . Most critically, he accepted no responsibility for the stunningly bad optics of having members of his caucus no-show, even if it likely wouldn’t have moved the needle.

This never should have happened in the first place. It was the result of a series of decisions by Jeffries and Clark about the vote that made clear it wasn’t important.

Momentum lost can’t be regained. If Jeffries doesn’t understand that, he’s not the man for the job purely on tactical grounds, and he should lay no claim to being a party standard-bearer to steer us through the next two years of Trump’s America.

Jeffries and his party seem doomed to repeat the past. In 2009, when President Barack Obama came into the White House on the back of a change election that gave Democrats huge majorities in Congress, including a filibuster-proof supermajority in the Senate, the party hobbled itself out of the gate by preemptively declining to pursue justice for the many crimes of eight straight years of George W. Bush.

“We need to look forward as opposed to looking backwards,” Obama told ABC News’s George Stephanopoulos in January 2009 , effectively ending any hope of accountability for the outgoing administration’s torture program and myriad other misdeeds . The ramifications of that decision arguably led to the war on Iran, a bipartisan immigration-deportation regime, and the end of Roe.

Democratic voters don’t want the party to rest on its laurels, they want blood.

Now, with a Republican president who is hated even more than W—something that would have seemed impossible to imagine almost 18 years ago—the Democratic Party’s establishment wing appears ready to repeat those failures. Taking on Trump and his corrupt, violent administration was one of the main messages that flipped House and Senate seats across the country but the party’s current leaders are allergic to action.

Entrenched Democrats also don’t seem interested in any sort of accountability. Stevens, the Michigan Democrat who broke ranks with her party and endorsed Republican Mike Rogers for Senate rather than back Abdul El-Sayed, was under pressure in the days before and after the election, with even establishment kingmaker Rep. Jim Clyburn signaling openness to expelling her from the caucus. By Tuesday morning, Pelosi — always in touch with party leadership — seemed to throw cold water on the idea: “I’m not supporting kicking her out…. Let’s focus on the very positive.”

This is such a complete misunderstanding of the mood of the electorate, one wonders if it’s intentionally obtuse. Democratic voters don’t want the party to rest on its laurels, they want blood. Anyone who’s been to a liberal rally since the start of the second Trump term can tell you that the signage is calling for, at minimum, accountability, not immediate compromise.

If Democrats rubber-stamp Jeffries as speaker and fail to adopt a more aggressive legislative and investigative approach, frustrations within the caucus and among the base will only continue to mount.

Jeffries is downplaying dissent, but this is more than just a battle between two wings of the Democratic Party. Democrats in New York have been looking to unseat the leader for years, frustrated with his closeness to AIPAC and financial institutions. He’s the kind of Democrat the base is fed up with, and that exasperation is widespread; polling shows just how deeply unpopular he is.

Now, multiple incoming and incumbent Democratic reps have told reporters that constituents and activist groups are demanding they not vote for Jeffries as speaker.

There is an alternative gaining steam: Rep. Ayanna Pressley, the Massachusetts progressive and member of the original “Squad” who were first elected in 2018 . Pressley has an uphill battle and has not yet announced that she’s interested in the job. The left is interested .

Voters gave Democrats a clear mandate on Election Day for what they want to see in Washington. Holding this administration accountable should be one of the top priorities. If the party fails to do all it can to advance that goal, it will once again earn its reputation for preferring failure to action. We should all push the next Congress to act as the exception to that rule—and they can start by picking a new speaker to meet the moment.

IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

scraped.h1: Hegseth Dodges Impeachment, for Now. And Tom Morello on Fighting for the World You Want
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

“When change is real, it comes from below. It comes from you and me,” says Rage Against the Machine’s Morello. “That’s what I've been singing about and screaming about in my songs for an entire career.”

Secretary of defense Pete Hegseth narrowly avoided impeachment on Tuesday, but his future is anything but secure as an enraged Democratic caucus prepares to take control of both the House and Senate in January.

“Tick, tock! Get ready, asshole, because we’re coming,” Congress member-elect Richard Ojeda, D-N.C., warned Hegseth at a press conference on Wednesday. Ojeda told The Intercept that he planned not only to impeach Hegseth but also to bring criminal charges against him.

On Tuesday, the House declined to move forward with impeachment proceedings introduced by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., which accused Hegseth of multiple “high crimes and misdemeanors.” Massie accused Hegseth of illegally waging war against both Iran and Yemen and of overseeing extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean.

This week on The Intercept Briefing, co-host Jessica Washington speaks with Nick Turse, Intercept senior national security reporter and editor of Tom Dispatch, about Hegseth’s legacy as “secretary of war.”

“Hegseth can spin it any way he likes,” says Turse. “He can use the troops as a shield, claiming that indictments of him are indictments of them. But in the end, he’s got a lot to answer for on his own, and none of it’s because he’s doing a good job.” Turse adds: “It’s because he’s committing high crimes.”

Co-host Jordan Uhl also sits down with musician and guitarist Tom Morello to talk about his new album “ Everyone Gets Everything They Want ” and his decades-long fight against forever wars and his resistance to fascism.

“My career has basically been rebellion as self-care,” says Morello. “But in this day and age, every act of art is an act of resistance. Every truth spoken is a light in the gathering darkness. And every song sung has the potential to be a trumpet of a bulwark against the rising tide of authoritarianism to help sound the bell for current and future generations to continue to fight for a more just and peaceful and decent planet.”

For more, listen to the full conversation of The Intercept Briefing on Apple Podcasts , Spotify , YouTube, or wherever you listen to podcasts.

Jessica Washington: Welcome to The Intercept Briefing, I’m Jessica Washington, politics reporter for The Intercept.

CNN : Republicans banded together and they killed this effort to impeach Pete Hegseth and largely stayed united. And the final vote here was 211 to 204.

NBC : Republicans uniting to block them from moving forward following Hegseth’s fiery rebuke of the outgoing congressman who introduced them, Thomas Massie.

ABC : The Republicans sticking together have essentially tabled or moved this resolution to the House Judiciary Committee, where it’s expected under Republican control these articles of impeachment will die. Pete Hegseth, for the moment, will not be impeached by the House of Representatives under this effort by Kentucky Republican Congressman Thomas Massie. Not a single Republican colleague joined him. All the Democrats stuck together, but there were not enough.

JW: On Tuesday night U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth narrowly avoided impeachment as House Republicans blocked a bill introduced by Republican Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky.

Rep. Thomas Massie : We’re not indicting him for being bad at his job. In fact, he was very effective at killing school children in Iran. He was very effective at extrajudicial killings. Joining me now to break it all down is Nick Turse, senior national security and foreign policy reporter for the Intercept and editor of Tom Dispatch.

Nick, welcome back to The Intercept Briefing.

Nick Turse: Thanks for having me on. It’s great to be here.

JW: Before we dive in, I also want to let listeners know we have a special interview with Tom Morello, the musician and original member of Rage Against the Machine.

Tom Morello: My job from day one is to try to make one guitar sound like a riot and to have my music be a contributing factor to social justice movements at home and abroad.

JW: So stay tuned for that conversation

All right, Nick, to start. What’s your reaction to Secretary Hegseth dismissing Massie’s impeachment articles, claiming :

Pete Hegseth: What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability. It’s a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.

JW: and that Massie is punishing him for a, “job well done”? What is your response?

NT: To start, it’s laughable. For half an hour at a press conference on the morning of the impeachment vote, Secretary Hegseth wove a web of lies designed to refute or obfuscate Massie’s eight impeachment charges. He repeatedly claimed that the effort to impeach him was just a stunt by one disgruntled congressman.

But, as we came to see, more than 200 members of Congress voted with Massie. So no, this wasn’t one man’s vendetta. When the new Congress is sworn in I think we’re going to find that the number in favor of impeaching him is only going to grow. And consequently, I think the list of high crimes and misdemeanors against him is also going to grow.

There’s almost a limitless list of high crimes that Hegseth can be charged with, and there are crimes within crimes. Waging unlawful wars in Iran and Yemen and Venezuela and specific war crimes within them that Hegseth may also be culpable for.

“Waging unlawful wars in Iran and Yemen and Venezuela and specific war crimes within them that Hegseth may also be culpable for. “

The boat strikes in and of themselves are criminal, and then there is, for example, the double tap strike on the first attack on a so-called drug boat, which is a crime in its own right.

Hegseth can spin it any way he likes. He can use the troops as a shield, claiming that indictments of him are indictments of them. But in the end, he’s got a lot to answer for on his own, and none of it’s because he’s doing a good job. It’s because he’s committing high crimes.

JW: High crimes and misdemeanors to a layperson, even to me, is not exactly indicative of what these actual crimes are. So what were the actual charges that Massie leveled against Hegseth?

NT: There were three charges for illegally waging war against Iran in violation of the War Powers Resolution. There was a charge related to Operation Rough Rider, which is the 2025 war in Yemen, which caused a tremendous number of civilian casualties. It’s become a forgotten conflict at this point.

The boat strike campaign which experts say are extrajudicial killings. There’s also a charge related to Hegseth’s efforts to undermine efforts at minimizing the possibility of civilian casualties. So these are some of the high crimes and misdemeanors of eight charges that Massie put forth.

JW: You just mentioned the drone strikes on so-called “narco terrorist” boats in the Caribbean and the Pacific, which to your estimate have killed more than 240 civilians . Those strikes, from my perspective, have gotten far less media attention than the Iran war, and obviously part of that is that much of what the U.S. is doing and who they’re targeting in open waters is shrouded in secrecy. But, how unprecedented are these strikes, and are these actions considered war crimes?

NT: The boat strikes, as you said, have largely been overtaken by the Iran war. But during his Pentagon press conference, Hegseth made a full-throated defense of his actions that actually drew attention to the unprecedented nature of the boat strike campaign.

Hegseth said that the charges that the American military targets civilians are a lie, and that the only people that target civilians are the terrorists that the U.S. hunts down. That itself is an outright lie. The U.S. boat strike campaign has only targeted civilians. Only. Not some, not inadvertently, not maybe. These are all civilians, period, full stop.

These summary executions of more than 240 people are a significant departure from the standard practice in the long-running U.S. war on drugs, in which law enforcement agencies detained suspected drug smugglers and then brought them to trial on criminal charges.

Experts in the laws of war, Pentagon officials that I’ve spoken with, and members of Congress from both parties say that Hegseth’s boat strikes are illegal, that they’re extrajudicial killings. The military is not permitted to deliberately target civilians, even suspected criminals.

Interdiction in these cases is possible. It’s preferable. It’s legal. We don’t execute suspected criminals in this country, or when the police do, it’s supposed to be a crime. If there was a declared war, these boat strikes might be war crimes, but no war exists, and there is no plausible legal justification for the strikes. And outside of armed conflict, the legal term for premeditated killing is murder. That’s what’s happening. That’s what Hegseth is responsible for, outright murder.

“Outside of armed conflict, the legal term for premeditated killing is murder. “

JW: Massie has not called Hegseth a war criminal or used the term murder like you have, but he did have this to say about Hegseth when discussing the articles of impeachment.

Thomas Massie: You won’t find a reference to war crimes. What I do say, though, is because he’s violated the international norms of war and violated our own conventions of war, he’s put our own soldiers and sailors at risk. When you go back for a second kill on people who are clinging to wreckage, you’re encouraging our adversaries to do the same. That’s why those laws — those international laws — are on the books.

JW: Nick, what did you make of Massie’s response just now?

NT: We were the first outlet to report that double tap strike in September 2025 . It caused a firestorm in Congress for the very reason that Massie’s talking about.

He’s right. Double tap strikes on helpless shipwrecked people, they’re in contravention of the U.S. military’s own law of war manual, and they undermine respect for the laws of war and encourage enemies to give Americans no quarter, which is a war crime, and a war crime that Secretary Hegseth has openly called for and advocated.

I’m going to out myself as a lapsed historian here, but to emphasize that this is a longstanding norm in armed conflict I’d mention that a great rallying cry of the Revolutionary War — the American Revolution —was “Remember Paoli.” It’s a town in Pennsylvania where British Redcoats reportedly offered no quarter and massacred American forces.

Back in 1777, this was considered a major breach of the laws of combat. This is what Secretary Hegseth has advocated [that] we are doing in these types of double tap strikes, executing those who are injured those who are surrendering. That’s outright barbarism.

JW: We were just discussing civilian casualties in the boat strike —intentional civilian casualties. I also wanted to talk about what happened in February when the United States conducted an airstrike on an elementary school in Minab, Iran. That strike killed at least 150 people, most of them children .

Now, U.S. officials said the strike was caused by a “targeting error” where the military mistook the elementary school for an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval base. What did this horrific incident tell us about how the military has been operating under Hegseth when it comes to civilian casualties?

“Hegseth made it inevitable that something like this mass killing of children would happen.”

NT: This horrendous attack — a massacre of children — was the predictable result of Pentagon policies that The Intercept has been spotlighting since the spring of 2025, just after Pete Hegseth came to office. Hegseth made it inevitable that something like this mass killing of children would happen.

We reported that immediately upon taking office, he began dismantling what is known within the military as CHMR, the shorthand for Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response, basically undermining everything he could that restrains the military in favor of his favorite dictum, which is lethality.

A group of Democratic lawmakers told Hegseth in July in a letter directly to him that this gutting of CHMR had left the Pentagon unable to comply with the law and also its congressionally mandated responsibilities to protect civilians. This is precisely what military officials told us would happen months earlier, and it all came to fruition.

These criticisms were echoed in another report that we revealed in July that found that Hegseth had gutted the premier center devoted to preventing civilian casualties in war zones, the Pentagon’s own Civilian Protection Center of Excellence. Its workforce was slashed from 40 personnel in January of 2025 to just nine at the end of last year.

Last week we published an exposé that quoted six current and former defense officials who served under Hegseth, and one of them was the former senior advisor to this Civilian Protection Center of Excellence. This former official Wes Bryant, served eight combat deployments calling in airstrikes on ISIS and other post-9/11 entities.

Then he served under Hegseth until he was pushed out for blowing the whistle on policies that would undermine protections for civilians. Bryant told me that Hegseth is conducting what he called, “state terrorism.” He said Hegseth is “100 percent a war criminal,” and that he needs to be prosecuted.

JW: To that last point, and I really don’t like to play devil’s advocate, but from my understanding, you choose to refer to Hegseth by his self-styled title, Secretary of War, and if I understand you correctly, your argument is that there’s no need to sugarcoat what the U.S. military is doing. The Army is not in the business of defense. It’s in the business of war.

Is there an argument to be made that Hegseth is simply stripping back the facade of the U.S. military as anything other than a war machine, or is he really changing how the U.S. operates in the theater of war and in the world?

NT: I take a lot of heat from from readers on social media and in my email inbox about this, and readers plead with me not to bend to Hegseth’s will and call him the Secretary of War, which is, as you said his preferred title.

But I’ve really jumped at the chance for the reasons that you mentioned. When Hegseth unilaterally renamed the department, it gave me license to do what I’d wanted to do for years to call it as it’s seen, as it’s experienced in the world. For years out in the field, I found it grating whether I was in Vietnam or Cambodia or Libya and Somalia, to talk to victims of U.S. military violence about the so-called Department of Defense. The DoD says this. The DoD spokesman says that. I don’t think these people cared about it, but I absolutely did.

The Defense Department made war on the world, killing, wounding, and displacing millions of people not in the defense of anything. It was an aggressive war-making organization, plain and simple.

I hate using milquetoast euphemisms, but journalistic conventions handcuffed me. I couldn’t go off on my own and start calling it “Department of War.” But when they freed me up to give readers a more accurate assessment of what they do now under Hegseth and what has been done since they changed the name going back to the 1940s, I took the opportunity that I was afforded.

Attacking an elementary school in Iran is an act of war and maybe a war crime. It’s not a defense of the United States or in defense of the United States. That’s the reason why I use that title.

JW: Do you think that Hegseth has changed what the department is? Did it becoming the Department of War change something fundamental about it, or is that what it’s always been? And then is Hegseth changing anything about the actual way it operates?

NT: Hegseth has pulled the veil off of what the department does. I think in a very real sense, he’s undermined protections on civilians that were only just starting to perhaps take hold. The Center of Excellence that I mentioned earlier only just came into existence and was needed because the Pentagon has a long history of attacking civilians whether purposefully or inadvertently as “collateral damage.”

So the Defense Department always did what the Department of War does now, but there were some measures that were perhaps just starting to take hold, and Hegseth has undermined them completely.

JW: I think to your point, yes, Hegseth has lifted the veil off of what this department does. It is a department that makes war on the world. But he’s also made that worse and deadlier for civilians around the world.

And, obviously on Tuesday, Republicans killed the possibility of Hegseth being impeached by the current Congress. But come January, there’s going to be a new Congress dominated by Democrats. Now, before the vote on Massie’s articles of impeachment, Massie had this really interesting argument actually for why Republicans should join him in impeaching Hegseth. Let’s hear that clip.

Thomas Massie: I’m being polite here. What is an impeachment? An impeachment is just firing somebody, really. You don’t go to prison. You don’t go to jail. You don’t pay a fine. OK, when the Democrats get in charge, they are going to be very vicious.

JW: He went on to say.

Thomas Massie: The Democrats are going to bring people in here who have served under him and with him, give them protection. They’ll be able to say what he’s actually done, the things that he has ignored, the things that he did that caused civilian casualties, the way he’s ignored the laws, and then there’ll be a full, robust trial over in the Senate.

JW: Nick, what do you make of Massie’s remarks, the failure of this vote now, and what do you think might be coming in the next Democratic-led House and Senate?

NT: So Hegseth was very fixated on Massie having a grudge against Trump, which he had transferred over to the war secretary. But Massie, as we heard there, throughout the process, was very vocal that he was doing Hegseth a huge favor. Massie suggested that his impeachment resolution was the legislative equivalent of a mercy killing, calling it a much gentler version of what the Democrats would do when they take control of Congress in January.

The Democrats can rain down relentless hellfire on Hegseth. Congressional committees have broad investigative powers including the authority to subpoena administration officials to testify under oath and compel them to turn over documents. They can paper the Pentagon with subpoenas.

Representative Yasmin Ansari , who filed articles of impeachment against Hegseth in the spring, told me that Hegseth surviving Massie’s impeachment only opened him up to a plethora of ways for Democrats to hold him accountable in the next session. Specifically compelling to testify under oath before Congress and before the American people.

She emphasized that he’s “not only one of the most incompetent members of the administration,” her words, “but also one of the most unpopular” on a bipartisan basis. What she believes is going to happen is that Hegseth is going to be hauled up before Congress, and he’s just going to be battered incessantly.

This is probably going to grow so great that he’s going to become toxic to the administration. Representative-elect Richard Ojeda of North Carolina told our colleague Matt Sledge just after the impeachment vote the new Democrats are spoiling for a fight with Hegseth. He said “I want Pete Hegseth not just impeached, I want him prosecuted.”

I personally think that Hegseth might relish this rhetorical combat on Capitol Hill as a prelude to a potential presidential run. But, I think at some point it’s going to become untenable for him to actually preside over the Pentagon.

JW: I was at a press conference where Richard Ojeda was as well, and he had even more colorful language for Hegseth.

Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda: Make no mistake about it, the 120th Congress, he will not be so lucky. Tick, tock! Get ready, asshole, because we’re coming.

JW: They certainly seem to have plans to really target Hegseth and Massie might have been right that he was trying to offer a mercy kill. But we’re going to have to leave it there.

Nick Turse, thank you so much for joining me on the Intercept Briefing.

Jordan Uhl: “Every act of art is an act of resistance,” says the legendary musician Tom Morello. Fighting for social justice and against fascism has been a staple of his art and career, from his work with The Nightwatchman to Rage Against the Machine to Audioslave.

And he’s at it again with his new album “ Everyone Gets Everything They Want .” The track “Adjourn it” denounces the rising tide of racism and anti immigrant bigotry.

[ Adjourn It plays ]

The song features Serj Tankian of System of a Down and Morello’s 15 year old son, Roman.

Tom Morello joins me now.

Tom, thanks so much for joining us on The Intercept Briefing.

JU: Tom Morello, it is an honor. Thank you so much for joining us on the Intercept Briefing

Tom Morello: It’s my pleasure. Thank you very much for having me

JU: Tom, you have a long history of activism, infusing that into your music and your art, and creating space for activism-oriented concerts and events like Power to the People. Your new album follows that tradition. It’s called “Everyone Gets Everything They Want.” Can you tell us about this new album, the themes that you explore on it, and if there are plans for future Power to the People festivals as we head into the presidential cycle?

“Every act of art is an act of resistance.”

TM: My career has basically been rebellion as self-care — rock and roll, especially in these troubled times. But in this day and age, every act of art is an act of resistance. Every truth spoken is a light in the gathering darkness. And every song sung has the potential to be a trumpet of a bulwark against the rising tide of authoritarianism to help sound the bell for current and future generations to continue to fight for a more just and peaceful and decent planet.

“Everyone Gets Everything They Want” is the 22nd album of my career. All 22 of those records have been built around a single purpose: that history is not something that happens, history is something that we make. Standing up in your place, in your time, in your place of work, whether it’s in a recording studio, whether it’s at the carpenter’s union, whether you’re a student, whether you’re an unhoused person, whether you’re a politician, is doing what you can with what you’ve got to try to be an advocate and an agent for a more just and peaceful planet.

JU: We are coming off of a massive rout in this election. Voters made it clear how they feel about this growing fascist movement in this country. Unsurprisingly, we are seeing the pundit class rush to quell people’s enthusiasm, insisting the left does not have a mandate and that the moderate policy is the answer. What is your response to that?

TM: I was the scheduling secretary for United States Senator Alan Cranston for two years, so I got to see how the sausage is made from inside the sausage factory, and it is worse than you could possibly imagine. While it is encouraging that here and in Hungary and in Serbia and in Brazil that the people have resoundingly said no to fascism but the idea is not to have a kinder, gentler oligarchy. The idea is the liberation of humanity. The idea is securing a planet — a healthy planet — for our children and grandchildren, generations to come.

“People have resoundingly said no to fascism but the idea is not to have a kinder, gentler oligarchy. The idea is the liberation of humanity. “

One thing that is encouraging in those other countries and in our most recent election is in addition to the terrible corporate Democrats who are also represented, there’s a new breed of politician. We have a socialist mayor in New York City. We have a socialist mayor in Los Angeles, the two biggest cities in our country.

The young people are once again the hope of the future. Rather than having me, a musician of a certain age saying, “This is what you should do,” I think that the main thing I can do is listen to what they have to say and encourage them in their efforts to build that more just and more peaceful planet.

JU: Do you have any thoughts on who should lead in the House and the Senate? We’re seeing calls for Schumer to step aside. Maybe if it’s new blood, maybe it’s Chris Van Hollen. Do you have any thoughts on who should lead Democrats in the Senate?

Obviously the Chuck Schumers and Hakeem Jeffries are just awful continuations of the awful policies that got us in this to begin with. You can trace it back to Clinton with the crime bill and with NAFTA, and the abandonment of the working class that got us in this mess to begin with.

“Aim for the world you really want without compromise.”

But again, I also think that it’s important to aim for the world you really want without compromise, without apology, and to not just go, “OK, well this is going to be better than the slippery slope to obvious this 50 percent clown show, 50 percent fascism that is the Trump administration.”

But what is the world you really want, and how do you build that? Not just what is a glazed-over version of what we’ve had, a reheated version of the terrible policies of both parties that got us in this situation of nearly environmental collapse and right-wing white Christian nationalism.

One thing I will say is that, there has been some reckoning that needs to be pushed even further of dealing with America’s original sin. The paradox of this country, which is demanding liberty while embracing white supremacy. That is the story of our country from day one in that some people’s lives just matter a lot more than other people’s lives, both at home and abroad. And a full rejection of that we’ve seen in some other countries, we’ve seen in part of the electorate here, and in some of the elected officials.

In my view, Election Day is harm reduction. I always vote. I vote my conscience, unless it is a contested election, and then I vote for the absolute most harm reduction.

“What’s the world you really want, and how do we fight for it?” That doesn’t just happen on Election Day. That happens the day after Election Day, and the day after that. ”

To go beyond that and be like, “What’s the world you really want, and how do we fight for it?” That doesn’t just happen on Election Day. That happens the day after Election Day, and the day after that.

Since I was 17 years old, I have been in the trenches of grassroots organizing via rock and roll to try to do what I can in my small way with a Marshall half stack to liberate humanity. And that work has only just begun.

JU: I want to touch on that. I live in Los Angeles, and we just watched California voters reject a billionaire tax. This was a fight you were directly involved in. TM: It’s easy to make sense of it. It’s money in politics. I’m a fan of sports. Every World Series game, every football game had 72 ads paid for by tech billionaires and featuring the heroes of the California Democratic Party saying, “Please don’t tax the billionaires, whatever you do.”

This is a firsthand account. I was the scheduling secretary for a U.S. senator. Let me tell you what I scheduled. I scheduled phone calls for him to ask rich dudes for money. That’s what the schedule was.

We would go to a hotel, and there were like 10 payphones in a row. I would commandeer them, and I would call up the first guy and say, “Can you hold for the senator?” He’d get on the phone and ask that rich dude for money. Nine more calls in a row, Republicans, Democrats, corporate people, whatever.

Then they would start again, and we would spend the whole day doing that. Those guys are bought, sold, and totally beholden to the oligarchs that have their hands on the lever of power. JU: Over $300 million by a handful of billionaires. It’s absolutely staggering.

I want to look ahead. You and through your music, you’ve always been ahead of the curve waiting for folks to catch up. So what are the emerging fights that you see now that people need to get plugged in on? Is there something that stands out?

TM: I would say one thing is to not sink into a complacency when there’s a euphoria in the aftermath of a in my view somewhat surprising rejection of to the level that we’ve seen of Trumpism. But that’s just the beginning. We’ve already seen, as you mentioned, the right-wing of the Democratic Party asserting their hold on, like, “Hold on now. Hold on now.”

What people need to realize is the world isn’t going to change itself. That is up to you. That is up to me. While that may sound like a daunting sentence and a daunting task, the good news is whenever the world has changed in progressive, radical, or even revolutionary ways, it has been changed by people who didn’t have any more money, courage, power, intelligence, influence than anyone listening or watching this right now. The world is changed by average, everyday, ordinary people standing up in their time, not just at the ballot box, but in all that intervening time. Change comes from below. When change is real, it comes from below. It comes from you and me. That’s what I’ve been singing about and screaming about in my songs for an entire career. But I think that just that realization that we are agents of history, not just on election day, but beyond.

JU: The song “Unconquered” on your album features Kneecap , the Irish rap trio who have been very vocal at their shows for the liberation of Palestine, and they faced backlash, losing gigs, revocation of visas. What do you make of this backlash from the industry, from venue owners, from the billionaire class?

TM: First of all, welcome to my life. There’s nothing new about that. From Rage Against the Machine to my own political organizing, the pushback is real when you threaten centers of power and established orthodoxy in that regard.

The one thing that artists should remember is that you don’t put down your First Amendment rights when you pick up a microphone or a guitar. A lot of people are like, “Just shut up and dribble in sports,” or, “Just shut up and play music.” I would encourage all artists, don’t leave behind who you are and what you do.

But not just artists. As journalists, whatever your job is, don’t leave behind your convictions in your vocation. Those artists, Kneecap and Macklemore, have done it, and they’ve paid a price. Well, thank God. If you are making music that everyone can like hold hands to and skip around, you’re probably making pretty shitty music.

But those artists have stood up at a critical juncture. They are the Rage Against the Machine of now, fearlessly standing up for an oppressed people in a time where the world pushes back, and they don’t give a fuck. TM: Thank you for your service, and The Intercept’s service in doing what you do. I think that you guys are upholding a long tradition of confrontational journalism, which the world needs now more than ever.

“My job from day one is to try to make one guitar sound like a riot and to have my music be a contributing factor to social justice movements at home and abroad.”

And also I’ve just started. I’M BEN MUESSIG, The Intercept’s editor-in-chief. It’s been a devastating year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

Israel’s War on Gaza

Jonah Valdez

“That’s not complicity," said a U.S. doctor. "That's active participation in the murder of physicians and other healthcare workers.”

Voices

Eoin Higgins

By not showing discipline on the Pete Hegseth impeachment vote, Democrats seem poised to repeat the mistakes of the past.

Voices

Seth Stern

When Democrats take power, they should take aim at the president’s censors, like Hegseth and FCC Chair Brendan Carr.
