scraped.title: Democrats Did Their Best Bernie Impression in the Midterms
scraped.description: Put their 2026 midterms side by side with previous campaigns, and it’s clear: Democrats won in red states by sounding less like Democrats and more like Bernie Sanders.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

Put their 2026 midterms side by side with previous campaigns, and it’s clear: Democrats won in red states by sounding less like Democrats and more like Bernie Sanders.

Democratic moderates have tacitly accepted what the Left has said for years: the Bernie Sanders pitch — of a corrupt, rigged system pitting billionaires against working Americans — has broad appeal that cuts across geographic, racial, and even partisan lines. (Tom Baker / Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

T he 2026 midterms saw historic gains for socialists and progressives. So, perhaps unsurprisingly, the Democratic Party’s corporate wing is hurriedly spinning the result as a victory for centrists and “moderates.”

Largely lost in this is the way that the Left has transformed what it actually means to run as a Democratic moderate or a centrist. Because looking at this year’s campaigns, there is no doubt that even the most uninspiring “moderate” candidates were taking several pages — whole chapters, really — from the books of Bernie Sanders, Zohran Mamdani, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.

It’s worth recalling that before 2025, standard Democratic campaign rhetoric was all about “defending democracy,” railing against extremism and authoritarianism, and advocating for abortion rights — all good things on their merits, but (with the exception of abortion rights) largely abstract ones that are not as animating or as high a priority for the majority of voters as their basic pocketbook concerns.

Just look at former President Joe Biden’s big kick-off speech for his reelection campaign, which was almost completely devoid of an economic message but heavy on talk of “MAGA extremists” and the “soul of America.” In fact, the absence of an economic message was a constant left-wing criticism of the party through the Biden era, including from this very magazine .

This has now completely shifted. While Democratic candidates in 2024 ran by far most of their TV ads on abortion , with immigration coming a distant second, this year, the overwhelming focus of their ad spending was “affordability,” dropping $401 million on the topic — a full quarter of their $1.5 billion total spend.

And where did the “affordability” frame come from? Well, both Democratic and Republican members of Congress happened to start spamming that word in their emails to constituents right after socialist Zohran Mamdani won the New York City Democratic primary with a campaign that put affordability at its very center.

But it’s more than just coming up with a pithy new word describing voters’ struggles with the economy. A number of the moderate candidates who won in red states sounded oddly like Bernie Sanders, railing against billionaires and the ultrarich, the corrupting influence of money in politics, and swearing off corporate money.

The clearest example of this was Texas Senator-elect James Talarico, who said that the fundamental divide in US politics was “top versus bottom,” called billionaires “the only minority destroying America,” charged that “for fifty years, billionaire megadonors have been buying politicians” like his opponent who then “rig the rules of the economy,” and who said that “we already have class warfare in this country” in the form of “the billionaires waging war against the rest of us” — a line almost directly borrowed from Bernie Sanders. He was rewarded for it by winning by one of the biggest margins of the night and doing it in one of the reddest states in the country.

The corporate center has tried to square this by simply retconning Talarico as one of them , a moderate , as Matthew Yglesias dubbed him. They point to the fact that he moved away from some of his support for trans rights, embraced an “all-of-the-above” energy policy, and eschewed Medicare for All in favor a public option (though the idea that’s a “centrist” or “moderate” policy would be surprising to anyone with a memory longer than five or six years).

But even if Talarico wasn’t viewed by nearly half of all Texas voters as “very liberal” on the eve of the election (and as “somewhat liberal” by a further 27 percent), this is a pretty hard sell.

To see why, look at Colin Allred. Just two years ago, Allred, a former NFL player, civil rights lawyer, and congressman, launched his own Texas Senate run with a campaign widely characterized as a “ centrist ” one against Republican Ted Cruz.

What did that campaign involve? Allred cast the GOP as having become too extreme and told conservatives who believed in the rule of law and the Constitution that they should vote for him. He proudly touted his US Chamber of Commerce endorsement . He “was unable to successfully develop” an economic message against Cruz and made abortion and reproductive rights “ central to ” and the “ banner of ” his campaign instead. During their debate, he hammered Cruz for supporting an abortion ban and being soft on the January 6 rioters, calling him a “threat to democracy” and only offhandedly mentioning he cut taxes on the rich. Again, these are all important issues but were unconnected to voters’ economic struggles.

The result: Cruz won by 8 points, nearly quadrupling his winning margin from six years earlier.

T his was not something unique to Texas and Talarico’s “moderate” campaign there. It was the case in every red state that Democrats just won a Senate seat in.

Take a look at Annie Andrews’s campaign that made her the first Democrat elected to a South Carolina Senate seat in twenty-eight years . Andrews hammered her initial opponent, the late Lindsey Graham, for “sell[ing] out to big money” and for being “willing to take food off our kids’ plates” and gut Medicaid “just so he can deliver tax cuts to billionaires,” and called on him to refund donations from Jeffrey Epstein–linked billionaires. She swore off “corporate PAC money” and pledged to “rein in the influence of corporations and billionaires in our elections.”

When Graham died and was replaced by his sister, Darline, Andrews hammered her for the same thing. Andrews called her “handpicked and bought by big corporations,” attacked her for doing the bidding of a data center industry spending millions of dollars of dark money to get her elected, and pointed to the $27 million that “outside Super PACs” had spent to support her. She won by nearly 5 points.

This was a very different campaign than the one former corporate lobbyist Jaime Harrison ran against Lindsey Graham six years ago. Since Harrison was relying on corporate bundlers and billionaire donors to raise obscene amounts of money to outspend Graham, he couldn’t and didn’t launch any of these attacks — in fact, Graham turned it around on him, complaining that outside dark money was flooding in to support the Democrat. Harrison’s attacks on Graham were focused on the idea that voters couldn’t trust him, because he had gone back on his word in supporting Donald Trump’s 2020 Supreme Court pick. He lost by 10 points.

Or look at Josh Turek, who won Iowa by four points against GOP candidate Ashley Hinson. Turek constantly talked about how Washington was full of millionaires “looking out for billionaires” and that he was “not one of them,” nor did he take corporate PAC money or was “owned by billionaires” (even as he quietly did take money from some billionaires). Iowa’s Republican senators and, he implied , his opponent , were “just looking out for billionaires and large corporations.”

During a debate , in attack ads , and in a Des Moines Register op-ed , Turek took aim at Hinson’s personal wealth, complaining that she had “gotten richer in her time in Washington” while slashing social spending on working-class Iowans, slamming her for her stock ownership, and saying that “we have a corruption crisis that’s leading to an affordability crisis because we’re sending people like Ashley Hinson up to DC” to line their pockets.

Not even Sanders went this hard against his wealthy opponents.

Then look at Michael Franken’s campaign for an Iowa Senate seat four years earlier. Though Franken prominently swore off corporate PAC donations, there was no talk of billionaires or wealth inequality. Franken appealed to “that middle segment who want logical, pragmatic, smart, dedicated, national servants to work for them,” and ran on a message that “we need to put country over party” and “people over politics.” He jabbed at his opponent’s age and long tenure in office, framed himself as defending democracy and minority rights, particularly those of women, whose right to an abortion he frequently brought up. And he ended up losing by 12 points.

Over in Mississippi, where prosecutor Scott Colom eked out a shock win to become the state’s first black senator, he did it by similarly assailing his Republican opponent Cindy Hyde-Smith’s donations from “millionaires and billionaires” out of state and accusing her of throwing tens of thousands of Mississippians off their health insurance “to look out for people in California and New York,” specifically “billionaires and millionaires” there, by giving them a “ billionaire tax break .” He ran on raising taxes on the rich and getting rid of corporate subsidies for billionaires, and hit his opponent for staying silent on data centers being pushed by “AI billionaires” while being backed by a pro-AI super PAC.

This did not happen two years earlier, when Ty Pinkins (who ran, to some controversy, as a third-party candidate this year) ran for the other Mississippi US Senate seat, once again eschewing any kind of bold economic message in favor of warning that “our very democracy is being threatened” by people attacking its “institutional safeguards,” in his announcement . Pinkins said his platform revolved around the vague motto of, “You talk, I listen, we do,” which he explained (in even vaguer terms) meant, “I can listen and hear what’s important to their communities,” and then “do what’s necessary to move these communities and our state forward.” That campaign lost by nearly 30 points.

A particularly instructive example is Sherrod Brown in Ohio, who lost reelection to his Senate seat by nearly 4 points in 2024, then won the other Senate seat this year by just under 5 points. Despite a long-standing and deserved reputation as a populist, Brown said very little about millionaires and billionaires two years ago, other than that they should “ pay their fair share ” into Social Security — even as they were spending massive amounts to defeat him, which they did.

In 2026, more or less the official motto of Brown’s campaign was “Workers Before Billionaires,” a phrase he put in press releases , merchandise , tweets , Substack posts , reels , TikToks , and video after video . Compare his demure response two years earlier to a question about Republicans backing personally wealthy candidates — “That’s who they are . . . I guess I’m not surprised by that” — to what he said about his 2026 GOP opponent, Jon Husted: “The disdain, the contempt they have for work and for workers tells you everything.”

This time Brown, who called for a tax hike on billionaires, went in on Husted’s connection to the ultrarich and what the campaign characterized as his “ corruption ”:

“Clevelanders have seen time and time again how Husted bows down to billionaires and corporations while leaving hardworking Ohioans behind.” ( August 29 )

“Jon Husted’s for sale and the billionaires and corporations pouring millions into this race know it.” ( September 21 )

“Ohioans have watched Jon Husted put billionaires and corporations before working families time and time again.” ( October 3 )

“From Elon Musk to Donald Trump, billionaires are spending hundreds of millions of dollars against me because they know they can buy Jon Husted’s votes.” ( October 29 )

For good measure, Brown ran at least three separate TV ads hitting Husted for taking more money from Les Wexner, the disgraced Epstein-connected Ohio billionaire, than anyone else in Congress.

It is hard to make the case that nothing has changed when the same candidate ran a completely different campaign just two years later.

Finally, take a look at North Carolina, home to the second largest US financial center after New York, and where former governor Roy Cooper beat the Republican candidate by nearly 20 points. “Time to elect a senator for everyday people, not billionaires,” Cooper said after winning the primary, a theme he came back to over and over again, whether saying that “we don’t have the billionaires they do,” that his opponent was “fighting for the billionaire friends he made while working as a Big Oil and utility company lobbyist in DC,” or hitting Trump’s bill “that gave tax cuts to billionaires” and had “driven healthcare premiums up.”

Again, Cooper has a well-established reputation as a moderate, but this kind of rhetoric simply bore no resemblance to the Senate campaign run by another moderate, former state Supreme Court Chief Justice Cheri Beasley in 2022. Beasley centered her campaign on abortion rights and health care generally, and talked about diversity and reforming the criminal justice system to fix the “disparities” that exist within it while touting her support from law enforcement. There was no talk of billionaires or dark money, since Beasley herself was backed by twenty-three billionaires and won her primary by being boosted by various out-of-state PACs. She lost by 3 points.

This is borne out by research by Eric Blanc. Going through candidate websites in 2024 and 2026, he found that while billionaires were referenced in only 19 percent of candidates’ websites two years ago, this year they featured in 78 percent. Meanwhile, research by the Center for Working Class Politics found that less than 20 percent of the candidates in 2024 attacked corporations, billionaires, or Wall Street for their role in the affordability crisis.

T he fact that these candidates used populist rhetoric doesn’t necessarily mean they are populists, or even progressive. A number of these candidates have taken money from the billionaires they decry, including Talarico, and did not necessarily run on very ambitious policies. Meanwhile, Cooper is a multimillionaire himself, and like several others, did not run on taxing the rich, for all the class-war-style rhetoric that was thrown around.

But it does mean that Democratic moderates have tacitly accepted what voices on the Left have been saying for years, which is that the Bernie Sanders pitch — of a corrupt, rigged system pitting billionaires and corporations against working Americans — has broad appeal that cuts across geographic, racial, and, yes, sometimes even partisan lines.

Whatever they may tell you now, centrists did not always feel this way. Third Way cofounder Matt Bennett, for instance, was one of the corporate centrists insisting that there was nothing remarkable about any of this, because Sanders was not “the first Democratic (adjacent) candidate to use populist rhetoric in the modern era.” This will be news to Third Way circa 2016, whose president celebrated Sanders’s loss in the Democratic primary that year, because if “liberal populism doesn’t win Democratic primaries,” then it can’t “be the path back for a party” in a general election, and showed that “voters are angry, but they don’t want to focus mainly on billionaires.”

Likewise, Matthew Yglesias today may mock clueless young people thinking “Bernie Sanders invented the idea of campaigning on economic fairness themes.” But back in 2016, he listed Sanders’s plans to “soak the rich to a much greater extent” as one of the supposedly risky, radical ideas that made “the vast majority of the party’s elected officials and interest group leaders” worry about him. Stances like that were “not popular,” Yglesias wrote, and made him unelectable, compared to Hillary Clinton’s “relatively modest, overwhelmingly popular tweaks to the tax code.”

Something interesting is happening here. For years, frustrated socialists and progressives have been arguing that opposition to billionaires, soaking the ultrarich, and getting money out of politics are the centrist positions: that Americans across all walks of life — white or black, college-educated or not, liberal or conservative, in blue, red, or purple states — were pretty united on this, regardless of their exact views on things like immigration, guns, or trans kids in sports. Whatever the pundits are saying, centrist candidates seem to have finally acknowledged that’s the case.

Branko Marcetic is a Jacobin staff writer and the author of Yesterday’s Man: The Case Against Joe Biden .

scraped.title: Possible Love Is a Cinematic Masterpiece About Class
scraped.description: Lee Chang-dong doesn’t have the same profile as fellow South Korean directors like Bong Joon-ho and Park Chan-wook, but his latest film should change that. Possible Love is a powerful study of class in the wake of a shattering real-life strike defeat.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

Lee Chang-dong doesn’t have the same profile as fellow South Korean directors like Bong Joon-ho and Park Chan-wook, but his latest film should change that. Possible Love is a powerful study of class in the wake of a shattering real-life strike defeat.

Lee Chang-dong has produced a series of outstanding films about contemporary South Korean society. His latest work, Possible Love , tackles the aftermath of a real-life strike whose defeat paved the way for a brutal assault on South Korea’s working class. (Joo Jae-bum / Netflix)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

P ossible Love is yet another masterpiece that South Korean director Lee Chang-dong has brought to us, after an eight-year hiatus since his last film Burning (2018). Unlike his younger Korean peers, such as Bong Joon-ho ( Parasite ) or Park Chan-wook ( Old Boy and No Other Choice ), Lee, now seventy-two, has often found himself confined to the independent film scene outside South Korea, where he has usually enjoyed modest commercial success.

Deeply rooted in humanity and class relations, Lee’s films deserve a wider audience beyond the ranks of art house aficionados (including Barack Obama, who named Burning among his favorite movies of 2018). Lee’s 1999 film Peppermint Candy weaves the life of a young man into the breakneck pace of South Korean capitalism, showing how innocence loses ground to violence, avarice, and lust. Burning explores the ways in which capitalism preys on and consumes poor young men and women.

Netflix’s funding and global distribution of Possible Love will likely expand Lee’s global reach. However, it has also revealed the maestro’s inability to raise further funds in South Korea, whose media giants — mostly outgrowths of chaebol conglomerates such as CJ ENM or Lotte Entertainment — no longer appear to be willing to bankroll Lee’s bold and unapologetic portrayal of South Korea’s economic system.

F or Netflix, Possible Love is a prestige project: an opportunity to bring home an Oscar with a highly accomplished director while reversing a viewership slump and enhancing its brand. Possible Love premiered theatrically in South Korea in September, meeting the Academy’s country-of-origin eligibility deadline . The streaming platform has also made Lee’s previous films available for its subscribers.

Possible Love is set against the aftermath of the 2009 brutal crackdown on the seventy-seven-day strike against massive job cuts at SsangYong Motor (fictionalized in the film as SP Heavy Industries). After crushing the strike, management and the government pushed through one of the country’s first massive layoffs by slashing 50 percent of SsangYong’s blue-collar workforce. In the film as in real life, workers refer to their laid-off colleagues as “the dead” and those who managed to escape the cull as “the living.”

Through the crackdown, corporations and the conservative government set a precedent for mass layoffs. After the defeat at SsangYong, corporations could cut jobs by invoking broadly defined criteria of managerial exigency. The repercussions of the strike and its vivid suppression resonated deeply throughout South Korea.

The strike even became part of the backstory of Squid Game , Netflix’s gamified portrayal of capitalist suffering. In his review of the series, Lee Chang-kun, a leader of SsangYong’s labor union, summed up the experience of an agonizing and prolonged factory occupation:

Out of the blue, we were left with no option but to squat at the factory. We first attempted to turn to each other to survive together. However, we were thrown into a life-or-death situation, often with no other option but to betray and dupe each other. At least once, as in Squid Game , we each had to hurt our closest friends.

Many workers or their family members have since died by suicide or from stress-related conditions such as cardiac arrest. There was probably no better place for Lee to begin Possible Love than the funeral of one such worker.

I n the film, Ho-seok (played by Peppermint Candy star Sul Kyung-gu) was one of the remaining seven hundred striking workers who faced the violent police raid. He had been a welder, proud enough to name his son “Iron.”

Having been injured in the crackdown and subsequently jailed, he has been drained of his blue-collar mettle and sense of purpose, leaving him with simmering feelings of anger and betrayal. His wife, Mi-ok ( Secret Sunshine star Jeon Do-yeon) is a good-hearted, innately resilient former seamstress who does her best to hold the family together against all odds in the wake of her husband’s layoff.

At this point, documentary director Ye-ji — played by Cho Yeo-jeong, almost typecast as the seemingly innocuous upper-class woman after her similar role in Parasite — encroaches on Ho-seok and Mi-ok’s fragile universe with her camera lens. A daughter of a small-business owner turned parvenu, Ye-ji is married to Sang-woo ( Hope star Zo In-sung), a private equity investor born into generations of wealth and power.

Ye-ji attempts to love Mi-ok and Ho-seok because she believes herself to be a good person. While she is probably sympathetic to Ho-seok and his family, she is strikingly lacking in empathy for their situation. Her superficial innocuousness is pernicious.

Ye-ji’s interest in laid-off workers from SP Industries began during a vacation at a resort in the middle of the Qatar desert, maintained by workers who, her husband tells her, labored hard behind the scenes. Ho-seok is a subject Ye-ji wants to capture through her camera before he disappears into obscurity.

Ye-ji’s husband, Sang-woo, is kind and well-mannered, probably because he has little reason to be otherwise. In his line of business, everything seems impersonal, reduced to numbers and valuations. Although he possesses greater worldly insight than his wife, he need not concern himself with the consequences of his spreadsheets for people like Ho-seok, who remain invisible to him.

There seems to be nothing Ho-seok can do better than Sang-woo. The latter is the better husband, always supportive of his wife, both morally and financially. He is also the better athlete, having tutored the welder’s son in tae kwon do, the sport in which Ho-seok was once a varsity athlete.

To add insult to injury, he is even a superior musician who can play the oboe while Mi-ok sings at karaoke. Ho-seok keeps his guard up around Sang-woo, but he seems to be free of personal jealousy toward him, as though he instinctively feels that the rift between them is one of class rather than individual attributes.

Rather, what has traumatized Ho-seok is the experience of his coworkers, who are now divided into the living and the dead. He has feelings of envy toward the living; they can still throw a fancy birthday party for their children. Emotionally overwhelmed, Ho-seok cannot open up during a group therapy session, where one of the dead laments that they were defeated despite being on the right side.

I t is painful to watch Ho-seok, especially if you understand how strikes and campaigns are defeated — how they implode before they can fizzle out or are violently crushed. We do not walk away from our collective struggles because we abruptly come to fear or love our adversaries. We walk away because we have grown disillusioned or lost trust in the people beside us.

It is before Ye-ji’s camera that Ho-seok finally breaks down in tears and confesses his deepest fear that his wife and former coworkers will discover the anger and sense of betrayal he has kept deep inside. Words like “solidarity” or “resistance” have been reduced to hollow shells of what they used to mean to him.

It is also when Ye-ji finally lowers her intrusive camera, perhaps stunned by the scene, or perhaps realizing she can never genuinely understand (or love) her subjects. Her very innocuity is a form of violence against Ho-seok and Mi-ok. “That’s enough!” both Ye-ji and Mi-ok yell after Ho-seok’s moment opening-up. The two couples part ways.

Director Lee appears to have built the narrative around one of the Ten Commandments, “You shall not covet,” which appears at the beginning of the film. Ye-ji has even coveted Ho-seok’s agonies. For Ho-seok, that suffering still constitutes part of his own dignity. After opening up, he appears to regain part of his strength.

When Mi-ok asks for the first time in the film about their future, “What shall we do?” he answers, “We will keep living on.” “It will rain tomorrow,” his wife says. “It hasn’t today,” her husband replies, as if that were how he has put himself together day by day since the strike was crushed.

Possible Love is difficult to watch because it relentlessly makes you uncomfortable, if not downright pained. Ho-seok is not an idealized figure: he is a wavering worker, trapped in divisions within his own class, rather than a bold and brave militant taking on his boss and the system. However, this makes his character all the more real: like Ho-seok and the film itself, we are all multilayered beings defying any simple definition.

Kap Seol is a Korean writer and researcher based in New York. His writings have appeared in Labor Notes , In These Times , Business Insider , and other publications. In 2019, his exposé for Korean independent daily Kyunghyang revealed an imposter who falsely claimed to be a US military intelligence specialist posted to the South Korean city of Gwangju during a popular uprising in 1980.

scraped.title: US Government Bureaucracy Is Designed to Punish the Poor
scraped.description: In The Time Tax, journalist Annie Lowrey ably documents the myriad ways US public services harm poor and working-class people and alienate them from the government. Yet she downplays the class interests that benefit from these Kafkaesque arrangements.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

In The Time Tax , journalist Annie Lowrey ably documents the myriad ways US public services harm poor and working-class people and alienate them from the government. Yet she downplays the class interests that benefit from these Kafkaesque arrangements.

The United States’ long, sordid history of racial oppression and especially stark class exploitation helped give rise to a government bureaucracy that punishes and demeans the poor. Fixing it will require class struggle. (Bettmann Archive via Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

Review of The Time Tax: How the Government Wastes Our Time — and How to Fix It by Annie Lowrey (HarperCollins, 2026)

F or several years, I lived in Norway and enjoyed the privileges associated with membership in Folketrygden , or the National Insurance Scheme. One privilege that I still think about often is the relative frictionlessness of interacting with the Norwegian government.

Seeing a doctor, for example, was effortless, and once my low annual deductible (as of 2026, ~$300) was paid, all testing and treatment for the year was covered without my involvement or input. My taxes were — without my prompting — prepared for me and sent for my amendment and approval. There was never anything to amend, of course. And because of the country’s leveringsfritak , or “silent acceptance” law, I did not even have to sign or submit a return.

The great difference between how things are typically done in Norway and how they are done in my home country, the United States, was never clearer to me than it was one day when I had to visit the US embassy in Oslo to handle some paperwork. At that time, the embassy was housed in an angular, charcoal-colored Eero Saarinen building across the street from the Royal Palace. It was not only conveniently located but, despite its popular reputation as a “fortress,” simple and straightforward to access — entering the compound required flashing my passport and was about as easy as doing anything else in Norway.

Imagine my surprise, then, when I arrived at the office where I was to complete my task: from the uncomfortable seating and oppressive lighting to the interminable wait and general feeling of disaffection, it was such an uncanny recreation of an underfunded Department of Motor Vehicles or post office that it could have been a movie set. There was even a small, cheaply framed photo of the president. The juxtaposition of this experience — which seemed designed to frustrate — and my happy dealings with Norway’s bureaucracies was, in its own way, radicalizing.

I sense that Annie Lowrey, author of The Time Tax , has been similarly radicalized, albeit through extensive personal and journalistic exposure to the myriad forms in which people in the United States have their time wasted and disrespected — or “taxed,” as she puts it — in almost every conceivable interaction with the government. She is clearly and justifiably pissed, and her book endeavors to show that the problem is, though widespread and deeply rooted in a particular national history of racial exclusion and class oppression, fixable. There is a world, she argues, beyond our current patchwork of fool’s errands and wild-goose chases.

B ut it is to this patchwork — and its associated “time taxes” — that most of the book is devoted. Through a mix of reporting, social scientific research, and reflecting on her own experience with an autoimmune condition, Lowrey has collected a cabinet of maddening curiosities: impenetrable forms, inexplicable rejections, multiyear wait times, and more. Page after page finds ordinary Americans trying to navigate a twisted institutional terrain seemingly designed by Franz Kafka or M. C. Escher. In the United States, you can buy, bid, and bet with the click of a button. Yet paying your taxes, voting, and getting benefits for which you qualify requires you to do American Ninja Warrior — with the proper forms of ID in hand.

Having cataloged the challenges people face when using public services in the United States, the first section of The Time Tax concludes with a tantalizing glimpse at the Estonian case, which, in many ways, resembles the Norwegian one with which I am more familiar (sans generous welfare state and strong labor rights). The story, as told by Lowrey, is that the small Baltic country, battered and bereft after exiting the Soviet Union, lacked the time, experience, infrastructure, and resources to recreate the comprehensive service architectures of other countries. So it didn’t. Instead, a generation of young and enterprising leaders leaned into speed, convenience, and digital integration to build an innovative e-government. In Estonia, Lowrey has seen the almost frictionless future of navigating government — and it works!

The Time Tax is at its most interesting and convincing when Lowrey is detailing the diabolical busy boxes that occupy millions of Americans. After the brief field trip to Estonia, the book could — and probably should — have ended with her proposals. It doesn’t.

Perhaps drawing inspiration from her subject, Lowrey decides that she requires more of her reader’s time to make her point. After a section break, we leave Estonia and arrive at . . . Fort Pillow in 1864? With Confederate general and future Ku Klux Klan Grand Wizard Nathan Bedford Forrest? It was disappointing to discover that The Time Tax was not in fact beginning its descent to a satisfying landing — it had been diverted to another destination: the past.

The middle third of the book draws on the extensive historical and social scientific scholarship devoted to the United States’ welfare system to recapitulate a story that will be familiar to anyone who knows the tortuous history of social provision in the United States. All the beats are there: Civil War pensions, Jim Crow, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and the Great Depression, Lyndon Baines Johnson and the Great Society, Ronald Reagan’s “welfare queens,” Bill Clinton and the “end of welfare as we know it.” Lowrey provides some useful context for twenty-first-century annoyances but breaks no new ground here, and the long historical detour saps the momentum of her opening chapters.

I worry that it also leads her to draw the wrong conclusions about her time taxes. She laments, for instance, that “diversity creates time taxes” and suggests that we are not Estonia due to “racial makeup.” Could it not be instead that time taxes transform diversity into inequality and hierarchy?

I n any case, the final part of the book picks up the threads of the first to make a final appeal and offer Lowrey’s solutions. This appeal takes for granted that the reader has not been entirely swayed by their own experiences or by the book’s emphasis on aggravation, injustice, racism, and inequality. Instead, Lowrey makes a persuasive closing argument that time taxes also hurt our health, teach us the wrong lessons about citizenship and government, and undermine social trust.

She concludes with her blueprint for change. Her proposed fixes include measuring time taxes via “sludge audits,” federalizing what are today state-run programs, reducing the use of means-testing in favor of universalism, and abolishing work requirements and pro forma interviews. These changes would, in the aggregate, make using public services faster, easier, more convenient, more empowering, and ultimately more fulfilling.

But I hesitate to call these proposals “solutions,” because I do not think that they actually address the problem at the heart of The Time Tax . This problem is not time taxes per se but the success of actors who weaponize bureaucracy to undermine our access to the goods and services of the social citizenship for which previous generations have fought and even died. The status quo in the United States is a nightmare not because elites are unaware of the fact that universalism promotes greater public investment and trust in government — it is a nightmare because they are aware. The history of many hitherto existing time taxes is also the history of class struggles.

Lowrey knows this — I think. She condemns TurboTax for helping to kill Direct File, Florida Republicans for fighting the reenfranchisement of convicted felons, and Donald Trump for the disaster of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE)–related cuts. She tells us that “time taxes are not just policy failures, but deliberate tools of social control.” And yet The Time Tax ’s antagonist is without question “Uncle Sam” (her chosen shorthand for the government) and his “bureaucratic excesses.”

The issue is that while she lambasts “Uncle Sam” again and again, she is hesitant to center the private interests for whom that control is useful and profitable. In her long historical excursus, she can acknowledge that poll taxes and other discriminatory laws were used by racist white elites to exclude black people, make their lives precarious, and destroy governmental alternatives to foster dependency on actors who rarely had their best interests in mind. But while the past has opponents, for Lowrey, the present only has design flaws.

A smaller rhetorical point: Lowrey undermines her cause with the book’s core metaphor. Calling the problem the “time tax” might sell books to tax-wary Americans, but it could reinforce the pernicious idea that taxes do not benefit ordinary people. This is odd, as Lowrey herself acknowledges that a sustainable remedy to “the headaches, snafus, and frustration imposed by Uncle Sam” requires the expansion and improvement of administrative capacity — a development that would almost certainly require, well, greater taxes.

Finally, there is a problem of conceptual imprecision, which becomes apparent in the book’s first pages. Lowrey opens The Time Tax with a montage, juxtaposing disconnected scenarios for the purpose of creating a connective thread — the time tax — between radically different people, places, and challenges. But as she moves from losing the right to vote, to trying to get insurance to cover therapies for an autistic child, to attempting to open a soft-serve ice cream shop, to practicing cosmetology without a license, to handing out burritos to the homeless without a permit, I began to question whether each of these is in fact an example of the same problem. After a while, she more or less abandons any attempt to persuade you that a given obstacle is or is not a time tax. Instead, she just asserts it, identifying one or more annoyances and then adding something like “ — a time tax,” as if it were obvious.

All in all, The Time Tax is laudable as a collection of curios. It is less useful as a blueprint. Though Lowrey knows — and sometimes says explicitly — that this maddening status quo reflects the desires of certain powerful and well-resourced actors, she offers no proposals for organizing to muzzle, defang, or otherwise diminish their influence. She writes that “change does not happen without awareness, and awareness is not possible without numbers and stories.”

But it also does not happen without an awareness of who or what benefits from keeping you trapped in a thousand purgatories and a strategy for organizing against them. The path to a Norwegian-style welfare state is not just a matter of design — it is one of politics, and class politics in particular.

Kelly McKowen is a cultural and economic anthropologist currently teaching in the Department of Anthropology at the College of William & Mary.

scraped.title: The politician-to-podcaster pipeline is getting crowded
scraped.description: It makes sense why so many politicians are hopping behind the mic. The 2024 election has been called "the podcast election."
scraped.author: Meagan O'Rourke
scraped.h1: The Politician-to-Podcaster Pipeline Is Getting Crowded
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Media

Meagan O'Rourke | 11.13.2026 2:45 PM

Did you catch the latest episode of Inside CentCom ? What about This is Gavin Newsom ? Did you listen to Hold These Truths with Dan Crenshaw ? Well, if you've somehow run out of pod content by politicians, you will soon be able to tune into World War Chi , a podcast by 28-year-old New York City Councilmember Chi Ossé. Ossé, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, will be hosting a show for Crooked Media , the media company founded by the Pod Save America hosts, Vulture reported last week. Ossé told Vulture he would squeeze in recording sessions on Saturday or Sunday evenings and that the show will mostly cover cultural topics. Still, there will "be a slow IV drip of socialism throughout each episode," he told Vulture .

If a "slow IV drip of socialism" is not your speed, you can listen to outgoing Rep. Nancy Mace (R–S.C.) talk about the Lindsay Clancy case, the WNBA , and Sharia law on her show, Get Maced . The tatted congresswoman launched her podcast back in August on YouTube, and she has over 100,000 subscribers.

And if none of these podcasts sound appealing to you, you are not alone. As Reason 's Robby Soave pointed out in April after Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. launched his own pod, "There are just too many podcasts."

It makes sense why so many politicians are hopping behind the mic. The 2024 election has been called "the podcast election," as both Donald Trump and Kamala Harris went on podcasts with large audiences to win support (obviously with varying degrees of success). And in 2025, when establishment Democrats realized they were losing their grip on the podcasting world, they desperately set out on a quixotic quest to find the "Joe Rogan of the left " to win back voters. That same summer, former Democratic National Committee chair Jaime Harrison even launched a podcast called At Our Table in a pathetic attempt to rebrand the Democratic Party. (In case you were wondering, his last episode has just cracked 100 views on YouTube). And political operatives know the power of podcasts is not going away. During the 2026 midterms, successful congressional candidates "made nearly three times as many podcast appearances as their losing opponents, according to Spotify data," reported Axios.

The democratization of the media via podcasting or platforms like Substack is a good thing , as major networks no longer control political narratives. But if politicians only appear on podcasts with politically aligned hosts or launch their own shows, they can evade tough questions while appearing transparent. And, as Soave noted in April, we may occasionally need our leaders to step away from the podcasting set to do their taxpayer-funded jobs.

Maybe the podcast market will soon be oversaturated, if it isn't already, and most of these podcasts will go the way of At Our Table . Not everyone has the podcasting magic in them. Plus, boring politicians will have to compete with hypnotizing AI fruit videos for the masses' attention. To win over 2028 voters, politicians may have to start thinking more about policies that will improve constituents' lives and less about their next MrBeast-style thumbnail.

scraped.title: Piecing Together The Timeline For The Rudofsky/Hiland Nominations
scraped.description: It is pretty clear that Hiland bombed his interview and the White House selected its first choice, Rudfosky.
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

It is pretty clear that Hiland bombed his interview and the White House selected its first choice, Rudfosky.

Josh Blackman | 11.13.2026 2:43 PM

We now have Senate Judiciary Committee questionnaires from both Judge Lee Rudofsky and Justice Cody Hiland . If we consider Justice Hiland's remarks to the law school, we can piece together a rough timeline of how this nomination zigged and zagged.

First, here is Judge Rudofsky's summary of the process:

In the Spring of 2026, I communicated to the White House Counsel's Office that, if a vacancy opened on the Eighth Circuit, would be interested in being considered for the vacancy. On or around June 19, 2026, the White House Counsel's Office asked me to interview for an Arkansas seat on the Eighth Circuit in the event of a vacancy. Shortly thereafter, I expressed my interest in the potential position to my home-state Senators. On July 1, 2026, I was interviewed in the Eisenhower Executive Office Building by attorneys from the White House Counsel's Office and from the Department of Justice's Office of Legal Policy. On or around July 20, 2026, Judge Shepherd formally announced his intention to take senior status upon the confirmation of a successor. On August 12, 2026, the President called me to tell me that he was going to announce his intention to nominate me to the Eighth Circuit. Throughout the process, I have communicated with individuals in the White House Counsel's Office and the Office of Legal Policy.

Second, here is Justice Hiland's summary of the process:

On June 17, 2026, I received a phone call from United States Senator John Boozman, who asked whether I would be interested in a potential vacancy on the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit. The next morning, I received a call from Senator Tom Cotton to further discuss the opportunity. On June 19, 2026, I received a phone call from White House Counsel's Office, and I interviewed on June 29, 2026, with staff from White House Counsel's Office and the Office of Legal Policy of the Department of Justice. On July 17, 2026, the White House Counsel's Office requested that I undergo a background investigation and prepare paperwork in anticipation of a potential nomination. On August 12, 2026, White House Counsel's Office asked about my interest in a potential district court nomination. [LOL ] On November 10, 2026, the White House Counsel's Office informed me that I was to be nominated and shortly after formally transmitted my nomination to the Senate. Throughout the process, I have had periodic communication with the Department of Justice's Office of Legal Policy to assist me in preparation of documents in support of my nomination.

Here is the timeline:

It is pretty clear that the White House wanted Rudofsky all along, and humored Boozman by giving Hiland an interview. Then, Hiland bombed his interview and the White House selected Rudfosky. But Senator Boozman wants his buddy to have a lifetime commission, and the President folded .

I should note that this morning, someone came up to me in the hallway at the Mayflower and said "I'm from Arkansas." I replied, as I often do, "Am I in trouble?" (I also met a Mississippian who gloated that "the Butler did it"; I don't think conservatives from Mississippi should be boasting about their skill in picking the right protein.) Fortunately, my interaction with the Arkansan went better. The person told me that Justice Hiland's voting record makes him indistinguishable from the Democrat Justices on the court. Here is a smattering of cases that the person shared with me:

Standridge, 2025 Ark. 42 (joined liberals in dissent, applying rule that "the primary rule of statutory interpretation is to give effect to the intent of the legislature)

Hause, 2025 Ark . 156 (wrote for majority, joined by liberals - Bronni's dissent, joined by conservatives, points out majority avoids answering the questions presented; issue in the case was a city ordinance used to block Airbnb-like rentals)

Paschall, 2024 Ark. 155 (Arkansas Supreme Court has a long liberal history; without questioning the precedent, in dissent, joined by liberals, Hiland writes that we must afford ballot titles "liberal construction and interpretation")

Boyle Ventures, 2025 Ark. 71 (writing the lead opinion, which the liberals joined or concurred, Hiland again uses legislative intent language, adding that the court "must look at the legislative history, the language, and the subject matter involved")

Eureka Gun and Pawn, 2026 Ark. 1 (joined liberals in dismissing an appeal over a municipality denying a gun shop a conditional use permit; conservatives concurred to explain there was nothing more to do on remand but grant the gun shop its permit)

Hughes, 2026 Ark. 69 (voted with liberals to dismiss an appeal as improvidently granted in a case that the court of appeals ruled that parents who live 15 minutes apart cannot have joint custody; case number is CV-23-749 and the docket shows the liberals, excluding Hiland, originally voted to deny the petition for review, Arkansas's version of cert petition)

I have reason to have hope for Judge Butler. Let's see what Justice Hiland does.

scraped.title: Iran War Day 259: Mossad Chief Visits U.S., Pushes for War
scraped.description: State of the Union: President Trump appears to have settled on a “neither war nor peace” strategy.
scraped.author: Andrew Day
scraped.body_text:
Roman Gofman, the director of Israel’s national intelligence agency Mossad, was in Washington, DC, on Friday pressing senior Trump administration officials to resume hostilities against Iran, Axios and Israeli media reported .

Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose government lost its majority in recent elections, has urged President Donald Trump to restart the war rather than make a deal with Tehran. A recent call between the two leaders degenerated into a shouting match, according to numerous reports.

Trump in recent days has opted for an apparent middle position, favored by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, between war and peace. The administration has sustained the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports, which was recently expanded to cover land routes. On Thursday, Trump said the U.S. doesn’t need an Iran deal and directed Vice President J.D. Vance, who has led peace negotiations, to shift focus to domestic issues.

Bloomberg reported Thursday that Trump has come to see the strategy as opening an opportunity to “leave the conflict in limbo and walk away.” Some Middle East experts warn America’s economic pressure campaign risks provoking an Iranian attack or leading to an escalation spiral.

Oil prices remain elevated but are set for a second weekly decline as traders see diminished odds of another round of war. Brent crude opened at $95.84 on Friday. In America, the average price of regular gasoline was $3.87 per gallon, continuing a decline.

Andrew Day is the senior editor of The American Conservative . He has a PhD in political science from Northwestern University. You can follow him on X @AKDay89 .

scraped.title: Now Rubio Wears the War
scraped.description: Our diplomacy-averse top diplomat’s Iran victory will prove Pyrrhic.
scraped.author: Andrew Day
scraped.body_text:
Our diplomacy-averse top diplomat’s Iran victory will prove Pyrrhic.

If you’re a fan of covert White House infighting bursting, if only partly, into public view, then Thursday must have been a fun day for you.

“We don’t need an Iran deal,” President Donald Trump declared , apparently giving up on diplomacy with Tehran.

This latest turn of the Trumpian diplomacy–war wheel was widely interpreted as bad news for opponents of the Iran War and for supporters of Vice President J.D. Vance, who has led peace negotiations.

It’s neither.

“We don’t need a deal” is an obvious and significant improvement over Trump’s previous position: “We’ll either make a deal or we’ll make a war.” That latter framing is how the U.S. got into the current Iran catastrophe in the first place. Trump has proven himself deal-incapable when it comes to the Islamic Republic, so the “deal or war” dichotomy was always, in addition to being false, counterproductive to peace, as I explained to Responsible Statecraft in June. And anyway, Trump has also proven himself willing—if not eager—to attack Iran amid negotiations.

As for the political repercussions for Vance, well, this will require some explaining.

Without question, the president was slapping down the Veep, removing him from the Iran file and siding with that faction of the White House, led by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, which opposes constructive diplomacy with Tehran. Trump’s announcement came in the form of a Truth Social post in which the president instructed Vance to focus instead on corruption and crime in Democratic-run cities.

In that sense, Trump’s unexpected pronouncement represents a political victory for Rubio, who has promoted the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports as a middle position between war and diplomacy. For now, the Rubio strategy prevails. But it won’t work. Rubio’s victory is a Pyrrhic one that will lead to his undoing as a viable presidential candidate.

Thanks, perhaps, to Rubio’s maneuvering, Trump has come to see the blockade as the easy “status quo” option, but as I explained in my other column this week (and on a recent episode of a popular online news show), that’s not right. The blockade builds pressure on Iran over time, and Middle East experts told me the Islamic Republic won’t stand idly by while the U.S. destroys its economy. In other words, Tehran is more likely to lash out than back down or collapse.

Moreover, the blockade is expensive to maintain and raises risks of an escalation spiral around the Strait of Hormuz. And even if the blockade somehow did effectuate state collapse in Iran, well, do you think the collapse of an enormous state in the Gulf region would be a good thing? To you and me, that would plainly be a very bad thing, but they’re not thinking very clearly over at the White House these days.

Rubio has made himself the most prominent and vocal supporter of this doomed strategy. And that means Rubio has made himself the face of the Iran War.

And that is a major development.

In case you haven’t noticed, our top diplomat hasn’t been doing a whole lotta diplomacy when it comes to the Iran War (or the Russia–Ukraine one, for that matter), and by that disgraceful means he’s managed to distance himself from the administration’s most unpopular policy.

No longer. The distance Rubio had cultivated has now collapsed.

Quite the opposite for Vance, the only cabinet member who has taken up the gargantuan task of securing a peace deal with Iran. Given Trump’s refusal to make the kind of concessions Tehran demands as part of a settlement, Vance’s good intentions weren’t translating into a lasting diplomatic—or political—win. Instead, Vance came to represent diplomatic failure, and in voters’ minds, however unfairly, he became closely associated with the war, since he was often on the teevee talking about it.

The whole situation was proving a political disaster for Vance—a Marine veteran who made his name lambasting forever wars in the Middle East—which helps explain his effort to subtly convey opposition to his boss’s misbegotten war. That effort culminated in a not-very-subtle social media post in which the Veep blamed the conflict for the GOP’s midterm-elections rout last week and made clearer than ever his preference for ending it ASAP. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said, rather bluntly.

Now, I’m more concerned with ending a war that is bad for America than I am with the political prospects of Vance or the Republican Party, but ask yourself, my Vance-adoring readers, and try to process these latest developments with as much cynicism as you can muster: Is it not better for Vance to become the guy who condemned and tried to stop the Iran War but was thwarted by Rubio? And is it not better for Vance that Rubio becomes the face of the Iran debacle, while the Veep turns his attention to crime and corruption?

It is better—much better, I humbly submit, even if few political analysts seem to agree with me.

As for the war itself and the prospects for peace, I harbor zero optimism. Maintain for another moment that cynicism that you mustered and confront this hard truth: There are no sources of hope in this Mideast fiasco, no obvious ways out, as Trump has laid for himself a hellish trap he cannot escape. Buckle up.

Andrew Day is the senior editor of The American Conservative . He has a PhD in political science from Northwestern University. You can follow him on X @AKDay89 .

scraped.title: Mark Levin’s Alternate Universe
scraped.description: The neocon commentator has never let the facts get in the way of a good war.
scraped.author: Juan Rojas
scraped.body_text:
The neocon commentator has never let the facts get in the way of a good war.

Mark Levin and reality have a complicated relationship .

This has been on full display recently in his crazed reaction to Republicans’ wipeout election loss , which was due largely to the Iran war—a conflict the neoconservative pundit has championed with unparalleled zeal.

“Everyone knows why we lost,” admitted Vice President J.D. Vance, blaming the war.

Well, not everyone .

Just before voters headed to the polls, Levin assured his viewers that if the GOP were to lose, it wouldn’t be “because of the Iran war.”

And after the GOP went down to its historic defeat, Levin claimed Iran “wasn’t even a big issue during this election.”

The data tell a different tale. Exit polls showed that 74 percent of voters said the Iran war was a crucial or major factor in their vote. A week before, Gallup reported that 77 percent of registered voters considered the war “extremely” or “very important” to their vote.

“It’s not my fault,” Levin cried .

“The GOP wipeout is absolutely the fault of Mark Levin and the Trump/Netanyahu Iran War,” noted the independent journalist Glenn Greenwald. “He knows it’s his fault which is why he’s crying that it isn’t.”

POLITICO reported in June that Levin was among a group of hawks that had been advising Trump on the war, including urging the president to resist a potential peace deal.

Despite this, for most of last week and this one, a wild-eyed Levin has lashed out at anyone who would dare say that the war he so avidly cheered cost Republicans the election. It had to be other issues instead, he fretted .

“Morning, Mark. You sound a little upset,” wrote the media personality Piers Morgan to Levin on the morning after the election. “[I]s it because America last night rejected the ruinous war-mongering, economy-shredding bullsh*t you’ve been spewing all year?”

“Sounds like I know what your fellow countrymen feel better than you,” the Englishman and Iran war critic said. “Maybe time to retire?”

But whether Levin retires or not, his complete detachment from reality is nothing new.

Mark’s most recent mania took me back to an earlier era, in which he was cheerleading for another Republican president and his disastrous Mideast conflict.

Almost twenty years ago, as Americans soured on George W. Bush’s venture in Iraq—which played a significant role in the election of Barack Obama—Mark Levin was in the cheer section for the war. Even as the scope of the tragedy became clear, he joined his neocon confreres in insisting that the war was undertaken in the service of a just cause, and that Bush was right to wage it even in the face of overwhelming popular opposition.

Just as today, war-lovers refused to let reality get in the way of their ultimate goal, manipulating language and attempting to gaslight the American people as to the character and costs of interventionism abroad.

In his 2009 book Liberty and Tyranny: A Conservative Manifesto , his early Obama era tome, Levin attempted to define a “conservative” foreign policy as distinctly “neo”: In other words, what Bush and Vice President Dick Cheney had just done in Iraq and beyond.

This would include the Global War on Terror and all its fruits: endless military operations, torture of detainees, warrantless searches, and mass surveillance. All of which Levin endorsed.

I reviewed the book for Taki’s Magazine at the time, and couldn’t help but call out the absurdity of some of Levin’s framing of these issues. Especially his bizarre and repeated use of the word “Statist” (always capitalized) as a pejorative for progressives or civil libertarians who took issue with controversial legislation like the PATRIOT Act or the illegal act of waterboarding .

On the PATRIOT Act, Levin wrote,

The Statist has also opposed the interception of enemy communications, such as email and cell-phone contacts, without approval from a court. But his position is contrary to all legal precedent, historical practice and highly impractical, given the speed by which such communications occur.

On waterboarding Levin wrote, “The Statist has succeeded in characterizing something as torture that is not torture, for the purpose of banning its judicious use.”

It was pure neocon drivel that was so typical of the Bush-Cheney era.

Oppose the PATRIOT Act? “Statist!” Oppose torture? “Statist!” Oppose the war? You guessed it.

I wrote in my review—which reads pretty gently in retrospect, given the ridiculousness of what Levin was saying—that the idea of calling people “‘statists’ who question the constitutionality of the PATRIOT Act or the morality of torture makes zero sense.”

“If he were honest, Levin would concede that increasing government power, whether by allowing it to spy on citizens or the executive branch redefining interrogation methods to circumvent the law, [requires] inherently ‘statist’ measures that he just happens to believe are necessary,” I noted.

When I talked about my review on the air in my local talk radio job in Charleston, SC, in 2009, Levin wanted me fired (we worked for the same umbrella company). But that’s a story for another time.

The lesson here is that neoconservatives will ignore existing reality to fabricate any narrative that protects or promotes their agenda.

“Where is the actual evidence of widespread civil liberties abuses against American citizens? It is nonexistent,” Levin wrote of curtailing citizens’ civil liberties.

That line might read differently to conservatives today, who are in full revolt against intrusive Flock cameras. Civil liberty protections were also probably important to right-wingers who participated in the January 6, 2021, Capitol Hill protests, particularly those who might have been ensnared in punitive legal situations . Just ask the family of Brian Cole, Jr .

But in 2009 and before, sacrificing those liberties was a core part of the neoconservative Bush administration. You disagree ? “Statist!”

Right now, Levin still contends that the Iran war was just and right, and that it definitely did not cost Republicans the midterm elections.

If that sounds completely unrealistic, that’s because it is.

It’s also vintage Mark Levin.

Jack Hunter is the former political editor of Rare.us . Jack has written regularly for the Washington Examiner , The Daily Caller, Spectator USA , Responsible Statecraft and has appeared in Politico Magazine and The Daily Beast. Hunter is the co-author of the The Tea Party Goes to Washington by Sen. Rand Paul.

scraped.title: Progressives say they can save US foreign policy from the blob
scraped.description: Matt Duss' edited volume presents a strong plan for reining in militarism, with one big concession to the status quo
scraped.h1: Progressives say they can save US foreign policy from the blob
scraped.body_text:
Matt Duss' edited volume presents a strong plan for reining in militarism, with one big concession to the status quo

In a stirring 1967 address in New York City, Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. proclaimed the death of the welfare state at the hands of the warfare state.

“The promises of the Great Society have been shot down on the battlefield of Vietnam,” King declared. “While the anti-poverty program is cautiously initiated, zealously supervised and required to be an instant success, billions are liberally expended for this ill-considered war. The security we profess to seek in foreign adventures we will lose in our decaying cities.”

Nearly six decades later, those who care about peace and dignity for the American people confront a similar dilemma. America’s post-Cold War pursuit of military dominance has generated resistance and destabilized nations abroad while enriching Pentagon contractors at the expense of the American public. It has led the United States into endless wars in the Middle East while pushing our politics in an ever more violent and paranoid direction.

The Pentagon budget continues to grow to an eye-watering $1.5 trillion as Biden administration alumni flood the zone with self-exculpatory memoirs and a Republican president who campaigned on purging neoconservatives now finds himself fighting a disastrous war with Iran . Reacting to the sorry state of U.S. foreign policy, a critical mass of Americans have come to recognize that the country’s foreign policy does not serve their interests, as the midterm elections made clear.

Congress responded to similar demands after the Vietnam War by initiating a bold (albeit insufficient) swath of reforms to rein in the imperial presidency and prevent U.S. arms from abetting human rights abuses. The question facing today’s progressives is whether they are up to the challenge of forging what Dr. King would call a “revolution of values” in American foreign policy.

“ A World for All , ” edited by progressive foreign-policy maven Matt Duss of the Center for International Policy, seeks to answer this question in the affirmative. The volume of essays from progressive scholars and foreign-policy practitioners is divided into three thematic buckets: one on U.S. policy in several world regions, another on economics and migration, and a third devoted to Congress, the military-industrial complex, and technology.

It is oriented, as Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) explains in the foreword, toward “articulat[ing] an affirmative vision” of a new foreign policy that “confronts global oligarchy, strengthens democratic institutions, and builds genuine partnerships.” Such a policy eschews delusions of global dominance while recognizing that “true security comes not from trillion-dollar arsenals but from addressing the root causes of instability: inequality, injustice, and environmental catastrophe.”

At times, the volume does not live up to these grand ambitions. Even as the war in Iran raises important questions about the survivability and utility of U.S. military bases, few of the essays detailed how U.S. force posture might need to change to support such a vision. In fact, the Europe essay does not discuss the future of the 80,000 American troops on the continent. Similarly, the book’s discussion of the Ukraine War — the central friction point between the United States and Russia today — largely repackages the status quo in arguing that “the key diplomatic instrument will not be rhetoric or the art of persuasion but the cumulative leverage over Russia that Ukraine and its partners are able to amass.” It does not interrogate whether Ukraine’s leverage diminishes as the war of attrition drags on, likely harming Kyiv’s position at the negotiating table.

This is a serious missed opportunity to chart an alternative course to the Cold War relic policy of many establishment Democrats and Republicans, which seeks worldwide U.S. military dominance without acknowledging the exorbitant costs this ambition incurs. These questions of prioritization should be front of mind for anyone trying to map the contours of a progressive foreign policy.

As a whole, however, the book is a vital opening salvo in the Democratic foreign policy debate that will play out between now and the 2028 presidential primaries. The chapters on corruption and the defense budget feature bold, actionable recommendations for cracking down on pervasive corporate or foreign influence and ensuring American foreign policy represents the will of the American public. The volume’s contribution on Congress’s abdication of its constitutional responsibilities in war and peace likewise proposes important reforms to rein in the imperial presidency and build transpartisan coalitions to challenge unchecked presidential war-making.

The book also rebuts some of the unhealthy ideological organizing principles of American primacy. Its prologue rightly pans “great power competition” with China and Russia for “prioritiz[ing] military solutions over diplomacy, undermin[ing] democracy and exacerbat[ing] inequality while exacerbating xenophobia and racism; and fuel[ing] jingoism…which heightens the risk of conflict. It also distracts from the problems with which the American people are most concerned.” In so doing, contributors Michael Brenes and Van Jackson make the provocative but essential argument that endless wars and interminable rivalries erode American democracy, in terms not dissimilar to King’s.

The authors lament that the United States has become a driver of regional conflict in the Middle East through its blank-check support for an “expansionist” Israeli government and autocratic Gulf regimes. Similarly, the authors rightly argue the Iran War is the logical endpoint of the flawed bipartisan precept that overwhelming American military power can solve the political problems that bedevil the region.

The authors are correct to observe that only sustained diplomacy with Iran can advance U.S. interests. Their conclusions that the United States should reduce or end its military presence in Iraq and the Gulf states and terminate U.S. assistance to Israel when it violates the laws of war or defies U.S. interests are compatible with a grand strategy of restraint.

In several essays, contributors rebuke the Biden administration’s shortsighted focus on a global competition pitting democracies against autocracies as the organizing principle of international politics. The volume recognizes that China’s authoritarian government is not going away and that the United States should strive for a grand diplomatic bargain to reduce the risk of war and help manage vital issues of mutual concern, like climate change, AI, and nuclear arms control. Indeed, the sections on the Middle East, Africa , and Latin America criticize the bipartisan blank check that U.S. military aid and security assistance have provided to authoritarian regimes at great human cost in the name of counterterrorism or the War on Drugs.

This represents a welcome break from post-Cold War Democratic foreign-policy orthodoxy. The 2024 Democratic Party platform , for example, characterized President Donald Trump as too soft on autocratic states like Iran and eschewed any mention of guardrails on competition with China. Democratic and progressive documents often suffer from critiquing the methods or decorum of U.S. policy rather than on the tangible outcomes of a faulty strategy of worldwide preeminence. The result has been old wine in a new bottle.

To its credit, A World For All avoids this trap. It recognizes that the primary competition between democracy and autocracy is within states rather than between them. It rejects the premise that more defense spending and less bureaucracy will restore American military dominance and keep Americans safe. Its epilogue, written by Heather Hurlburt, notes that for too long, internationalists “have been prone to overpromise on what U.S. leadership can deliver and how ‘indispensable’ we are.”

The Biden administration pursued a strategy that rejected the reality of a more multipolar world. If the next Democratic administration forges a new path and heeds the book’s call for humility, diplomacy, and discipline, it can break the cycle of endless war and give the American public its long-awaited peace dividend.

scraped.title: The hypersonic missile race is unnecessary boondoggle for US
scraped.description: Washington's existing weapons systems are more than capable of dealing with threats to American interests, say experts
scraped.h1: The hypersonic missile race is unnecessary boondoggle for US
scraped.body_text:
Washington's existing weapons systems are more than capable of dealing with threats to American interests, say experts

Last year, a group of high-ranking former military personnel and weapons company executives issued an ominous warning in an Atlantic Council report . U.S. adversaries, they said, were making rapid advances in hypersonic missile technology, “posing a severe challenge to US battlefield dominance.”

“Now is the time to act decisively to close the hypersonic gap and defend the nation’s interests for the future,” the report declared.

But is this really an existential threat? Will these technologies be as truly groundbreaking as the defense-tech industry claims? Experts who spoke with RS cast doubt on these positions, arguing that the spending is wasteful because despite the hype, hypersonics won’t provide unique advantages for the United States.

Hypersonic missiles can reach speeds of over Mach 5 and remain maneuverable mid-flight to confuse defensive systems. The missiles are designed to evade traditional ballistic missile defense systems by flying at low altitude, leaving them difficult to detect until minutes or even seconds before striking a target. In comparison, traditional ballistics follow high, extraatmospheric, parabolic arcs, allowing radar systems to detect them before they reach their zenith, sometimes affording defenders more than 20 minutes of warning before impact.

Claims about the difficulty of intercepting hypersonics aren’t airtight. Despite successful tests of some hypersonics, some experts doubt the feasibility of the claimed maximum speeds, maneuverability, and stealth abilities, according to Scientific American . The Congressional Budget Office agrees, insisting that “technological challenges must still be overcome to field hypersonic missiles.” According to the CBO, if fielded, the weapons would cost at least 30% more per unit than their ballistic counterparts. Even then, they would be more useful than ballistics only against extremely advanced, long-range defense systems, which no US adversaries currently possess.

Still, claims of successful tests or deployments of hypersonics by Russia , China , North Korea , and Iran have caused concern in the national security establishment about growing risks to Washington’s aerial dominance and, particularly, the ability of these weapons to get past U.S. missile defense systems. As of October 2026, Russia has reportedly tested two maneuvering hypersonic systems, and it has used regular hypersonic missiles (Oreshnik) in the war against Ukraine.

Iran and North Korea ’s claims of hypersonic capabilities remain unverified by independent observers. China has a confirmed hypersonic weapon, with unconfirmed reports suggesting additional successes.

The chase for hypersonics ignores a larger geopolitical context, says Kelly Grieco of the Stimson Center , who argues the United States’ major adversaries are acting out of a sense of vulnerability rather than a desire for escalation. For Russia and China, this stems from the transfer of U.S. THAAD (Terminal High Altitude Area Defense) missile defense systems into Ukraine and South Korea. U.S. adversaries see these batteries as giving cover to U.S. activities in their respective regions, making it easier for the U.S. to attack without having to worry too much about defending its equipment and personnel in the region. If hypersonics can evade such defenses, these countries can theoretically respond effectively to any American incursions in the region, thus acting as a deterrent.

In this context, these advanced, but expensive and rare, munitions make strategic sense. For a country like Iran , which can manufacture missiles more cheaply and has more limited resources, investing in a few highly advanced long-range missiles to increase deterrence in a future conflict makes strategic sense. In hypothetical wars — and indeed, in the ongoing war in the Persian Gulf — Iran is defending itself close to home against a militarily superior enemy. A country like Iran or China knows that even the threat of a strike to key U.S. sites, or even against the American homeland, would be intolerable for the U.S. and perhaps prevent an attack.

However, Grieco felt that, given expensive military supply chains, a less developed missile manufacturing sector, and a different overall strategic orientation, these munitions would do little to enhance American security. The U.S. typically aims to maintain aerial superiority to carry out offensive strikes against an enemy with comparably minimal aerial defenses. Grieco says existing, cheaper ballistic missiles launched en masse would be just as effective at evading or overwhelming any countermeasures. Additionally, she believes the United States’ nuclear triad already serves as a more than effective nuclear deterrent that wouldn’t be improved by hypersonic development.

Yet the U.S. is moving ahead with large-scale hypersonics development. Recently, the Pentagon offered private industry incentives to help close the alleged gap, with procurement contracts totaling over $12 billion for FY 2027 . This staggering sum excludes additional research and development spending. Although traditional players like Boeing , Lockheed Martin , and Northrop Grumman are in the mix, defense-tech startups are also trying their hand. Pentagon procurement overhauls in 2025 changed the rules to benefit younger, more innovative companies. Since then, venture capital investment in the hypersonic sector has more than tripled , rising to $1.2 billion in 2025 from $220 million the year prior.

Newcomer Castelion demonstrates this trend well. As of September 2026, the company is valued at $14 billion after raising $1 billion in Series C funding , largely from venture capital, and winning nearly $500 million in Defense Department contracts this year alone. In September 2026, the Navy placed a nearly $44 million order for 444 rounds of the Castellion hypersonic strike missile, known as the Blackbeard, making it one of its largest such contracts to date.

Grieco advised caution toward large-scale investment in immature technologies like hypersonics.

Pointing to a Government Accountability Office (GAO) report, Grieco said the projects are already behind schedule. The GAO reported in July that the Army and Navy alone have already approved over $50 billion in investments and procurement of hypersonic missile technologies. As of July , the Navy Conventional Prompt Strike (CPS) Program is 24 months behind on modifying ships to carry the $50 million-a-piece CPS missiles . The Dark Eagle, a missile developed jointly by the Army and Navy that will serve as the backbone of the Army’s hypersonic arsenal, is already delayed by two years .

There is no central strategy for hypersonic investment. Julia Gledhill , a researcher and defense budgetary expert at the Stimson Center, explained there is no easy way to get a single number for the total U.S. investment in hypersonics today. “You have hypersonic funding in Golden Dome, in the Defense Production Act Money that is focused on industrial base expansion,” she said, adding that they were on the new Pentagon Munitions Acceleration Council’s list of 12 critical munitions.

Grieco and Gledhill both said any strategic gains from hypersonics would be marginal at best and that greater investment risked entering a costly escalatory spending cycle with countries like Russia and China, as each strives to gain a technological upper hand with increasingly complex counter systems. Gledhill pointed to Trump’s “Golden Dome for America” as an example, comparing it to the ill-fated Reagan-era “Star Wars” initiative . Estimated to cost at least $1.2 trillion over 20 years , the program aims to build an orbital nuclear missile defense system. Scientists have already dubbed it a “fantasy,” and experts say it would be an unprecedented escalation in militarizing space .

Grieco offered a simple explanation for why Washington is continuing this pursuit despite its myriad challenges. Hypersonic investment is “a culture thing,” she said. “There seems to be discomfort with being behind.”
