scraped.title: Exclusive: Teacher Recruitment Programs Accused Of Racial Rigging
scraped.description: Four teacher preparation programs are under investigation for "credible reports" that they target aid toward non-white teachers.
scraped.author: Breccan F. Thies
scraped.h1: Exclusive: Multiple Teacher Recruitment Programs Accused Of Racial Rigging, Prompting Civil Rights Investigations
scraped.body_text:
OCR is also opening investigations into 11 universities to determine if they are violating similar civil rights law with their program offerings.

Four teacher preparation programs receiving federal dollars are under investigation by the U.S. Department of Education after it received “credible reports” that they illegally discriminate by targeting aid toward non-white teachers.

According to information obtained by The Federalist, these programs are “designed to recruit, retain, and support future educators,” but some also operate with explicit racial intent to artificially alter the “diversity” of a teacher workforce by providing services based on race. The Office for Civil Rights (OCR), which is conducting the investigation, said the programs could be in violation both of Title VI and Title IX of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 for race or sex discrimination, respectively.

“Race, national origin, or sex should not decide who will shape America’s next generation, yet many states and universities seem to prioritize recruiting and training ‘minority’ candidates rather than evaluating candidates based solely on merit,” Assistant Secretary for Civil Rights Kimberly Richey told The Federalist. “Education agencies and institutions that consider race, national origin, or sex as a means to withhold opportunities in selecting, supporting, and preparing teaching candidates violate federal law and compromise education excellence. The Trump Administration will fully investigate these allegations and ensure a future where students are once again judged on their hard work and merit, not prejudged by the color of their skin or their sex.”

The programs come from both institutions of higher education and state education agencies.

The City University of New York (CUNY) is under investigation for its NYC Men Teach Program which “aims to improve the diversity of the NYC teaching workforce by adding 1,000 male teachers of color into the teacher pipeline,” according to its website . The program surpassed that racial quota goal in 2018, and maintains finding candidates from the 16 CUNY campuses as well as a new effort to find candidates from high schools.

The University of Maryland (UMD) School of Education received a nearly $100,000 grant from the Maryland Higher Education Commission’s Teacher Quality and Diversity Grant Program, providing aid to “students from groups historically underrepresented in the teaching profession.” It specifies that “historically underrepresented” meant “African Americans, American Indians/Alaska Natives, Hispanics/Latinos, those from low-income backgrounds, first-generation college students, and individuals with disabilities.”

However, although it is possible groups like “low income,” “first-generation college students,” and disabled persons could be white, the “eligibility” portion of the program states “priority is given to historically black colleges and universities and Hispanic-serving institutions with a track record of preparing diverse and high-quality teachers.”

White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller has stated that removing diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) discrimination and other left-wing ideologies from universities will be one of his focuses in the role.

UMD also has the EdTerps CARES Network which is “designed to recruit and retain community college transfer students — particularly those from racially and ethnically minoritized backgrounds — into teaching programs at UMD.”

The program boasted the ability to get non-white candidates through transfer students, stating that between 2017 and 2019, 47.2 percent of the transfer students “identified as Black, Indigenous and people of color (BIPOC), compared with just 28.8% of first-year students.” It called transfer students the “essential strategy for increasing the recruitment and retention of multilingual and racially and ethnically diverse teacher candidates who will help diversify the educator workforce.”

Minnesota has two entities under investigation: the state Department of Education and the state Office of Higher Education.

Through its Education Tuition Assistance Program, which provides scholarships and stipends to teacher preparation programs, the department is able to target grants toward “teacher candidates of color and American Indian teacher candidates.”

The program has had this racial focus since its creation in 1997, with the explicit purpose of increasing the number of non-white teachers, thereby decreasing the number of white teachers.

Using the acronym TOCAIT, which stands for “Teachers of Color and American Indian Teachers,” the program tracks the percentage of these non-white teacher candidates at the state’s universities.

From 2024 to 2026 alone the program has doled out $5,872,960.21 to universities, most of which was awarded in 2026.

The Minnesota Office of Higher Education is under investigation for its Aspiring Teachers of Color Scholarship Pilot Program and the Underrepresented Student Teacher Grant, “both of which conditioned eligibility for receiving the awards on the applicant’s race,” OCR stated.

The Aspiring Teachers program says it is for “teachers of color” in the title, as also makes race a contingency, stating it is “designed to provide postsecondary financial assistance to undergraduate and graduate students who are preparing to become teachers, have demonstrated financial need, and belong to racial or ethnic groups underrepresented in the Minnesota teacher workforce.”

Even more explicitly, the program states, “in order to receive an award the institutions are required to verify if the applicants identify as a race or ethnicity underrepresented in the Minnesota teacher workforce.”

The Underrepresented Student Teacher Grant uses nearly identical wording.

In addition to the four programs, OCR is also opening investigations into 11 universities to determine if they are violating similar civil rights law with their program offerings.

The schools are: University of California – Berkeley, University of California – Los Angeles (UCLA), Campbell University, Drake University, College of DuPage, Middle Tennessee State University, University of North Iowa, University of Tennessee – Knoxville, University of San Diego, Seattle University, Westfield State University.

The U.S. Department of Education that the complaints received detail how the schools allegedly restricted scholarships, educational opportunities like fellowship programs, and support services on the basis of race or sex. However, the department was unable to provide more detail on the specifics of the allegations, as it is not their policy to discuss complaints.

scraped.title: After Midterms, Alito Warns Of Threats To Judicial 'Independence'
scraped.description: Justice Sam Alito is warning about potential efforts by a soon-to-be Democrat-run Congress to undermine the judiciary's 'independence.'
scraped.author: Shawn Fleetwood
scraped.h1: As Dems Ready To Take Power, Alito Warns Of Threats To Judicial ‘Independence’
scraped.body_text:
Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito is sounding the alarm about potential efforts by a soon-to-be Democrat-run Congress to undermine the judiciary’s longstanding “independence.”

The warning came during Alito’s appearance at The Federalist Society’s annual Antonin Scalia Memorial Dinner on Thursday. The senior justice was interviewed by Federalist Editor-in-Chief Mollie Hemingway, who published a bestselling biography about him earlier this year.

“Congress can turn off the lights at the Supreme Court and stop everything from happening if they want to defund their activities. And there are many, many, many other things that they can do, or at least try to do,” Alito told Hemingway.

The Bush 43 appointee further underscored the importance of “preserv[ing] the independence of the judiciary.” “If that is eliminated,” he said, “then the Constitution as adopted in 1789 will no longer be the same.”

Had the pleasure of interviewing Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito about America250 and his jurisprudence tonight at the Federalist Society’s Scalia dinner. pic.twitter.com/5Fjr8AfBL2

While not specifically mentioned, the justice’s comments appear to be in reference to last week’s Democrat midterm victories, and the party’s ongoing threats against the high court and its conservative majority.

[READ: Democrats’ War Against The Supreme Court Is About To Get Even Worse ]

Throughout the past several years, Democrats, with help from leftist-funded propaganda firms like ProPublica , have launched a series of phony “ethics” smears against Alito, Clarence Thomas, and the other conservative justices. In doing so, the party has sought to dishonestly paint the court (and its decisions) as corrupt and lay the groundwork for its ultimate aim: court-packing .

Numerous Democrats — including incoming congressional leaders and potential 2028 presidential candidates — have recently ramped up calls for increasing the high court’s number of justices. Despite claims to the contrary, the goal of this scheme is to stack the court with left-wing activists who will rule based on what’s favorable for Democrats instead of what law calls for.

[RELATED: Here’s Where Every Major Democrat Senate Candidate Stands On Packing SCOTUS ]

Among the other issues addressed by Alito during Thursday’s discussion was that of judicial power. While agreeing with the notion that the judiciary is the “least dangerous” branch and “vulnerable” to the other branches, the justice cautioned that judges can also abuse their authority.

Lower court judges “are dedicated and they are skillful, but they’re not perfect and they make mistakes,” Alito said. “And in some instances, I think they have gone far astray in abuse of their powers.”

The comments are seemingly in reference to lower courts’ overreaching rulings against the Trump administration. Alito and several of his colleagues have previously chastised some of these judges for such antics in the high court’s recent decisions.

items.title: The GOP Midterm Loss Is Not A Mandate For Amnesty
items.summary: Republicans want to use the midterms as a pretext for an 'immigration deal' that would reward big business with cheap foreign labor.

scraped.title: The GOP Midterm Loss Is Not A Mandate For Amnesty
scraped.description: Republicans want to use the midterms as a pretext for an “immigration deal” that would reward big business with cheap foreign labor.
scraped.author: John Daniel Davidson
scraped.h1: The GOP Midterm Loss Is Not A Mandate For Amnesty
scraped.body_text:
Republicans want to use the midterms as a pretext for an ‘immigration deal’ that would reward big business with cheap foreign labor.

In the wake of Republicans’ historic midterm wipeout, there’s a narrative push underway in Washington that it was Trump’s immigration policy, especially ICE deportations, that drove Latino voters who voted for Trump in 2024 to vote Democrat this time around.

This narrative is demonstrably false, but it’s being pushed by Washington Republicans who want to return the GOP to its pre-Trump form once the president leaves office (which is a fantasy because the pre-Trump GOP is completely dead, never coming back). In the meantime, they’d like to cut an immigration deal with Democrats to grant amnesty to illegal immigrants — specifically, to illegals who work in certain industries.

They are of course denouncing the term “amnesty,” as DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin did in a recent interview, even as Trump himself did in his 60 Minutes interview with Ross Douthat. But what they describe — granting legal status to foreign nationals who came to the U.S. illegally and allowing them to remain and work here legally — is amnesty, plain and simple.

What’s really happening here is that the GOP establishment, the people who have always hated Trump’s America First coalition and the MAGA agenda, are trying to ram through amnesty as a way to secure cheap foreign labor for favored industries before Democrats take over completely.

First, consider the argument they’re using to push amnesty. As my colleague Jordan Boyd explains in these pages , the idea that Latinos voted Democrat in the midterms because of Trump’s immigration policy isn’t backed up by polling data, which shows that economic issues, not immigration, drove Latino voters into the arms of Democrats. “One NBC exit poll found that 45 percent of Latino voters said the economy was their biggest concern going into the 2026 election,” wrote Boyd. “Only 15 percent reported ‘immigration’ as ‘the most important facing the country.’ Of those who prioritized immigration, six in 10 voted Republican.”

The vast majority of Latino voters — 94 percent — said cost of living was a crucial or major factor in their midterm vote. And as Boyd noted, exit polling showed that the more a Latino voter said that immigration was an important factor in how they voted, the more likely they were to vote Republican. Another Federalist colleague, Shawn Fleetwood, broke down exit polling data last week that showed the same thing. In one CNN exit poll, 73 percent of respondents said Trump’s immigration enforcement was a “crucial” or a “major factor” to their vote. Republicans won this group 51 to 47 percent.

For Latino voters, as for voters generally, the main concern was the economy — which was a concern precisely because gas and grocery prices spiked after Trump decided to attack Iran. It was the unpopular and costly Iran war , not ICE deportations, that turned voters away from the GOP (along with a host of lesser issues like corruption and lack of transparency around the Epstein files).

The Washington Republicans who blame the midterms on immigration of course have little to say about the Iran war. When they say anything at all, it’s to claim that the real problem is Trump didn’t go after Iran hard enough, that Vice President J.D. Vance tried to negotiate an end to it, that we didn’t pursue an insane policy of arming the Kurds or invading with ground troops. They will say almost anything, however untethered from reality, before they admit that the war was a terrible idea to begin with and we never should have done it.

And now they’re saying that what the American people really want is for Republicans to strike an immigration deal with Democrats and grant some form of amnesty to entire classes of illegal aliens. This week on Fox News, Rep. Marlin Stutzman of Indiana, a Freedom Caucus Republican, argued for a Republican immigration reform that includes amnesty for certain illegal aliens and no mass deportations.

“What’s happened is first President Trump did what he said he was going to do by securing the border. That was step number one, that’s happened. And now we need to look at our laws,” he said. “I think we should be focusing on those who are here that haven’t broken criminal laws, that are working, that could be paying taxes, they would be willing to be sponsored by somebody. There’s room for that, I believe, and that’s what people are looking for.”

Stutzman went on to denounce the idea of mass deportations, which Trump campaigned on successfully in 2024. “I just don’t think it’s possible,” he said. “You’re looking at 20 million people that you would have to deport out of this country.” Never mind that Trump explicitly promised 15-20 million deportations during his 2024 campaign, even vowing to use the military to accomplish it. That was a popular message.

Unfortunately, Trump himself is now talking about an immigration deal for “the good ones,” as he calls them, immigrants who came illegally but are now working in certain industries. Indeed, there seems to be a broad agreement among GOP officeholders that illegal immigrants who provide cheap labor for farms, hotels, and construction companies should be exempt from U.S. immigration laws.

For example the GOP-backed farm bill, filed back in June, would allow illegal immigrants working in a variety of agricultural-related industries to obtain H-2A visas and avoid deportation . The bill, H.R. 9535, called the “Securing Agriculture’s Workforce Act,” is sponsored by House Agriculture Chairman Glenn Thompson, a Republican, and has a total of 52 Republican cosponsors. It basically creates a permanent underclass of foreign agricultural workers who will be issued H-2A visas and be employable on a permanent year-round basis. Whatever the Trump 2024 coalition voted for, it wasn’t that.

Time and again, Republicans pay lip service to immigration enforcement but advance policies that ensure big business has access to cheap foreign labor. They don’t really care what their voters want, they care what their donors want. That’s why Sen. John Thune was just reelected majority leader by Senate Republicans after an historic midterm wipeout. Voters spoke, they said they were angry with the GOP, they handed control of the Senate to Democrats, and effectively destroyed the Republican Party for a generation. The message was clear. Republican senators responded by saying, we don’t care.

They’re saying the same thing about immigration. Voters support mass deportations, they support ICE enforcement, they support Trump immigration policy. And in response, Washington Republicans are falsely claiming that immigration was a major cause of the midterm route, and then using that as a pretext to do what they wanted to do all along: pass amnesty for their friends and donors in big business.

Doing this is worse than doing nothing. Much worse. After a defeat this thorough, the establishment Republicans should resign in shame, not try to cram amnesty down our throats on their way out the door. As pollster Rich Baris said , “Put simply, the best thing people who betrayed voters and cost the party their trust can do, is go away.”

That they refuse to go away is a blatant slap in the face to GOP voters. Whatever comes after these people, it has to be a party that actually cares about what voters want and does what they promise to do. Until Republicans figure that out, they will remain in the wilderness where they belong.

scraped.title: Bring Back the America of ‘You’ve Got Mail’
scraped.description: We still care about the film—as the announcement of a remake shows—because we miss the country it embodied: brick-and-mortar stores; falling in love in real life; good, old-fashioned competition.
scraped.author: Liel Leibovitz
scraped.body_text:
I live on the Upper West Side of Manhattan, which means that every time I take a stroll around the neighborhood, I’m walking right through the set of You’ve Got Mail . That storefront on 83rd Street? That’s the café where Meg Ryan’s Kathleen sat waiting for Tom Hanks’s Joe, not knowing that the man she met online is the owner of the big, bad bookstore about to run her much smaller bookshop out of business. You can see that bookshop, too, if you saunter on over to 69th Street—it’s an organic dry cleaner now, but the flower garden in Riverside Park and 91st Street where Joe and Kathleen finally kiss looks pretty much the same as it did in the movie.

Hey, I’m far from the only one obsessed with this rom-com: Just this week, Warner Bros. announced that a reboot was in the works, with director Jason Orley at the helm. But can a reboot of You’ve Got Mail even work these days?

scraped.title: The Biggest Scandal of the Trump Administration? Plus. . .
scraped.description: In today’s Front Page, Pottinger on why the Nvidia scandal is a political scandal of epic proportions, Dhillon tells all to Audrey Fahlberg in her first interview since leaving the Trump administration, and more.
scraped.author: The Free Press
scraped.body_text:
It’s Friday, November 13. This is The Front Page , your daily window into the world of The Free Press —and our take on the world at large. Today: Audrey Fahlberg interviews Harmeet Dhillon on why she quit the Trump administration. Roy Altman memorializes the federal judge who wasn’t afraid to talk politics outside the courtroom. Yuval Levin on how Congress’s new Democratic majority will move both parties to the right. And much more.

But first: the scandal of the decade?

Jensen Huang’s fall from grace this week is one of the year’s biggest spectacles in business, technology, and international politics. Yet now that the Nvidia founder has been ousted from the chip company he built into a titan, the world is still not sure what we’re looking at. The possibilities range from a salacious sex scandal à la Bill Clinton to a strategic betrayal akin to the Rosenbergs .

The plot thickened on Thursday as members of both parties called for Huang to testify before Congress. Lawmakers want to know whether the alleged Chinese spy with whom Huang had an affair helped smuggle restricted chips to her homeland—with or without Huang’s knowledge. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is facing similar heat, as critics allege that he loosened barriers on foreign chip sales despite being warned of a possible scheme.

These suspicions point to a gut-wrenching possibility: that the Donald Trump administration and major players in America’s AI industry undermined national security by turning a blind eye to Beijing scheming to evade export controls designed to stop U.S. chips making it into China.

That’s the theory that Matt Pottinger and Liza Tobin explore in their report today. A former top national security official and a leading China strategist, respectively, they chart the timeline of the administration’s moves and talk to former officials who say they were sidelined or pushed out of the Commerce Department after devising tighter technology restrictions. The details, they argue, amount to “a story of brazen regulatory capture: how Jensen Huang gained personal, persistent access to the president of the United States.” No matter which way you look at it, it doesn’t look good.

—Mene Ukueberuwa

In her first interview since resigning from the Trump administration, Harmeet Dhillon tells all to Audrey Fahlberg. The former assistant attorney general for the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division reflects on her fight to clear illegal immigrants from voter rolls, why she thinks most conservatives are too timid when it comes to the law, and why she’s not afraid of scrutiny from Democrats in the next Congress.

Most judges are tight-lipped outside the courtroom. But Richard Posner, who died this week after serving for nearly 36 years as a circuit court judge, turned this assumption on its head. In doing so, writes Judge Roy K. Altman, he reminded the American people of an under-discussed role of judges in our democracy: to explain the judiciary, offer a window into it, and remain connected to the people whose disputes they adjudicate. “His example should encourage the rest of us to take a more active role in the public conversations that matter to our fellow citizens,” Roy writes.

Even those dismayed by Democrats’ midterm gains should find reason to celebrate the end of the fifty-fifty split in Congress, argues the conservative intellectual Yuval Levin. “Simply by making large majorities imaginable again, and so focusing political competition on the median voter and the challenge of building broad coalitions, this election could allow for some renewal in our constitutional system,” he writes. Read Yuval’s essay about how the midterms might reinforce American democracy.

America loves a sex scandal—which is a problem when there’s a much more serious national security scandal attached. Such may be the case with the biggest news story of this week: Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Huang’s philandering got him ousted as the CEO of Nvidia, the semiconductor giant behind the AI revolution. But if his Chinese mistress was smuggling Nvidia chips into China—and he knew about it—his problems are a lot bigger than most people thought, argues Patrick McGee . Read his piece on why the implications of the Huang affair stretch from the bedroom to the boardroom—perhaps, even, to the White House Situation Room.

This high-profile honeypot scandal is the first of many to come, writes Tyler Cowen . “Life is going to feel much more cloak-and-dagger, especially for the wealthy and influential,” he argues. Read his column on what Huang’s affair portends for the coming age of the AI wars—and the spy-thriller games that may soon unfold.

The other sex-scandal news of this week was the prison sentence handed down to British actor Russell Brand after his recent conviction for rape and sexual assault. From his lurid and highly public sexcapades in the 2000s to his eyebrow-raising pivot to Christianity in the 2020s, Brand was always shape-shifting to evade accountability, argues Douglas Murray . Now, not only have his deplorable actions caught up with him, they’ve revealed a fraught cultural shift wrapped up in #MeToo, Covid vaccine skepticism, and changing sexual mores.

When Ross Douthat interviewed the president for 60 Minutes last week, Trump surprised him—and the nation. The commander in chief conceded an actual political failure. He suggested one domestic policy choice that would create a true political earthquake, and expressed an openness to guardrails on artificial intelligence. Read Ross’s column on the takeaways from that interview—and the decisions Trump still has to make that will determine his legacy.

The GOP’s midterms reckoning continued this week with slightly less finger-pointing and more soul-searching—while Democrats congratulated themselves on a new dawn in politics. But the midterms were a regular shellacking, not a political paradigm shift, argues Niall Ferguson . In his latest column, he traces the lessons of history, from Dwight Eisenhower to Richard Nixon, about what happens when a second term turns sour.

In New York City, e-bikes sometimes travel up to 70 miles per hour. As they speed through traffic lights and on sidewalks, they’re leaving people maimed, paralyzed, or dead. This week, River Page reported on the fight brewing in New York City politics over e-bikes: the victims, the food deliverymen, and the progressive politicians who can’t decide what’s more important—fighting racism or reducing e-bike deaths.

scraped.title: Is This the Most Serious Scandal of the Trump Era?
scraped.description: If Jensen Huang’s mistress was channeling Nvidia’s chips to China—and the administration looked the other way—it will constitute a breathtaking breach of national security, write Matt Pottinger and Liza Tobin.
scraped.author: Matt Pottinger
scraped.body_text:
Jensen Huang may have resigned from the AI-chip behemoth he founded, but the investigation into what he knew and when he knew it—about his mistress Alice Huang, and about where her company was delivering Nvidia’s most advanced chips—that’s just beginning.

Congressional investigators will soon be asking whether Jensen Huang helped Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese spy, to circumvent U.S. export controls to supply powerful chips to China’s AI companies. Did he have access to—and pass on—U.S. classified information? As a member of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, Jensen Huang was eligible for a security clearance and may have been briefed on sensitive intelligence. And given Alice Huang’s alleged ties to the Ministry of State Security (MSS), was she then feeding information to the Chinese government?

We’ll return to Alice Huang and the MSS in a minute.

But first we mustn’t overlook the companion narrative that only adds to the scandal. That is a story of brazen regulatory capture: how Jensen Huang gained personal, persistent access to the president of the United States, the secretary of commerce, and other key officials—and how he used that access to advocate policies that have put America’s foremost adversary, the People’s Republic of China, within reach of becoming the dominant power in artificial intelligence.

“China is going to win the AI race,” Jensen Huang told the Financial Times last November. He blamed American “cynicism” about AI and contrasted it with Beijing’s lavish subsidies for the technology. Jensen Huang released a statement later the same day saying, “It’s vital America wins” the AI race.

You wouldn’t know it from his lobbying efforts.

scraped.title: Gen Z’s favorite rabbi
scraped.author: Nikos Mohammadi
scraped.h1: Gen Z’s favorite rabbi Yosef Mizrachi is the tough Dad they never had
scraped.body_text:
Recent years have witnessed an explosion of online anti-Semitism, particularly among Gen-Z men. Some of what is called anti-Semitism is legitimate criticism of the Israeli government. But plenty of it is straight-up, old-school Jew hatred. An obvious example is the onslaught of Instagram reels to the tune of “Hava Nagila,” with stereotypical caricatures of “ the happy merchant ,” often captioned, “Well, well, well,” or accompanied by Nazi imagery. Then there are the Groypers and others who openly, unabashedly attack Jews as Jews.

It’s a paradox of our online life, then, that one of the most popular figures among this very cohort is an ultra-Orthodox rabbi who believes that Jews do and should run the world: “The goyim gets angry, ‘the Jews in control, the Jews in control, they control the money.’ So who will control the money — you ?” he exclaims. “You compare yourself to the chosen people? … It’s good for you that they run the country.” (“Goyim” is the Hebrew word for Gentiles, or non-Jews.)

His name is Rabbi Yosef Mizrachi, and he has rapidly ascended over the past year on online shows and X, the app formerly known as Twitter. “Your entire story, it’s a made-up story,” he said flat-out of the New Testament, much to the anger of one interlocutor. Mizrachi has also debated the manosphere-icon-turned-Islamist streamer Sneako, who opened the stream by praising Mizrachi for being “a breath of fresh air, because at least you are honest about what you believe in.” And the rabbi has become the subject of a whole genre of memes — first on X, and now increasingly on Instagram, where more “normies” are encountering him for the first time.

One type of self-help reel, featuring a speech of Mizrachi’s set to a melodramatic tune, is especially viral on Instagram at the moment. It goes : “I’m not interested to be religious, but I don’t have a choice. If I stay the same bum I am, in the clubs of Manhattan, smoking grass all day, walking like a goy everywhere I go, what kind of a girl will I get?”

It is this latter type of message that especially attracts younger men to the rabbi’s message. His voice is like that of the tough but benevolent father many of them never had, whether because Dad was absent or permissive to an excessive and destructive degree. As he tells me in a recent interview at UnHerd ’s New York headquarters, “every teenager — 16, 17 — when he begins to take drugs, he knows that’s not a positive thing to do. What makes him take that risk anyway to destroy his life, to destroy his future marriage, to destroy his future family, to destroy his own parents? Why would he jeopardize his future in such a horrible way? The answer is pure desire.”

It helps that the rabbi, in his strong Israeli-inflected accent and somewhat broken English, cuts to the chase and says what he actually believes, however controversial. And he is hilarious, to boot. His viral quips about the goyim also come at a time when the use of the word “goy” is being popularized. Some of the term’s usage is obviously anti-Semitic: look at those all-powerful Jews, demeaning us goyim . But in Zoomer parlance, it also has a light-hearted valence, as a means for distinguishing between positive attributes and degeneracy.

For something to be “goy-coded” means it is déclassé, for the masses, and dumb. Indeed, Jews themselves can be “goyim.” And a Gentile doesn’t necessarily have to be a “goy.” Studying for your classes, working hard at your job, and eating healthily are definitively not “goy-coded.” Endlessly watching Sunday “goyball” (football), consuming “goynip” (marijuana), and binge-eating your DoorDash “goyfeed” (caloric fast food) are, as their prefixes would entail, “goy.” Mizrachi himself has mocked “some Gentiles” who “are very stupid, they never think. They only want the beer, and the alcohol, and the sport, and the football, and the Fourth of July barbecue, and the beach, and the tattoos, and the clubs … Nothing in life, no values, no ethics, no conscience, no calculation about where I am heading.”

Strip away the hard-line sectarianism — and some of it is unquestionably gross — and Mizrachi’s message to young men, Jewish and non-Jewish, is simple: clean up your act. The impulse to enjoy lower pleasures, Mizrachi believes, must be tempered — and the problem is that too often in today’s society, it isn’t. As he tells me, summing up the prevailing consumerist ideology: “‘Let me enjoy the moment and deal with the problem later on.’ But that’s pure stupidity, because people are not supposed to be that stupid.”

By Nikos Mohammadi

The rabbi was born in Israel in 1968 and moved to New York nearly two decades later. He now lives in Monsey, the ultra-Orthodox hamlet in Rockland County, and teaches night classes on the Torah in Brooklyn and Queens.

Mizrachi’s journey to becoming a rabbi started with his fatherly impulse: “I saw that I have influence on my friends to starting to change their lifestyle, and that’s — it’s like God was pushing me to that direction.” He was already married, but he wasn’t religious. In his telling, he came to be influenced by religious lectures being delivered by rabbis in the New York area. Mizrachi would go to these lectures, where he discovered that he “had power to influence people.” In 1994, he started his own religious lectures, which initially drew small crowds. Eventually, his followers made him a website, and he started to gain a limited online following.

The “turning point,” Mizrachi tells me, was in 2015, when he had a debate with a Jewish believer in Christ and teacher at the New York School of the Bible, Daniel Mann, whom he simply calls the “Christian professor.” In response to Mann’s message, Mizrachi tells me, he set out to prove that “Christianity is not a divine religion, no connection to God.” Christianity, as Mizrachi explains, has “a lot of good values, and they learn a lot of things from the Torah and from Judaism. They have one major issue: they took a human being and turn him into a god, and that’s against the Ten Commandments.” “Righteous Gentiles” are those who follow the Noahide laws, which he believes everyone can.

From this early provocation against Christianity to his widespread virality today, the rabbi has been mired in controversy. In 2015 and 2016, he came under fire for suggesting that the Holocaust had taken the lives of only 1 million halachic Jews (those recognized as Jews by traditional Jewish law). He later issued a formal apology after having been shown “the accurate statistics” and realizing that “those that were not halachically Jewish were a very small minimal number.”

Also in 2016, the chief rabbi of Britain had warned that a planned visit by Mizrachi to the country would elicit “widespread offense and upset,” particularly due to Mizrachi’s comments that sick children were being punished for sins in a previous life. Mizrachi canceled the trip amid the uproar. Three years later, when he yet again sought to go to Britain, he was barred by the UK Home Office.

There have been other low points: in 2020, Mizrachi claimed that blowing a hair dryer in one’s mouth was “guaranteed” to stop the novel coronavirus; in 2023, an Israeli court found him liable for defaming the mother of former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, whom Mizrachi had alleged was not Jewish.

At the same time, Mizrachi can sound surprisingly universalist notes for a religious leader widely known for his Jewish supremacism and mocking of the goyim. He tells me, “I wouldn’t like a Gentile that is Nazi, but I also wouldn’t love a Jew that is a terrorist. There’s no difference. I don’t discriminate between Jews and non-Jews.” He adds that he’d rather live in an apartment building full of religious Muslims, even if he believes their religion is wrong, than to raise his children next to “wicked Jews.” When it comes to people, as individuals, he emphasizes, “the last thing I care about [is] if they are Jewish or not Jewish.”

So what about his apparent belief that “goyim are not people,” a saying widely ascribed to him on social media? Mizrachi replies unequivocally: “I never say and never dare to say such [a] thing.” Later on, he contextualizes some of his more demeaning statements about the Gentiles: “When I say sometimes in my speeches, ‘He dresses like a goy,’ meaning there’s a Jewish religious dress code, and there is the way that the rest of the world dress, right? So it’s not necessarily an insult.” Moreover, “when I speak in Hebrew,” the rabbi mentions, “I tell the people you look like Chiloni . Chiloni means secular, you know. And the Chilonim are not offended by that. They’re proud of how they dress.”

Such statements can seem disingenuous. Mizrachi has made many demeaning statements about the goyim, though he’s never precisely said “goyim are not people.” The closest thing might be when he once said , “At least 6 [or] 6.5 billion people are idol-worshippers that, according to the Torah, do not have the right to live. Idol-worshipper goy [deserves the] death penalty.” And he counts Christians, Buddhists, and Hindus equally among the ranks of “idol-worshippers.”

It is also hard to believe he has all due respect for the goyim and secular Israelis, when in one viral clip , he blames the IDF’s inability to beat Hamas on half of Israeli soldiers being “Russian goyim and other goyim,” and the others being earring-wearing, tattooed, secular Israeli Chiloni , who, “when they join the army, 20% to 30% of them are gays, hate religion, hate rabbis, make fun against Hashem [God] all day on the internet. That’s the army. So why should Hashem help us when half of our soldiers makes fun at him all day?”

He is, to some extent, shirking responsibility for the uglier side of his statements, a contradiction from a leader who believes his following stems from his honesty, as Mizrachi tells me, with all appearance of sincerity. “The most popular compliments that I get from all the people — Jews, non-Jews, Muslims, Christians, even atheists, is we like you because you are honest.”

The arch-Groyper Nick Fuentes, for one, is a fan: “I saw Rabbi Mizrachi challenge me to a debate. Increasingly, I’m not even interested only because I don’t know what we’d debate about.… I think Rabbi Mizrachi was right about literally everything.” Among the areas of agreement, Fuentes believes, is that some goyim don’t have souls, with Fuentes’s own, rival online anti-Semites (of the more conspiratorial variety) — Dan Bilzerian, Jake Shields, Ian Carroll, and Candace Owens — being the prime examples.

And the fandom is mutual. “Even though he’s an anti-Semite,” Mizrachi says of Fuentes, “I actually admire some of the things he says because at least you can see that he has some kind of truth in him.” Mizrachi is against “stupid liberalism”: “they want to push all kinds of immigrants into the country. They want to bankrupt the country. They want to give freedom and rights to people that nobody even know who they are.” Among these liberal people are Jews, and white supremacists, in the rabbi’s telling, frame all Jews for liberalism’s excesses.

Fuentes, Mizrachi says, “makes a lot of noise, and it’s a very interesting theater, you know, his shows.” Mizrachi also makes the distinction between genuine anti-Semites and those he believes are in it solely for the clicks, with Tucker Carlson as an example. “For years, he works for Fox News. He’s an extreme Righty, is pro-Republicans, is pro-Israel, is you know, has a lot of Jewish friends. All of a sudden, Qatar buys him out,” Mizrachi alleges, and Carlson “becomes a representative of Qatar, number one sponsor of terrorism.” (There is no evidence that Carlson is on the Qatari dole.)

More ugliness comes, also, in Mizrachi’s treatment of Israeli Arabs. “Stupid liberalism,” as he calls it, which he believes rules in his native Israel, has led to a situation in which Arabs, apparently, “have the best rights than any other Arab country in the world.” Israel’s hospitals “are full of Arab doctors, Arab nurses. It’s enough that 1% of them are jihadists, and they catch all the time these guys with ISIS, these guys pro-Hamas, these foolish doctors. They write in their social media, ‘It’s time for jihad, kill all Jews.’” So, Mizrachi asks, “Do you want to go as a Jewish person to a hospital to be operated by a doctor that last night wrote in his Facebook page that you have to kill all Jews and he’s supposed to save your life? Do you understand the contradiction? This is the price of just liberalism.” (The idea that some Arab-Israeli doctors seek to kill their Jewish patients is false and has been condemned by the Israel Medical Association.)

By Valerie Stivers

Mizrachi’s unlikely emergence as a Gen-Z icon says something about the state of the Gen-Z soul: it reflects the emptiness and spiritual fatherlessness into which three generations of ultra-permissive liberalism has plunged them. To the audiences that fall for his style of edgelording, Mizrachi also offers a spiritual balm of a kind — and this may be the secret of his appeal. Maximum “freedom” and “acceptance” have been bad for many young men, especially the hyper-online. Mizrachi uses their favorite medium to urge them to restraint, self-respect, and the acceptance of limits.

On addiction, a plague of this generation, Mizrachi laments: “I can’t say today that goyim smoke more marijuana than Jews. I think the statistic is just about the same. Secular Jews, secular Gentiles, they consume drugs. Unfortunately, alcohol, drugs, anything you can think of.” Cigarettes are “killing, everybody knows it’s killing. When people argue with me in my lectures, it always will be smokers.” Instead of arguing back, the rabbi thinks it would be healthier to say: “‘I’m a weak character. I’m an addict. I wish I can overcome that addiction,’” but most people aren’t willing to admit as much, because “most people are not honest.”

“Ego, pride, and money, greed, desire,” are the evils he believes we must grapple with. And on this front, the rabbi’s concern is once again universal. “And what do you think: Gentiles think different than Jews?” he asks me. “Don’t they know what’s right and what’s wrong? They also know. And people are tired of the corrupted society we live in, they are tired of this. They look at the politician. They look how the president talk. They see his ego. They see everyone around. One day, they say one thing, and an hour later, they say … the exact opposite.”

President Trump, somewhat like the rabbi, was also once a favorite among hyper-online Gen-Z men, and may have fulfilled a similar aspirational-authority-figure role. Mizrachi, perhaps, offers something better. He appreciates the president for his support for the Jewish state, he tells me, but “his personality, his personal character, needs a huge improvement, starting with his ego and pride and insulting people in public. That’s not the way of a president.”

The same Tucker Carlson whom Mizrachi now demonizes as a Qatari operative, said about Trump at a Turning Point Action rally in the run-up to the 2024 election: “If you allow people to get away with things that are completely over the top and outrageous, if you allow your hormone-addled 15-year-old daughter to like slam the door of her bedroom and give you the finger, you’re gonna get more of it. There has to be a point at which Dad comes home.”

Is Mizrachi that imperfect Dad? Like Trump, Mizrachi delights in offensive provocation and dabbles in conspiracy theories. But unlike Trump, he offers a normative account of good behavior: to dress respectably, to cultivate good manners, to stay off drugs. The young men are loving it — because many of them have no one else to tell them these things.

Nikos Mohammadi is an academic fellow at UnHerd US.

scraped.title: Who will defend the stranglewankers?
scraped.author: Kathleen Stock
scraped.h1: Who will defend the stranglewankers? Censorship is becoming a lazy British habit
scraped.body_text:
'At the core of this proscription, then, is a fear about representation.' (Juno Baisla/EyeEm)

'At the core of this proscription, then, is a fear about representation.' (Juno Baisla/EyeEm)

How many feminists does it take to change a lightbulb? Answer: about a hundred or so, working together to chuck people who ignore faulty lightbulbs in jail. So ran my thoughts as I heard about the new anti-porn laws.

A quiet addition to the Crime and Policing Act has made pornographic images that depict realistic-looking acts of strangulation and suffocation illegal, along with images of adults pretending to be minors, or pretending to be engaged in incest (otherwise known as the immensely popular category of “fauxcest”). Several feminist organizations back the change as a good one for women generally. Controversy has erupted about the clauses pertaining to suffocation in particular; for it turns out that there are many creative ways to block the airways while on a porn shoot, and nobody really knows what is now allowed. But while definitions of criminality remain vague, the penalties cited are chillingly specific: up to five years imprisonment for producers and distributors, and two years for possession, including the retention of previously legal downloads.

As you might expect, these events have produced some sober and dignified online exchanges. Professional femdoms are complaining about the sudden censoring of their monetized content, and the Government’s failure yet again to back the small business owner. Incensed libertarians are speculating that the authorities might come for murder mysteries next, since these too depict dangerous activities not to be tried at home. Labour MP Jess Asato has unwisely weighed in on whether face-sitting counts as suffocation or not, while justice minister Alex Davies-Jones denies being a “modern day Mary Whitehouse”, urging all those engaged in “legal, safe, and consensual” sexual activity to “crack on”. Meanwhile the real Mary Whitehouses — namely, radical feminists — have been hurling the newly minted insult “stranglewanker” at anyone online who dares complain.

But I’m afraid there are several good reasons to feel concern about this law, without signaling undying commitment to the stranglewanking cause. You might dislike unclear, confusing criminal legislation; exactly the same goes for the draft Conversion Bill, attracting the righteous ire of many feminists at the moment. You might object to the practice of foisting late stage amendments onto existing bills, meaning they bypass the committee and/or report stages of scrutiny — the same tactic that recently brought us the decriminalization of late abortion without much discussion at all.

By Kathleen Stock

Alternatively, you might be worried about censorship on spurious “protective” grounds becoming a lazy Government habit: Spotify , YouTube Kids, eBay and Vinted are just some of the sites being mooted as off-limits for minors this week. Or perhaps you just don’t like the hypocrisy of clamping down on an erotic medium mostly used by men, while allowing women to keep enjoying books with titles like Taken By My Alpha Triplet Stepbrothers .

My own concern is partly about the infuriatingly high-handed strategy, and why some campaigners seem so happy to use coercion to get the changes in public morality they want. (One might even say that anti-porn feminists love a top-down directive, if it were not very dangerous to make such jokes.) Personally, I think porn is a spiritual blight on the soul. But it is also a mistake to have turned a set of common, easily committed, and widely tolerated private behaviors into imprisonable crimes from one day to the next — and even more so when the collapsing court system can barely accommodate graver offenses. Indeed, it seems deeply perverse for the Government to be making relatively new electronic offenses imprisonable, while including those with GBH and firearm convictions in early release schemes . Do they just want a less scary kind of prison inmate, or what?

Polling suggests there is broad support for some kind of ban of the images in question. Still, I am skeptical there will be much enthusiasm for punishing individual users once the details are properly grasped. The reception on Mumsnet has been distinctly mixed , and is likely to become more so when sentences on blindsided family members start being handed down. For it is hard to defend a law that means someone can be banged up for possession of an image, yet where no actual offense occurred in front of the camera; and especially where the viewer is also fully aware he is looking at pretense. Or to put it another way: if you enjoy role-playing of the kinds in question, and it is consensual and safe for all participants, Davies-Jones will tell you to crack on. If you film it for later use, she thinks you should be in jail.

That this is the case is clear from the drafting. To count as an offense, the depiction must be “realistic”: a similar sounding word to “real” but which usually implies the opposite. When you say that a piece of acting is realistic, you are signaling awareness of an element of pretense. Meanwhile the clause on fauxcest requires that a reasonable person, inspecting the image, would judge that the participants “were related or pretending to be related”; and similar wording is applied to depictions of sex involving adults pretending to be minors. In other words: the image is the crime, but not necessarily what it records. And the viewer can know perfectly well that no crime has been recorded, but only a feigned one; yet still be committing a crime by possessing the image at all.

At the core of this proscription, then, is a fear about representation, and not reality directly; about the supposedly harmful effects of pretending or fantasizing, using staged images as props. Campaigners tend to obscure this point by mixing up concern about the direct dangers of sexual role-playing behaviors for participants with suppositions about their indirect effects on viewers. It is true, for instance, that there are physical risks in what is referred to, horribly coyly, as “breath play”; and that the normalization of such practices provides a convenient criminal defense for violent males. But these points have no bearing on a separate argument, also emphasized: that performing make-believe versions of transgressive activities on camera encourages viewers to do them for real. That this is the complaint is underlined by the fact the new rules censor AI-generated images, involving no real people at all.

To this argument about causation of harm, critics reply that the evidence presented has been underwhelming so far; that most people can keep track of the distinction between fantasy and reality, even when props are realistic; and that feeling excitement while vividly imagining doing something does not mean you are actually tempted to do it. The question is complicated, and I’m not sure what I ultimately think. But — as the actress probably said to the bishop — wading in with a judicial cudgel and a Mommy-knows-best face is only likely to make the law look like an ass.

There is a growing trend here. This week, we also heard of politicians’ plans to get rid of webcamming for its links to sexual exploitation; and to install spyware into every phone in the name of combating child sexual abuse. Meanwhile, in the wake of Bralliams — the biggest double feature since Barbenheimer — there have been plenty of calls to change the legal age of consent. The general, basic-as-hell formula for action seems to be: allege some sort of eye-catching harm to a vulnerable group; then intimate you can magically reduce that harm, simply by banning or criminalizing something. (Alternatively, if the allegedly vulnerable group is the one being criminalized — as in late-term abortion — then use a simple sob story to get the howwible, mean penalty taken away.)

If your aim is criminalization, don’t worry about unintended consequences for civil liberties, or any other abstract matter. As no heart-rending story can be told about a favored set of victims here, nobody is going to care about those. And if you get objections or protests, smear the objectors as filthy perverts, or else construe the criticism as intolerable abuse. Repeat as necessary, then proceed smoothly to the King’s speech.

Arguably, the tendency to stitch up the law like this stands in inverse proportion to campaigners’ ability to persuade people to stop doing things by other means. This is not necessarily their fault. It is difficult to make a persuasive moral case against anything these days, thanks to decades of be-cool liberalism telling us that pretty much anything goes. Indeed, it is telling that even when campaigners are blatantly moralizing on behalf of a better deal for women — and nothing wrong with that — they like to pretend they are doing something science-y and objective. Ludicrous psychological studies involving word-association tasks are cited as revealing something about misogyny generally. Actively defining the limits of immoral sexual behavior is presented as countering “rape myths”, as if some historian were debunking medieval beliefs about the weather.

By John Maier

Thanks to said liberalism, there is also deep squeamishness about translating any knowledge of the sexual dangers women face into practical parenting measures; and particularly when it means laying down rules that the kids might not like. Enlightened mothers can no longer comfortably decree “you aren’t going out like that!” to a teenager venturing forth dressed only in knickers and a coat, for fear that some sort of autonomy-suppression or victim-blaming is going on. When your gormless 16-year-old says she is in love with a creepy comedian, it seems easier to lobby your MP about the age of consent than to take away her phone. In the wake of the gentle parenting revolution, we appear to need Big Brother more than ever.

If online discourse from this week is anything to go by, some anti-porn campaigners are likely to respond to my points here by suggesting I need my hard drive checked. They act like there are only two possible categories for behavior, illegal or positively good; and only one possible motive for arguing against illegality, secret approval. Probably in vain, my hope for these law fetishists is that they have their own lightbulb moment. The rumors are true — you really can hate something without immediately wanting to see it banned.

scraped.title: "A Deal For The World": Russian Diesel Exports Double Under Trump's Waiver, And America Gets None Of It
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: "A Deal For The World": Russian Diesel Exports Double Under Trump's Waiver, And America Gets None Of It
scraped.body_text:
Five weeks after Trump announced that Putin would "immediately" supply diesel to the "American and Global Marketplace," we can now check the receipts.

The global marketplace did fine. The American one got nothing.

According to the FT , citing Kpler data, Russia shipped 271,000 barrels a day of diesel in October, double the 135,000 b/d it exported in September . The extra barrels went to Brazil, Turkey and elsewhere. Meanwhile, not a single cargo generated by the sanctions waiver has reached a US port , two US-bound tankers have changed course, and the last one is idling off the East Coast waiting for someone, anyone, to buy it.

Regular readers know we have been tracking the diesel crisis since March , and we were skeptical of the Trump-Putin deal from the moment it hit the tape on Oct 9, mostly because of the arithmetic. It turns out the arithmetic was the least of the deal's problems.

First, the numbers. Kpler's tally is backed by Energy Aspects, whose head of geopolitics Richard Bronze told the FT that Russian diesel exports rose from 120,000 b/d in September to 260,000 b/d in October. That sounds impressive until you see the comparison he offered: the five-year average for October is roughly 700,000 b/d . In other words, Russia doubled its exports to barely a third of a normal October .

S&P Global's Commodities at Sea data tell the same story in tonnes: Russian diesel and gasoil loadings totaled 985,000 mt in October, against roughly 2.7 million mt in November 2025. Moscow says it wants to export about 2.15 million tonnes this month, though Deputy PM Alexander Novak himself conceded that renewed refinery strikes could cut that number. (We'll take the under.)

The White House, for its part, says that is all according to plan. A White House official told the FT that more Russian diesel on the global market will help ease prices for Americans, in line with the deal Trump struck with Putin:

“As the President has said, this is a deal for the world. This deal was made to add diesel supply to the global market — lowering prices for Americans and the world — which is exactly what will be done. ”

That is a convenient reading of a Truth Social post that promised diesel to the "American" marketplace first. Then again, diesel is a global commodity, and a barrel that lands in Santos is a barrel the Gulf Coast doesn't have to ship to Brazil, so the White House isn't entirely wrong. It is just a much less exciting claim than the one made on Oct 9:

*TRUMP SAYS PUTIN AGREED TO RELEASE DIESEL INTO GLOBAL MARKET

Then there is the US leg of the trade, which so far exists mostly on vessel-tracking screens.

As we reported on Oct 21 , the first US-bound cargo, the Malta-flagged Agioi Fanendes, loaded about 40,000 tonnes of ultra-low sulfur diesel at Primorsk on Oct 22 and signaled New York, due around Nov 7. Two more tankers, the Leruo and the Talisman, followed, for a combined ~140,000 tonnes. Then the lawyers showed up:

The result, as we noted on Nov 3 : the Leruo switched its destination to Brazil, the Talisman diverted into the Mediterranean , and the Agioi Fanendes changed its destination to "for orders." Per Bloomberg, it turned around roughly 400 nautical miles from New York; Reuters later found it halted off the East Coast, and the FT says it is still there, waiting for a buyer. The White House says negotiations with the vessel's owner are continuing, which is a remarkably candid way of saying nobody has bought it yet.

Meanwhile, the barrels that did leave Russia found homes quickly. Brazil has overtaken Turkey as the top destination for Russian diesel so far in November, per Bloomberg, which is also when we tweeted this:

Russia Fuel Flows Hit Four-Month High as Diesel Curbs Eased: BBG

Some perspective on what America is missing: the 40,000 tonnes aboard the Agioi Fanendes are roughly 300,000 barrels. The US burns about 4 million barrels of distillate a day, so the last US-bound cargo of Russian diesel covers less than two hours of American demand (napkin math, but not by much). Phillips 66's Brian Mandell said as much on his company's earnings call, calling Russian supply "a drop in the bucket" relative to how much distillate is offline.

Why did Russian exports double in the first place? Energy Aspects' Richard Bronze was blunt about what did the work: Russian refineries were able to ramp up because Ukraine paused its drone campaign. “If we want to attribute it, it would be the US pressure and Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire,” he said.

That pause is over. Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries resumed on Oct 30 after a two-week break , and on Oct 31 Moscow extended its diesel export ban yet again (it had already pushed it to Oct. 31 ), this time through the end of January, with exceptions carved out to keep the Trump deal alive on paper. Bronze told the FT he now expects Russian exports in the coming months to be very lackluster. Kpler's Sumit Ritolia added that Moscow will prioritize the home market, especially as it is now running short of gasoline and rationing it:

“Russian refinery operations remain under significant pressure. We expect them to remain constrained around 4mn b/d in the near term, with limited prospects for a meaningful recovery as attacks continue ,” he said.

Recall our point back on Oct 9: Russia's binding constraint is its refineries , and a six-month OFAC waiver doesn't fix a crude unit that was hit by a drone last week.

Goldman's numbers show just how big that refinery problem is. In its October commodity index commentary ( available to pro subs ), the bank's commodities desk wrote that distillate cracks traded a roughly $15/bbl range during the month on headlines about strategic stock releases, refinery strikes and, yes, Russian diesel exports, before laying out the damage:

Singapore middle-distillate stocks were down 44% year-on-year, while ARA jet-fuel stocks were down 56%. Refiners continued to prioritise diesel output, constraining the availability of other products. Persistent refinery damage continues to constrain product supply, with Middle East outages around 1.6mb/d above seasonal norms and Russian outages 4.2mb/d above seasonal norms. Planned global refinery maintenance was down 1.7mb/d, or 27%, year-on-year, largely driven by postponed US maintenance. Deferred maintenance was expected to prolong product supply weakness into 2027, with planned maintenance rising sharply in Q2.

Put differently, Russian refinery outages alone are running about 4.2 million b/d above seasonal norms , a hole that dwarfs October's entire 271,000 b/d of diesel exports. Goldman's Asia refining team (in " Asia Refining: Robust 2027 margins even in near-term de-escalation scenarios ", also available to pro subs ) models combined Middle East and Russian outages as peaking near 7 million b/d this summer, and in its baseline they don't normalize until December 2027:

Which brings us to the punchline, at least for anyone hoping that a diesel deal (or a peace deal) delivers cheap fuel by spring.

Goldman's base case says the global refining system stays tight well into 2027 even in a scenario where every Middle East and Russian outage magically disappears in January, as Goldman's Jerry Shen summarized the bank's Asia refining team's work in a note to clients ( available to pro subs ):

Surprisingly, even in the most aggressive normalization scenario—where Middle East and Russian refinery outages completely vanish by January 2027—GIR still models the 2027E Singapore gross refining margin (GRM) at a highly profitable $19/bbl. To put that into perspective, the historical mid-cycle average is just $10/bbl. Under their baseline scenario, margins surge to $33/bbl.

In other words, Goldman's best case for refining margins is still almost double the historical mid-cycle , and the reason is mundane: product inventories have built far less than crude. Singapore middle-distillate stocks are down 44% y/y, per the desk, and the US is in worse shape. As we reported earlier this month, US diesel inventories slid below 100 million barrels for the first time since 2003.

There is also a timing problem nobody is talking about. Refiners postponed this fall's maintenance to run flat out, so global planned maintenance is down 27% y/y, which means a lot of it lands next spring. Goldman expects 2027Q2 maintenance to be especially elevated, with Russia and the Middle East running near seasonal norms while Asia ex-China runs about 50% above its normal level:

Translation: the next diesel squeeze is already on the calendar , and it doesn't need a single drone to happen. No wonder the global diesel crunch is set to last well into 2027 .

So where does that leave the diesel deal? Probably about where the skeptics put it on day one. Russia got a sanctions waiver through April 7 and a political win; Brazil and Turkey got the barrels; and US consumers got the indirect benefit of a few hundred thousand extra barrels a day sloshing around a global market that is short several million. AAA had pump diesel around $6.29 a gallon at the start of November, down from the $6.50+ record in September , which has a lot more to do with Iran headlines than with anything leaving Primorsk.

Could the White House still be right that the world gets a bit more diesel and Americans pay a bit less? Sure, at the margin. But with Ukraine back to hitting refineries, Moscow rationing its own gasoline, and Goldman modeling a tight product market into 2027 even in the rosiest scenario, the more likely outcome is that Russian exports fade back toward "lackluster" just as US inventories hit multi-decade lows . Relief, if it comes, will come from Hormuz and from refiners' maintenance calendars, not from the Kremlin.

And the Agioi Fanendes? Last seen idling off the East Coast, carrying less than two hours of American demand that nobody is allowed to buy. A deal for the world indeed.

Much more in the full Goldman " Asia Refining " note and the GS commodities desk's October commentary, both available to pro subs .

scraped.title: This Case Is Insane...
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: This Case Is Insane...
scraped.body_text:
Authored by Steve Watson via Modernity ,

In Britain's two-tier policing system, law-abiding citizens who try to report real dangers now risk prosecution for private mutterings inside their own vehicles , while actual criminals face little consequence.

A Glasgow father handed over dashcam footage after nearly being forced off the road, only for Police Scotland to charge him instead.

The case, detailed by Free Speech Union general secretary Toby Young in The Spectator , centers on a man referred to as Craig. He was driving his four-year-old son home to Glasgow after a day at an amusement park in Falkirk. Exiting the motorway, another vehicle cut him up, forcing him to swerve to avoid a collision. Suspecting the other driver was drunk, Craig called the police from his car. Both vehicles stopped; officers arrived, declined to breathalyze anyone, and took Craig's dashcam footage to check for offenses .

?? FSU VICTORY! A Scottish FSU member was driving on the M80 with his four-year-old son after a day at an amusement park when another car cut him up, nearly causing a collision. Under his breath, he muttered something racist. The windows were down, but the other driver wasn't looking at him. The only witness was his young son in the back seat. Convinced the dangerous driver had been drinking, our member contacted the police. They eventually stopped both cars and reviewed his dashcam footage. A week later, the police contacted him to say that an offence had been committed - not by the dangerous driver, but by our member, for words he had muttered under his breath in the privacy of his own car. He was prosecuted for allegedly causing alarm and distress, even though only he and his young son were in the car. It is extraordinary. The Free Speech Union found him an excellent barrister, and he was acquitted by the Justice of the Peace within minutes. This is the closest we have come to defending someone prosecuted for thought crime. This is the extent of police overreach in speech and thought policing. They need to get their priorities straight. Watch the Free Speech Union's General Secretary, Lord Young, below ?

— The Free Speech Union (@SpeechUnion) November 12, 2026

A week later the officers returned the footage and informed him an offense had been committed - by him, not the other driver .

His "crime" was muttering the words "smelly black bastard" under his breath seconds after the near-miss.

As the article notes, the windows were closed, so no one outside the vehicle could have heard him . The other driver was not looking in his direction and could not have seen the words. The only person who might have heard was the four-year-old in the back.

The bizarre story of the man charged with 'threatening or abusive behaviour' with a racial aggravator for muttering to himself. In his car. https://t.co/lvmFg9JTDr

— Stephen Knight ?? (@GSpellchecker) November 12, 2026

The sole evidence was the dashcam Craig had voluntarily supplied in the hope of seeing the dangerous driver brought to justice.

Craig asked the officer reading him his rights: "How could you charge me for saying it in my car?" He added: "I was saying it to myself." The officer replied: "The language was still racist."

He was charged with "threatening or abusive behaviour" with a racial aggravator and faced court.

Young described the episode as "a near-perfect illustration of 'anarcho-tyranny,' a phrase often used to describe contemporary Britain in which law-abiding responsible citizens are persecuted and criminals go unpunished."

To secure a conviction for "threatening or abusive" behavior under the relevant Scottish law, the Crown must show the conduct would be likely to cause a reasonable person fear or alarm and that the accused intended that outcome or was reckless as to whether it would occur.

Because Craig spoke only to himself, with no realistic possibility of anyone outside the car hearing or being alarmed, he was found not guilty. The Free Speech Union, which has handled more than 7,000 cases since 2020, defended him.

Young put the resource waste in context: in Glasgow four out of five burglaries go unsolved, and there were 11 car thefts per 10,000 people in the year to June 2026. "In the Yookay," he concluded, "trying to bring criminals to justice is far more likely to get you into trouble than breaking the law."

This is not an isolated curiosity. The same forces that pursued private words in a sealed car have, as previously documented, treated people merely standing in public spaces as a "dangerous new threat."

Officers have threatened arrest for filming in public places on the grounds that the presence "might" wind someone up, or for simply existing in a square while actual violent crime elsewhere draws less urgency.

The pattern sits alongside other high-profile overreaches. Graham Linehan, the Father Ted writer, described stepping off a flight at Heathrow to find five armed officers waiting: "Not one, not two - five. They escorted me to a private area and told me I was under arrest for three tweets."

He noted the contrast with a country "where paedophiles escape sentencing, where knife crime is out of control," yet the state mobilized armed officers for social-media posts. Young cited the Linehan arrest as the supposed low point before the car-muttering case showed it was not.

Two further FSU cases involving the word "pikey" illustrate the same selectivity. In one, a mother on a country lane in Cambridgeshire called 999 while two men abused her 14-year-old daughter; she used the term during the call.

Police took no action against the men but threatened her with a hate-crime charge unless she attended a racial-awareness course.

In another, a Hampshire special constable with decades of service was dismissed after a private WhatsApp message to his then-boyfriend about locking doors to "keep the pikeys out"; the ex later complained. Privacy arguments failed at the Police Appeals Tribunal.

The Craig prosecution fits the broader picture of police energy directed at private speech and non-crime "hate" while clearance rates for burglary and vehicle crime remain abysmal.

Citizens who install dashcams and cooperate with police in the hope of accountability for dangerous driving discover that the footage can be turned against them for words never directed at anyone and never heard outside the vehicle .

The officer's response - "The language was still racist" - reveals the priority: the content of the thought itself, not any public effect or risk of alarm.

Britain's police forces have repeatedly demonstrated that they will expend significant time and court resources on private remarks that cause no fear or alarm to any reasonable person outside the speaker's immediate family, while large volumes of property crime go unsolved.

The not-guilty verdict in Craig's case was the only sane outcome; the decision to charge him in the first place was not .

scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: Watch: Greta Laughs Off The Climate Kids She Left Behind For Gaza
scraped.body_text:
Greta Thunberg burst out laughing on camera when told that the climate movement she founded was still holding demonstrations , in a 27-second scene from a new German documentary that has ricocheted across X this week. She launched the Fridays for Future school strikes as a 15-year-old in 2018.

The clip comes from Auf Panzern in die Klimakrise ("On Tanks Into The Climate Crisis"), a 100-minute independent film by German YouTuber and filmmaker Hubertus Koch. Meeting Thunberg in Berlin, Koch tells her it is "kind of symbolic" that their interview fell on the day of a Fridays for Future demonstration in the city.

"Is it?" Thunberg asks, before dissolving into loud laughter. "Really?" When Koch says yes, she follows up: "They still do that?"

Schaut mal wie Greta Thunberg euch auslacht XD pic.twitter.com/0KgBR3ru1i

The companions laughing along at the table were Hebh Jamal and Judith Scheytt, who sailed with Thunberg on the Gaza flotilla, according to Apollo News , which reported that the scene was shot at a Palestinian café in Berlin. Visegrad 24's post of the clip alone drew more than 380,000 views within a day.

Koch's film is built on the argument that the climate movement didn't fizzle out on its own but was crushed by police, prosecutors and the press, and is now coming back as an anti-war movement, per a write-up of the documentary. In the film, Thunberg says she didn't take up protest to save trees or frogs but for justice and equality , and her focus is now fighting capitalism, Apollo News reported.

In Germany, where Fridays for Future still marches, the movement's best-known face shrugged it off. Luisa Neubauer said she stays focused on the cause and won't be distracted , and told Welt TV that activists don't have to agree on everything, including forms of protest and narratives, Tagesspiegel reported. The split is not new: German Fridays for Future distanced itself from Thunberg in 2023 over her posts on Gaza after the Hamas attack on Israel, t-online reported at the time.

Since then, Thunberg's activism has run mostly through the Palestinian cause . She was detained by Israeli forces aboard a Gaza-bound aid boat in June 2025, after which she said she had been "kidnapped" , and again when Israel intercepted the Global Sumud Flotilla in October 2025; Israel dismissed reports that she was abused in custody as "brazen lies." In December, as we reported, she was arrested in the City of London under the Terrorism Act for holding a placard supporting jailed Palestine Action activists, a group Britain has banned as a terrorist organization.

The clip landed the same week Thunberg returned to the UN climate talks for the first time since Glasgow in 2021, where she waved off world leaders' promises as "blah, blah, blah." Arriving at COP31 in the Turkish resort city of Antalya on Tuesday, she called the summit a hypocrisy : "It's a hypocrisy every year that the host countries are given an opportunity to whitewash themselves and we know that these negotiations are filled with lobbyists, paid by the very destructive industries which are benefiting from our extremely violent status quo," she said .

Climate activist Greta Thunberg emphasized the need to prioritize people and the planet over profits as she arrived at the U.N. climate meeting in Turkey. This year’s Conference of the Parties, or COP31, follows a year of climate-induced disasters. pic.twitter.com/6eO7jko18e

She also called for an oil embargo against Israel and "justice for Kurdistan" (translated) at the summit, according to Tagesspiegel. The talks, co-hosted by Turkey and Australia, run until Nov. 20.

Climate change, Thunberg told reporters in Antalya, is "threatening everything" - "everything and everyone we love is at stake."

scraped.body_text:
Get woke, go broke.

Cosmetics giant Maybelline is at it again and waging a new war on women.

After decades of selling products to women (and happily taking their money), Maybelline is now erasing women from its iconic tagline.

For more than three decades, Maybelline used its iconic tagline in all of its advertising campaigns: “Maybe she’s born with it, maybe it’s Maybelline.”

The cosmetics giant changed its tagline from “she” to “we” — “Maybe we’re born with it” – to exclude women.

“At Maybelline, “Maybe” means possibility. We believe everyone is born with infinite possibility. It’s not a question about what you could be; it’s a statement about all you can become. A new shade, a different look, a new mood, makeup can help you explore what feels possible, express yourself and feel more confident,” the company said on its website .

“Maybe. Is in our DNA,” Maybelline said.

After 35 years, Maybelline is giving one of beauty’s most recognizable slogans a makeover.

The brand is moving away from its famous “Maybe she’s born with it. Maybe it’s Maybelline” tagline, shifting from “she” to “we” with a new message about identity and possibility.

“MAYBE. IS IN OUR DNA,” the company says, adding that everyone is born with the potential to become anyone they choose.

Download the Fox News app or go to https://t.co/gPHiho5zni for more.

— Fox News (@FoxNews) November 12, 2026

Maybelline received intense backlash from women.

“Trying to erase women is a sure way to erase your brand,” one social media user said.

“Well then maybe “WE” won’t be buying any of their products,” another said.

“Maybe “It’s” Born With It. Maybe women should boycott the brand,” a social media user said.

“Get woke, go broke,” another said.

Maybelline’s new woke tagline comes after it ran a ‘bearded beauty’ campaign in which the cosmetics giant featured a bearded man using their products.
