scraped.body_text:
An illegal alien semi-truck driver has been charged with three counts of involuntary manslaughter after causing a deadly crash in Kansas City, Missouri, earlier this week.

Ukrainian national Eldar Skander, 39, was charged on Wednesday with three counts of involuntary manslaughter in the deaths of a mother and her two young sons.

According to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Skander entered the country illegally during the Biden administration. ICE has placed a detainer on him.

According to court records, Skander was driving a white Volvo semi‑truck at a high rate of speed Monday afternoon and failed to slow for congested traffic. He struck a Honda Odyssey carrying the Sorbalo family, killing Olga Sorbalo, 35, and her sons Luis, 8, and Samir, 4. Olga’s husband and their youngest child reportedly suffered critical injuries.

The collision triggered a chain‑reaction crash involving multiple vehicles and causing additional critical injuries.

A police investigation found a tablet in the cab was open to YouTube and no sign of braking before impact.

Skander, who lives in Chicago, is currently held on a $150,000 cash‑only bond and also under an ICE detainer.

“Reckless open-border policies have resulted in countless preventable tragedies,” ICE said in a statement.

“Three more innocent American lives were lost. Two children who will never get to grow up, and a mother who will never get to watch them grow.

These deaths were tragic and preventable. No other family should have to endure this loss. This is our WHY.”

scraped.h1: Home Sales Dropped In October to Their Lowest Level Since 2010
scraped.body_text:
Sales of existing homes in the U.S. dropped 5.5 percent in October to their lowest level in 16 years, after spending the last 4 years hovering at low levels.

The National Association of Realtors (NAR) reported that sales of existing homes fell during October, to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 8.8 percent–the lowest level since the subprime crisis era in 2010.

🇺🇸 U.S. existing home sales falls to lowest level since 2010 https://t.co/h33JXW8s9z

— Hedgeye (@Hedgeye) November 12, 2026

NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement , “Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023. As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010.”

Zero Hedge reports that Yun sounded an optimistic note that most of the country’s 88 million homeowners remain comfortable thanks to accumulated equity and that “there could be sizable pent-up demand if mortgage rates decline.”

Total house inventory was 1.59 million units, up from 1.3 percent from September and 4.6 percent from October 2025.

The unsold inventory represented a 5.1-month supply, which was up 4.7 months in September and up from 4.4 months in October 2025, according to NAR.

Meanwhile, the median existing-home price for all housing types was $416,700, an increase of 0.4 percent from one year ago, making it the 40th consecutive month of year-over-year price increases.

Higher financing costs are pushing monthly payments out of reach for many prospective buyers with 30-year fixed mortgage rates hovering above 7% and hitting nearly a three-year high.

The NAR reports that month-over-month sales dropped across the Midwest, South, and West. Activity held steady only in the Northeast.

Contract signings—a forward-looking indicator of closed sales—slumped 7.3 percent in September to a record low on the National Association of Realtors index.

The trend has shifted buyer leverage as active listings have grown while seller demand softens, resulting in widespread price cuts and builder incentives, according to Realtor.com.

The U.S. housing market took another leg down in October.

With existing sales hitting their lowest level since 2010.

3.75M annualized sales took place in Oct 2026, which is down 44% from the pandemic peak.

Adjusted for the size of the housing stock, demand is in its biggest depression ever. (worse than post-2008)

The reason sales are so low is because homebuyers have no interest in paying record prices at 7% mortgage rates.

Sellers need to get the memo: cut the price, or else your house will sit.

To track sales in your market, search your ZIP: https://t.co/NCo5SoC0G0

— Nick Gerli (@nickgerli1) November 12, 2026

scraped.body_text:
Good Friday morning.

Here is what’s on president Trump’s agenda today:

8:00 AM THE PRESIDENT participates in Executive Time

12:30 PM THE PRESIDENT participates in a Policy Meeting

3:00 PM THE PRESIDENT participates in a Policy Meeting

4:00 PM THE PRESIDENT participates in a Policy Meeting

4:30 PM THE PRESIDENT participates in a Policy Meeting

Two minutes of hate:

Stephen Miller has been chief of staff for four days, and K Street is already wailing and lamenting. A memo from his office, first obtained by Politico , says White House staff now need sign-off from the White House Counsel before meeting with a registered lobbyist about policy.

A dozen GOP lobbyists told Politico that Miller will be hard to work with. One called him impossible to lobby. Another complained that he’s insular, with relationships only among the ideological true believers. In Washington, that counts as a scandal.

Look at who he’s replacing. Susie Wiles built her career at Ballard Partners and Mercury Public Affairs before running the White House. Ballard is on pace to clear more than $100 million this year, more than four times what it made in 2020. This week Brian Ballard had to publicly deny that his firm enjoyed improper access to his old colleague. Wiles’s daughter is a partner at another lobbying shop named in the same accusations. Everyone involved denies wrongdoing. If it looks like a revolving door and swings like a revolving door, it’s a revolving door.

In Washington D.C everyone is doing their current job, in the service of their next job.

Miller’s financial disclosures show two outside paychecks since the first term, both from organizations he founded. No K Street retainer. No firm holding a corner office for him on the way out.

The lobbyists’ complaint boils down to this: he decides based on policy outcomes supporting the president’s agenda rather than relationships. A Ballard lobbyist who worked with him said exactly that, and meant it as a warning. It’s the most flattering thing anyone in this town has said about a chief of staff in years.

The memo itself is modest. Get approval first. Route outside requests through the Office of Public Liaison. It’s a speed bump. If a speed bump has caused this much hand-wringing you can imagine how much traffic was on the road.

Some lobbyists already have a plan B. Skip Miller, work the Domestic Policy Council and the National Economic Council, or try to call the president directly. A Fortune 500 lobbyist told Politico the goal for the next two years is avoiding land mines rather than hitting home runs. That’s the sound of an industry discovering the front door is locked.

See you at the White House Christmas party, K Street. Bring your counsel’s approval.

scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/140738092630206
scraped.h1: Secretive US military agency announces giant leap toward mega-structures in space
scraped.body_text:
America has unlocked in-orbit construction that 'can scale to your imagination.'

A U.S. defense agency says it has accomplished what has never been done before in outer space and that it didn't need advanced artificial intelligence to do it.

The landmark event is being called a historic first and could mean rapid expansion for the United States in (or out) of the Earth's orbit.

'Good old-fashioned rigorous engineering.'

Four years into its NOM4D space program, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency has demonstrated an outstanding capability it says is the first of its kind.

With the help of advanced engineers from the California Institute of Technology, DARPA says it is the first agency to autonomously build a structure in space.

The inaugural moment was achieved using Caltech's Autonomous In-Space Tensioned Reflector Assembly robotics system, which ScienceDaily described as an automated arm that assembled structural tubes and joints from storage dispensers into repeating sections that form a truss .

Even more impressive, the team at DARPA said the project was completed without the use of advanced artificial intelligence models (or astronauts) and was simply a product of "good old-fashioned rigorous engineering."

The ASTRA builder was launched with two pre-built bays , the lab explained, with a third bay built by the system in orbit. Photos captured by one of the 11 on-board cameras showed additional composite fiber tubes and "netlike reflective material," Caltech stated.

RELATED: Vanderbilt hackers claim a MILLION Social Security numbers stolen — as seething students beg for answers

"This is the first time that a structure has been autonomously constructed in space," said Sergio Pellegrino, senior research scientist at Caltech's jet propulsion laboratory. "Developing a payload of this complexity on such a short timeline was an enormous undertaking for our small team," he added.

NOM4D program manager Andrew Detor boasted about the program's future capabilities to scale at large, adding to Caltech's claim that the team has demonstrated the feasibility of the concept.

"This approach that the Caltech team is taking can scale to your imagination. It can scale to very, very large things. They've done it in a way that is really elegant," Detor said.

For comparison, Detor explained that current approaches had modular structures being built on Earth and sent into space over "many, many launches," including the International Space Station that took "over 40 launches to build up its roughly 100-meter size."

RELATED: Beware: The top AI detector is now shockingly good — even at video

NOM4D refers to the defense agency's Novel Orbital and Moon Manufacturing, Materials, and Mass-efficient Design program, with the stated goal of manufacturing and assembling enormous structures in space.

These structures are meant to be "precise, mass-efficient" space structures that withstand "maneuvers, eclipses, damage, and thermal cycles inherent to the space environment."

The project began in 2022 with the intent of eventually ferrying "raw materials from Earth for in-orbit manufacturing," which has now seemingly been accomplished.

The latest demonstration served as the third phase on the project timeline, with the first being the development and design of the concept, followed by a demonstration in Earth settings.

scraped.h1: Suicide toll at NSA and US Cyber Command hits 11 — with 5 in just one month: Report
scraped.body_text:
A disturbing 'cluster' of suicides has rocked America's highly isolated national security workplaces.

A recent string of suicides at government agencies has the White House's attention, a recent report claims.

The cluster of deaths came just months after a series of disappearances and deaths tied to U.S. space and nuclear programs were reported.

... working in isolated environments inside secured, windowless facilities.

At the National Security Agency and United States Cyber Command, both located in Fort Meade, Maryland, at least 11 workers have died by suicide in about a year's time.

A recent report cited public records and unnamed U.S. officials who spoke under the condition that they not be identified.

During one specific period — early June to early July — Bloomberg reports that there was a "suicide cluster," with five employees from the NSA and Cyber Command taking their own lives.

Subsequent alleged suicides included a 21-year-old Army soldier and a 59-year-old civilian contractor working for the NSA in September. A government official, allegedly familiar with their employment, confirmed the situation, speaking anonymously because the official was not authorized to discuss the matter.

These deaths reportedly prompted White House and congressional staff to question the agency leaders behind closed doors, and seemingly to order military officials to better monitor working hours and the toll it takes on employees. Apparent details included mental health support to government employees working in intelligence and hacking, whose workloads have allegedly surged due to foreign conflicts.

RELATED: Speculation mounts over mysterious deaths and disappearances tied to US space and nuclear program

Brooks Kraft LLC/Corbis/Getty Images

In a follow-up report , spokespersons for the government agencies told Bloomberg that they take a "comprehensive, integrated approach to suicide prevention" with the various armed services.

The officials said they have been working with other parts of the military to "ensure there is embedded care in our secure workspaces."

Contributing factors to the deaths were characterized in the reports as including long, strenuous work hours that involve largely classified tasks, while working in isolated environments inside secured, windowless facilities.

RELATED: 'I'm not suicidal': Rep. Burchett says US would fall apart if we heard truth about UFOs

SAUL LOEB/AFP/Getty Images

In April, Blaze News reported on eight dead or missing personnel who were linked to space and nuclear activities within the United States government.

This included a contractor who was working at a national security campus, a former Air Force Research Laboratory major general, and a rocket scientist, all of whom went missing.

Among the dead were a German-born rocket scientist, a Caltech astrophysicist, and a director of Plasma Science and Fusion at MIT. The latter was assassinated.

scraped.h1: VIDEO: Stephen A. Smith says he's making his teen daughter do one thing before she can support socialist Mamdani
scraped.body_text:
Smith had a debate with Trevor Noah on his podcast about the free-market capitalist system.

Sports commentator Stephen A. Smith appeared incensed that his teenage daughter supports socialist New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D), and he has a plan to dissuade her.

Smith made the comments on the "What Now?" podcast episode that published Thursday after host Trevor Noah asked him to defend the free-market capitalist system in the U.S.

'I want to see what you say then. Yeah, Nyla, I’m talking about you! I can’t wait because I ain’t having it!'

Smith said that he opposes socialism based on his paying between 50 and 60 percent of his paycheck for a government that doesn't work well. Then he said his daughter supports Mamdani.

"My daughter loves Mamdani. And I know exactly why: 'cause she ain’t pay a damn bill yet. She ain't pay a damn bill!" he said.

Noah and co-host Eugene Khoza burst out in laughter.

"I knew you were gonna say that," Noah responded.

"She ain’t pay a damn bill. Let me tell you, she’s about to turn 18. And when that happens, fellas, she’s going to have a job," he continued.

"Amen!" said Khoza.

"I don’t give a damn if it’s for a month. ’Cause I want to see her face when she sees that check," said Smith.

"And I’m going to make sure she’s working in New York. I want to see the check. You understand? When you went to work thinking that this is the money that you were earning, and then the check comes home, and more than half your s**t is missing," he added.

"I want to see what you say then," Smith said. "Yeah, Nyla, I’m talking about you. I can’t wait because I ain’t having it!"

The exchange was light-hearted and comical, but Smith and Noah also debated the merits of socialism as opposed to the free-market capitalist system.

Noah pushed back and claimed that all of the great things America introduced to the world were socialistic in nature. Smith defended the free-market system and excoriated socialists who claim to support the community but fail to actually help their constituents.

RELATED: Stephen A. Smith apologizes 5 years later for saying vaccine skepticism made player look 'flat-out stupid'

Smith also expressed extreme skepticism in all politicians, claiming politicians are a major reason to oppose socialism.

"I don't like none of your asses. I don't believe none of y'all!" he exclaimed.

He also said that he gave up on the possibility of running for president in 2028, even though he thinks he could win, after being told he would have to be immediately pulled off the air and lose his paycheck as soon as he announced a run because of FCC rules.

items.title: Hakim Adi’s “Pan-Africanism and Communism”: A pro-Stalinist attempt to erase the Trotskyist alternative — Part Eleven
items.summary: This is the eleventh and concluding part of a series reviewing British historian Hakim Adi’s book on the Communist International and Africa. It examines how the book erases Leon Trotsky’s role in founding the International and his theory of Permanent Revolution.

scraped.title: Hakim Adi’s “Pan-Africanism and Communism”: A pro-Stalinist attempt to erase the Trotskyist alternative — Part Eleven
scraped.description: This is the eleventh and concluding part of a series reviewing British historian Hakim Adi’s book on the Communist International and Africa. It examines how the book erases Leon Trotsky’s role in founding the International and his theory of Permanent Revolution.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
This is the eleventh and concluding part of a series responding to British-based historian Hakim Adi’s recently republished book, Pan-Africanism and Communism: The Communist International, Africa, and the Diaspora, 1919–1939.

[ Part One ] [ Part Two ] [ Part Three ] [ Part Four ] [ Part Five ] [ Part Six ] [ Part Seven ] [ Part Eight ] [ Part Nine ] [ Part Ten ] [ Part Eleven ] Against the Post-Soviet School of Falsification: Recovering the Trotskyist Alternative

Hakim Adi's dishonest Pan-Africanism and Communism is part of a broader trend in contemporary academic writing that selectively appropriates socialism to give revolutionary credentials to Pan-Africanism, post-independence states, and petty-bourgeois nationalist movements on the continent.

In his epilogue, Adi declares that the Comintern's approach to the Negro Question had 'a lasting impact not least on the wider Pan-African movement'. He identifies the 1945 Manchester Pan-African Congress as a major expression of this influence, citing its focus on the 'masses' as the driving force of the anti-colonial struggle. He notes that its participants included George Padmore, I. T. A. Wallace-Johnson, Jomo Kenyatta and others formerly associated with the Comintern and its International Trade Union Committee of Negro Workers (ITUCNW). [ 1 ]

But what did the Fifth Pan Afican Congress held in Manchester produce? Organised principally by Padmore and Kwame Nkrumah, with W. E. B. Du Bois presiding, it brought together trade unionists, anti-colonial activists, and future leaders of independent African states. Its declarations demanded an end to colonial rule and called upon workers and peasants to organise through strikes and boycotts. Among its participants were Nkrumah, subsequently Ghana's first president; Kenyatta, Kenya's first president; and Hastings Banda, who established an authoritarian regime in Malawi.

The ascendancy of Pan-Africanism within the anti-colonial movements of the late 1950s and early 1960s took place under definite historical conditions. The international working class had suffered devastating defeats through fascism and Stalinist counterrevolution, while its established organisations in the imperialist centres remained under the political domination of reformist and Stalinist bureaucracies. The postwar economic boom had provided the basis for a period of relative capitalist stabilisation, reinforcing the grip of these bureaucracies over the working class. The revolutionary traditions of the early Communist International had been suppressed, and the Fourth International confronted the immense political consequences of Stalinism's destruction of revolutionary leadership.

Under these conditions, bourgeois nationalist movements were able to present formal independence and state-directed capitalist development as the culmination of the struggle against imperialism. Within two decades, these figures had assumed political power. Nkrumah pursued state-led economic development under the banner of “African Socialism”, Kenyatta became a darling of the West as he looted the country, while Banda established a brutal dictatorship. None overcame the domination of imperialism.

Yet Adi's falsification of the Comintern reflects a broader rehabilitation of the political traditions that dominated Africa following formal independence.

In Socialist De-Colony: Black and Soviet Entanglements in Ghana's Cold War (2025), Nana Osei-Opare presents Nkrumah's Ghana as a socialist state and seeks to establish the Leninist credentials of its capitalist economic programme. Osei-Opare argues that Nkrumah's encouragement of foreign investment and private enterprise followed the precedent of Lenin's New Economic Policy (NEP) of the early 1920s. But the NEP was a tactical retreat carried out by the workers' state established through the October Revolution. Nkrumah's policies were pursued by a bourgeois nationalist government that preserved capitalist property relations. Osei-Opare uses the Bolsheviks’ temporary concessions to capitalism under proletarian rule to theoretically justify capitalist development under bourgeois nationalist leadership.

Adam Mayer carries this rehabilitation of nationalism and Stalinism into the domain of military rule. His Military Marxism: Africa's Contribution to Revolutionary Theory, 1957–2023 (2025) argues that bourgeois military-led regimes across the continent are a distinctively African contribution to Marxist revolutionary theory. Mayer constructs a historical lineage from Nkrumah's writings on guerrilla warfare and the nationalist movements of the 1960s to the self-proclaimed “Marxist-Leninist” military dictatorships of Mengistu Haile Mariam in Ethiopia and Siad Barre in Somalia, alongside the military-led government of Thomas Sankara in Burkina Faso. Military Marxism, he claims, is the very “backbone” of Africa's socialist tradition. He argues that those seeking revolutionary change must abandon what he calls their “formalistic frames of mind when it comes to democracy.”

Leon Trotsky (1879-1940), was the co-leader of the 1917 Russian Revolution, socialist opponent of Joseph Stalin, founder of the Fourth International, and strategist of world socialist revolution.

Such falsifications occur amid the resurgence of military coups in West Africa, with the juntas in Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger having exploited widespread hostility to French imperialism and the corrupt, pro-imperialist regimes they overthrew. Their anti-imperialist rhetoric, denunciations of Western domination, and invocations of Thomas Sankara have generated considerable illusions among workers and youth, who see these military officers as champions of African national liberation and social transformation.

Mayer intervenes directly in this political climate. He hails the emergence of “popular military governments,” describes junta-ruled Niger as “revolutionary Niger,” and insists that these movements possess a “genuine Marxist theory” and an intellectual tradition rooted in Africa's anti-colonial struggles. He declares that “armies also represent working-class agency,” arguing that military forces can represent the interests of workers and peasants. Mayer appropriates Marxism to confer revolutionary credentials on bourgeois military rule.

This revisionism is not confined to Africa. In Britain, the US and other imperialist countries, it forms part of a decades-long ideological offensive against Marxism, in which the centrality of class struggle has been displaced by racial, ethnic and other forms of identity. Such conceptions serve to divide the working class and provide ideological prop for imperialism, while privileged layers of the middle class present themselves as representatives of the oppressed.

The dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991 did not signify the failure of Marxism. It was the culmination of the nationalist and counterrevolutionary programme of Stalinism, vindicating Trotsky's analysis of the Soviet Union as a degenerated workers' state. Trotsky insisted that the working class could save the gains of October only through a political revolution to overthrow the bureaucracy and extend the 1917 socialist revolution internationally. Without this, the Soviet Union would regress to capitalism. The Stalinist bureaucracy's 1991 restoration of capitalism confirmed Trotsky’s theory of permanent revolution: the socialist revolution could not be completed within the USSR under the nationalist program of “socialism in a single country”. As new generations enter struggle across Africa, we must return to Trotsky’s struggle to recover the only theoretical and political framework capable of explaining the twentieth century's victories and defeats, and arming the working class for the struggles of the twenty-first.

The Fourth International, founded by Trotsky in 1938, and represented today by the International Committee of the Fourth International, remains the sole embodiment of this programme — based on the fight against Stalinism, social democracy and bourgeois nationalism, and the perspective of world socialist revolution — is the indispensable foundation of revolutionary struggle in the 21st century.

But the conditions facing the African working class are not those of the early 1960s. Decades of capitalist development, urbanisation and the global integration of production have created a powerful, youthful proletariat across the continent, tied through countless economic and social connections to workers in the imperialist centres. Africa's mines, factories, ports, transport networks and agricultural industries form part of an international system of production dominated by the same banks, corporations and financial institutions that exploit workers throughout the world.

The deepening crisis of world capitalism is bringing these objective connections increasingly into the open. Across Africa, workers and youth are entering into struggle against austerity, unemployment, dictatorship and imperialist domination. In Europe, too, strikes, demonstrations and mass protests are developing against declining living standards, cuts on public services, militarism and war. These struggles are unfolding alongside one another on an unprecedented international scale.

Africa is simultaneously becoming a central arena in the intensifying struggle for the redivision of the world. The US and European imperialist powers, confronting the expanding economic influence of China, are competing for control over the continent's resources, markets, transport corridors and military positions. Africa's immense reserves of oil, gas, cobalt, copper, lithium and other critical minerals are indispensable to global industrial production and the expanding war industries. The growing struggle over access to these resources threatens to draw the continent ever more deeply into the military and geopolitical conflicts between the major powers.

There is no programme of national capitalist development, no alliance with one or another imperialist power, and no scheme for a united capitalist Africa that can resolve this crisis. The African bourgeoisie, bound to international finance capital is incapable of carrying through the struggle for genuine liberation from imperialism.

The alternative is the Trotskyist perspective of the United Socialist States of Africa, as an integral part of the world socialist revolution. This requires the independent mobilisation of the working class, drawing behind it the oppressed rural masses, the overthrow of capitalist rule, and the revolutionary unification of the continent across the borders imposed by colonialism. The banks, mines, plantations and major industries must be placed under democratic workers' control so that Africa's immense resources can be directed towards meeting social needs rather than enriching the corporations and ruling elites.

Such a transformation cannot be achieved within the confines of Africa alone. The struggle for socialism on the continent must be united with that of workers in Europe, the United States and throughout the world. This is the essential content of Trotsky's theory of permanent revolution, which rejected the Stalinist subordination of the working class to the national bourgeoisie and insisted that the struggle for democratic and national liberation was inseparable from the fight for workers' power and international socialist revolution.

The decisive task is therefore the revival of revolutionary Marxism in Africa. This demands a conscious reckoning with the crimes and betrayals of Stalinism, the recovery of the revolutionary heritage of the October Revolution and the early Communist International, and the assimilation of the historical and political lessons of the struggle waged by Trotsky and the Fourth International against Stalinism, reformism and bourgeois nationalism. On this foundation, sections of the International Committee of the Fourth International must be built throughout Africa, and the world.

Concluded .

Op. cit., p. 404.

David North visited Trotsky’s final residence during his exile (1929-33) on the island of Prinkipo, and paid tribute to the life of the great theorist of world socialist revolution.

items.title: World Bank's cure for poverty: More jobs, so the poor can produce more wealth for the oligarchy
items.summary: Globally, one in 10 people live on less than $3.00 a day, while 3.7 billion people, almost half the world's population, are highly insecure, living on less than $8.30 per day.

scraped.title: World Bank's cure for poverty: More jobs, so the poor can produce more wealth for the oligarchy
scraped.description: Globally, one in 10 people live on less than $3.00 a day, while 3.7 billion people, almost half the world's population, are highly insecure, living on less than $8.30 per day.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
Figures released by the World Bank show that 811 million people, one in 10, are living in extreme poverty, defined as living on less than $3.00 per day.

Poverty, Prosperity and Planet Report 2026 tracks progress in reducing extreme poverty and increasing prosperity. It states that poverty reduction has stalled, changing little since 2019. Had the 2000-13 pace been maintained, 243 million additional people would have escaped poverty.

Extreme poverty is set to concentrate further because of demographic patterns. More than half the extremely poor live in just nine countries: Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, India, Ethiopia, Pakistan, Sudan, Tanzania, Uganda and Mozambique. By 2030, 87 percent will be living in Sub-Saharan Africa, in fragile and conflict-affected situations. Since populations are growing fastest in many of the countries with the highest poverty rates, the absolute number of people living in extreme poverty may continue to rise even where the incidence of poverty is falling.

Even more telling is the fact that nearly 3.7 billion people, almost half the world’s population, are highly insecure, living on less than $8.30 per day. They are, to use the World Bank’s words, just “one shock away from falling back into extreme poverty”. This number has remained broadly stagnant for decades.

The “global middle class”, those living on between $8.30 and $28.00 a day, has roughly doubled as a share of the world’s population, but this expansion has largely been concentrated in the upper-middle-income countries, where they are now the majority. The vulnerable group, living on less than $8.30 a day, constitute by far the largest group in the low-middle-income countries. This “middle class” remains a tiny minority in low-income countries.

The report’s message is that the world is not on track to meet international poverty goals without a significant acceleration in economic growth and job creation.

The 2026 Global Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), published last month by the UN Development Programme (UNDP) and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative (OPHI), University of Oxford, using a very different methodology, presents a complementary and, in some respects, even more disturbing picture. It says that for the first time since the index was established in 2010, the estimated number of people living in multidimensional poverty has increased.

Beyond income alone, the MPI combines 10 indicators across living standards, including inadequate nutrition, schooling, healthcare-related deprivation, sanitation, electricity, housing, and access to clean water. A person is considered poor if they are deprived in at least one-third of the weighted indicators.

Its study covered 108 countries and 6.3 billion people. It found that 1.2 billion people are living in multidimensional poverty or 18.9 percent of the population covered, a 51.5 million increase over the previous comparable estimate. Nearly half, 534 million people or 44.6 percent of these impoverished people, are considered severely poor, meaning that they face deprivations across more than half of the MPI’s weighted indicators. A further 952 million people, in addition to the 1.2 billion living in multidimensional poverty, are considered vulnerable: they face deprivations across multiple indicators without crossing the poverty threshold.

Over half of the world’s 1.2 billion poor (617 million) are children under 18. One in every three children is multidimensionally poor, compared to one in seven adults. Children account for more than half (57.7 percent) of the poor in Sub-Saharan Africa and 56.6 percent in the Arab states despite being only 41 percent of the total population. In East Asia and the Pacific, older adults (60 years old and above) are overrepresented relative to their population share.

The rural population accounts for a disproportionate share of all those living in poverty—83.3 percent (998 million). The incidence of poverty is 28.7 percent in rural areas, compared to 7 percent in urban areas. Not only is poverty more frequent in rural areas, but it is also far more acute, as reflected in the overall MPI value.

More than one third of all poor people (422.2 million) are to be found in 21 countries, where the incidence of poverty is greater than 50 percent. Eighteen of these 21 countries are in Sub-Saharan Africa, the region with the highest levels of multidimensional poverty and the highest number (616 million). In some cases, this is because the population has grown; the report cites Angola and Zambia as examples where poverty incidence fell but the total number of people in poverty still increased because population growth was faster.

The country-level results reveal important reversals. Nigeria’s multidimensional poverty rate rose from 33 percent in 2021 to 38.7 percent in 2024, with the number of people affected rising from 72.2 million to 90.1 million.

The long-term implications are horrific. An entire generation of undernourished children will suffer chronic illness, perform poorly in school, and face low incomes and a dearth of opportunities. According to the World Health Organization’s August 2026 regional humanitarian response plan, in the Greater Horn of Africa alone, more than 4.9 million children are projected to suffer acute malnutrition in 2026. Of these, more than 1.5 million are expected to require treatment for severe acute malnutrition (SAM), the most life-threatening form. These devastating conditions compound the social and economic pressures that fuel local and regional instability and conflict. Conflict, in turn, destroys livelihoods, displaces populations, and intensifies hunger and malnutrition, driving those able to flee their homes in search of security and income for their families.

The UNDP report, whose mission is poverty reduction, is essentially descriptive, quantifying deprivation. It avoids the key questions: what has caused this social catastrophe? What resources exist globally to resolve these problems? Who controls them? What policies and programmes are necessary to secure the funding required to eliminate those deprivations?

Likewise, the World Bank’s 2026 Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report does not provide a single global dollar figure for eliminating or even alleviating poverty. Estimates from researchers at the United Nations University World Institute for Development Economics Research (UNU-WIDER) in 2024 suggest that the direct cash transfers needed to end extreme poverty and absolute monetary poverty worldwide by 2030 would cost about $70 billion and $325 billion per year, respectively. These estimates cover the direct cash transfers required to eliminate monetary poverty; they do not include the wider investment necessary to provide adequate healthcare, education, housing, sanitation and other essential services. Nevertheless, they indicate the relatively modest financial resources required to eliminate even the most extreme forms of income poverty. This represents only 0.1 percent and 0.6 percent of the gross national income (GNI) of the OECD’s high-income countries.

The scale of these annual requirements becomes more striking when compared with the accumulated wealth of the world’s 3,428 billionaires, which has reached $20.1 trillion, according to Forbes’ latest World’s Billionaires List. That is roughly one-fifth of annual world GDP. The annual cost of ending extreme monetary poverty would be a tiny fraction of this accumulated wealth. The billionaire class increased its wealth by about $4 trillion in a single year, between 2025 and 2026. The 20 richest billionaires alone hold about $2.9 trillion.

The contrast is not simply between the wealth available and the cost of alleviating poverty. It is evident in the chronic underfunding of the international humanitarian system. UN humanitarian chief Tom Fletcher has reported that only about 20 percent of global humanitarian appeals were funded, the lowest proportion in a decade.

The World Bank frames the problem as creating more and better jobs, increasing earnings, raising productivity, expanding employment, especially among women, and achieving stronger per-capita economic growth. It argues that poverty reduction has stalled because growth and job creation have been insufficient, not because of how resources are owned and distributed. The report repeatedly presents employment and earnings as the main route out of poverty.

The problem is not that these countries lack employment or that their populations are unwilling to work. Millions already work long hours in low-paid, insecure, and often dangerous conditions in agriculture, mining, manufacturing, and the informal economy. The question is who captures the wealth generated by their labour.

Much of the value is appropriated further along the production and distribution chains by commodity traders, processors, brand owners, retailers, and financial institutions that capture interest payments, repatriation, and ownership of productive assets, and intellectual-property holders who own the patents, platforms, and technological infrastructure. Their wealth is invested in and managed by the same financial institutions and private equity firms that hold the sovereign debt of these less developed countries. The workers and countries producing the wealth retain only a fraction of it.

The World Bank naturally has little to say about who captures the wealth, or that the wealth created by the working class is expropriated by the capitalist class. As the executive arm of the imperialist financial powers, it has spent four decades imposing structural adjustment, privatisation and austerity on the world’s poorest countries. Now its remedy— more jobs so that the poor can “produce more wealth”—reveals the logic of capitalism and imperialism. The poor are not human beings with needs; they are a labour force whose productivity must be raised so they can be exploited more efficiently.

The Bank’s admission that poverty reduction has “stalled” implies that poverty reduction was taking place and had merely hit a snag or a slowdown that could be resolved by more growth and more jobs. Far from being some aberration of capitalism that can be corrected, poverty is a permanent and necessary feature of an economic system based on the extraction of surplus value from the working class by the capitalist class. The Bank’s own “solution”, to intensify the exploitation that causes poverty, confirms this.

The elimination of poverty requires a unified struggle against the entire capitalist system, by workers and rural masses in rich and poor countries alike, to expropriate the expropriators. The means of production, including factories, land, banks, public infrastructure, and the vast productive forces that capitalism has developed, must be taken out of private ownership and placed under the collective, democratic control of the working class. Production must be reorganised not for profit but to meet human need.

The working class must build its own independent political party, break with all the capitalist parties, and take state power, dismantling the existing state apparatus and replacing it with organs of workers’ power. Only then can the productive forces be reorganised on a socialist and humane basis, ending poverty forever.

items.title: COP31 convenes in Türkiye: The climate theater of the capitalist oligarchy
items.summary: As COP31 opened in Antalya with its president admitting the 1.5°C target will be breached, Turkey’s coal and oil conglomerates are being showcased as “climate partners”, while the imperialist powers escalate war and refuse funding to poorer countries.

scraped.title: COP31 convenes in Türkiye: The climate theater of the capitalist oligarchy
scraped.description: As COP31 opened in Antalya with its president admitting the 1.5°C target will be breached, Turkey’s coal and oil conglomerates are being showcased as “climate partners”, while the imperialist powers escalate war and refuse funding to poorer countries.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
The 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) opened November 9 in Antalya, the tourism capital on Türkiye’s Mediterranean coast.

The conference will continue until November 20. It is being chaired by Murat Kurum, Türkiye’s Minister of Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change. The negotiations are being led by Australia’s Minister for Climate Change and Energy, Chris Bowen.

“This is the first COP where it is clear beyond a reasonable doubt that the world will overshoot the 1.5-degree target,” Kurum said. He then declared the target to be a “compass.” The 1.5-degree target was set by the 2015 Paris Agreement, which rested on non-binding national pledges that were not subject to any sanctions.

Kurum announced that, rather than setting new targets, the summit would focus on the “implementation” of existing commitments. The hosts are marketing the gathering as the “Implementation COP.” What will actually be implemented in Antalya is the same policy that has been implemented for three decades: the subordination of the planet and the lives of billions of people to the profit and geopolitical interests of the giant corporations and the imperialist powers.

The summit has convened after a year marked by scorching heat waves in Europe, forest fires in Indonesia and devastating floods in Nepal. The World Meteorological Organization has placed 2026 among the hottest years ever recorded.

In the October 14 floods, nine people lost their lives in Istanbul and Kocaeli. Most of the dead were workers, among them a child worker and a migrant worker. In the aftermath of the floods, the World Socialist Web Site (WSWS) stressed that summits such as the upcoming COP31 serve to give a “green” veneer to the horse-trading between the imperialist powers and the energy monopolies, and to open up new fields of profit such as carbon markets.

Addressing the Leaders’ Summit on November 11, UN Secretary-General António Guterres declared: “The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us.” He added: “This is the path to mutually assured destruction.” Guterres noted that even if current national plans are fully implemented, “the world would be above 2.5 degrees [hotter] by the end of this century.”

Drawing a concrete comparison, Guterres said: “In the last quarter alone, the nine largest oil companies pocketed $95 billion in profits. Meanwhile, the Loss and Damage Fund has received around $600 million. That is what these companies made in about 14 hours.” As Reuters reported, ExxonMobil, Chevron, BP and Shell have posted windfall profits since the war against Iran began at the end of February.

The UN chief’s proposed solution was the bankrupt perspective of appealing to governments: “It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits.” The reality is that the capitalist oligarchies that control governments everywhere are not going to tax themselves. They are determined to finance rearmament and state debt through a ferocious social assault on the working class. It is this class struggle that lies behind the movement of young people and workers into the streets, in Europe and many other parts of the world.

At the opening session on November 9, Guterres had called on leaders to “get serious.” But what “seriousness” looks like became clear immediately. An item proposed by African countries calling for the tripling of adaptation finance was kept off the agenda following objections from the European Union (EU). According to the UN, developing countries will need $305 billion a year for adaptation by 2035. That is roughly ten times what they receive today. Before the summit, a senior EU official had already stated bluntly that there would be “no political will” for new commitments.

Most of the finance on offer comes in the form of loans, not grants. According to Oxfam and CARE, developing countries pay back roughly $7 for every $5 they receive. The bill for the catastrophe created by the imperialist centers is being handed, with interest, to the workers and peasants of the poorer countries.

Previous summits had already demonstrated, if only through the choice of their hosts, how seriously this critical global issue is taken. COP28 in Dubai was presided over by Sultan Al Jaber, CEO of the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company (ADNOC). COP29 in Baku was chaired by Mukhtar Babayev, a former executive of the state oil company SOCAR. The WSWS characterized the Baku summit as an expression of “the normalization of mass death” and described its final text as “another empty agreement.”

As was noted at the opening and in the aftermath of last year’s COP30 in Belém, a significant number of world leaders did not even attend. The fossil fuel lobby, meanwhile, with some 1,600 people, formed the largest delegation apart from that of host Brazil. The final text did not so much as mention fossil fuels by name, and the “roadmap” backed by more than 80 countries was relegated to a voluntary basis.

The United States, the world’s second-largest greenhouse gas emitter, is absent from Antalya. The Trump administration has pulled the country out of the Paris Agreement for the second time and did not send a single official to COP31. The Democrats arrived with a congressional delegation. But the Obama administration, which signed the Paris Agreement, and the Biden administration, which rejoined it, both drove oil and shale gas production to record levels.

The largest conglomerates of the Turkish bourgeoisie occupy the summit’s shop window. Koç Holding is the “Global Business Partner” and Sabancı Holding the “Electrification Partner,” while Cengiz Holding is among the sponsors. Limak, IC Holding, Rönesans and Sinpaş top the list of “climate supporters.” Conglomerates that operate coal-fired power plants and are planning new mines and power stations are being welcomed in Antalya under the title of “climate partner.” Alongside the construction monopolies and the major energy and real estate companies, the sponsors include banks. Garanti BBVA is present as the “global banking partner.”

The record of these “climate partners” speaks for itself. Cengiz Holding operates a 1,320-megawatt imported-coal power plant in Karabiga, in Çanakkale province, and has launched an environmental impact assessment process for a new 1,050-megawatt unit. Limak and IC are partners in the Yeniköy-Kemerköy lignite power plants in Muğla and bear responsibility for the destruction of the Akbelen Forest to make way for a coal mine. In October, the Council of State, Türkiye’s highest administrative court, rejected the lawsuit seeking the annulment of the urgent expropriation order. According to Climate Home News , Koç Holding and Tüpraş, the oil refiner it controls, cut their 2030 reduction targets for emissions from their own operations from 27 percent to 20 percent in 2025.

On November 9, the day the summit opened, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan heralded the discovery of 135 million barrels of oil in place at Gabar, in Şırnak province. According to Global Witness, gas production by the state oil company TPAO is expected to nearly triple, from 8.2 billion cubic meters in 2025 to 22 billion cubic meters in 2035. Companies in co-host Australia are on the same course. Woodside is preparing to double its LNG output by 2032, while Santos plans to increase its crude oil output eightfold by 2035.

Addressing the Leaders’ Summit, Erdoğan declared: “Today, humanity is experiencing perhaps one of the deepest existential crises in its history, driven in part by the greed of excessive consumption.” But the cause of this existential crisis is not the “greed of excessive consumption.” It is the capitalist system, which subordinates the global economy and the fate of humanity to private profit and the accumulation of wealth, and the rule of the oligarchies that control it.

Erdoğan went on: “Wars, crises, migration, hunger and poverty are increasing the need for international solidarity day by day. Alongside people, nature too is paying the heavy price of armed conflicts.” These words come from the leader of a country that has NATO’s second-largest army and is a military-strategic ally of US imperialism.

COP31 convenes amid an escalation of imperialist war stretching from Eastern Europe to the Middle East. The US-Israeli war of aggression against Iran and the accompanying blockade have sent oil prices rocketing, while the war waged by the NATO powers against Russia through Ukraine continues to escalate. The European governments are raising military spending to record levels, even as they declare there is “no political will” for climate finance. The world’s militaries are among the largest consumers of fossil fuels, yet their emissions are largely excluded from climate accounting.

Much of the debate in Antalya centers on the transparency of the sponsors or on the lack of “political will.” But the problem is the capitalist system itself, which is based on the profit motive and divides the world into rival nation-states. The scientific and technical means exist to take the steps needed to rapidly reduce global emissions. What blocks their implementation are the interests of the capitalist oligarchy that controls energy, construction, finance, the entire economy and the nation-states themselves.

The lesson of three decades of COP (Conference of the Parties) summits is clear: the climate crisis cannot be resolved through appeals to the governments of the capitalist class that created it. The energy, construction and banking monopolies must be expropriated and placed under the democratic control of the working class. Production worldwide must be reorganized to meet social need, not private profit. This requires the unification and mobilization of the working class all over the world in the struggle to take power and implement socialist measures.

The Socialist Equality Party is organizing the working class in the fight for socialism: the reorganization of all of economic life to serve social needs, not private profit.

scraped.description: The midterms exposed an important contradiction: millions want a break with the status quo, yet the elections strengthened the grip of the Democratic Party on U.S. politics. AOC 2028 makes DSA's choice immediate: mobilize behind the Democrats and negotiate a platform acceptable to them, or build an independent organization to resist the Right and fight for all of our demands?
scraped.author: Maryam Alaniz, James Dennis Hoff
scraped.body_text:
The midterms exposed an important contradiction: millions want a break with the status quo, yet the elections strengthened the grip of the Democratic Party on U.S. politics. AOC 2028 makes DSA’s choice immediate: mobilize behind the Democrats and negotiate a platform acceptable to them, or build an independent organization to resist the Right and fight for all of our demands?

Maryam Alaniz and James Dennis Hoff

The Democrats’ midterm victory expressed a popular rejection of Trump and everything his administration has done since he was re-elected. From the rising cost of living — a direct result of the war on Iran — to the genocide in Gaza, the violent deployment of ICE in cities across the country, and the onslaught of attacks on democratic rights, millions of people loudly said “no more!”

But the results were not only a rejection of Trump. They also expressed the aspirations of an electorate that is feeling its power and is eager for change. This includes support for such ideas as Medicare for All, taxing the rich, abolishing ICE, and ending U.S. support for Israel. Ironically, these are all policies that the Democrats, the big winners of this month’s midterms, have repeatedly rejected, watered down, avoided, or otherwise undermined every time they have been in office. These are also demands Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) members have organized around for decades, keeping them alive even as Democratic officeholders have repeatedly refused to act on them. This rejection of Trump is obviously a positive development. But there is a catch. The immediate electoral form this opposition has taken has simultaneously strengthened the very party that failed for eight years to check Trump and which has spent a decade proving it will not satisfy the popular aspirations of the masses. The Democratic Party now has a mandate for change, but nothing about its class composition, its leadership, its funding, or its record suggests it intends to deliver. On the contrary, as we saw in California, where the Democratic establishment actually worked with billionaires to defeat legislation to tax billionaires , they are more likely to resist such demands whenever they think they can get away with it.

Many on the Reformist Left, including the writers and editors over at Jacobin , have attempted to grapple with this contradiction between the popular rejection of Trump and the inadequacy of the Democratic Party. For instance, in an article laying out his analysis of the election results , labor historian and Jacobin regular Eric Blanc warns against repeating what he calls the disaster of 2008, when, as he claims, Barack Obama squandered a historic mandate, demobilized his base, and opened the road to reaction. For Blanc, “Everything depends on breaking the destructive doom loop of Democratic victories, dashed hopes, and increasingly reactionary Republican comebacks.” Likewise, Catalyst editor Vivek Chibber emphasizes the need for mass organization, noting that “winning office is not the same as winning power.”

Yet they seem determined to draw all the wrong conclusions. For Blanc and Chibber, both of whom explicitly reject the idea of building an independent working-class party now, “winning power” ultimately means lining up behind the Democrats. In the case of Chibber this means working with them in order to “shift the political culture through the party.” Meanwhile, Blanc argues that the immediate task before us now “is to organize enough independent working-class power to make the anti-MAGA (i.e., Democratic) coalition succeed in meeting workers’ urgent needs, rather than lob critiques from the sidelines about how betrayal and disappointment are inevitable.” Both believe that working-class power can be built in coalition with capitalist parties rather than in opposition to them, but such a strategy — where the workers’ movement supplies the organized force and the Democrats retain political leadership — is exactly the lifeline the Democratic Party needs to draw disenchanted working people back into its political orbit. By subordinating workers to the interests and limitations of a bourgeois party, it strengthens the capitalist state while simultaneously weakening independent organization and working-class power as a whole.

For the generation now joining DSA, especially after the genocide in Gaza under Biden’s administration, there is an enormous distrust and hatred of the Democratic Party. Even Blanc had to concede that the election was “a repudiation of Donald Trump, not a vindication of Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries” — the same pro-Zionist leaders who mounted no serious fight against Trump’s reactionary offensive and now claim credit for his defeat when it was communities and workers that dared to confront Trump from Los Angeles to Minneapolis . In fact, the movement against Schumer and Jeffries as they mount their leadership campaigns shows that working people remain fed up with the Democrats and are willing to fight for our demands independently of them.

That is why the central question now is not how we can help the Democrats pass this or that piece of legislation. Instead, we have to ask ourselves how best to build the independent working class power we need to force the Republicans and the Democrats, including DSA electeds, to answer to us on our own terms. In this regard, socialists can learn a lot from the popular struggles in France, the Spanish State and Minneapolis.

A recent exchange within DSA highlighted the tensions over what political “independence” means in practice. Sid C.W., a National Political Committee (NPC) member from Marxist Unity Group, argues that organizing “independently” in this moment requires wrestling with the fact that the Democrats will not be able to deliver what working people want them to. In response, Blanc contends that simply denouncing Democrats amounts to “propagandizing”: telling people that the party will not deliver without offering a concrete way to organize and act. But his alternative — focusing on pressuring Democrats — becomes mere opportunism if winning concessions from a capitalist party becomes the organizing goal. Socialist demands and tactics then come to be judged by whether they can move Democratic officials, rather than whether they strengthen the masses’ capacity to organize and act independently.

That exchange reflects a broader argument: for Blanc, as well as many of the leaders of the DSA, the current weakness of the Left is not a strategic problem to overcome, but a justification for making the Democratic Party its indefinite political horizon. Chibber provides a more explicit defense of this logic. For him, the Left is just too small to accomplish anything without using the Democratic Party as a vehicle for its politics. And this is why he argues that those in DSA who are calling for class independence are essentially small-minded sectarian purists, while those who insist on continuing to work within the Democratic Party are doing “actual politics.” However, his own account of what an organization can do once it reaches a certain size complicates that argument:

Once your organization reaches a certain size, like in New York City or in Chicago, it can actually move things. You can move events. You can actually mobilize people in large numbers and, at least to some extent, even think about setting the political agenda. What happens when you’re very, very small is that you’re piggybacking on things that other people are doing.

But DSA is no longer a small organization, not in New York City, where it has almost 17,000 members, and not nationally, where it has over 130,000 and is growing every day. That does not mean DSA can win everything on its own or that DSA is the party the working class needs, but it does mean the question is no longer simply whether it is large enough to act independently. Most important is whether it uses that capacity to build working-class politics and organization or channels it into a program of pressuring the Democrats.

And DSA’s growth is only part of what has changed.The social forces confronting bipartisan imperialism have also grown dramatically in the last period. From the Black Lives Matter uprisings of 2020 and the hot labor summer of 2023, to the campus movement for Palestine and the fightback against ICE in Minneapolis, Chicago , and Los Angeles, not to mention the absolutely massive No Kings protests against Trump, people are clearly fed up with both parties and have shown a capacity to act beyond the electoral timetable of the Democrats.

And in many ways, the election confirmed that shift: Abdul El-Sayed won in Michigan despite the millions that AIPAC spent to defeat him. And of course many people, including those who voted for Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier, came out explicitly to register their hatred of ICE — an organization funded every year by every Congress since it was created in 2002. These were Democratic victories, but the aspirations expressed through them clash with the Democrats’ role as an imperialist party of capital. In the streets and in the elections, people were not simply following the Democrats’ lead: they were starting to put forward demands of their own.

The growth of DSA and the recent wave of class struggle, especially in Minneapolis, show the material possibility of acting and organizing independently for more than just elections. An electoral strategy centered on the Democratic Party and not on using independent candidates to further a socialist program squanders this opportunity. Independent candidacies can help build the fight for a working-class party that challenges the political order itself; no change in the law will simply open the way for that party — we have to win the space to build it through struggle. In fact, such a strategy would only draw the DSA further into the trap of working within an institution that has steadfastly refused to take the demands of working people seriously, and which, further, is materially incapable of actually delivering them without abandoning its fealty to the capitalist system it defends.

In fact, the current debate in the organization over whether Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (AOC) should run for president in 2028 makes this choice even more salient. While the NPC of the DSA has not yet formally endorsed AOC, it has made its intention to do so very clear. In September, the 27-member NPC rejected plans for a special presidential endorsement conference, which would have allowed elected delegates to debate and decide the issue. Instead, it is organizing internal discussions and chapter-level polls under the slogan “It’s time for you to decide.” But it’s obvious that such discussions are purely advisory.

This is no way to decide such an important issue. The NPC must put the strategic choice before the membership before committing DSA’s resources to another presidential campaign that subordinates its program and organizing to the Democratic Party; members must be able to decide the organization’s electoral strategy — including whether to run an independent candidate around the DSA’s own program.

The question facing DSA now is: will it use this moment to funnel our energy and aspirations into supporting a presidential candidate working on behalf of the interests of bipartisan imperialism, or will it finally begin to organize the kind of independent power needed to win all of our demands?

Many of the caucuses lining up behind AOC 2028 have already made it clear that they don’t believe this is the right time for such a fight. Their wager is that supporting AOC will help build a mass Left rooted in labor and organized around popular economic demands, creating the strength they argue is necessary before a break with the Democrats becomes possible. But building a working-class constituency is not the same as building its political independence. If that constituency is organized primarily to elect and pressure Democrats, its growing numbers can strengthen its role within the party without increasing its capacity to act against it. The missing link is a strategy for turning organizational growth into independent political power: preparing workers to pursue their demands even when doing so means confronting the candidate they once supported and breaking with the party that put her in office.

All over the world, independent action from below is driving mass politics, from the fight against declining living standards in France to the general strike a few days ago in the Spanish State against the housing crisis which forced parliament to deliver on some of the movement’s demands. And we saw the same thing happen in Minneapolis , where workers and communities were able to confront and limit the ability of ICE to operate in the city. The fight for popular demands such as Medicare for All will require the same kind of self-organization, not as a base for pressure campaigns that accommodate the insurance industry, as Obamacare did, but in the form of workplace and neighborhood committees of healthcare workers and working-class people who are denied care, empowered to make decisions, take action, and build the capacity to fight the interests standing in their way. The point is not to build an alternative alongside existing society, but to organize the working class to confront the forces that govern it. Struggles over the ongoing ICE raids, the AI-driven attack on jobs and communities, and the imperialist attacks in the Middle East are opportunities to start coordinating action to develop a common program — not by narrowing our politics to economic demands deemed electorally popular, but by connecting the fights over bread-and-butter issues like health care, education, wages, and living standards to the fight against repression and imperialism. In a moment where states like Florida are ramping up their attacks against the DSA and buildings are collapsing in working-class communities like Flatbush, seeds of struggle are likely already developing around questions like housing and the attacks against the Left. For instance, an assembly on housing in a city like New York, where there are around 17,000 DSA members, not to mention many more people who are willing to organize and put their energy behind alternatives to the Democrats, could have profound political effects. Instead of tailing the narrow reforms of the Mamdani administration or settling for what the Democratic Party and the state are willing to allow, it could bring together workers, students, activists, and community members to discuss and decide a way forward, connect the struggle over housing to other questions like policing, and build a movement that can confront the forces blocking our demands locally and nationally. This is where democratic organization from below connects to the struggle for a working-class party. An assembly can decide demands and organize action, but confronting the forces blocking those demands requires more than a single local movement. It requires a common program and an organization capable of coordinating struggles nationally and fighting for political power. DSA could help build that organization through these fights, rather than treating movements as sources of volunteers and pressure for Democratic campaigns.

That work cannot wait until 2028. This weekend’s NYC DSA convention will be a space for delegates to debate campaign proposals, including AOC’s presidential campaign, but the right to elect delegates does not by itself give members the power to collectively develop a different political strategy for the organization. Democracy must mean more than voting on previously drafted proposals and supplying the volunteers to carry them out. DSA is growing because people are looking for an alternative to top-down politics. They will not stay if they are treated as a volunteer pool rather than political subjects with a say in the organization they are building.

Genuine “base building” means organizing inside and outside DSA. Mass branch meetings, housing assemblies, and workplace committees where workers, students, and community members decide demands, organize action, and hold leaders accountable, are mass politics that can organize hundreds of thousands around a shared program for working people and the oppressed.

An organization like DSA has the capacity to connect such bodies through a common socialist program and act on their collective decisions — not treat their participants as simply volunteers for AOC 2028. The task after the midterms is to give the clear desire for a break from both parties of capital an independent political form and ultimately an independent party, capable of fighting for our demands even when Democrats stand in the way.

Maryam Alaniz is a socialist journalist, activist, and PhD student living in NYC. She is an editor for the international section of Left Voice. Follow her on Twitter: @MaryamAlaniz
