scraped.body_text:
Spain’s first general strike in 14 years shut down car plants, ports, and highways. Electricity demand dropped almost 10 percent, and employers estimate more than 2 billion euros in lost output. Santiago Lupe goes through the data to show where the strike hit hardest, how it compares to the strikes in 2010 and 2012, and why linking labor demands to housing could open a new phase of struggle.

Santiago Lupe

November 11 left behind a scene not seen in the Spanish State for years: picket lines starting at dawn, blocked entrances to industrial parks, paralyzed transportation, major production centers operating at minimal capacity, and roads blocked in several regions. The general strike, despite the difficulty of extending it to all sectors and despite regional differences, managed to make its presence felt at strategic points throughout the economy.

Initial assessments by the Workers’ Commissions (CCOO) and the General Union of Workers (UGT) point to particularly high participation in industry, the automotive sector, ports, and transportation. The Confederation of Tenants’ Unions, for its part, has highlighted the strike’s nationwide reach; demonstrations took place in more than 100 cities through a network of 1,130 neighborhood strike committees.

Employers’ associations and various government agencies have sought to downplay the day’s impact, while labor unions have emphasized its significance. But beyond the dispute over percentages, there is a reality that is difficult to hide: November 11 succeeded in disrupting the operations of key productive sectors and shifting the social conflict from workplaces to the streets and highways.

An indicator that provides insight into the strike’s impact is the shift in electricity demand. This is not a perfect gauge — it also depends on temperature, economic activity, self-generated power such as rooftop solar, habits, and other factors — but it offers an important clue: when factories, logistics facilities, and other centers of activity reduce or halt production, energy consumption reflects this.

And November 11 sent a significant signal. According to data from grid operator Red Eléctrica compiled by public broadcaster RTVE, at 8 a.m., demand stood at 28,746 megawatts, compared to 31,856 at the same time the previous day: a 9.8 percent decrease. At 11 a.m., demand was 7.46 percent below forecast, according to data released by Red Eléctrica.

The decline was particularly pronounced from 10 a.m. to 11 a.m. The fact-checking outlet Newtral, comparing actual consumption with the average for weekdays over the past month, recorded a drop of nearly 9 percent at the peak of the decline and 6.12 percent at noon.

Usage gradually increased as the day went on. But the trend during the early hours — coinciding with factory shift changes, picket lines at logistics centers, and transportation disruptions — shows that electricity demand dropped significantly precisely when the strike was expected to disrupt productive activity.

Comparing these figures with those from the country’s most recent major general strikes provides further context. On September 29, 2010, during the strike against the labor reform of José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero’s government, electricity demand fell by an average of 14 percent compared to Red Eléctrica’s forecast. Two years later, on March 29, 2012, during the strike against the labor reform of Mariano Rajoy’s government, the drop was 14.84 percent.

The figures for November 11, 2026, are lower than those for either of those days. By this indicator, participation appears to have been lower than during the strikes of 2010 and 2012. This should come as no surprise. The 14-year truce granted to the Rajoy and Sánchez governments by the bureaucratic leaderships of the CCOO and UGT has taken its toll.

After all these years, however, November 11 has once again placed the general strike at the center of social confrontation, and it has done so without being called by the CCOO and UGT. It has also shown that significant reserves of militancy still exist in the industrial, transportation, and logistics sectors, and that they have been reignited by a strike call linking labor demands to the housing crisis.

Participation data allow us to analyze where the strike’s strength was concentrated and which sectors effectively halted their operations. All the data indicate that the impact was most noticeable in manufacturing, ports, and logistics — those sectors with the strongest tradition of union organization and the greatest capacity to paralyze production.

According to the CCOO and UGT’s joint assessment of the first shifts, participation was particularly high in the automotive sector, ports, the meat-processing industry, waste collection, the energy sector, and logistics.

In the automotive sector, 90 percent of workers participated in the strike. The unions highlighted the complete production stoppages at Volkswagen Navarra, SEAT, and Ebro in Barcelona.

The ports were another major focal point of the strike. According to the unions, Algeciras and Valencia recorded 90 percent participation, while disruptions also occurred at the port facilities in Barcelona, Tarragona, and A Coruña. In A Coruña, activity came to a near-complete halt.

In the meat industry, participation reached 85 percent on what was its third day of strike action over the national collective bargaining agreement, which covers 35,000 workers.

Logistics also played a prominent role. In Guadalajara and Illescas — two strategic hubs for the distribution of goods in central Spain — unions estimated participation at around 80 percent.

Street cleaning and garbage collection ground nearly to a halt, with 82 percent participation. Many large cities woke up to find their trash bins full of the previous day’s garbage, which had not been picked up during the early-morning hours.

The energy sector saw 75 percent participation, and the postal service, 35 percent. Participation was more limited in some public services and in health care, retail, and finance. There were notable exceptions, such as the education sector in Madrid, which had 50 percent participation as part of its indefinite strike, and the Catalan education sector, which had similar overall participation, reaching 70 percent in the Barcelona metropolitan area.

Much of the available data also shows that participation was affected by minimum service requirements — staffing levels that the government mandates during strikes — which in certain sectors, such as health care, prevented workers from completely halting operations.

The regional distribution of the strike also offers some insights. Union data and reports published throughout the day agree that participation was highest in Catalonia, Galicia, Asturias, and Aragon, although there was also significant participation in Andalusia, Madrid, and the Valencian Community.

Catalonia was one of the epicenters of the strike. CCOO estimated overall participation at 84 percent in its final report and highlighted 92 percent participation in sectors such as the automotive and transportation industries. Barcelona was left without buses or the metro during the hours when minimum services were not in effect, from 9:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. Port operations were also affected, and universities closed completely.

According to the CCOO and UGT, Asturias recorded participation of around 75 percent. The impact was particularly significant at large industrial companies such as ArcelorMittal, Thyssen, Fertiberia, and Rioglass, as well as in Gijón’s urban transit system and the logistics sector.

In Madrid the impact was particularly noticeable in transportation and logistics, and operations at Airbus came to a complete halt. The CCOO estimated overall participation at 65 percent, while the metro saw a 54 percent drop in ridership during rush hour, and the city’s EMT buses saw a 63 percent drop.

The Basque Country was one of the regions where industry was hit hardest. Production came to a virtual standstill at companies such as Petronor and CAF, while the workforces at Mercedes and ACB Sestao managed to significantly reduce operations. Also notable were the shutdowns at Irizar and Ulma, which the workers themselves decided on. The strike also spread to the education sector — with 60 percent participation, according to the unions — as well as to retail, sanitation, and outsourced services.

Aragon saw participation of over 70 percent, according to the unions. Companies such as Saica, CAF, and FCC experienced significant work stoppages, with operations at some workplaces coming to a virtual standstill.

Galicia stood out for the impact on industry and ports. The unions reported 100 percent participation at the Alcoa plant in Lugo and a total shutdown at the port of A Coruña. The Galician union CIG’s mobilization in Vigo also saw very high participation.

Andalusia saw significant participation in industry and port operations. The CCOO and UGT estimated industrial participation at around 70 percent, with 90 percent participation in agribusiness and 100 percent at the port of Algeciras. In its final assessment, CCOO also put overall participation in the region at 70 percent.

In the Valencian Community, ports and industry were the main areas affected. The CCOO estimated overall participation at about 60 percent, with significant disruptions to port operations.

At the other end of the spectrum, Extremadura, Castile–La Mancha, and Castile and León were among the regions with the lowest participation during the first shifts, although there were significant pockets of strike activity at certain logistics and industrial centers.

If anything visually characterized November 11, it was the widespread presence of picket lines and roadblocks. The strike was not limited to company gates; it managed to disrupt access to major industrial centers, wholesale markets, logistics hubs, and key transportation routes.

In Catalonia the blockades affected about 20 roads, according to reports published throughout the day. Among them were the AP-7, the A-2, the C-58, and the B-10, as well as Barcelona’s Ronda Litoral. There were also actions at the entrances to industrial parks and in the areas surrounding Mercabarna (Barcelona’s wholesale food market) and the Zona Franca. The picket lines disrupted traffic at various points throughout the metropolitan area.

In Madrid the blockades affected some of the city’s main thoroughfares. There were blockades on the A-1, A-42, and A-5, as well as on the M-30 near Legazpi, Vallecas, and Ventas, and on the M-40 in Moratalaz. Mercamadrid (Madrid’s wholesale food market), the EMT bus depots, and various logistics access points were the sites of picket lines from early in the morning.

In the Valencian Community, the protests affected the V-21, the Ronda Nord, Avenida del Cid, Paiporta, and the access roads to Villareal. Picket lines were also set up at the ports, where activity was severely limited.

In Zamora the police arrested strikers at the municipal bus depots. There were also incidents at Valladolid’s municipal sanitation depots and in Granada, where police intervened against transportation picket lines.

In Málaga, EMT workers staged actions at the municipal bus depots. In Zaragoza, picket lines were set up at the FCC access points to try to paralyze street-cleaning operations. In Guadalajara and other logistics hubs, actions were also organized to disrupt the operations of distribution centers.

Police repression was another feature of the day. At Mercamadrid, police used pepper spray, and more than a dozen people required medical attention. Police also charged picket lines at public transportation depots in Madrid, Málaga, and Granada, and made 50 arrests during the day, with at least as many more once the demonstrations ended.

The roadblocks and picket lines expressed the workers’ determination to make the strike count for something more than just an absence from the workplace. Their goal was to bring the conflict into the public eye, broaden participation, and disrupt the functioning of economic circuits that usually remain hidden.

Beyond participation rates, one way to measure the scale of a general strike is to calculate the volume of economic activity that is not undertaken during the day. The Research Service of the General Council of Economists (CGE) has produced an estimate placing the net loss of GDP at up to 2.1 billion euros in a high-participation scenario of 70 percent.

The calculation is based on average daily output of about 6.76 billion euros. From there, the CGE outlines three scenarios: with 30 percent participation, 2.03 billion euros in goods and services would go unproduced, although the resulting net loss would be about 900 million euros; with 50 percent participation, the initially interrupted production would total 3.38 billion euros, and the net loss would stand at 1.5 billion euros; and with 70 percent participation, the activity not generated that day would total 4.73 billion euros, with an estimated net loss of 2.1 billion euros.

This distinction is important, since not all production halted during a 24-hour strike is permanently lost. Some of it can be recovered later through additional shifts, reorganization of operations, or catching up on orders. But another portion — especially in certain services, transportation, commerce, and production processes subject to deadlines — cannot be fully recovered.

Other estimates published before and during the strike point to a similar potential impact. Professor José Ramón Pin Arboledas of IESE Business School calculated a cost of at least 2 billion euros in GDP, factoring in not only the absence of striking workers but also the effects on workers who could not reach their workplaces or carry out their normal activities.

For its part, the employers’ association CONPYMES estimated a loss of 1.85 billion to 4.56 billion euros, with workers’ participation ranging from 30 to 70 percent. From a different perspective, the Spanish Exporters and Investors Club estimated that, in a scenario of widespread participation, 1.6 billion euros in goods and services intended for export could go unproduced. This figure refers solely to the export sector.

BBVA Research also considered a scenario with an impact of up to 0.2 percent of GDP — equivalent to about 3.5 billion euros — compared to its more moderate baseline estimate of around 0.1 percent. The think tank Funcas, while cautioning that it is difficult to make a definitive estimate before knowing the level of participation, put the potential impact at up to 5 billion euros in a scenario of total shutdown.

In short, the various estimates place the volume of production that could have been affected at roughly 2 billion to 5 billion in the highest-impact scenarios. These are not final recorded losses but calculations of potential impact based on different methodologies and assumptions. They do, however, allow us to gauge the capacity of a general strike to disrupt the economy’s production, distribution, and service networks.

The assessment of November 11 must be approached without triumphalism and without concealing its limitations. Participation was not uniform across all sectors and regions, and electricity consumption data do not allow us to automatically equate its impact with that of the general strikes of 2010 and 2012. Nor, however, can it be reduced to a day of limited participation, as employers’ associations have sought to portray it.

Work stoppages in major industries, disruptions at ports, roadblocks, transportation mobilizations, and the widespread nature of the protests demonstrate that the capacity for collective response has not disappeared during these 14 years without general strikes.

Furthermore, November 11 had an important and novel feature: it linked the labor conflict to the housing crisis, connecting what is happening in the workplaces with a massive youth and social mobilization that has sent shockwaves through the government and the political regime. The demand for living wages, the fight against exorbitant rents, and the condemnation of speculation have made it possible to have an impact in workplaces — which are constrained by the control of union bureaucracies — and to bring in social sectors that do not always take part in traditional union calls to action.

The hundreds of neighborhood strike committees and the experiences of coordination among labor organizations, housing collectives, students, and workers point to a path for expanding this capacity for mobilization.

The challenge is to ensure that all this momentum does not dissipate now that the day of action is over. The assemblies, strike committees, and coordinating bodies that have emerged or been strengthened must cohere this organizing and extend it into the workplaces.

Ensuring that these processes of self-organization develop within workplaces is essential to preventing the leaderships of the CCOO and UGT from imposing another truce on us under a potential new Sánchez government — or a controlled management of the conflict if the right wing comes to power, as it did under Rajoy.

On this issue, militant unionism bears a fundamental responsibility. It must seek the greatest possible unity with the rank and file, members, and delegates of the major unions who don’t go along with their leaderships’ policies, and build synergies and alliances with the housing and youth movements to revolutionize the workplaces.

The experience of 2010 and 2012 also taught us a lesson: a one-day strike, no matter how massive, does not guarantee victory for our demands. What is needed is continuity, organization in workplaces and neighborhoods, and the ability to sustain mobilization regardless of electoral calendars and agreements between union leaderships and governments.

November 11 has shown that the social force exists to impose the movement’s demands, such as rent reductions and the expropriation of large property owners. We must wrest from the government and employers a wage restructuring like the one being fought for in France — with an increase in the minimum wage and across-the-board raises by decree for all workers. We need to coordinate the ongoing struggles and secure victory. We must confront the reactionary agenda — whether implemented by the right or the “progressives” — and overturn rearmament plans and racist immigration policies.

The question that remains open — and which we should debate in the assessment meetings to be held in the coming days — is how to transform all this social force into a sustained movement that operates democratically from the grassroots and that is combative, that can impose real solutions to the housing crisis and the deterioration of living conditions for the working majority, and that can halt — together with the working class and the youth of the continent — the war machine that is spreading across Europe.

November 5 brought 1.6 million to the streets in France and high strike rates on the railways and in education, confirming workers are joining the youth movement. While the government seeks to channel discontent through negotiations, we need a plan of action for a general strike.

Damien Bernard

Ari Aalto

October 17 opened a pre-revolutionary period in France. The question now is whether the students and their working class allies can expand, organize themselves, and win the political independence required to fight for its own way out of the crisis.

scraped.title: Florida’s Subpoena against DSA is an Attack on the Entire Left - Left Voice
scraped.description: Florida’s Attorney General issued a subpoena against DSA, accusing them of having connections to foreign governments. This is the latest attack in a growing campaign of repression against the entire Left.
scraped.author: Samuel Karlin
scraped.body_text:
Florida’s Attorney General issued a subpoena against DSA, accusing them of having connections to foreign governments. This is the latest attack in a growing campaign of repression against the entire Left.

Samuel Karlin

Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier is attacking the state’s Democratic Socialists of America chapter. On Tuesday, November 10 — a week after the midterm elections which saw DSA make gains across the country and nearly win a senate seat from Florida — Uthmeier issued a subpoena accusing DSA of having ties to the governments of Cuba and China, citing the organization’s history of participating in delegations to these countries.

This is an act of repression that the entire Left should oppose. As DSA has grown numerically and in relevance in national politics, the organization has been subjected to increasing attacks by both the Right and establishment Democrats. An attack on the largest socialist organization in the country has implications for everyone who identifies as a socialist or is beginning to identify with the term.

The attempt to delegitimize and criminalize socialist organizations by linking them to foreign governments has a dangerous history in the United States. Most recently Secretary of State Marco Rubio has used this method to paint a conspiracy theory that Cuba’s government is infiltrating the United States through relationships with left-wing organizations and activists. This line that any organization which questions the U.S. government’s pro-war foreign policy must be acting on behalf of a foreign government has previously been used to justify investigations and legal attacks against organizations like the Party for Socialism and Liberation and CODEPINK.

This attack must further be understood as part of the Trump administration’s escalating repression against social movements, particularly the movement against ICE and pro-Palestine solidarity. The sentencing of immigrant rights activists who held a noise demonstration outside an ICE jail in Prairieland, Texas showed just how far the administration is willing to go to crack down on dissent. Now the administration is attempting to repeat this attack against 15 activists who confronted ICE in Minneapolis and eight pro-Palestine activists in Michigan . The list of attacks goes on, from the ongoing efforts to deport pro-Palestine activists Mahmoud Khalil and Leqaa Kordia, the bogus assault charges against Green Party leader Jill Stein, and the many cases of attacks on academic freedom including Tom Alter in Texas and the CUNY Fired Fourth .

While many of these examples have important differences, together they demonstrate the larger climate of repression which has developed under Trump, though importantly predates him as the repression of the movement for Palestine began under Biden.

Left Voice fully condemns Uthmeier’s attack on DSA. A socialist organization in the United States should have every right to engage in international exchanges without being slandered as foreign agents. The capitalists are an international class and they regularly convene to exchange about how to exploit workers and make us kill each other in their wars, but international exchange is then treated as a crime when workers and socialists do it. This double-standard should be firmly rejected as its aim is not just to repress the Left, but to keep Americans isolated and obsessed with our own national interest at the expense of greater connection with our class siblings around the world.

In the face of escalating repression it is essential that the Left in the United States stand in solidarity, despite any political differences, against all attacks from the state. Uthmeier should withdraw the subpoena. The labor movement, civil-liberties groups, and the broader Left should oppose efforts to criminalize DSA.

Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)

Repression

Subpoena

scraped.h1: American Indian College Fund and Pendleton Woolen Mills Student Blanket Design Contest Opens November 15
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

The American Indian College Fund and Pendleton Woolen Mills are accepting submissions for their seventh annual Tribal College Blanket Design Contest, offering Native students the opportunity to showcase their artwork, earn scholarships and cash prizes, and have their designs featured in Pendleton’s internationally distributed wool blanket collection.

The American Indian College Fund and Pendleton Woolen Mills are inviting American Indian and Alaska Native students attending tribal colleges and universities (TCUs) to showcase their artistic talents through the seventh annual Tribal College Blanket Design Contest. Submissions open November 15, 2026, with a deadline of January 15, 2027.

The annual contest celebrates emerging Native artists by providing an opportunity to have their original designs featured in Pendleton’s renowned wool blanket collection. The first-place winner will see their design incorporated into Pendleton’s American Indian College Fund blanket collection and distributed on products internationally. Second- and third-place winners will also receive scholarships and cash prizes.

American Indian and Alaska Native students enrolled at a TCU are eligible to submit up to two designs. Applicants do not need formal artistic training or previous textile design experience to participate.

Your contribution is appreciated.

The 2026 contest offers significant financial awards to support students in their educational journeys:

Winning designs are selected by a committee composed of Native American artists and representatives from the American Indian College Fund and Pendleton.

Pendleton Woolen Mills has partnered with the American Indian College Fund since 1995, providing more than $1.5 million in scholarship support for American Indian and Alaska Native students attending tribal colleges and universities.

Often located on Indian reservations and in remote rural communities, TCUs play an essential role in expanding access to higher education, career opportunities, and Indigenous knowledge. The American Indian College Fund provides millions of dollars in annual support to thousands of TCU students. The blanket design contest builds on that commitment by combining educational assistance with opportunities to celebrate Native creativity, culture, and storytelling.

The 2025 grand prize winner, Belle Brings Plenty, a citizen of the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe and 2025 graduate of United Tribes Technical College, created the Journey blanket in honor of her late brother, Cole Brings Plenty.

The design incorporates geometric shapes commonly found in traditional Lakóta artwork, with a dragonfly at its center representing healing medicine. The Lakóta word for “journey,” Oómani , also appears in the design’s ledger art elements.

Brings Plenty hopes the blanket will offer comfort and connection to those who encounter it.

“I just want people to be able to connect with this blanket in their own ways. I hope people can be able to wrap themselves in this blanket and feel loved,” she said.

Eligible American Indian and Alaska Native students attending a tribal college or university may submit up to two original designs. Formal art education and textile design experience are not required.

The submission period opens November 15, 2026, and all entries must be received by January 15, 2027 .

CLICK for complete contest guidelines, eligibility requirements, and application.

Through this longstanding partnership, the American Indian College Fund and Pendleton continue to create opportunities for emerging Native artists while investing in the education, cultural expression, and future of Indigenous communities.

scraped.author: Elyse Wild
scraped.h1: ‘Colonization F—ed All of Us’: Q&A with Native Comedian Joey Clift on Native History, Humor and His New Book
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

There’s one thing award-winning comedy writer Joey Clift (Cowlitz) wants people to know about the rez: “If you hang out on a rez with other Native folks, you’re going to hear a lot of laughter. You’re going to hear a lot of joy.”

Clift brings that joy into his literary debut as he examines the untold history of America’s first people. We’ve Been Here The Whole Time! A Not-So-Sacred Guide to All Things Native America which hit shelves last month, dives into iconically misunderstood figures like Pocahontas, the forgotten I ndigenous iron workers that built NYC, Native American sports mascots, the Land Back movement, Lily Gladstone, and more.

Native News Online’s Elyse Wild talked to Clift about Native humor, using satire to learn about hard truths, and which historical figures are invited to the powwow.

Tell me where you grew up and what you really loved about it.

I’m an enrolled member of the Cowlitz Indian Tribe in Washington state, and I grew up on the Tulalip Reservation, about 45 minutes from Seattle.

I think what I loved about the Tulalip Reservation was how beautiful it was to be surrounded by Coastal Salish culture throughout much of my upbringing. Going to school on the reservation and having assemblies that included things like dance performances was so cool.

Other than that, one thing I really loved about the reservation was the easy access to illegal fireworks. The Tulalip Reservation had an entire city called Boom City that’s just a sea of fireworks stands. That truly made every Fourth of July and New Year’s the most fun. I probably still have scars from third-degree burns.

One thing that really caught my attention about the book was the title, We’ve Been Here the Whole Time . We often hear the message, “We’re still here.” That’s a sobering, serious message that speaks to how marginalized Native communities have been and calls up the attempts at erasure. But “We’ve Been Here the Whole Time” seems to have a little edge of humor. Am I reading too much into that, or can you tell me a little bit about the title and whether that aligns with your thought process? Thanks so much for asking. I think the book title does a great job of capturing the book’s tone. That was something I talked with the publisher, Andrews McMeel Publishing, about a lot as we figured out how to package it.

I think the original title for the book was going to be Your School Never Taught You About Native People . That was one option, but we thought we needed something a little shorter and punchier. The title was actually a suggestion from the publisher: We’ve Been Here the Whole Time .

I really love it. I feel like it nails the truthful but comedy-forward approach I wanted the book to have.

Tell me how your Nativeness and the culture you grew up in influenced your work as a comedian.

I think the Native sense of humor influenced my career and how I approach comedy in a couple of different ways. Most of them are pretty indirect. I don’t wake up every morning trying to write Native jokes specifically. I write what’s funny to me.

Growing up on a reservation and having a lot of super funny family members influenced me. My uncle is very funny, and my mom was constantly making poop and fart jokes when I was a kid, which I didn’t appreciate at the time. Now I’m like, “Oh, my mom had jokes and still has jokes.” She’s very funny.

Your contribution is appreciated.

I’ve grown to really appreciate the comedic rhythm of Native jokes as I’ve become a professional comedy writer. I feel like there are two types of delivery for Native jokes. One is saying the meanest thing you’ve ever heard anybody say, followed by the most vicious burst of laughter. Or somebody will say the driest, most serious, intense-sounding thing you’ve ever heard, followed by, “Just kidding.”

I catch it whenever I’m hanging out with other Native folks or watching anything where Native folks are in conversation. I’ll hear somebody from a reservation across the country from where I grew up tell a joke the way I tell one. I’m like, “Oh, that feels like something I never really thought about influencing even how I deliver jokes.” But it definitely does.

Tell me about researching the book and using your skills as a comedy writer to write about these really difficult things in a way that’s also funny and easier to read.

My friends and I often joke that if you hang out with a group of Native folks, you’re always three seconds away from the conversation shifting to genocide. It’s such total whiplash for people who aren’t used to it.

I think if you hang out on a reservation with other Native folks, you’re going to hear a lot of laughter and joy. A lot of that is probably a coping mechanism for what we’ve gone through as a community and are still going through.

For this book, I view it as a comedic look at Native history, people, and contemporary Native culture. But it felt like if I wanted to write a book called A Not-So-Sacred Guide to All Things Native America , it would be disingenuous not to cover the darker stuff, like boarding schools, genocide, and the MMIW epidemic.

When I covered those topics in the book, I tried to honor the experiences people went through and write from a really sensitive place. But this is also a comedy. The primary goal was for people to learn, but also to laugh while doing it.

The way I approached that specifically in the boarding school chapter is something I’m really proud of. The chapter immediately after that is called, “Because the Past Two Chapters Were Pretty Heavy, Here’s a Picture of Cherokee Activist and Leader Wilma Mankiller Kicking the Founder of Indian Boarding Schools, General Pratt, in the Nuts.”

It features the most cartoonish drawing of Wilma Mankiller kicking this colonizer right in the dick. After that, there’s a chapter about how great that casino is.

I really tried to use my comedy writer hat as much as possible and make sure I was taking care of the audience comedically and tonally while people were reading the book. Whenever I’ve covered the darker stuff, I’ve always tried to find moments of levity to give the audience permission to experience a range of emotions while reading.

I see comedy as a fantastic tool for narrative change and education. Jokes are like the candy coating you put around cough medicine. Or, if you have a dog, it’s like the big gallon of peanut butter you put the pill into to get the dog to eat it.

There’s a lot of great research from organizations showing that comedy is a great tool for helping people take in and retain information in a way they might not from a two-hour college lecture or a 500-page history book.

What did you learn while researching the book that surprised you?

I grew up on a reservation, and many of the basics in the book were things I’ve known my entire life, or at least most of it.

But as I was researching the book, I traveled to many different tribal communities. I talked to Native folks from other communities about their experiences and the things they’re going through.

Something so interesting is that there are more than 570 federally recognized tribes and hundreds more at the state level. Our experiences are vastly different in terms of our relationships with the U.S. government, tribal enrollment, and how our tribal governments work.

It was really interesting to talk to other tribes about their specific situations regarding treaty rights and the issues facing their communities. It really underlined for me that my tribe is from Washington State and has its own specific challenges. Still, the issues facing even another tribe in Washington are probably going to be vastly different from those of my own tribe.

The way I think about it is that colonization fucked all of us a little bit differently, but it did fuck all of us. This really underlined that for me.

Another thing I should say is that I have a series of chapters in the book explaining why different historical figures are not invited to the powwow. There are chapters about why Christopher Columbus isn’t great, why Andrew Jackson sucks, etc.

In a lot of those chapters, like the Columbus chapter, I went in knowing, as a lot of Native folks do, that Christopher Columbus wasn’t a good dude. But when I actually looked into him, I had no idea how dumb he was.

He thought the Earth was shaped like a pear, with a nickel on top.

He was the governor of a country after he “discovered” the Americas, and he was so bad at his job that he was fired and arrested for being incompetent. I describe him in the book as a genocidal Mr. Bean, and that’s not inaccurate.

What do you hope Native readers take away from the book, and what do you hope non-Native readers take away from it?

I hope Native readers take away a lot of levity from knowing that somebody is cracking jokes about all this stuff that we’ve been talking about as communities for a long time.

Something I really love about Native readers reading this book is that many of them read it and then tell me there’s a lot they learned. We’re not a monolith. We don’t all have encyclopedia-level knowledge of every aspect of Native identity, culture, and history, just as I don’t.

It’s so cool to see Native folks reading this book, learning from it, and appreciating all the jokes and fun illustrations.

For non-Native people, I hope the main takeaway is that we’re still here. Native people represent many different cultures, and we’re all flourishing and living in 2026 in our own ways.

I hope people learn a basic understanding of Native history and culture. Something I’m very proud of in the book is that one of the last pages is an Indian 101 diploma with space for the reader to sign. After reading the book, you officially graduated from Indian 101.

Something I talk about a lot in the book that I hope non-Native readers take away is just how good my tribe’s casino is. It’s 20 minutes north of Portland, so it’s a short drive. There’s a hand-drawn map in the book showing how to get to my tribe’s casino.

I’d say the takeaways are that Native people are still here, readers will get a basic education on many different Native topics, and they’ll learn just how great the Cowlitz Casino is.

Joey, thank you so much for talking with me. Is there anything you want to add, or anything you were expecting me to ask that I didn’t?

One thing I should probably add is that, up until now, most ways to learn about this stuff in the book world have been really long, in-depth academic history textbooks or books that are ultra-focused on our trauma.

My goal with this book was to create an accessible way for non-Native people to learn about this stuff while also making something fun and funny for Native folks to read.

Especially now, when any history that runs counter to the American exceptionalism narrative is being removed from institutions and schools, I think it’s really important for our history to be accessible.

Something so cool, even in the months since this book came out, is that I’ve already heard from many middle schools, high schools, and colleges adopting it as part of their curricula.

We sold out our first two printings on the first day of its release.

Last week, we were the No. 1 best-selling nonfiction book in Oklahoma. Technically, it might have been two weeks ago, but recently we were the No. 1 best-selling nonfiction book in Oklahoma. I think we were the No. 7 or No. 8 best-selling nonfiction paperback book in Southern California.

It’s so cool and validating to see that people want to learn about Native history and culture, and to hear our stories.

I hope that this book’s success shows people there’s a desire for Native satire and Native comedy in literary spaces. I hope it shows people that they don’t just want to learn about Native people; they also want to laugh at funny jokes by Native writers. There’s a desire and a market for this.

Guest Opinion I am not sure it’s worth spending many brain cells […]
scraped.author: Mark Trahant
scraped.h1: Don’t Waste Brain Cells on Interior’s Plan to Sell Off Public Lands
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

The Trump administration’s Interior Department strategic plan prioritizes oil and gas development and threatens public lands, prompting concerns about potential executive actions and legal battles while invoking Theodore Roosevelt’s conservation legacy in ways that contradict his historic record of protecting public lands.

I am not sure it’s worth spending many brain cells on the Interior Department’s 2026-2030 Strategic Plan. If it was released before the election, then we’d all be mad and worried. But now? Not a chance.

To read more articles by Mark Trahant, go to: Marktrahant.substack.com

Even Western Republicans don’t like the idea of a sell off of public lands. Former Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke told the Associated Press that he “remains firmly opposed to the sale or transfer of public lands.” And he would vote against any measure.

Of course the Trump administration will try to do much of this by executive order. And that means a lot of litigation ahead.

Your contribution is appreciated.

The report, really a love letter to oil and gas, misappropriates history. In his letter Interior Secretary Doug Burgum writes:

As President Theodore Roosevelt, who helped shape and define our department, explained: “Conservation means development as much as it does protection.”

Perhaps it’s worth thinking about Roosevelt’s actual record. He added roughly 230 million acres to the public land base.

A summary from the The Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History:

“In the early twentieth century, President Theodore Roosevelt was a dynamic force in a relatively new movement known as conservationism. During his presidency, Roosevelt made conservation a major part of his administration. As the new century began, the frontier was disappearing. Once common animals were now threatened. Many Americans, including Roosevelt, saw a need to preserve the nation’s natural resources. He wanted to protect animals and land from businesses that he saw as a threat. Roosevelt said, “the rights of the public to the natural resources outweigh private rights, and must be given its first consideration.” By the end of his time as president, he had created five national parks, four game refuges, fifty-one national bird reservations as well as the National Forest Service. It could be said that Theodore Roosevelt, through laws, executive orders, and his strong personality, opened the nation’s eyes to the natural wonders of the land. Roosevelt had changed the attitude of America. As we begin the twenty-first century, conservation is once again an issue that the United States faces.”

Roosevelt was imperfect, but these ideals remain worthy.

scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

Since March 2025, Inuit children aged two to five have been found to have lower hemoglobin levels and are likelier to have anemia than during the period when HFV was operating: report.

A new report on access to food in Nunavut says the territory continues to be in a “food security crisis” and children are most affected.

“Existing survey data show that 7 in 10 Inuit children in the territory live in households that make sacrifices — skipping meals, eating less, and/or eating lower-quality food to make ends meet,” the report said.

The 146-page report was written by more than two dozen researchers looking into grocery supports and the Hamlet Food Voucher Program for Nunavut Inuit.

Researcher Vandna Sinha told APTN News that she hopes the new report will be the last word on the subject.

“We brought together a really great team of researchers from across disciplines and across universities so that we could look at food insecurity, and the effect of these initiatives on food insecurity, in a really comprehensive way and put something out that would hopefully eliminate the need for people to say we need more research,” said Sinha, an associate research professor at the University of Colorado Boulder’s Faculty of Education.

The report, Strengthening Food Access in Nunavut: Lessons from the Inuit Child First Initiative funded Grocery Supports and the Hamlet Food Voucher Program , is the product of work by four researchers from Qupanuaq, which advocates for Nunavut children and youth in partnership with 22 researchers from six universities along with the Institute for Circumpolar Research and BetterCart Analytics.

Sinha, who began research on Jordan’s Principle while working at McGill University in Montreal, said Qupanuaq contacted her to discuss potential research about food supports in Nunavut. She said the research team and the number of local advisors has expanded over the years.

Beginning with five pages of quotes from Nunavummiut about the strain and challenge of struggling to get enough food — and sacrifices that parents make to give their children better access to food — the report is unequivocal in its findings.

“Food insecurity surveys usually ask about events during the year,” the report noted, “but families in Nunavut faced much more consistent challenges: 8 out of 10 families we interviewed faced daily, weekly or monthly struggles to make ends meet.”

New report about an old problem

Hunger, food access, food security and food sovereignty are all longstanding concerns in Nunavut, the report noted.

In 2019, the federal government launched the Inuit Child First Initiative (ICFI) — an Inuit parallel to the Jordan’s Principle program designed to provide First Nations children with equal access to health, social and educational services.

Initially, the ICFI offered “Grocery Supports” to individual Inuit families who requested them. By 2023, the report notes, individual-family requests for Grocery Supports were overwhelming bureaucrats and creating a large backlog, which led Nunavut hamlets to apply for funding for food-voucher programs that would feed all Inuit children and youth in the communities.

This was known generally as the Hamlet Food Voucher program (HFV).

“By the end of 2024, these programs reached Inuit children in 24 of 25 communities, for an estimated annual cost of just under $100 million,” the report said. “They operated without complex or time-consuming application processes and allowed families to use the funds in ways that complemented their other budget-stretching strategies.”

The consequence was immediate; the report found the HFV seems to have reduced physical and psychological harms “by reducing hunger, increasing nutrition, improving physical health, improving quality of life and giving both families and communities greater resources to devote to needs that extended beyond nutrition.”

In March 2025, Indigenous Services Canada ended the program, forcing families to make requests for Grocery Supports once again.

However, the report notes, “After that, very few requests for individual Grocery Supports have been approved. The treatment of ICFI-funded Grocery Supports requests does not appear to meet the legal standards for responding to urgent cases that have been established for services to First Nations children through Jordan’s Principle, the southern parallel to ICFI.”

The number of people seeking daily meals from Iqaluit soup kitchen Qajuqturvik Community Food Centre saw a steady decline after HFV — which reversed when the program ended.

Likewise, since March 2025, Inuit children aged two to five have been found to have lower hemoglobin levels and are likelier to have anemia than during the period when HFV was operating.

Resilience isn’t enough to beat hunger

The research behind this report, Sinha noted, predated the emergence of the HFV program, but provides solid proof of arguments about the programs many advocates have made for years.

“We’ve been working on it for a couple of years, and this is the culmination of all those different kinds of research,” she said. “We already know what we need to know. We know that hunger has been a long-term problem. We know that it’s a structural problem. “There’s no way that Inuit in Nunavut can learn their way out of food insecurity. There’s no way they can love their way out of food insecurity. There’s no way that they can just hunker down and be strong and get through the problem, because it’s a structural problem. It needs structural solutions.”

The report, Sinha said, explains in detail the ways in which the HFV program worked.

“It was pretty efficient. It reached a large number of people really quickly for a cost that, in policy terms, is pretty reasonable,” she said. “It looks like it improved nutrition, improved physical health outcomes, decreased hunger, improved quality of life.”

By contrast, Sinha pointed out the consequences of inadequate nourishment are also well documented, and are likewise understood by most people on an individual level.

“I’m not my best self when I’m hungry. Children don’t learn well when they’re hungry. Parents don’t do their best parenting when they’re hungry. It has severe consequences in terms of health.”

Further, she noted, research has begun to track sprawling mental-health impacts of food insecurity over the long term, which she said were tied to depression, anxiety, impulsivity and suicide.

These factors can weigh upon quality of life, Sinha said, since it’s hard for any person to realize their full potential and thrive when the primary focus of their energy is on meeting basic needs.

This is true for individual people, she said, but it also extends to the collective impact on society.

“When we talk to people, what’s really, really obvious is the love, the strength, the sharing that they do, the resourcefulness,” she said. “But all of those strengths and resources are being tied up in these basic needs, and that means that people individually and collectively aren’t being allowed to think about more, to dream about more, to invest in more. That’s not equitable. It’s not just.”

New funding

Sinha said she and many of her fellow researchers saw little encouragement in the federal government’s budget that promises to allocate $575 million to the Inuit Child First initiative over five years. Ottawa has negotiated that program — called Pirutsiagutiit — with Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami as well as four Inuit treaty organizations and plans to launch it on April 1, 2027.

At that point, ITK and Inuit organizations will take over administering the program.

“The funding for that in the new budget is not nearly enough to cover the Hamlet Food Voucher program alone,” Sinha explained, “and because that’s supposed to be the way of addressing children’s complex needs, if it all gets sucked up dealing with the basic need around food, then the other needs that families have that are acute and so important don’t get addressed.”

She said the budget would maintain the status quo following the $100 million cut to funding for food for Inuit children.

“It’s ongoing about what the terms of the new funding would look like, but we are hopeful that they’ll give more [than they have announced at present],” Sinha explained. “The funding level has not increased in any measurable way.” The consequence, she argued, is that Inuit children get limited access to respite care, occupational therapy and other services available to First Nations children in the south through Jordan’s Principle.

“I hope that the federal government and the [territorial] government would work with Inuit leadership to find a way to make sure that families in Nunavut are getting equitable support. And that sounds pretty basic, I think because it is, but that’s certainly not happening.”

The cost of living was already high in the North, she said, but it has increased dramatically as prices have risen everywhere else. As a result, she argued, Inuit children cannot access the same support available to Indigenous families who don’t live in Nunavut.

“We know what’s needed,” she said. “We need a locally-based system of preventative and supportive programs so that people get their needs met without having to go into the child welfare system, and every major review that you will look at in any jurisdiction has said that over a couple of decades.”

Funding issues extend to the federal Nutrition North food-security subsidy, whose amounts also increased under the new budget.

“It’s a fraction of what would be needed to solve the price differential in Nunavut,” she said. “As with the ICFI funding, what they’ve allocated for the entire North is a fraction of what we would need in Nunavut.”

Read more:

With no end to hunger crisis in Nunavut, community orgs work hard to keep residents fed

First bowhead whale harvest since 2022 brings Iqaluit abundant meat

Cost of living adjustment

Sinha said that the Qupanuaq organization, the lead partner on this research project, is calling for a cost-of-living adjustment under the Canada Child Benefit.

“Based on our comparison of different options, based on existing research,” Sinha said, “we think that’s the most efficient way to move forward.”

She argued such an adjustment would essentially double the Canada Child Benefit, with which the lowest-income families would experience roughly the same level of support they got from the Hamlet Food Voucher program.

For Sinha and her colleagues, there are two discussions about relieving hunger in Nunavut that need to happen simultaneously: one is a long-term plan to bring about food sovereignty in the territory in order to address deep structural issues driving hunger. The other discussion is about how to feed hungry people right away.

“We’re talking about immediate increases in food access, because people shouldn’t go hungry while they’re working towards those long-term solutions,” she said. “A cost-of-living adjustment to the Canada Child Benefit would be a fairly large policy shift.

“The U.S. already adjusts food benefits, for instance, for cost-of-living. So it’s not unprecedented if the U.S. is doing it. In the scope of how policy works, it seems like it’s a pretty straightforward way to go.”

Sinha said the team that carried out the study has worked in close partnership with Nunavut Tunngavik Inc. in order to ensure research findings would be shared with the federal government. “We continue to do this and hope that the research findings will be able to inform policy discussion moving forward.”

Jesse joined APTN as a producer after 16 years as a print and web journalist. During seven of those years, he covered the Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee for community newsmagazine The Nation. Jesse’s writing on Indigenous issues has also appeared in Canadian Geographic, the Toronto Star, the Rover, The Eastern Door, Metro, and the Huffington Post.

scraped.title: second-generation cutoff needs to end says FNLC
scraped.description: An open letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney and Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull Masty calls for an end to second-generation cut-off.
scraped.author: Leanne Sanders
scraped.h1: First Nations Leadership Council sends open letter to the prime minister, Indigenous Services over delay in passing Bill S-2
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

B.C. First Nations ‘deeply alarmed’ by new standalone legislation touted at First Nations-First Ministers meeting. Photo: APTN.

In an open letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney and Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull Masty, the First Nations Leadership Council (FNLC) is calling for an immediate end to the second-generation cut-off .

The FNLC is made up of the B.C. Assembly of First Nations, First Nations Summit and the Union of B.C. Indian Chiefs. It’s calling for an end to sex and race-based discrimination in the Indian Act, and removal of the second-generation cutoff.

“We fully support the amendments to Bill S-2 made by the Standing Senate Committee on Indigenous Peoples and adopted by the Senate of Canada on December 4, 2025,” the FNLC said in the letter.

“Further, we are concerned with the Minister of Indigenous Services Canada’s (ISC) use of a secretive process regarding the new standalone legislation, which violates the legal duty to consult in good faith.”

The second-generation cutoff is when a person, under section 6(1) of the Indian Act, passes status to a child no matter who the other parent is. But a person under section 6(2) can pass it on only if the other parent is also registered as “status” under the Indian Act.

After two generations of parenting with someone who is not registered, the third generation is out. That is the second-generation cut-off.

The FNLC maintains that the immediate elimination of the second-generation cut-off is supported by UN human rights bodies including the UN Human Rights Committee, the UN Committee on the Elimination of Discrimination Against Women, and, in May 2026, the UN Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples .

“For months, Bill S-2 has been stalled in the Standing Committee on Indigenous and Northern Affairs (INAN Committee), while the Minister insisted upon further consultations and then argued for broader registration reform and confused the issues of band membership and self-determination over citizenship with Indian status, and is now proposing new draft legislation. These deceptive tactics are a red herring to distract and delay the passage of Bill S-2,” the letter stated.

First Nations Summit Political executive Robert Phillips said in an interview with APTN News that it’s frustrating that “we’ve governed ourselves for thousands of years. And to remove second-generation cutoff and maybe replace it with universal one parent rule, or introducing legislation-and then it’s stalling?”

“We’re getting to the point where now we’re in argumentative stage…I do believe we need to be at a table and say that the authority should rest with First Nations and those that have treaties or those that have Aboriginal rights like here in British Columbia…,” Phillips said.

According to Phillips, Gull-Masty has invited “select First Nations leaders” to consult with ISC on new draft legislation to address the second-generation cut-off.

In the letter to Carney and Gull-Masty, the FNLC said, “we understand that… the minister has invited select First Nations leaders to consult with ISC regarding new draft legislation to address the second-generation cut-off, on the condition that they sign a Non-Disclosure Agreement (NDA), which binds them to not disclose any information that is shared with them for a period of five years, unless that information is disclosed to the public by the Minister.”

That doesn’t sit well with the FNLC.

“Using NDAs to convene meetings with selected leaders blocks First Nations leaders from consulting their Nations, members, technical and legal advisors. This secretive and selective process is an alarming escalation of the government’s tactics to undermine the broad support of First Nations.”

Read More:

Senators vote to end the second-generation cutoff for ‘status Indians’

According to a statement from Gull-Masty’s office, a “collaborative process” on the second-generation cut off and section 10 voting thresholds concluded at the end of July, where the government invited First Nations to “put forward their own proposals and solutions to address these inequities in the Indian Act.

“We heard a range of perspectives, proposals, and priorities, alongside a shared sense of urgency: the second generation cut-off must be addressed,” according to a statement provided by Gull-Masty’s office. “While the Collaborative Process has now concluded, the work continues. We are currently reviewing the proposals, feedback and perspectives shared through the process to inform next steps, including legislative reform.”

The FNLC said the process goes against “the vast majority of First Nations across Canada” and introducing new standalone legislation ignores “broad support from First Nations and First Nations rights-holders…and directly contravenes the mandate of the vast majority of First Nations across Canada, who are on record supporting the immediate passage of Bill S-2 as amended by the Senate.”

Leanne has a certificate in broadcasting and has more than 12 years of radio news experience, both as an anchor and reporter in Saskatchewan and Alberta. The Métis journalist is a passionate writer and born storyteller and loves to connect with people and learn about their life experiences.

scraped.title: Gull-Masty surprised premier raised abolishing Indian Act
scraped.description: Mandy Gull-Masty says she was surprised when Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew raised the idea of abolishing the Indian Act at a meeting.
scraped.author: Fraser Needham
scraped.h1: ISC minister says she was not expecting Kinew’s comments about abolishing the Indian Act
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty says she was as surprised as anyone when Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew raised the idea of abolishing the Indian Act last month and was hoping for more information on what role the province would play.

“I think it’s interesting to see somebody who’s a provincial premier wanting to frame up that space,” she said. “Clearly, in his role he would have to indicate his responsibility in the provincial seat and how you would serve those off-reserve community members.

“I think that’s the initiative I was hoping to see as a minister coming out of that space because you have to increase the responsibility, the partnership, the role of the provincial government in the path beyond the Indian Act.”

The idea of getting rid of the Indian Act was raised by Kinew during a press conference at the First Nations First Ministers meeting in Ottawa on Oct. 26.

“What you saw was a spontaneous moment where premier Kinew wanted to speak about status. Wanted to speak about the Indian Act.”

The Indian Act , passed in 1876, continues to govern matters of Indian status, First Nations governance, and reserve lands. The federal government has tried, and failed, to abolish it a number of times in the past 50 years.

At a later press conference, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he was open to the idea as long as it was co-developed with First Nations and has tasked some of his ministers to look into the issue.

He said he was directing Gull-Masty to chart a path with First Nations on amending or abolishing the act.

‘Overrated’

Conservative MP Billy Morin says the 2026 federal budget is disappointing on a number of levels.

“This might be the most overrated Prime Minister (Mark Carney) I’ve seen in quite some time,” the MP for Edmonton Northwest said. “Even more overrated than his predecessor (Justin Trudeau). This guy’s apparently a banker, a guy who knows how to do finances.

“He’s running deficits bigger than Trudeau. Bigger deficits than Trudeau and he takes great pride in that?”

The budget projects deficits of well over $50 billion over each of the next five years.

The 2023/24 deficit, the last budget under Trudeau, came in at $61.9 billion and the 2026/27 deficit is projected to be $62.3 billion.

Morin is the Indigenous Services critic for the Conservatives.

Metis disappointed

The president of the Manitoba Métis Federation says leaving Métis people out of the 2026 federal budget is not a mistake the Carney government can afford to make.

“It shouldn’t be something that we need to worry about whether it’s a budget or not,” David Chartrand said. “It should be automatic. It’s part of the fiduciary responsibility and constitutional responsibility of Canada,” he said.

The 2026 budget makes roughly $50 billion over ten years in investments in Indigenous priorities but makes no mention of Métis-specific investments.

Some have expressed fears the government is returning to a non-distinctions-based funding model that largely focuses on First Nations people.

Chartrand said the government collects billions of dollars in taxes from Métis people every year and it needs to invest that money back in their communities.

Fraser spent the last 20 years working in both print and radio in Saskatchewan – mostly in the northern part of the province. Before joining APTN’s Ottawa bureau, he was news director for the Missinipi Broadcasting Corporation working out of their Prince Albert office. He holds a bachelor of arts degree in political science from Carleton University and a diploma of journalism from Algonquin College.

scraped.author: North Dakota Monitor
scraped.h1: North Dakota unveils application process for first potential charter schools
scraped.body_text:
ICT

This story was originally published by North Dakota Monitor.

Michael Achterling North Dakota Monitor

North Dakota’s first charter schools are potentially on the horizon for fall 2027 as the Department of Public Instruction released application materials last week and a timeline to set the new schools in motion.

North Dakota public charter schools were authorized by the Legislature in 2025 with the passage of Senate Bill 2241 .

“Opening a public school is a serious responsibility, and North Dakota families deserve confidence that any new school has a clear plan to help students succeed,” said Superintendent of Public Instruction Levi Bachmeier in a statement.

The state will provide an average per student payment of about $8,300 to each charter school based on its enrollment. The new schools are not eligible to receive funding from property taxes, according to the department.

Applications for new charter schools under the ND ANCHOR program, Authorizing North Dakota Charters for High-Quality Outcomes and Results, can be submitted to the department beginning Dec. 2 and will continue until March 2, 2027, according to the DPI website .

Under state law , public charter schools will operate within the state’s public education system and cannot charge students tuition. They also must enroll all students who apply and use a lottery system, if enrollment surpasses the school’s capacity. Public charter schools must not base admission criteria on ethnicity, national origin, religion, gender, income level, English proficiency or disabling conditions.

The schools are also prohibited from engaging in religious educational programming and operations, according to state law.

Arlene Wolf, director of school approval and opportunity for the department, said the application materials, process and timeline were the results of nearly two years of work looking into best practices.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

“We’re ensuring that we’re really, truly opening those that are high quality schools with really good plans and have the best interests at heart,” Wolf said. She added the department consulted with national charter school organizations and other states.

A public charter school is not something that can be opened quickly, she said, and potential schools should take some time to weigh whether becoming a public charter school would be the best fit.

Wolf said the performance agreements with the department will be a key mechanism in setting the benchmarks for the new charter schools and evaluating their success.

As part of the application, prospective charter schools must enter into performance agreements that measure student academic proficiency and growth, attendance and recurrent enrollment, graduation readiness, financial and governance performance and community engagement. The school’s results in those areas will determine renewal eligibility and potential corrective action if performance goals are not met, according to the department.

“They are kind of held to that,” Wolf said. “It is a contract.”

Nick Archuleta, president of ND United, a union representing teachers and public employees, said the charter school performance agreements are an important guardrail to ensure quality education.

“If you are covering the academic, financial and governing structures of these things, that’s a very good place to start,” Archuleta said. “I think it is a sustainable path and I think it’s a good path because it does put those guardrails in right away so there isn’t any gray area.”

He also commended the department for requiring licensed teachers and staff members for the charter schools, as well as, an in-person learning requirement that would prevent online academies from sprouting up across the state.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

“We know that education is predicated on relationships,” he said. “And it’s hard to form those relationships, if you are going to be constantly online.”

Each potential charter school must also submit to a public interview with department officials before any approval decision is made.

Established North Dakota schools are able to convert to public charter schools under the law.

Private schools that could potentially shift to a public charter school may already have a lot of the information needed for the application, she said.

The department will release an informational video Monday to explain the application process.

“We wanted to get it out. We wanted people to look it over,” Wolf said. “It’s gonna take time.”

Dave Archambault Sr., a member of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe, a former principal and superintendent of tribal schools in South Dakota, told members of the department during a December administrative rules hearing that charter schools give opportunities for communities to try something new, which is needed in tribal education.

“I want a lot more for our children on these reservation schools to do better,” Archambault said. “It (charter schools) has such great possibilities for developing human potential and that’s what I want.”

He said having more options for Native American families choosing where to send their children to school could lead to more successful outcomes.

During the 2021-22 school year, the average graduation rate for students across the U.S. was 87 percent while the rate for Native American students was 74 percent during the same time period, according to the National Center for Education Statistics .

A few people and groups have reached out to the department since the application was posted last week, Wolf said, but interest has waned a little since the law went into effect in 2025.

The department also plans to open another application window for public charter schools next fall, she said, and hopes to have an annual application window opening every fall.

scraped.title: What if we had the land to be nomadic again? - ICT
scraped.description: I went to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification COP17 in Mongolia to witness their nomadic way of life.
scraped.author: ICT Opinion
scraped.h1: What if we had the land to be nomadic again?
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Anpo Jensen Oglala Lakota

I landed in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, around 9 o’clock at night, exchanged my currency for tugrik and found a taxi. It was dark, but there was still a bright white light on the horizon, like the sun had just gone down. While sitting in the back of the taxi, it hit me. I can’t believe I’m here. I was so far north and away from home that I got nervous just thinking about it. But deep down, I knew I had to come. There was a reason, and it was up to me to uncover it.

I was there for UNCCD COP17, the United Nations conference on land degradation and drought, as part of the international youth delegation. Rangelands, which cover 54 percent of the Earth’s land , were at the center, and the focus was on implementation and community-led restoration . I am an Oglala Lakota environmental engineer, and I study international frameworks and legally binding instruments intended to protect land and water. I also came to witness Mongolia’s nomadic way of life. As someone who comes from a nomadic history, I wanted to see what it looked like before our nomadic lifestyle was brought to a forced halt by reservations.

I had never seen a place that mirrored the Great Plains – the vast grasslands, the horse culture, the sustainable homes, even a clan system like our tiospaye systems. There I hiked Turtle Rock, where offerings were left and it reminded me of hiking Black Elk Peak at home.

But this is what shocked me the most. Nearly 30 percent of Mongolians are still nomadic, according to the Asia Foundation . This isn’t ancient history. Most live with their families and move four times a year with the seasons and the stars, the way we used to. Before traveling outside of Ulaanbaatar, I couldn’t even imagine this reality. Could there be a timeline or a future where we, as Oceti Sakowin, also still moved four times a year? Is it still possible for us?

The land itself makes that possible. Mongolia has a free land policy where every citizen is entitled to a plot of land of their own, at no cost. The pastureland stays public and shared, so herding families can keep moving across it. About 72 percent of the country is open, shared rangeland , and that openness gives families access to a sustainable food system.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

I was so impressed that I wished we still lived in our thiíkčeya . I wished it was normal again, the way living in a ger is normal in Mongolia. Still, what I saw was beautiful and peaceful, and I wanted it for us.

Mongolia has its own struggles. Like us, Mongolians have experienced mining and extractivism on their lands. Yet their nomadic way of life continues. When I asked our tour guide if young people who live nomadic still go to college, he said of course. And like ours, their young people face pressure from mainstream society to choose between living in the city and returning home to their communities.

Over dinner with Mongolian friends, we found that we carried the same pressure to retain our culture through graduate school. At one point, every friend at the table knew their clan and its origin story, and I shared mine too. This reminded me that the Lakota way connects me with the rest of the world.

I also saw the numbers. About 77 percent of the land is degraded, and 21 percent of lakes and 12 percent of rivers have dried up . Overgrazing is part of it too, responsible for about 49 percent of the desertification .

But the research is clear that moving herds is not the problem . In Mongolia, degradation has been driven by larger herds and less movement, as families settled closer to markets and many cut back their seasonal migrations . Among the Maasai in Kenya, land that stayed shared and moved with the seasons held more grass and more wildlife than land divided into private plots, according to the Journals of Arid Environments and Biological Conservation Overgrazing comes from being fenced in and pushed to produce more, not from moving with the land. That is what our ancestors understood when we followed the buffalo.

Home is facing the same problem. Between 2000 and 2007, wells in the Madison aquifer dropped anywhere from a few feet to more than 100 feet. An earlier South Dakota Mines study found the region could not meet current demand in a drought. The answer on the table is a $2 billion, 161-mile pipeline from the Missouri River that could take decades to build.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

We have seen this answer before. The Mni Wiconi pipeline already brings Missouri River water to the reservation. And yet families on Pine Ridge still wait years to be connected to a water line that runs right past their homes. There is no reliable count of who on the reservation lives without running water. That gap in the data is part of the problem, and it is why Anpoetry, the initiative I started, exists.

There’s another way forward, one our ancestors already practiced. We can restore our connection to the land and water as one system, beyond the borders of the reservation. That is why the treaty territory of the Oceti Sakowin matters.

The research backs this up. A study across Australia, Brazil and Canada found that Indigenous-managed lands have equal or higher biodiversity than protected areas. A 2026 review led by the University of British Columbia found they protect forests, biodiversity and carbon as well as or better than government protected areas. Indigenous-led solutions are proven solutions, and that is why we are the ones to lead this work.

Today, the world is still building legally binding instruments to protect land, water and biodiversity . The UN Convention to Combat Desertification, which brought me to Mongolia, and the Convention on Biological Diversity both bind the countries that join them, and nations are still negotiating a legally binding treaty to end plastic pollution. The 1851 and 1868 Fort Laramie Treaties are legally binding instruments too, and they protected a land base large enough for our people to remain nomadic. In that sense, our treaties were ahead of their time.

The treaty council taught me why we protected that land. Protecting the land meant protecting the water systems within that territory too. What if our treaties were honored as intended?

I figured out what the reason was. Mongolia showed me that a nomadic life isn’t something lost to history. It is happening right now. With the land, it could happen for us too. I was there to be reminded to dream bigger. Dream bigger than what is.

Anpo Jensen is a Lakota environmental engineer and co-founder of Anpoetry Climate, an Indigenous-led initiative advancing environmental stewardship and sovereignty through science, storytelling, and community-led solutions. She is also the founder of Anpoetry.
