scraped.h1: New Zealanders won’t know for weeks who won the election as neither side secures clear victory
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Charlotte Graham-McLay Associated Press

WELLINGTON, New Zealand — New Zealanders will wait for weeks to discover who will lead the country after Saturday, Nov.7, election failed to deliver a decisive win for the right or the left, leaving fraught negotiations for a wafer-thin governing majority the only apparent path to victory for either side.

The tightest vote in years delivered a stinging rebuke to the major parties which have long dominated New Zealand politics, Christopher Luxon’s center-right National party and center-left Labour led by Chris Hipkins, as voters threw more support behind minor parties on the ideological flanks than before. On Saturday’s, Nov. 7, numbers, minor parties would enter negotiations for a governing deal with leverage to extract deeper policy concessions from a weakened National or Labour.

The near-deadlock was partly produced because voters, apparently weary of New Zealand’s economic woes and apathetic about both Luxon and Hipkins , chose to propel a new entrant group to Parliament for the first time in years. Opportunity, led by 38-year-old business consultant and political newcomer Qiulae Wong, is unaligned with either bloc and Wong has said she could work with either side to form a government.

Wong’s pledges of evidence-based centrism and an end to partisan bickering had on the results secured seven seats for Opportunity — enough to frustrate both left and right in a simple path to power. It was a staggering ascension for a party that made three failed attempts at Parliament before Wong became leader less than a year ago.

The conservative bloc has a simpler route to victory, but results could change

Other winners were harder to identify and on Sunday, Nov. 8, “who won the election 2026” was the top trending Google search in New Zealand. So unclear was the result that parties won’t begin negotiations to form a government until final tallies are released on Nov. 27, confirming the exact number of seats they’ve won.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

With 2.8 million ballots counted on election night, the conservative incumbent government led by Luxon’s National party appeared close to the slimmest possible return to power — by just one seat. However, Luxon didn’t claim victory, instead striking a note of cautious optimism that he could negotiate a second term in power.

Speaking to reporters, Luxon blamed public dissatisfaction on global shocks which have buffeted New Zealand’s trade-based economy, noting that other incumbent governments worldwide have faced voters’ rancor over living costs.

Yet his opponent Hipkins, who was turfed from office in 2023 largely over discontent about the same economic issues, didn’t appear to benefit on Nov. 7. The left-wing bloc appeared to fall short of a majority but was still hopeful it could triumph — though that seemed a more remote prospect.

Electoral officials were due on Sunday, Nov. 8, to begin counting nearly 400,000 so-called special votes, including from New Zealanders who live abroad, a process expected to take three weeks.

Those ballots have historically granted an additional seat or two in Parliament to left-wing parties, which could snatch the current razor-thin majority from the right, although such an outcome would likely leave the left struggling to form a majority too. If a government can’t be formed, New Zealand could face a fresh vote.

Incumbent Luxon urges people to ‘calm down’ and enjoy a break from politics

“I think everyone’s over politics so let’s all have a bit of a break for the next three weeks,” Luxon told reporters on Sunday. He will lead a caretaker government until an outcome is reached.

Luxon suggested that National had a viable path to power and boasted that it had secured more seats in Parliament than any other group. However, election night was bleak for his party.

Several of National’s most senior lawmakers would exit politics on results so far, including the ministers of finance and defense, the speaker of parliament, and the attorney general. With the party’s traditional governing partners winning increased support, Luxon faces a more strident list of policy demands to secure their backing.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

Libertarian ACT won 13 seats and populist New Zealand First won 12. Both are led by canny veteran politicians, and detractors of Luxon, a former business executive who entered politics in 2020, said his dealings with them in the three years since he took office had highlighted his political inexperience.

The vote was a slap for both major parties

New Zealanders don’t vote for prime ministers. Instead they cast two votes, one for their preferred party and another for the candidate they want as their local representative.

The country has one house of Parliament and no states, so the central government holds ultimate sway over New Zealand’s direction. Governments in the South Pacific nation of 5.6 million people are elected every three years.

National won just 29.21 percent of the preferred party vote as of Sunday, Nov. 8, a collapse of its previous result, and secured its 42 seats entirely by winning local constituency races. Luxon, who unusually faced two separate confidence votes among his own lawmakers this year, further slumped in popularity as leader close to election day.

However, Labour also won just 29.36 percent of the party vote, a result that appeared to suggest a second election defeat for career politician Hipkins. Despite winning about the same party vote percentage as National, Labour has secured only 36 seats on numbers so far because they won fewer local races.

Minor parties on the left saw bolstered support. The environmentally-focused Greens won 16 seats and Indigenous rights group Te Pāti Māori secured five.

The total number of seats in New Zealand’s Parliament changes due to quirks in how seat allocations are calculated. There would currently be 131 lawmakers elected, with 66 seats required for a majority.

Luxon’s conservative bloc would currently hold 67, a razor-thin margin likely to discomfit a leader managing a three-way government with two emboldened minor parties. However, the left bloc held only 57 seats before the historically left-leaning special votes were counted.

Even if the final tally boosted the left bloc’s seats slightly, Hipkins would apparently need support from newcomer Wong to govern.

Before the election, Luxon repeatedly ruled out negotiating with Wong. He sidestepped questions on Sunday, Nov. 8, about whether his vanishingly slim lead had changed his mind.

scraped.title: Usher and Chris Brown reportedly still at odds despite putting on a united front for fans
scraped.description: Usher and Chris Brown reportedly clash over creative control and concert delays as their joint R&B Tour loses Los Angeles and Miami dates.
scraped.author: Peter Kerich
scraped.h1: Usher and Chris Brown reportedly still at odds despite putting on a united front for fans
scraped.body_text:
Two upcoming performances in Los Angeles and Miami have been canceled as questions about the singers' working relationship continue.

Usher and Chris Brown may be sharing the stage, but apparently, they aren’t exactly getting along behind the scenes.

The R&B superstars’ joint tour is reportedly dealing with some serious interpersonal drama, with a source close to the situation telling PEOPLE that the relationship between the two singers has deteriorated to the point that they can barely stand each other.

In an exclusive report published Friday, PEOPLE detailed the alleged fallout , which reportedly intensified following a disagreement during the tour’s Atlanta stop earlier this month. According to the insider, the tension stems from longstanding personal differences, competing egos and disagreements over creative control.

The situation allegedly came to a head when the Atlanta concert began nearly two and a half hours late. Brown reportedly wanted to delay the performance because of heavy traffic around Mercedes-Benz Stadium, hoping to give fans more time to arrive. Usher, however, was reportedly frustrated with the delay and confronted Brown backstage.

The singers eventually appeared together onstage, performing several songs and exchanging hugs, giving fans the impression that any disagreement had been resolved. But according to PEOPLE’s source, the friendly display was largely for appearances.

“They were doing it for show,” the insider reportedly said, adding that the artists were still not speaking backstage.

The reported friction comes as two additional performances on the joint R&B Tour have been canceled. The Nov. 16 show at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California, and the Dec. 6 performance at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami are no longer moving forward. The source disputed speculation that poor ticket sales were responsible, instead pointing to the singers’ inability to work together.

Their Nov. 15 Los Angeles performance remained listed as of the report, although even members of their respective teams reportedly weren’t certain both artists would appear.

For now, the tour’s financial commitments and obligations to fans appear to be keeping the two performers on the same bill. Whether they can put their differences aside long enough to finish the run remains another question.

scraped.author: Peter Kerich
scraped.h1: Tems named executive music producer for ‘Children of Blood and Bone’ film
scraped.body_text:
The Nigerian singer will help shape the soundtrack for the highly anticipated fantasy adaptation, featuring Burna Boy, Ayra Starr and other African artists.

Nigerian singer Tems has been named executive music producer for the upcoming film adaptation of “ Children of Blood and Bone ,” adding another major international project to her growing career.

The announcement, reported by Album Talks on Nov. 12, revealed that Tems will help shape the musical direction of the film, whose soundtrack is expected to feature an impressive lineup of African artists, including Burna Boy , BNXN, Fireboy DML, Kold AF, Ayra Starr and Obongjayar, alongside additional performers yet to be announced. The film is scheduled to premiere in January 2027.

Tems’ executive music producer role places her at the center of the film’s musical identity, bringing together established and emerging voices from across the African music scene.

The announced lineup spans different sounds and generations of contemporary African music. Burna Boy, Ayra Starr, BNXN, Fireboy DML and Obongjayar have built international audiences, while Kold AF adds another name to the soundtrack’s diverse roster.

The project creates an opportunity to introduce a wider global audience to African musical talent through a major cinematic production. The film is based on Nigerian-American author Tomi Adeyemi’s bestselling fantasy novel of the same name. Drawing inspiration from West African culture and mythology, the story follows a young woman navigating a world where magic has been suppressed and explores themes of power, identity, oppression and resistance.

The adaptation is among the highly anticipated fantasy releases scheduled for 2027, bringing Adeyemi’s fictional world to the screen for an international audience.

scraped.title: ‘Me and her good’: Offset opens up about where things stand with Cardi B
scraped.description: The rapper opened up about their relationship after separating, revealing how ongoing online criticism has affected their children.
scraped.author: Bolarinwa Oladeji
scraped.h1: ‘Me and her good’: Offset opens up about where things stand with Cardi B
scraped.body_text:
The rapper opened up about their relationship after separating, revealing how ongoing online criticism has affected their children.

Offset knows how the internet sees him, and he says it is starting to cost his family more than it costs him.

The Atlanta rapper appeared on the New York Times’ “Popcast ” and spoke candidly about the reputation that has followed him through his marriage to and split from Cardi B.

Years of headlines and social media commentary have made him an easy villain online, and he admitted that the image gets to him. “I hate when people think that I’m a bad person, bro,” he said. “It bothers me.”

He was quick to say he wasn’t fishing for pity, stressing that he didn’t want any kind of sympathy. His concern, he explained, is what the narrative does to the people around him.

He has parents and children who see what is written about him. He said his oldest son, now 16, has gotten into trouble at school after seeing things posted about his father and hearing others repeat them.

The irony, as Offset described it, is that the conflict people keep circulating is no longer real.

“What’s so crazy is we good. Me and her good,” he said of Cardi B, explaining that the two have worked through their differences with their children as the priority. He said he has been spending time with his kids and has no issue with his former wife. “I salute everything that she doing,” he added.

What he will not do is put that peace on display to win back public opinion. Asked whether he wanted to show the world a more positive version of the relationship, Offset said no.

As long as he and Cardi B are on good terms and their children are doing well, he said, there is nothing to prove. “It’s not a show,” he said, acknowledging that he might “take the hit” for keeping it private because their mutual respect comes first.

He also pointed to how separate their lives have become. “She got her own whole world. It’s two different worlds now,” he said, adding that he would never want to merge those worlds and make anyone uncomfortable, especially when fans already make things harder than they need to be.

Offset and Cardi B married in 2017 and share three children; Kulture, Wave and Blossom. Their separation in 2024 played out under heavy public scrutiny, and both have since moved on with their own lives.

The interview offers a rare look at the other side of a story much of the public believes it already knows.

PARIS, FRANCE – JUNE 27: (EDITORIAL USE ONLY – For Non-Editorial use please seek approval from Fashion House) Rihanna, Riot and ASAP Rocky attend the AWGE Menswear Spring/Summer 2026 show as part of Paris Fashion Week on June 27, 2025 in Paris, France. (Photo by Arnold Jerocki/Getty Images)

It might be difficult for just anyone to outshine Rihanna, but one person has managed to do so: her second-born son, Riot Rose. The 3-year-old made his magazine cover debut in Arena Homme+ with a set of photos that have fans losing their minds over how adorable he is.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

Last month, folks were going crazy over all three of Rihanna’s kids—RZA, Riot, and Rocki Irish—featuring in her Savage X Fenty holiday season line, but now Riot is taking the spotlight for himself in an iconic photoshoot that shows he has the same modeling chops as his parents.

Styled by Rihanna’s longtime stylist Jahleel Weaver, the young model is draped in Chanel jackets, Chopard jewelry, and other designer pieces that fashion lovers could only dream of having in their closets, Page Six reported.

In one picture, Rihanna is holding Riot in the background, wearing the red jumpsuit she wore for her Super Bowl performance in 2023, while Riot wears a matching black one, leaving folks teary-eyed as they remember that the “Diamonds” singer was pregnant with her second-born son at the time.

waitttt Rih recreated the superbowl outfit because she was pregnant with Riot at the time 🥹 pic.twitter.com/O0U73FesPR

“Nephew finally gets his cover,” commented another user on X.

In a second image, the tiny model is sporting a sideways flat cap, with a white turtleneck and a shimmering suit jacket for a ’90s look that has folks online typing, “ARE YOU KIDDING?! He’s adorable.”

ARE YOU KIDDING?! He’s adorable 🥹😭😭 pic.twitter.com/sX0jRXsoNR

Other users have noted how Riot is a natural in front of the camera with poses that rival models with decades-long careers.

“Damn, he was born for this. Look at that perfect pose. He’s so cute omg,” posted one fan.

Damn, he was born for this. Look at that perfect pose 🥹 he’s so cute omg 🥰 pic.twitter.com/lN9cG06jem

User @livingthroughJ exclaimed, “STOP PLAYING WIT EM RIOT!!!!!”

User @Mrmouthalmighty commented that Riot is a mini Rihanna. Others have gone so far as to show the similarities between Riri and Riot by putting pictures of them side by side, and we have to agree he is on the same fashion trajectory as his style icon mom.

items.title: Charles Blow Predicted the Blue wave in the South
items.summary: In 2021, Charles Blow argued that Black Americans should participate in a reverse Great Migration by returning to the South in his book, 'The Devil You Know.' The 2026 midterms just proved him right.Read more...

scraped.title: How Charles Blow’s Thesis Played Out in the 2026 Midterms
scraped.h1: Charles Blow Predicted the Blue wave in the South
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

In 2021, Charles Blow argued that Black Americans should participate in a reverse Great Migration by returning to the South in his book, ‘The Devil You Know.’ The 2026 midterms just proved him right.

By

Angela Wilson

Published

NEW YORK, NY – MARCH 26: Panel moderator/journalist Charles Blow attends screening and panel discussion for HBO’s “King in the Wilderness” on March 26, 2018 in New York City. (Photo by Slaven Vlasic/Getty Images) | Charles Blow, “The Devil You Know” book (Photo: Amazon)

After Keisha Lance Bottoms and Scott Colom ‘s historic wins in Georgia and Mississippi, and another Democratic Senate flip in South Carolina, Charles M. Blow’s bold thesis laid out in his book, “The Devil You Know: A Black Power Manifesto,” was resoundingly validated—five years after he predicted a Southern political awakening as a historic midterm wave reshaped the nation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

In his 2021 manifesto, the former New York Times columnist argued that the 20th-century Great Migration —which saw millions of Black Americans flee the Jim Crow South for Northern and Western cities like New York, Chicago, Pittsburgh and Oakland from 1910-1970—inadvertently diluted Black political power by dispersing into regions where they remained a numerical minority.

Blow explained that racism existed everywhere, but only in the South did Black voters possess the concentrated population needed to truly dismantle Republican dominance from within. His prescription was a “reverse migration” back to the South to wield decisive power over statewide races—an idea critics dismissed as impractical and “complete hogshit.” Five years later, after the 2026 midterms, his vision materialized.

“’The south got something to say!’” Those were the words of André 3000 of OutKast in 1995 who thought the south was being overlooked and disrespected,” Blow wrote in a special election edition of “How We Win,” an opinion series for the Guardian.

RELATED: Scott Colom’s Father Reflects On His Son’s Historic Win and a New Future for Mississippi

The author explained how folks should “listen to the South,” whose message was “loud and clear” after a historic midterm election. “One of the big stories of the midterms is that the south is no longer solid Republican territory. The southern strategy has a term limit, and the region’s diversity is now paying political dividends for the Democrats,” Blow said.

Although Blow didn’t explicitly name-drop his book in that Nov. 4 blurb, commentators on social media resurfaced Blow’s book, noting that the Southern midterm outcomes validated his thesis about Black political power in the region.

“Democrats should make serious investments in the South going forward,” one X user wrote on Nov. 3. Another X user seemed to agree, replying how the blueprint was already laid out years prior. “Charles Blow laid it out in The Devil You Know.”

Charles Blow laid it out in The Devil You Know https://t.co/L4MKnCXt6n

Blow, who himself moved from Brooklyn to Atlanta, pointed to organizing efforts and demographic shifts in states like Georgia and North Carolina as evidence of growing Black political influence in “The Devil You Know.”

Blow wrote that Black Americans had long traded “the devil they knew for the devil they didn’t” by fleeing the South—forced, as he put it, to ask white majorities “to see you, acknowledge your equality, and grant you justice.” His remedy was simple: stop asking and start governing by reclaiming state-level power across the South. On Nov. 3, that blueprint became reality—and the rest of the country is now living in the results.

In South Carolina, Democrat Annie Andrews made history as the first woman elected to the U.S. Senate from the state, flipping a seat held by Republicans since 1998, according to the Guardian . Meanwhile, Democrats scored key victories in Iowa and Ohio—states where Republicans have long controlled state government—and swept both the U.S. Senate and gubernatorial races in Texas.

The wins delivered a majority of governorships to Democrats for the first time in two decades, allowing them to put up a stronger defense against President Donald Trump’s second-term agenda.

scraped.title: Then and now photos of celebrity parents and their kids
scraped.h1: Then and Now: Iconic Black Celebs and Their Doppelgänger Children
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Take a stroll down memory lane and look at these pictures of iconic celebrity parents with their kids then and now.

By

Mahalia Otshudy

Published

Getty Images, L, Zoë Kravitz & Lisa Bonet, 1989 (Photo by Vinnie Zuffante/Getty Images); R, Lisa Bonet & Zoë Kravitz 2020 (Photo by Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for InStyle)

One of the biggest trends in pop culture is looking back on the nostalgia of the 2000s, ’90s, and even earlier, with fashion trends, film remakes, and TV show reboots constantly being made. Yet what better way to see the passage of time than by watching Hollywood kids grow up before our eyes alongside their legendary parents —from Denzel Washington and his sons, John David and Malcolm Washington, to North West becoming an outspoken fashion icon like her dad?

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

Here is a nostalgic look back on celebrity parents and kids who have grown up together over the years.

Tracee Ellis Ross used to appear beside her mom, Diana Ross, on television specials before she made a name for herself in Tinseltown as a hilarious comedic actress. Now, fans might not immediately realize that Tracee comes from Hollywood royalty, but the two stars not only look alike, but they have also built powerful legacies.

Jaden and Willow Smith have been hitting red carpets with their parents ever since they could waddle, but they are no longer the adorable siblings posing beside Jada Pinkett and Will Smith. They have become icons in their own right: Willow has a successful music career, while Jaden leads operations as the Men’s Creative Director at Louboutin.

Related: Black Celebrities You Didn’t Realize Have Famous Parents

Kanye West has always been known for being outspoken, a generational musician with impeccable fashion taste, and North West has followed in her father’s footsteps. The 13-year-old is always experimenting with her fashion and already showing off her music-producing chops.

Folks have been obsessed with Blue Ivy ever since she appeared on stage alongside her mom and dad as a 2-year-old, and now the youngster is showing up with her parents at the Met Gala. Her internet aunties are definitely holding back tears.

Before building an acting career of her own, Nico Parker used to appear beside her mom, Thandiwe Newton, at all types of Hollywood events, and now she is playing co-lead in the hit 2025 live-action remake “How to Train Your Dragon” and its upcoming sequel.

In the ’80s, Zoë Kravitz was hanging on Lisa Bonet’s waist as she carried her wherever she went, but now the mother-daughter pair are both superstars across TV and cinema, and their resemblance is striking, too.

Usher can be proud of the legacy he has built within music, but he also has more reason to be proud of the two young men, Usher “Cinco” V, 18, and Naviyd, 17, who have gone from the cute toddlers climbing over his head in photoshoots to carving out their life paths. Cinco is at Howard University, and Naviyd is a social media star with a budding music career.

Brandy’s baby girl, Sy’rai Iman Smith, is all grown up now, and not only does she have the exact same smile as her R&B icon mother, she is also building a music career of her own with singles like “Late Night,” “Bad Guy,” and “On My Own” already under her belt.

Niecy Nash must feel like she is staring into a mirror every time she looks at her daughter, Dia, because the resemblance between them is scary similar, and Dia showed off her acting chops in Lifetime’s “Sister Wife Murder” as the lead.

Nothing shows the passage of time more than LeBron James Jr. going from visiting his dad on the basketball court to playing alongside him on the Lakers for a brief time. If you looked up the word legacy in the dictionary, their picture would come up.

Kimora Lee Simmons is fashion royalty, so it only makes sense that her daughters, Ming and Aoki Lee, who grew up in the world of glitz and glam, would become stylish queens themselves, carrying on the Baby Phat torch.

As a baby, Kaavia Union Wade always had folks laughing at her hilarious facial expressions, which often became memes, but now she has grown into an adorable young girl, slaying on the red carpet beside her parents and still rocking matching outfits with her mom, Gabrielle Union.

Denzel Washington was joined by his sons, John David and Malcolm, when he was cementing, literally, his place in Hollywood in 1998 with a hand-and-footprint ceremony in Los Angeles. Cut to almost three decades later, and those young boys are now grown men making their own moves in cinema.

Angelina Jolie took Hollywood by surprise when she decided to adopt multiple kids into a gorgeous blended family, and now those kids have grown to have a strong bond with their mom, with the confidence to build their own life paths, with Zahara Marley being a Spelman sister.

scraped.title: Arnold Schwarzenegger Opens Up About the Moment Trump Asked for His Support — and Why He Refused
scraped.description: Arnold Schwarzenegger explains why he refused to back Trump in 2016, but their political differences were only the beginning of a long-running feud.
scraped.author: Yohance Kyles
scraped.h1: Arnold Schwarzenegger Opens Up About the Moment Trump Asked for His Support — and Why He Refused
scraped.body_text:
Arnold Schwarzenegger explains why he refused to back Trump in 2016, but their political differences were only the beginning of a long-running feud.

Hollywood legend Arnold Schwarzenegger and President Donald Trump have a lot in common.

However, both Republican stalwarts did not see eye to eye on who should run the country.

Schwarzenegger, 79, left his mark on the worlds of entertainment and politics. In some ways, the Austrian-American served as a template for Trump, 80, to rise from television personality to federal officeholder.

Back in 2003, Schwarzenegger won the California recall election to become the 38th governor of the state. His emergence as a successful Republican politician followed a three-decade career as a movie industry A-lister.

Similarly, Trump turned his hosting gig on NBC’s “The Apprentice” reality show into leadership of the conservative MAGA movement, which led to the billionaire winning the White House in 2016 and 2024.

Both Schwarzenegger and Trump ran as GOP candidates in their respective races, but their different political agendas created a divide. That difference of opinions prevented the two power players from aligning.

“When he ran for the first time, for the presidency, in 2016, we talked to each other several times, and because we had a good relationship, we were very good friends,” Schwarzenegger said on the “Jimmy Kimmel Live!” show .

Schwarzenegger went on to discuss how Trump asked for his endorsement in the 2016 race.

According to the action movie icon, issues such as climate change and pollution prevented him from siding with MAGA at that time.

“I said, ‘I know. I’ve worked on that issue for so many years. Pollution kills seven million people, and you want to ignore that?’ I said, ‘Are you crazy?’ I said, ‘So, I cannot do that. I cannot go with you because of that issue alone,’” Schwarzenegger recalled about speaking to Trump.

The seven-time Mr. Olympia added, “He understood, and I understood that he thought differently. I respect that fully, so he went off, and he did his thing.” Schwarzenegger did not blatantly slam the increasingly unpopular POTUS.

Even though Arnold refused to publicly support Trump in his bid for the presidency, “The Terminator” actor still identifies as a Republican. That party affiliation did not stop him from voting for Democratic nominee Kamala Harris in 2024.

The seeming frenemy relationship between Trump and Schwarzenegger dates back years. They have known each other since at least the 2004 Republican National Convention.

Trump later donated $10,000 to Schwarzenegger’s 2007 re-election bid for California governor.

The five-figure contribution was reportedly allocated to help pay off campaign debts.

“The Governator” made a guest appearance on a March 2007 episode of Trump’s “The Apprentice: Los Angeles.” That cameo unexpectedly became a precursor to the franchise’s future direction.

Trump announced his presidential campaign in June 2015 with a divisive speech critics claimed disparaged Mexican immigrants. That same month, NBC announced it would end ties with the businessman due to the statements.

In 2016, Schwarzenegger announced he would not vote for the Republican nominee for the first time since becoming an American citizen.

To the shock of many Beltway pundits, Trump won that election against former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton.

Trump and Schwarzenegger essentially switched roles in the mid-2010s. “The Art of the Deal” author became a governmental chief executive, while the Gold Globe Award winner took over his TV gig.

NBC tapped Schwarzenegger to host “The New Celebrity Apprentice” in 2017. Trump used his speech at that year’s National Prayer Breakfast to mock the show’s television ratings with Schwarzenegger at the helm.

“They hired a big, big movie star, Arnold Schwarzenegger, to take my place, and we know how that turned out,” Trump said at the annual Christian gathering. “The ratings went right down the tubes. It’s been a total disaster.”

Schwarzenegger fired back in a selfie video. He said , “Hey Donald, I have a great idea. Why don’t we switch jobs? You take over TV, because you’re such an expert in ratings, and I take over your job. And then people can finally sleep comfortably again.”

Trump delivered another shot in the rivalry when Schwarzenegger’s version of “The Apprentice” ended after just 13 episodes.

Schwarzenegger blamed “baggage” tied to the polarizing president for leaving the show.

However, Trump pushed an alternative narrative. The ever-petty real estate mogul tweeted that his replacement was “fired” for “pathetic” ratings. He closed out his social media jab by writing, “Sad end to great show.”

The feud continued. Schwarzenegger blasted Trump following the Jan. 6, 2021, attacks on the U.S. Capitol. A mob of MAGA supporters tried to block the presidential transfer of power to Democrat Joe Biden in a chaotic scene that left several people deceased.

Schwarzenegger accused Trump of fomenting a “coup” and called the GOP standard-bearer a “failed leader” in a video shared online.

The Hollywood Walk of Fame recipient also declared that Trump will “go down in history as the worst president ever.”

A post shared by Jimmy Kimmel Live (@jimmykimmellive)

scraped.title: Video Shows Virginia Cops Telling Woman They Don't Need to Show a Warrant Before Turning Her Home Upside Down Looking for Her Estranged Husband
scraped.description: Video shows Virginia officers shoving Black woman aside and searching her home for nearly an hour after she demanded to see a search warrant. Police were there looking for her estranged husband.
scraped.author: Carlos Miller
scraped.h1: Video Shows Virginia Cops Telling Woman They Don’t Need to Show a Warrant Before Turning Her Home Upside Down Looking for Her Estranged Husband
scraped.body_text:
Video shows Virginia officers shoving Black woman aside and searching her home for nearly an hour after she demanded to see a search warrant. Police were there looking for her estranged husband.

Virginia cops barged into a Black woman’s home, shoving her aside when she demanded to see a warrant, telling her they did not need a search warrant to arrest her estranged husband for missing a court date.

“The guy pushed me out the way,” Trice Riddick said in an interview with Atlanta Black Star after posting the video on Instagram, where it has gone viral. “He said, ‘We ain’t got to show you sh-t.’ And ran up in my house, guns out.”

Portsmouth police entered her home on Sept. 22 to arrest Edward Riddick for missing court over a parole violation, searching her home for about an hour before finding him hiding in a small space inside a closet.

They told her they had an arrest warrant that listed her address on it — not an actual search warrant — but Riddick said she had kicked him out of the house three weeks earlier and had yet to see the actual arrest warrant with her address listed on it.

“He doesn’t live here. He just happened to come over that day and asked for a ride,” Riddick said. “I didn’t care if he got arrested. I told him he needed to turn himself in weeks before.”

Her main beef with the cops is that they told her they had spotted him on the street but waited to arrest him inside her home because they needed to assemble a team of cops.

“Y’all don’t need no team for no 150-pound —he probably 90-pound soaking wet,” she said. “Why y’all needed 20 officers to arrest one skinny-ass man for?”

Riddick sent video showing her estranged husband running up the stairs after the cops began banging on the door.

“You have an arrest warrant for Ed, but you don’t have a warrant to come in my house,” Riddick tells the cops through the closed front door.

The video shows her walking up the stairs to find him, then back down to say she couldn’t find him, and opening the front door after the cops threatened to break it down.

“Ma’am, you have to step out,” a cop tells her.

“You have to show me a warrant,” she responds.

But the officers push past her and head upstairs, apparently because they saw Edward Riddick run upstairs and decided not to search downstairs. One officer tells her they have an arrest warrant listing her address, but no officer shows her the warrant in the footage Atlanta Black Star reviewed. The officer, who appears to supervise the others, also repeatedly tells her they followed Edward Riddick to her house.

“If you seen him come in the house, then that means you seen him walking to the house,” she said. “Why didn’t you arrest him on the street?”

About an hour later, they found him hiding in a small space in the closet and walked him downstairs in handcuffs.

He remains incarcerated on a parole violation that appears to stem from a 2012 conviction for cocaine distribution, online court records show.

“I still to this day have not seen a warrant,” she said.

Riddick, who posted the video to Instagram about a month later in October to raise awareness, says she had been trying to find an attorney to file a lawsuit but has had no luck.

“I definitely want to hold these officers accountable for what they did,” she said.

Whether the entry was lawful remains unresolved. In United States v. Brinkley, the Fourth Circuit, whose jurisdiction includes Virginia, held that officers entering a home under an arrest warrant alone must have probable cause to believe the wanted person resides there and is inside.

Entering a third party’s home generally requires a search warrant unless officers have consent or exigent circumstances justify entry.

Riddick said she had put her husband out three weeks earlier. She has not established what information officers had about his residency before they entered.

Although he seemingly no longer lived there, Riddick said he returned that morning to ask for a ride to a medical appointment. While waiting, he walked to a convenience store and called her to say he had seen officers nearby, she said.

She said he later returned to the house and fell asleep on the living room couch, and the cops began banging on the door about 30 minutes later.

“Y’all seen him on the street and y’all waited till he came up in the house to come harass me and y’all don’t even have a warrant,” she said.

“This has caused me so much mental anguish. I feel weak. I feel violated.”

“It makes you feel like not even safe in your own home. And that’s where you’re supposed to be safe at,” she added.

scraped.title: Trump’s Visa Restrictions Keep Two African Beauty Queens Out of Miss Universe. Two More Are Still Waiting
scraped.description: The Republic of Congo will miss its Miss Universe debut as delegates from Zimbabwe and South Sudan await U.S. visas ahead of the Nov. 24 final in Puerto Rico.
scraped.author: Jaidyn Bridgeforth
scraped.h1: Trump’s Visa Restrictions Keep Two African Beauty Queens Out of Miss Universe. Two More Are Still Waiting
scraped.body_text:
The Republic of Congo will miss its Miss Universe debut as delegates from Zimbabwe and South Sudan await U.S. visas ahead of the Nov. 24 final in Puerto Rico.

Roseanna Hall was supposed to leave for Puerto Rico on Nov. 8, when contestants began arriving for the 75th Miss Universe pageant.

The Zimbabwean beauty queen had spent weeks in South Africa trying to secure a U.S. visa. By Friday, Nov. 13, she was still waiting, with the Nov. 24 finale just days away.

Two African delegates have already withdrawn.

Zambia’s Mubanga Pamela Hatyoka, a 25-year-old registered nurse, and the Republic of Congo’s Georgina Kambongo will miss the pageant after being unable to secure U.S. visas, The Associated Press reported .

Kambongo planned to become the first woman to represent the Republic of Congo at Miss Universe. South Sudan’s Adut Deng was still waiting for clearance after months of efforts by her national organizers.

“She earned her crown, she earned her title, and she deserves the opportunity to represent the nation she proudly serves,” Miss Universe Zambia organizers said in a statement announcing Hatyoka’s withdrawal.

Puerto Rico is a U.S. territory, so international contestants traveling there are subject to federal immigration and visa restrictions.

President Donald Trump’s December 2025 proclamation expanded restrictions his administration first imposed that June.

The updated rules took effect Jan. 1, 2026, and partially suspended entry for nationals of Zambia and Zimbabwe seeking certain visas, including tourist, business visitor, student and exchange visitor visas.

South Sudan joined the list of countries facing full entry restrictions, while the Republic of Congo remained on it.

The restrictions generally apply to people who were outside the United States and lacked a valid visa when the rules took effect.

The proclamation includes an exception for athletes, coaches, team personnel and their immediate relatives traveling to the World Cup, Olympics and other qualifying major sporting events. It also allows case-by-case exceptions for travel deemed to serve the U.S. national interest.

Kambongo’s planned debut would have added another chapter to a pageant history stretching across the Black diaspora. In 1977, Trinidad and Tobago’s Janelle Commissiong became the first Black woman to win Miss Universe.

In 1999, Trinidad and Tobago hosted the competition as Botswana sent its first delegate, 19-year-old Mpule Kwelagobe.

She made history as the first Black African woman to win the crown and later used her platform to champion HIV/AIDS prevention, particularly among young people.

At the time, Trump co-owned the Miss Universe Organization with NBCUniversal. He sold his interest in the organization to WME/IMG in September 2015.

Twenty years later, South Africa’s Zozibini Tunzi took the crown at Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta. Tunzi wore her short natural hair as she discussed growing up in a world that rarely considered women who looked like her beautiful.

When asked what young girls should be taught, she answered, “Leadership.” Her response drew a standing ovation from the audience.

In San Juan, the national costume competition is scheduled for Nov. 21, with the crowning set for three days later.

As of Friday, Hall and Deng were still waiting to learn whether they would get to walk that stage.

scraped.title: Mother Emanuel’s New Memorial Confronts the Hate That Killed Black Worshippers
scraped.description: More than a decade after the massacre, the site honors the Emanuel Nine and educates visitors about the enduring scourge of anti-Black racism.
scraped.author: Brandon Tensley
scraped.h1: Mother Emanuel’s New Memorial Confronts the Hate That Killed Black Worshippers
scraped.body_text:
Capital B News

Read them in Seen & Heard, our free, twice-weekly newsletter.

Chris Singleton remembers vividly how one phone call and a horrific act upended his life in South Carolina.

On June 17, 2015, the collegiate baseball player had recently finished a successful freshman season . As he relaxed on the couch, a woman called from his mother’s phone, urging him to get to Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church. The 18-year-old sensed that something terrible had happened.

Earlier that evening, a white supremacist had entered the Charleston church, known as Mother Emanuel, and fatally shot his mother, the Rev. Sharonda Coleman-Singleton, and eight other worshippers after sitting with them for an hour during Bible study.

More than a decade after the attack, Singleton, now 30, will witness the unveiling of the Emanuel Nine Memorial. Established by the Mother Emanuel Memorial Foundation, the ceremony on Nov. 14 will feature tributes to the victims and performances of gospel, jazz, and poetry. Located near the church at 120 Calhoun St., the memorial is intended not only to honor the slain worshippers but also educate visitors about the ongoing terrors of racism — work that the community says is especially vital at a time when Black history is being erased.

“You don’t want people to forget why my mom and eight other people aren’t here anymore,” Singleton told Capital B. “We need to address why it happened and how we’re going to stop it from happening in the future.”

The other victims of the shooting were Cynthia Graham Hurd, Susie Jackson, the Rev. DePayne Middleton-Doctor, the Rev. Clementa Pinckney (who also was a state senator), Ethel Lance, Tywanza Sanders, the Rev. Daniel Simmons, and the Rev. Myra Thompson.

The memorial was a long time coming, its completion not always assured.

It began as a labor of love among Mother Emanuel members and the wider Charleston community, who wanted to establish a permanent site to commemorate the victims. But development was slowed down by construction delays. After breaking ground in 2023, the foundation hoped to finish the memorial in 2025, the 10-year anniversary of the shooting. The project, however, took longer than expected, as the foundation sought to close its fundraising gap and as supply shortages impacted the timeline.

To bring its vision to life, the foundation tapped Michael Arad, the architect behind the National September 11 Memorial in New York City. He worked with victims’ families, church members, and other Charleston residents to get it right and forge a space that the community would deem worthy of the nine victims. Arad drew inspiration from Mother Emanuel’s history of resisting racial oppression. This includes periods when Black worship was prohibited but Mother Emanuel still offered fellowship, Lee Bennett Jr., the church’s historian, told Capital B.

At the heart of the memorial is the Fountain of Grace, with the names of the victims etched around the edge. There are also two Fellowship Benches facing each other like protective wings, and a Cross of Hope, designed to be a place of solemnity where visitors can pause and reflect. A Survivors’ Garden, intended to honor the five survivors, is soon to come. The foundation has so far secured about $19.9 million toward its $25 million goal. The additional funds are needed to help complete the garden and maintain the memorial.

“The same way the families and survivors showed resilience, the foundation has had to show a good deal of resilience to get this project completed,” Deona Smith, the foundation’s executive director, told Capital B. “For so many young people and future generations, this will be history, and so the memorial ensures that we won’t forget.”

Memory, though, is about more than preserving the past, some in the community say. It’s also about reckoning with the forces — the white supremacy — that shaped the past and continue to shape the present.

The foundation’s goal is to fuel that reckoning through its Crossroads Education and Outreach program, intended to bring people together to discuss how communities might confront racism, including the kind of online radicalization that incubated the gunman’s hatred. (In 2025, the U.S. Supreme declined to hear an appeal in a lawsuit against Meta alleging that its algorithms had a hand in radicalizing the shooter by exposing him to racist propaganda.) The foundation hopes that its programming will reach not just older generations but also those who have no real memory of the massacre.

“These programs will allow us to hold conversations that will probably make some people uncomfortable, but they’re absolutely necessary,” Smith said.

As the Rev. Sharon Washington Risher sees it, these conversations are overdue. She was comforting a grieving family at a Dallas hospital when she began receiving calls about the shooting. Her mother, Ethel Lance, was one of the nine people killed. Since then, Risher, 68, has become a vocal gun control advocate, devoting her time to challenging policies that contributed to the massacre. She has worked with organizations such as Everytown for Gun Safety to focus attention on the consequences of gun violence and to push for stronger firearm regulations.

While she acknowledges that these measures can’t completely eliminate gun violence, she insists that not doing anything isn’t an option.

“It’s never going to go away, but if we can do something to try to [curb] the violence and just save even one life, then that’s better than nothing,” Risher told Capital B.

The memorial’s focus on confronting the roots of violence also raises questions about how the massacre has been remembered. For Risher, one of the most troubling aspects of the aftermath was the national fixation on the forgiveness that some victims’ families offered the killer. Within days of the shooting, this grace had seized the country’s attention. But Risher worried that this behavior allowed people to move on without actually wrestling with the hatred behind the slaughter.

Risher, who also lost two cousins and a childhood friend, recalled that she was nowhere near ready to forgive.

“I was very hurt and angry. It took me a long time to get to thinking about forgiveness,” she said. “I felt like the media latched onto that [narrative] to make themselves feel better about what had happened.”

Her concerns echo what other relatives of the Emanuel Nine have told Capital B. In a 2025 report , several family members — including Malcolm Graham, whose sister, Cynthia Graham Hurd, was killed in the shooting, and Alana Grant, a granddaughter of the Rev. Daniel Simmons, another victim — expressed frustration with the country’s fascination with forgiveness. They saw it as coming at the expense of hard conversations about racial hatred and the political changes that might help to prevent another massacre, such as enacting state hate crime legislation.

Those in the Charleston community say that the need for a fuller reckoning has only grown in importance as efforts to undermine Black history threaten to make it more difficult for younger generations to understand the country’s long struggle with racism. The Trump administration this year removed and later replaced exhibits about nine people enslaved by George Washington from a historic site in Philadelphia, drawing criticism that it was sanitizing history.

The Charleston memorial stands as a counterweight to such efforts, ensuring that the story of the Emanuel Nine won’t be erased.

Singleton has seen firsthand why that education matters. Since his mother’s death, he’s traveled across the country speaking with students about racism and inclusion. While he’s encouraged by the progress he’s witnessed, he knows that the hatred that killed his mother hasn’t disappeared.

Seven years after the shooting, a white gunman traveled to a predominantly Black area of Buffalo, New York, and killed 10 shoppers — all of them Black — at a supermarket. And in 2023, another white gunman killed three Black people at a Dollar General store in Jacksonville, Florida.

“There’s still work to be done,” Singleton said. “There’s still kids who grow up to hate people who look like me, just based on something I don’t control and you don’t control.”

scraped.title: Honduras declares 'environmental emergency’ in Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.h1: Honduras declares ‘environmental emergency’ in Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

Deforestation, organized crime and the expansion of cattle ranching have led the government in Honduras to announce an “environmental emergency” in the Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve, the largest protected area in the country.

The 36-month emergency, issued as a presidential decree on Nov. 10, will devote 1.5 billion Honduran lempiras (more than $55 million) over the next three years to halt “environmental deterioration,” according to an official statement .

“The initiative represents a commitment by the government to move from addressing threats to sustained intervention, with defined resources and institutional responsibilities,” presidential legal advisor Roberto Zacapa said in the statement.

The more than 832,000-hectare (2 million-acre) reserve stretches across the departments of Gracias a Dios, Colón and Olancho, and includes numerous Indigenous Miskito, Pech and Garífuna communities. In 1982, a section of it was designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site .

The reserve’s remote location along the Nicaraguan border has made it vulnerable to deforestation , drug trafficking, cattle ranching, gold mining , wildlife trafficking, roadbuilding and other illegal activities .

At least 6,691 hectares (16,533 acres) of forest were cut down between 2023 and 2025, according to the Forest Conservation Institute (ICF), the agency managing the country’s forests.

Since 2011, the reserve has been on UNESCO’s List of World Heritage in Danger , a list of sites facing serious threats to their environmental or cultural heritage.

“It’s like the wild west, where there’s no law and people come in and do whatever they want, and the rights of Indigenous communities are violated,” Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) Honduras program director, Edgard Herrera Scott, told Mongabay.

WCS attended preliminary meetings about the emergency. It wasn’t shown the final version.

A copy of the decree hasn’t been made public, but the funding will likely be spent on increasing law enforcement presence in the core zone of the reserve, Herrera said. That could include new patrol posts.

The Secretariat of Natural Resources and Environment, the Secretariat of National Defense and the ICF will work together on the effort, according to the statement.

“[The institutions] will coordinate resources and capabilities to protect the forests, biodiversity and ecosystems of the reserve,” the statement noted.

This isn’t the first time that the country has used a state of emergency to combat environmental crimes. In 2024, the National Defense and Security Council declared an emergency for all the forests in Honduras. The move was part of a zero-deforestation resolution that added funding for conservation and laid out measures to increase state presence in protected areas.

However, some environmental groups have criticized the 2024 initiative, saying the plan hasn’t been completely carried out and deforestation continues to threaten protected areas like the Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve.

Herrera said he hopes the recent funding will lead to substantive change.

“We have to turn what’s on paper into action,” he said. “That much is certain.”

Banner image: Honduran Navy officers patrol in Patuca river, near Ahuas, a remote community in La Mosquitia region, Honduras. Image by Rodrigo Abd via Associated Press.

scraped.h1: Bigger and more-frequent wildfires threaten water supplies across the US
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

A record number of wildfires burned more than 14,062 square miles in the U.S. this year, leaving behind charred trees and scorched vegetation. But less-obvious are the impacts they had on the streams and rivers that provide drinking water to urban and rural communities across the country. After a wildfire burns a watershed, rain will carry ash and organic matter into the streams that feed water treatment plants for towns and cities. Utilities must turn off the intake to keep the sediment-filled water from contaminating their systems and switch to another source, if it’s available. New studies found that wildfires can contaminate water for up to 15 years. These findings are especially concerning as climate change has led to an increase in the number and size of wildfires in the U.S.

By Martha Bellisele, Associated Press

scraped.title: There’s no substitute for getting out of the classroom and into nature (analysis)
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.author: Erik Hoffner
scraped.h1: There’s no substitute for getting out of the classroom and into nature (analysis)
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

Leading a group of ecology students down a trail through the forest behind Merrimack College, in North Andover, Massachusetts, U.S., where I teach biology part-time as an adjunct professor, I spot a garter snake. As it rapidly starts crawling away, I grab the snake by its tail. Excited students gather round to check out the foot-long striped serpent, while taking photos with their cell phones.

I tell them a bit about garter snakes and ask if anyone wants to hold it.

“I do!” one of the students says.

I gently hand her the snake.

“That’s really cool. I’ve never held a snake before,” she says, before handing it to another eager student. Then we turn the snake loose and continue on our way.

Since I began at Merrimack in 1997, I’ve taught mainly ecology labs. Most of the ecology lab sessions are outdoors, so they’re like weekly field trips. They give students the opportunity to step outside of laboratories and classrooms and interact with nature.

Field courses provide the same opportunity for teachers. When I head off into the woods with students in tow, I’m in my element. Whether I’m diving into the bushes and scrambling on my hands and knees to catch a snake or a frog to show the class, pointing out a hawk circling overhead, or teaching students how to identify various species of trees, shrubs, and wildflowers, my enthusiasm shows.

Sharing my love of nature and biology with my students and teaching them about the natural world around them — whether in a far-off exotic location or close to home — is rewarding. I often tell people I can’t believe I get paid to do something I enjoy so much.

But the biggest beneficiaries of field courses are the students. Whether it’s a student seeing wild monkeys or parrots in the Amazon rain forest, or kangaroos in Australia, or a myriad of colorful tropical fish swimming across a coral reef in Belize, it’s always a thrilling, and sometimes life changing experience for them. Even interacting with nature close to home — such as seeing carnivorous plants in a local bog, holding a snake for the first time, or watching a beaver swimming underwater in a stream — can be an exciting and memorable experience.

I’ve had many students over the years tell me that the ecology labs were their favorite class and they looked forward to them every week, because the labs gave them a chance to get outdoors and learn about the natural world around them. And field experiences like outdoor labs or field courses not only help students to develop an understanding and appreciation for the natural world, but also to develop a conservation ethic.

What’s that Baba Dioum quote? “In the end we will conserve only what we love; we will love only what we understand; and we will understand only what we are taught.”

Professor Bill McDowell, who teaches ecology and conservation biology at Merrimack, said courses with field components are important for a variety of reasons.

“First and foremost, field labs are unpredictable and can inspire a sense of wonder and curiosity in students. Whether it is discovering the life that lives within the small pond on campus, or having a snake (thankfully a non-venomous one!) fall from a tree onto a student while sampling tree diversity, these are undoubtedly memorable experiences,” he said.

Natural systems are inherently complex, he continued, saying we don’t always have clear cut explanations for the phenomena we observe.

“This serves students well because it forces them to think critically and flexibly to try and explain the observations they see. It also emphasizes the unfinished, open-ended nature of science. At its heart, science is something that you do, rather than something you learn. With field labs, you are seeking explanations, rather than simply learning them from a textbook.”

Field-based labs also help students to develop a sense of place, he said. For example, as part of his conservation biology course, students visited a local protected area close to their home and assessed what activities were allowed, and what the trade-offs were between human use and protecting natural systems.

“While the primary goal of the assignment was to apply concepts from lecture,” McDowell said, “I heard from many students about how the activity led them to discover a place they loved, or to reconnect with a place that they had not visited in a long time.”

Professor Larry Kelts, who retired in 2008 after teaching for nearly 30 years at Merrimack (and is now deceased), developed the Global Field Studies Program, which provided students with opportunities to study environmentally significant locations around the world, including the Brazilian Amazon, the Great Barrier Reef in Australia, the Serengeti Plain in Tanzania, the desert Southwest, the Galapagos Islands, and Belizean coral reefs and rain forests. Kelts and his colleague, Professor Marcia Walsh, taught semester-long courses that dealt with the ecology, conservation, and human cultures of these ecosystems, and culminated in field trips to these locations that lasted for two to three weeks each.

These were amazing experiences that inspired several students to follow in Kelts’s footsteps and become biology and science teachers themselves, including myself: I was a continuing education student on the Amazon course in 1996, and it was while I was on that trip that I was offered the opportunity to join the biology faculty at Merrimack as an adjunct professor, where I ended up assisting with several future field courses.

Along those lines, Professor Kristy McDowell, a lecturer and Chair of the Department of Environmental Sciences and Sustainability at Merrimack (and Bill McDowell’s wife), launched a new field course over winter break in 2024-2025.

“I was offered the opportunity to lead short-term study abroad in Costa Rica, and I jumped at it. I did dissertation research for my PhD in Costa Rica, and it is a place that I deeply love,” she said. The trip is tied to her environmental policy course, although it is voluntary and open to all Merrimack students.

“In the course, we spend the semester comparing and contrasting environmental policy in the United States and Costa Rica,” McDowell explained. “The trip entails a tour of several different locations and biomes and meeting with conservationists who are doing the work on the ground, so that students can see the policies in action and investigate the realities of interpreting and enacting policy. Overall, students have loved the experience. They particularly love that we go off the beaten path and dig deeper than the common tourist itineraries. They get to meet local people dealing with real environmental issues and participate in a meaningful way.”

She also said that field courses allow students to participate in the material in a hands-on way that is impossible to replicate in a classroom: “For environmental science in particular, there is no substitute for students actually going outside. Teaching in the tropics takes it to another level as well. Students who have spent most or all of their lives in the United States are blown away both by the biodiversity of the tropics, and by how closely many people live to nature in a country like Costa Rica. While I can describe these things to them, showing them firsthand makes it real for them and allows them to think about environmental science issues from a new perspective.”

Her favorite thing about the Costa Rica course, McDowell said, is watching her students enjoy the experience.

“I love sharing a place that holds so much meaning for me and watching them fall in love with it as well. When they say that they don’t want to leave, or they can’t wait to come back, it highlights how valuable the experience is for them. I also love the impromptu moments that you can’t plan for, like running into a squadron of peccaries on the trail or a fleeting glimpse of a blue morpho butterfly.”

Jim Hanken, Professor of Biology, Emeritus, and former director of the Museum of Comparative Zoology at Harvard University, said that Harvard incorporates field components into many of its courses, and has policies and procedures in place to help facilitate field studies.

Hanken emphasized that instructors of field courses need to follow regulations regarding alcohol consumption, sexual harassment, and other basic safety precautions during field trips just as they would while on campus. He said that several years ago, the Department of Organismic and Evolutionary Biology began offering symposiums for basically everyone who was planning to conduct or lead fieldwork — regardless of whether it was course-related or research-related — over the subsequent year.

“It quickly proved to be so valuable that the science division now offers it to members of several academic departments,” he said. “It doesn’t cover academic-specific subjects, like what kind of binoculars are best for birding, or how to catch a lizard, but instead topics that are common to fieldwork of all sorts, ranging from emergency preparedness to collecting permits.”

Field courses that involve travel may add additional personal and institutional impediments for both faculty and students, Hanken added.

“Depending on duration and distance of the destination, the trip can be very expensive to put on, and students of lesser means will not be able to participate unless the college or university foots the bill,” he said, which the Museum of Comparative Zoology has done for some.

Regarding field trips for courses associated with the Museum of Comparative Zoology (MCZ) and taught by its faculty — such as a week-long Costa Rica field trip that was part of a herpetology course he co-taught with colleague Jonathan Losos — Hanken said the MCZ paid the entire cost of the field trip for all students.

Losos, now an evolutionary biology professor at Washington University in St. Louis, Missouri, U.S., said he’s observed the positive effects that field courses have had on students. “I used to teach herpetology [at Harvard], where we would go to Costa Rica for a week,” he said. “What a spectacular experience. I had many students who told me this trip was a life-changing experience. Some have ended up going into science, in part as a result of how this trip affected them.”

John Morrissey, a biology professor at Sweet Briar College in Virginia, U.S., who retired in 2025, is a marine biologist and shark researcher and has brought nearly 1,000 students to the ocean on various field courses. The most memorable aspect of these field experiences for him, he said, was taking students who had never seen coral reefs in person on marine biology trips to the tropics.

“Hundreds of times I have been able to watch a student slide into the water over a coral reef for the first time,” he said, “and hundreds of times, I’ve had the honor and pleasure of listening to their squeals of amazement and delight as they observe the cacophony of shapes, sizes, colors, and activities of reef-dwellers for the first time.”

Morrissey added that field courses impacted his own career. Although he was a dinosaur fanatic as a kid and went to college to study biology and geology in preparation for a career as a paleontologist, a two-week field course in coral reef ecology on the north coast of Jamaica changed his career trajectory.

“I traded in my rock hammer for a snorkel and never looked back!” he said.

Morrissey also cautioned that faculty teaching field courses need to be willing to accept the good with the bad. Field courses often take place in remote areas where emergency services are non-existent, for example.

“They need not to be intimidated by the hazards, they need to be able to handle the strenuousness of the course, and to welcome the awesome responsibility of trying to keep 15 to 20 students safe, 24/7,” Morrissey explained.

But the pros far outweigh the cons, he added.

“I believe that there is no appropriate substitute for field components within courses, and even whole field courses,” Morrissey said. “Sitting in a forest or drifting over a coral reef can be a spiritual experience, to paraphrase Carl Sagan. Being in nature, being surrounded by and immersed in nature, is the only way to grasp its beauty and complexity, its fragility and power, its mystery and its majesty.”

Don Lyman is a science journalist, biologist, adjunct college professor, and health care professional.

scraped.description: Illinois’ Climate Works Pre-Apprenticeship Program provides people from underserved communities with free training.
scraped.author: YCC Team
scraped.h1: Ironworkers in high demand as wind energy booms
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

Transcript:

In an iconic photo from the 1930s, ironworkers eat lunch, perched on the steel beam of a skyscraper. The photo documents the critical role these tradesmen played in building city skylines.

And now, ironworkers are also essential for building another kind of tall tower – wind turbines.

Noah Mihaly, a union ironworker for White Construction, is helping build the Coles Wind Farm in Illinois.

Mihaly: “It’s almost entirely ironworkers that are preparing the engine rooms, preparing the blades … and then putting together all the pieces, as well as constructing the foundations.”

Given their vital role in building wind farms, ironworkers are in high demand as the clean energy industry expands.

So to recruit and prepare more people for these jobs, Illinois established a workforce training program under the state’s Climate and Equitable Jobs Act.

Called the Climate Works Pre-Apprenticeship Program, it provides people from underserved areas with free training and help applying to apprenticeships.

Mihaly: “The pre-apprenticeship program was my jumpstart. It was the main reason I was able to get into the ironworker’s union.”

And Mihaly says he finds the job rewarding.

Mihaly: “I just like the idea that I’m able to help put together renewable energy.”

scraped.title: ‘Electrify everything’ hits the global stage
scraped.description: The world gets most of its power from fossil fuels. Mass electrification, promoted by this year’s climate conference, is still a climate solution.
scraped.h1: ‘ Electrify everything’ hits the global stage
scraped.body_text:

Canary Media

13 November 2026

This analysis and news roundup come from the Canary Media Weekly newsletter. Sign up to get it every Friday.

World leaders — well, some of them — gathered in Turkey this week for COP 31 , the annual climate conference, for discussions focused on how we power our world. Specifically, conference organizers proposed that attendees join in on a goal of meeting 35 % of the world’s final energy demand with electricity by 2035 , up from just over 20 % today.

Achieving that target demands participation from across the global economy. Everyday drivers and shippers will need to replace gasoline- and diesel-powered cars and trucks with plug-in alternatives. Manufacturers will need to swap in industrial heat pumps and electric boilers. Steel and ironmakers must embrace electric arc furnaces and other cleaner technologies.

But if the power that supplies all those electric vehicles, heat pumps, and furnaces comes from fossil fuels , will electrification still make a dent in global emissions? Yes, and there are a few reasons why.

For one, electrification is a necessary step to ditching fossil fuels. And it can take a long time to make the switch, whether it’s your home’s heating or an industrial-scale system providing steam to a factory. Getting more homes and processes electrified now means a larger portion of the world’s energy demand will be cleaned up as soon as more renewables arrive on the grid.

Electric-powered machines are also way more energy efficient than fossil-fueled options, as energy and climate policy expert Jan Rosenow has explained . A lot of energy gets wasted when you burn fossil fuels, particularly in small localized applications like a boiler that heats up a home. But you can get the same result with less fuel — and fewer carbon emissions — if you burn natural gas at a big power plant and then use that electricity to power a heat pump.

Electrification has a benefit beyond emissions, too — one that has become especially pertinent as the war in the Middle East has sent global oil and gas prices through the roof . It lets countries reduce their reliance on imported fossil fuels.

In Europe and Asia, people have responded by buying electric stoves and cars to curb their reliance on imported oil and natural gas. And the EU , learning both from the Iran war and the ongoing struggle in Ukraine, announced plans in July to ramp up electricity’s share of energy use to 46 % by 2040 .

Whatever comes out of this year’s COP meeting, expect these climate, efficiency, and security benefits to keep nudging countries toward ever-greater levels of electrification.

What’s next for the permitting bill?

The Senate’s bipartisan permitting bill passed its first big test this week as legislators voted 73 - 25 to formally take up the proposal. The bill as written would speed up permitting timelines for transmission, clean energy, and fossil fuel projects, but it’s likely to undergo a lot of edits before it becomes law.

Monday’s vote was the Senate’s first since Election Day, when it became clear Democrats would have resounding majorities in both houses of Congress next year. Many Democratic senators voted against advancing the permitting bill, with some saying they could use their newfound power to beef up the legislation’s clean energy benefits — and address concerns that the bill is too generous to fossil fuel interests.

It’ll face a challenge there from Democrats who say they didn’t have enough input in the bill’s creation, though House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) says his party will guarantee its passage.

One step forward, one step back for SMRs

Small modular nuclear reactors’ murky future is no clearer this week as the industry notched one win and one setback.

On a bright note for the industry, the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission approved X-energy and Dow Chemical’s plans to build four Xe- 100 advanced reactors in Texas, reports Brian Martucci . The NRC OK ’d the application in a record 18 months, following its approval of two other small reactor projects from Kairos Power and TerraPower.

Up in Canada, the news was a bit more drab. Ontario Power Generation said Tuesday that its SMR , poised to be the first in North America, won’t be online by its 2030 target, nor will it stay within its budget, Dan McCarthy reports . That’s especially problematic given that the project uses the same technology behind most of the world’s existing nuclear fleet — and a design that developers in the U.S. are eyeing themselves.

scraped.description: Most of the GOP lawmakers targeted by the Invest in Tomorrow Coalition lost reelection. The PAC is now looking toward 2028.
scraped.h1: Solar PAC got revenge on clean energy’s enemies in Congress
scraped.body_text:

Canary Media

13 November 2026

Before this election cycle, it was hard to identify any politician who feared the solar industry. The Invest in Tomorrow Coalition PAC set out to change that, and now has a roster of wins to back up its threats.

The super PAC , funded and led by solar entrepreneurs and investors, emerged during the midterm primaries with pledges to spend millions of dollars on attack ads against politicians who undermined clean energy policy. ITC got the outcomes it wanted in all six primaries it targeted. Its ads didn’t mention renewables, but instead used messages that tested well with voters — for instance blasting archconservative members of Congress for not being MAGA enough.

In the general election, ITC engaged in 17 congressional races, many of them in districts that President Donald Trump won by double digits, said Tom Matzzie, who chairs the PAC . ITC saw its desired outcome in 13 of those races, counting the apparent , though not totally final, loss by Republican Lauren Boebert in Colorado’s 4 th District. ITC ’s targets won election in four cases: Arizona’s 2 nd District, Florida’s 13 th, Florida’s 27 th, and New York’s 21 st.

“ We definitely sent a message that we can make an impact no matter where you are,” Matzzie said. Of the Republicans who signed a letter in May 2025 calling to ​ “ fully repeal ” the Inflation Reduction Act, 40 % won’t be returning to their jobs in Congress.

The PAC lost its perfect hit rate, but after spending $ 17 million across the election cycle, it’s on track for 19 wins out of 23 races, or 83 % success.

ITC wasn’t solely responsible for all Republican losses. The group exploited a political environment that had soured on unified GOP control of Washington, amid rising costs, an open-ended war in Iran that disrupted the global energy trade, novel and highly lucrative forms of corruption, and masked federal operatives attacking immigrants and citizens alike in the streets of American cities.

But the group demonstrated a knack for homing in on its targets’ weaknesses and amplifying them to voters who might not have gotten the message otherwise. The PAC also frequently trolled the candidates to get under their skin. After the election, the group issued press statements calling Brandon Herrera, who lost in Texas’ 23 rd, ​ “ one of the most despicable candidates we’ve ever seen run for office,” and saying of the incumbent in New Jersey’s 2 nd, ​ “ Jeff Van Drew always looked out for Jeff Van Drew, and now he can do it full time.”

In several races, ITC ’s targets ended up corroborating the group’s effectiveness, by giving interviews venting about how the PAC was making reelection harder for them. Boebert recently guest-hosted ​ “ The Matt Gaetz Show” — a conservative talk show — and spent some of that time in the spotlight criticizing the solar PAC for obscuring its true policy aim behind ads on other topics.

To maximize its impact, the PAC deliberately chose races where promising Democratic candidates weren’t getting much outside funding. It became the biggest spender in Indiana’s 5 th District, dropping more money on ads than either candidate’s campaign mustered. After the Republican lost, the group released a braggadocious statement to the press: ​ “ Tell Victoria Spartz. We want her to know it was us.”

While that assertion would be tough to prove, the PAC ’s founders previously told Canary Media that their goal is to establish narrative influence: If members of Congress believe that voting to strip incentives from the solar industry will cost them in their next election, they may think twice about it next time. Now that nearly all the PAC ’s targets, many of whom hail from the ultraconservative House Freedom Caucus, have indeed lost their jobs, the threat is credible.

The last two sessions of Congress delivered historic highs followed by historic lows for the clean energy industry, emphasizing the value of not just passing policy but also making it stick. That’s where ITC ’s retributive style has the most to offer, and its well-publicized results will still be on file if a future Congress has a chance to revisit laws that help the clean energy industry thrive.

“ Our overall hope is we can come to a place of peace with politicians of both parties and move forward,” Matzzie said. ​ “ I’d much rather our industry was boring.”

For the next few years, at least, the diminished Freedom Caucus won’t have the sway it exerted over the last two years, when Republicans had a threadbare majority. Battles over energy policy will now unfold within a pro-clean-energy Democratic caucus.

Election season never really stops, however, and the 2028 presidential primary will offer high-impact opportunities to push candidates to support clean energy, or hound them for past attacks against it.

“ We are not going away,” Matzzie said.
