scraped.title: The Iran war will cause global fossil fuel emissions to fall
scraped.description: Counter to analysts’ early expectations, planet-warming pollution from fossil fuels is set to dip in 2026 — the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic.
scraped.h1: The Iran war will cause global fossil fuel emissions to fall
scraped.body_text:
This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

This signup form requires necessary cookies.

Allow marketing cookies to load the newsletter signup form.

Canary Media

13 November 2026

See more from Canary Media’s ​ “ Chart of the Week” column .

Global fossil fuel emissions are expected to dip this year for the first time since 2020 .

This time it was not plague but war driving the decline. The Iran war has caused brutal increases in oil and natural gas prices, leading many countries to cut their consumption of the fossil fuels and seek alternatives.

It’s not an especially large drop. Fossil-fuel-related emissions will tick down by less than half a percent this year, compared to 2025 , per new data from the Global Carbon Project . Nevertheless, it’s a surprising development: Analysts had initially expected emissions to rise this year.

It was clear from the earliest days that the Iran war would reshape the world’s energy use.

Iran shut down the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly 25 % of the world’s crude oil and 19 % of its liquified natural gas flows, shortly after the first U.S.-Israeli strikes began. But it was not obvious what that would mean for global emissions in the near term.

Yes, countries were trying to use less of those fuels to avoid spiking costs. And, yes, plenty of nations were racing to backfill their needs with EVs or renewables. At the same time, however, several countries sought refuge in coal — the dirtiest fossil fuel of all.

It’s now evident that the bump in coal use has been offset by the stark decline in oil consumption in particular.

The question is whether this is the start of a trend — or an aberration, like the pandemic-fueled drop of 2020 . The answer is hotly debated. Some analysts argue oil and gas demand will come roaring back whenever the war eventually ends. Others say it has kick-started a wave of cleantech adoption that is here to stay.

Shady Khalil, Global Policy Senior Campaigner, Oil Change International said:

“The first draft of the COP31 cover decision has some promising ingredients, but it's far too early to know whether governments will turn them into a meal worth serving. There is welcome recognition that wealthy countries are failing to deliver on climate finance promises and their obligation to provide public finance, triple adaptation finance, and the need for countries to develop roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels .

“Some key ingredients are missing. Governments must strengthen this draft with concrete commitments to end fossil fuel expansion, deliver fair and funded fossil fuel phaseout roadmaps, and ensure wealthy countries pay their fair share without saddling Global South countries with more debt. Other ingredients are rotten and should be taken out, such as dangerous distractions like CCS and CDR or a thinly veiled push for fossil gas expansion. Negotiations over the next days will suggest if governments need to prove they can deliver.

“The success of COP is not determined by the cover decision alone, but also the health and progress of negotiated agenda items, such as the establishment of just transition mechanism.”

Oil Change International is a research, communications, and advocacy organization focused on exposing the true costs of fossil fuels and facilitating the ongoing transition to clean energy.

scraped.description: The Trump administration’s fuel blockade has already been likened to an act of war by critics.
scraped.author: Sharon Zhang
scraped.h1: Fresh Off Electoral Defeat on Iran War, Trump Floats New Military Front in Cuba
scraped.body_text:
The Trump administration’s fuel blockade has already been likened to an act of war by critics.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

President Donald Trump said this week that he wants to “get Cuba done” before his term is over, casually saying that he is considering opening yet another military front in a country whose civilian population is already being killed and starved by his sweeping sanctions campaign.

When asked by conservative talk show host Hugh Hewitt on Thursday whether or not he would use military force in Cuba, Trump said he “would certainly consider” a military campaign on the small island nation.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave, yeah,” said Trump.

“We have a very good, talented guy for Cuba named Marco,” Trump went on. “Because Marco’s parents are from — Marco Rubio, his parents are from Cuba, as you probably know and he would love to do that. So we’re watching it very closely. It’s doing very poorly, it’s essentially a failed place, nation, whatever you want to call it, it’s failed. And we’re watching it. I would like to be able to do it.”

The suggestion to open a new military front comes despite voters delivering Trump and the Republicans a historic loss in last week’s midterm elections, due in large part to his failed war on Iran .

Cuba is indeed “doing very poorly” due in large part to the U.S.’s decades-old sanctions regime. The U.S. has held an embargo prohibiting U.S. businesses and citizens from conducting trade with Cuba since the 1960s, which had already had severe deleterious effects on the country.

Trump’s severe escalation in the sanctions regime, including the fuel embargo, is currently killing even more people in Cuba. As of June, childhood cancer survival rates in the country had declined from 85 percent to 65 percent since Trump’s sanctions were imposed, with medicine supplies reaching critically low levels. Infant mortality also doubled in that time, to 9.9 per 1,000 births, compounding on the existing effects of U.S. sanctions; according to an analysis this April by the Center for Economic and Policy Research (CEPR), the U.S.’s sanctions regime caused 1,800 excess deaths of infants between 2017 and 2025.

“The Trump policy of ‘maximum pressure’ on Cuba has killed a lot of babies — and, although we don’t yet have data for the last few months, it’s highly likely that more babies are dying now, and at an even higher rate than last year as a result of the current U.S. fuel blockade targeting Cuba,” said CEPR report coauthor Alexander Main at the time.

The U.S.’s fuel blockade, meanwhile, has led to numerous near-total or total blackouts across Cuba this year, leaving Cubans literally in the dark as they clamor for basic food and medicine supplies. Experts have said that the blockade is akin to an act of war .

The Trump administration has not shown any signs of letting up on Cuba. Just last week, Rubio and the Trump administration instituted yet another wave of sanctions targeting Cuba. Trump and Rubio have openly called for regime change. Two weeks ago, Rubio issued an open call on X for people to open a “discrete [sic] partnership with the CIA” if they seek change in Cuba, in concert with the CIA’s Cuba task force set up earlier this year.

In remarks on Monday, Trump said, on Cuba, that he “imagine[s] it will fall fairly soon.” The same day, Rubio criticized the Cuban “regime” and said that the U.S.’s goal is for Cubans to “wake up and realize that there is no future on the path they are on right now.”

scraped.title: Poll: Most US Voters Want a Popular Vote Model for Picking Future Presidents
scraped.description: Democrats in several states have indicated support for the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.
scraped.author: Chris Walker
scraped.h1: Poll: Most US Voters Want a Popular Vote Model for Picking Future Presidents
scraped.body_text:
Democrats in several states have indicated support for the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

New polling demonstrates that a majority of registered voters in the United States support changing the method through which presidents are selected.

Currently, the Electoral College is the mechanism used to pick presidents . Each state receives electoral votes equal to its number of congressional representatives — the number of House districts in the state plus its two Senate seats. These electors are directed by their states to vote for a presidential candidate following an election.

For most states, their entire slate of electors is given to the presidential candidate who won the most votes in their state. To win the presidency, a candidate must receive a majority of the tallied Electoral College votes, which is currently 270.

Due to significant population differences among states that are not accurately reflected in the Electoral College, the model can sometimes choose a presidential winner who did not win the popular vote among voters nationwide. Indeed, there have been five elections in U.S. history — including two elections since 2000 — in which the popular vote winner did not end up becoming president .

The post-midterm Economist /YouGov poll , conducted November 9-11, asked respondents whether they favored keeping the Electoral College or preferred to replace it with a popular vote system. Among registered voters, 51 percent said they wanted presidents to be selected through a popular vote, while only 28 percent said they wanted to keep the current system in place. Another 21 percent said they were unsure.

According to the poll, one in five registered voters (22 percent) have either heard of the Electoral College but don’t know how it works, or have never heard of it at all. It’s possible that a large segment of this population of voters would also support a popular vote model if they learned more about the undemocratic way in which the Electoral College functions.

With the results of the midterms flipping several state governments to Democratic Party control, there now exists a real opportunity for lawmakers to implement a popular vote system.

Complete abolition of the Electoral College would require a constitutional amendment. But advocates for a plan called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact say the rules of the Electoral College can actually be used to create a popular vote system.

Per the Constitution, each state determines for itself how its electors are chosen. If the compact was implemented, states totaling a majority of Electoral College votes would direct their electors to the candidate who won the majority of votes nationwide, rather than the candidate who won the majority of votes in their state.

The compact doesn’t kick in until states totaling a majority of Electoral College votes sign on. As it stands right now, just 48 electoral votes are needed for the compact to go into effect.

In this month’s midterm elections, Democrats won new trifecta governments (e.g., states in which Democrats have control of the state legislature and governor’s office) in Wisconsin, Michigan, Nevada, Arizona, and Pennsylvania. Each of those states has yet to back the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact — but if they do, they would represent more than enough of the remaining electoral votes needed to put it in place.

Lawmakers from those states have indicated that they are planning to pursue that route or are open to the idea of doing so.

Even if those states pass the compact, there’s one more hurdle: Article I Section 10 of the Constitution also requires Congress to approve most interstate compacts . That means the incoming Democratic-controlled Congress must pass a resolution to approve the idea — and that a filibuster by Republicans in the Senate could block it.

That is, unless Democrats change rules in that chamber to limit how and when a filibuster can occur, a matter that is presently dividing members of the party .

scraped.title: Critics Slam Department of the Interior’s New Strategic Plan for Public Lands
scraped.description: They say data center developers, mining firms, and energy companies could seize the opportunity to acquire vast tracts.
scraped.author: Lisa Sorg
scraped.h1: Critics Slam Department of the Interior’s New Strategic Plan for Public Lands
scraped.body_text:
They say data center developers, mining firms, and energy companies could seize the opportunity to acquire vast tracts.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News , a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here .

The U.S. Department of the Interior could transfer swaths of public lands to state, local and tribal governments through sales or land swaps, according to the agency’s new strategic plan .

Critics are concerned that many states, cities and counties can’t afford to maintain the lands, and would sell them to private interests — the first step toward a wholesale privatization of lands that have belonged to Americans for more than 150 years.

“This is the biggest attack we’ve ever seen on public lands,” said Kate Groetzinger, communications director for the nonprofit Center for Western Priorities.

The Interior Department did not respond to requests for comment.

The agency manages more than 500 million acres of land in addition to 3.2 billion acres of offshore resources and 700 million acres of underground minerals. All told, the department manages 20 percent of the country’s lands, from national parks to wildlife refuges.

Data center developers, mining firms and energy companies — all favored industries of the Trump administration — could seize the opportunity to acquire vast tracts for their environmentally harmful operations, critics say.

The plan says Interior “will work to decrease the size of the federal estate” through the sales. That will allow the department to “focus its resources on primary federal responsibilities and nationally significant federal lands,” according to the plan, with some of the sales proceeds going back to “the purchasing entities to use for conservation purposes.”

The plan also says the agency will “consolidate its workforce to advance operational efficiencies.” Interior has already lost more than 17 percent of its workforce under the second Trump administration.

In the plan’s introduction, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote that the agency will streamline environmental reviews and expedite leasing and permitting for energy companies. Nowhere in the plan does the agency mention wind or solar power. The first goal outlined in the plan is “Increase American Prosperity,” and the opening pages feature pictures of an oil rig and an offshore oil operation.

“Together, we can simplify processes and remove red tape that creates drudgery for our team members and impedes progress,” Burgum wrote. “We can bring forward new ideas and better ways of working. For the first time in human history, we can turn electricity into intelligence.”

Burgum has made millions of dollars off investments in artificial intelligence, powered by data centers, ProPublica reported Nov. 6 .

The plan doesn’t specifically identify data centers as potential customers to purchase federal property, but the White House previously asked Bureau of Land Management state offices to identify lands that would be appropriate for these uses .

Last June, BLM approved an AI data center on 81 acres of public land near Boulder City, Nevada. The builder had received federal approval in 2023 to construct a solar farm, but amended its application to include a data center.

A federal judge has halted the project because BLM did not conduct a new environmental analysis but rather used the previous one for the solar project, a likely violation of the National Environmental Policy Act.

Energy and mining interests have long sought — and received — access to the oil, gas and minerals beneath public lands via leases. The new Interior plan would allow BLM to sell or transfer those properties outright to agencies that could then resell them.

The plan runs from fiscal year 2026 to 2030. However, the Trump administration has already begun planning to offload some public lands in particular.

This September, the Forest Service, which is under the U.S. Department of Agriculture, issued a permit to Pitkin County in Colorado to manage a section of the White River National Forest that contains the Maroon Bells Scenic Area, the gateway to stunning burgundy peaks where hundreds of thousands of recreators visit annually. Critics see this move as a trial run for public land transfers.

In Alaska, the federal government is expected to soon open 28 million acres to new development and land ownership, according to the Juneau Independent .

Last March the Forest Service officially transferred a sacred indigenous site to Resolution Copper, a mining company .

BLM needs congressional approval to sell public parcels over 2,500 acres. However, federal law contains loopholes, Groetzinger said. The sales, for example, must serve the national interest, which can be broadly interpreted. The plan lays the foundation for that claim by repeatedly justifying future sales on national security grounds.

Not only does the Interior Department propose shrinking its current inventory of public lands, but the plan also forecloses the possibility of buying more. Instead of using the Land and Water Conservation Fund to purchase additional acreage, the agency says it will “shift its investment focus” to buying recreational and conservation easements on privately owned lands.

The Land and Water Conservation Fund protects thousands of parks, natural areas, historic sites and other projects nationwide from private development. “That’s an important function of the fund,” Groetzinger said. “For them to not use any of those funds to buy new land is just unprecedented.”

Jayson O’Neill is a spokesman for Save Our Parks and lives in Montana, where recreation and tourism driven by access to public lands and waters is critical for the local economy. “We need somebody that actually understands how important this is to the economic viability of our communities and also our way of life,” O’Neill said. “Instead they’re literally calling to give away federal public lands and public resources to industry.”

Inside Climate News reporter Jake Bolster contributed reporting.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $42,000 in the next 6 days. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

Lisa Sorg is the North Carolina reporter for Inside Climate News . A journalist for 30 years, Sorg covers energy, climate environment and agriculture, as well as the social justice impacts of pollution and corporate malfeasance. She has won dozens of awards for her news, public service and investigative reporting. In 2022, she received the Stokes Award from the National Press Foundation for her two-part story about the environmental damage from a former missile plant on a Black and Latinx neighborhood in Burlington. Sorg was previously an environmental investigative reporter at NC Newsline , a nonprofit media outlet based in Raleigh. She has also worked at alt-weeklies, dailies and magazines. Originally from rural Indiana, she lives in Durham, North Carolina.

scraped.title: Seven ways Democrats can help ordinary Americans and stand up to the oligarchs
scraped.description: If Trump vetoes them all, Republicans will have to answer for it.
scraped.author: Michael Mechanic
scraped.h1: Seven Ways Democrats Can Help Ordinary Americans and Stand Up to the Oligarchs
scraped.body_text:
Mother Jones illustration; Getty(2)

The historic repudiation of President Donald Trump’s agenda on Election Day had lots of ingredients. Voters were outraged over data centers , ICE cruelty , DOGE’s trashing of the federal workforce , the gutting of science funding and environmental protections and more, but blatant corruption and high prices seemed to be the top concerns.

The incoming Congress will conduct hearings and investigations, and perhaps even impeach a few officials, but if the Democrats don’t promptly address the economic elephant in the room, as Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told the New York Times last week, “we’re going to be screwed.”

The inflation resulting from Trump’s ill-conceived tariffs and war of choice in the Middle East have caused Americans’ living expenses to grow faster than their wages, while the AI-fueled stock market boom has only paid off for America’s wealthiest 10 percent (which holds more than 88 percent of the stock).

Taming consumer costs is one obvious goal, and Democrats have floated a number of interesting proposals , but voters may also appreciate efforts to redistribute back to the poor and middle class some of the economic spoils that Republicans redistributed to the rich in 2017 and 2025.

The scale of the Democratic sweep, as Paul Krugman wrote in a recent Substack post , “showed that Americans want fundamental change, a decisive break with Trumpism. Yet with Trump still wielding the veto pen, what should they do in the remaining two years of his term?” His answer: “Pass highly popular legislation that would clearly benefit ordinary Americans and not the oligarchs, knowing full well that Trump will veto the legislation.”

Here are seven ways the Dems could help the people who delivered them their landslide—along with ideas to pay for them. Ambitious stuff, but who knows: With 2028 approaching, and Republicans desperate to win back voters, maybe some of it will survive the veto pen.

Trump stubbornly refuses to accept that the world needs to wean itself off its oil addiction, but the Iran war he launched without congressional approval has made that point crystal clear. For now, though, we depend on the global flow of oil to keep prices in check. Congress could help restore that flow by refusing to keep funding the war, which will pressure the administration to end it quickly. For that to succeed, Democrats will need to completly reject the nearly 50 percent raise Trump is seeking for the Pentagon. His budget request is totally bananas—especially given that actual US military spending already exceeds $1.5 trillion , and the increase Trump desires would boost it to between $2 trillion and $3 trillion, according to an analysis by the Project on Government Oversight . That exceeds the combined military spending of every other nation combined.

How to pay for it: No need. Ending the war would save the government tens of billions—and the American people much more .

Pretty basic. Congress has the power to place limits on a president’s tariff authority. Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), the ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, introduced just such a bill in July, and the odds of it passing have now increased dramatically. Plenty of Republicans are not down with the tariffs, which are costing American families a lot of money. With Trump weakened, they may be willing to defy him, at least on tailored legislation. The tariffs on Canada, for instance, have badly damaged the US relationship with one of our best allies and trading partners, and imposed high costs on US consumers and businesses—especially in northern border states, but elsewhere, too, because America’s automobile and construction trades rely on Canadian inputs. Unless he’s reined in, Trump will keep doubling down—literally. Just yesterday, he threatened to double tariffs on another top trading partner, Mexico.

How to pay for it: More like, how can we afford not to do it?

Under the Working Americans Tax Cut Act , introduced in March by Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) and Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), a single filer would pay zero tax on their first $46,000 in earnings ($92,000 for a couple filing jointly), a baseline tied to median income. An eligibility phaseout ensures that people earning up to $80,500 (couples: $161,000) get a partial exemption, but no freebies for anyone who makes more. The main winners, according to the Penn Wharton Budget Model ‘s analysis, are households in the second through fourth income quintiles—whose average 2024 earnings ranged from $49,380 to $136,800. Depending on which quintile, they would see average tax cuts of $465 to $1,545. Families in the 81st through 99th income percentiles are not affected.

How to pay for it: Van Hollen and Beyer propose a hefty surcharge on taxable income in excess of $1 million a year, starting at 5 percent and rising to 12 percent on income over $5 million ($7.5 million for a couple). Don’t weep for these folks: Most families with income that high are reaping far more in untaxed investment gains . Subtracting the middle-class breaks from the zillionaire surcharges, Penn Wharton calculates a net revenue gain of about $264 billion over a decade if the bill becomes law.

This would address affordability concerns for many low- and middle-income Americans. The ironically named One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which slashed the safety net for America’s poorest by about $900 billion , was projected to cost the average family in the lowest income quintile $805 a year (after taxes and transfers) while boosting the average income of top 10 percent households by more than $15,000—top 1 percent households got about $63,000 extra. A Yale study conducted prior to the bill’s passage found that, when likely voters were informed of such effects, Republican opposition more than doubled and overall public support for the bill fell to 11 percent.

The Medicaid and food stamp (SNAP) cuts are being accomplished largely by imposing burdensome bureaucratic requirements that cause people to fall off the rolls. Recipients, for example, must repeatedly provide proof of employment, which may sound reasonable but is actually a nightmare for people just scraping by—even more so now that the world’s richest man has gutted the federal workforce, resulting in extra-abysmal customer service. (See: “The IRS is imploding.” )

The Affordable Care Act, meanwhile, helped millions of families get health insurance, but the premiums are increasingly unaffordable. Congress increased premium subsidies for low-income people in 2021. The next year, as part of the Inflation Reduction Act, lawmakers temporarily extended subsidies to middle-income households that had been priced out. Then the Republicans took over and let the expanded subsidies expire at the end of 2025, a move the Congressional Budget Office has projected will result in up to 7.4 million people losing health insurance by 2030. Retaining the expanded subsidies for a decade, the office calculated, would cost about $335 billion.

How to pay for it: Restoring all of these cuts will cost roughly $1.2 trillion over a decade, which is substantial, but the government spends more than twice that much on undeserved tax breaks for investors. The top marginal tax rate on wage and salary income, which applies only to earnings in excess of $751,601 for a couple, is 37 percent. But if that same couple gets all its income from long-term investments, not work, they pay just 23.8 percent on the portion over $600,050, and only about 19 percent up to that amount.

I’ve covered tax policy for a while now, and I’ve never once heard a reasonable rationale for the steeply discounted rates, which, based on estimates from the Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT), will cost the federal government more than $2.5 trillion over the coming decade.

Our for-profit healthcare system “is designed to return profits rather than to improve health.”

The Equal Tax Act , introduced in March by Sen. Edward Markey (D-Mass.) and Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.), tackles this worker vs. investor disparity by applying the 37 percent wage rate to any investment earnings in excess of $1 million a year ($1.5 million for a couple). That portion of the bill alone could raise hundreds of billions of dollars, and more if the cutoff were reduced to $500,000.

The tricky thing is that tax legislation always prompts changes in people’s behavior: Faced with a higher tax on income from selling stocks and other assets, some wealthy taxpayers will opt to hang onto those assets and instead take out loans against their holdings to cover expenses—part of a popular strategy known as “ buy, borrow, die .”

Markey and Ramirez address this by placing limits on “step up in basis”—the rule that lets wealthy people pass unsold investments to their heirs at death without anyone paying tax on these gains they accumulated over a lifetime. The Equal Tax Act, which includes protections for family farms and small businesses, treats these intergenerational wealth transfers as “liquidity events”: heirs are taxed as though the inherited assets were sold at fair market value on the day of transfer. The bill also has provisions to prevent families from using complex trusts to avoid taxation. Eliminating the “step up in basis” rule entirely, based on JCT’s estimates, would save the government some $618 billion over a decade—and even with this bill’s $1 million allowance, it could save hundreds of billions.

Markey and Ramirez go even further by capping the “pass-through” deduction. That’s a provision of the tax bill Congress passed in 2017 that lets owners of private businesses deduct 20 percent of “qualified business income” from their personal taxable income. It’s basically a $400 billion giveaway to the rich. Pass-through businesses, as I’ve written previously, are “dominated by S corporations and limited liability partnerships, nearly 70 percent of whose profits flow to the wealthiest 1 percent of the population…while ‘ virtually no ‘ pass-through income goes to people in the lower 80 percent.” The Markey-Ramirez bill caps the deduction at $200,000—and one could go lower.

Congress created the CFPB to rein in the sort of predatory Wall Street behavior that brought about the Great Recession of 2007-2009 and devastated middle-class wealth— Black wealth in particular .

Launched in 2011, the CFPB was funded by the Federal Reserve to safeguard its independence. Championed by Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), it tackled sleazy junk fees, abusive debt collectors, and discriminatory lending practices, and it didn’t hesitate to go after giants like Wells Fargo and Bank of America. The agency claims to have secured some $14.4 billion in consumer relief in its first 10 years alone, collecting $1.7 billion in civil penalties from the offending institutions.

Then, last year, Elon Musk crushed it. By June 2025, according to the nonprofit group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, DOGE had “effectively shuttered an agency which returned over $26 billion to the American people…but only cost taxpayers a fraction of that amount to run.”

Reviving the CFPB would help protect consumers, who are now even more vulnerable to predatory corporations in this age of AI enshittification . The big challenge is to protect the agency in a way the Supreme Court would tolerate, so that nobody can come back and DOGE it again.

How to pay for it: It pays for itself.

The elders among us remember how, when Congress was working on Obamacare, Republicans wouldn’t even allow a public option to compete with private health plans. That would be “socialism,” they claimed—and by god, they will make that accusation 1,000 times over with Medicare for All, which would kneecap the private health insurance industry. But is that a bad thing? Americans who are forced to deal with private insurers on a regular basis are fed up and frustrated—so frustrated that when a United Healthcare exec was gunned down in the street, plenty of people shrugged and said the guy had it coming.

The core problem with for-profit insurance, Dr. Ed Weisbart, national board secretary for Physicians for a National Health Program , told me in an interview soon after the killing, “is that the system is designed to return profits rather than to improve health.” It does so largely by delaying and denying claims—and placing patients who try to appeal the decisions into a bureaucratic labyrinth, the goal of which is to wear people down until they give up.

For-profit insurance is tremendously inefficient, Weisbart told me; the industry has overhead costs of roughly 15 percent, compared with about 2 percent for traditional Medicare. In 2018, JAMA published a study conducted at a large academic medical center that calculated the annual cost of dealing with insurance and billing red tape at nearly $100,000 per physician, which is bonkers. “And where does that money come from? ” Weisbart said. “It comes from jacking up prices.”

Indeed, a Yale analysis published earlier this year concluded that replacing commercial insurers with an expanded Medicare system that covers everyone would reduce US healthcare expenditures by more than $1 trillion per year and save 114,000 lives annually.

How to pay for it: It pays for itself.

By JCT’s estimates, over the next decade, the government will expend a mind-boggling $5 trillion on tax breaks to help Americans save for retirement. Encouraging people to save is laudable, but the majority of the population gets next to nothing out of this arrangement, and there’s no ceiling at the top end. (See “How Congress Made Sure the Rich Retire in Luxury—at Our Expense.” )

In 2021, JCT reported that more than 28,000 Americans had IRA (individual retirement account) balances exceeding $5 million, and nearly 500 had holdings of more than $25 million—Peter Thiel had managed to accumulate more than $5 billion in a Roth IRA, from which any disbursements are tax free. That’s in addition to any other tax-advantaged accounts they might hold, including pensions and 401(k)s.

Such people need no handouts, and the government could save a fortune by limiting tax breaks to people with no more than, say, $2 million in their combined retirement accounts. It could use the savings to shore up Social Security , which benefits everyone.

How to pay for it: See above.

These two quickies (and there are many others), won’t put money into the pockets of the middle class—directly, anyway—but they would help put a dent in this nation’s runaway wealth .

Tax unrealized investment gains: The untaxed growth of unsold investments is the foundation of the soaring oligarchic wealth that remains a dire threat to our republic. Imposing such a tax, Wall Street propaganda notwithstanding, is doable in theory, but as I wrote in “ How to Tax a Billionaire ,” the Supreme Court has signaled that it won’t tolerate such a thing. The Fair Tax Act , which is discussed in the article, offers a partial workaround. It has yet to be introduced as a bill, but the primary author, economist Brian Galle, told me he’s been meeting with legislators. We’ll see how he fares.

Neuter the GRATS: Estate lawyers and wealth managers for the richest families in America have embraced grantor retained annuity trusts (GRATs) as a zero-risk way to transfer hundreds of millions of dollars, even billions, to their heirs without paying a dime in inheritance tax. Congress “blew it,” the lawyer who pioneered the so-called Walton GRAT told me prior to his death—circa 1990, it unwittingly passed legislation that enabled these trusts and has yet to undo its mistake. A bill introduced in April by Sens. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Angus King (I-Maine) would do precisely that, if—like any of the above—it can get past Trump’s Sharpie.

scraped.title: The Florida teacher who turned “MAGA Meg’s” district blue
scraped.description: Elizabeth Holmes says voters were sick of her predecessor’s “political vanity projects,” which included renaming the airport after Trump.
scraped.author: Laura C. Morel
scraped.h1: The Florida Teacher Who Turned “MAGA Meg’s” District Blue
scraped.body_text:
Mother Jones illustration; Elizabeth Holmes Campaign; Florida House of Representatives

One of the many Democrats who flipped state House seats during the historic midterms was a public school teacher in Florida’s Palm Beach County. Elizabeth Holmes hadn’t even considered politics before 2026, and within months, she unseated Meg Weinberger, a Donald Trump–endorsed Republican known as “MAGA Meg” who had won the seat in 2024. Earlier this year, Weinberger sponsored legislation to rename the Palm Beach airport after the president, a project that cost $5.5 million . Holmes’ win there highlights how the MAGA movement is losing some of its power—even in the county Trump calls home.

The genesis of Holmes’ dizzyingly rapid campaign and victory can be traced back to April 15, an especially hard day at work. One of Holmes’ special education students ended up in the hospital after a mental health crisis. When Holmes got home later that day, she saw the news that during union contract negotiations, the superintendent offered the district’s teachers a 1.5 percent raise—a far cry from the 3.5 percent they’d been hoping for. Holmes channeled her frustration into a Facebook post.

“Today, after one of my hardest, most emotionally draining days of my teaching career, I am reminded that no matter how much we care, no matter how much we do, we are not valued,” she wrote, explaining how a 1 percent raise, after accounting for an increase in health insurance, would leave her with a $414 pay increase for that year. “School district leaders need to take a seat at a student desk and learn something from today’s teachers.” Nationwide, Florida consistently ranks in the bottom in teacher pay.

The post went viral and attracted the attention of Florida 180, a political committee that recruits and provides resources to Democratic candidates running for seats in Florida’s GOP-dominated legislature. In a message, Florida 180 co-founder Sara Miller asked Holmes whether she had ever considered running for office. Holmes’ husband initially thought the message was a scam, but she agreed to meet. She decided to run as a Democrat in the 94th District, which encompasses swaths of western Palm Beach County. “Given the opportunity to be supported in running for office and to make real change at the state level, it didn’t take me long to make that decision,” she told me this week.

Holmes, a mother of four in a blended family in Palm Beach Gardens, ran on promises to address the rising cost of living, support teachers, and protect communities from overdevelopment. Aside from renaming the airport after Trump, Weinberger, who leads the Palm Beach County Moms for Liberty chapter, had also filed legislation to rename a portion of Southern Boulevard after the president. Holmes highlighted these proposals in her campaign ads and social media posts, calling them “vanity projects.” In one Facebook post , she stands under the airport sign emblazoned with Trump’s name. “Do you hate this?” she asked, pointing toward the sign. “It’s time to get Meg Weinberger out of Tallahassee.”

Enough voters apparently agreed. Last week, Holmes defeated Weinberger by less than 3 points. She is among about 17 Democrats who flipped state House seats, ending the GOP’s supermajority in the state legislature and with it their ability to fast-track legislation and limit floor debates. Although Florida did not see any top-of-the-ticket races—such as governor or US Senate seats—flip blue, the House wins are a sign of the Democratic Party gaining momentum in the state as Trump’s unpopularity continues to crater the GOP. The seats are also part of a nationwide trend of Democratic gains in other statehouses. As HuffPost reported, Democrats “flipped 549 state legislative seats from Republican to Democratic, flipped control of 12 chambers and broke up 13 Republican supermajorities.”

“Stop ignoring Florida. We are on the ground doing phenomenal work with very little.”

Among the other Democrats who overturned Florida House seats are an infectious disease doctor in Orlando, the first Democratic Socialists of America member elected to the House, and an algebra teacher born in Mexico. Additionally, about a dozen other Democrats in state House races yielded between 47 and 50 percent of votes, a sign that there is potential for more flipped seats in 2028 with enough funding, which was sorely missing this election cycle. The lack of investment by major Democratic donors was a point of contention in the statewide races as well, where US Senate candidate Angie Nixon and gubernatorial candidate David Jolly lost by just a few points. “Stop ignoring Florida. We are on the ground doing phenomenal work with very little,” former Rep. Anna Eskamani, a Democrat who termed out this year from the state House and is now running for Orlando mayor, told me last week . “I want to see us build upon these successes to secure bigger wins in 2028.”

Holmes’ campaign was scrappy. She fundraised about $53,000 compared to Weinberger’s more than $800,000 , which funded several mailers against Holmes, including one showing her next to a drag queen that referred to Holmes as a “liberal teacher.” “Keep classrooms focused on quality education,” it read.

Holmes’ campaign was largely made up of volunteers, many of them Gen Z students in college or high school, among them some of her former students. Her only paid staffer was campaign manager Hannah Russell, a 17-year-old senior at Jupiter Community High School. She and Holmes, who teaches at another high school, met earlier this year during a district meeting regarding teacher salary negotiations. Russell and other students had gathered thousands of signatures in support of a teacher raise. A 3.5 percent increase was ultimately approved by the school board.

Holmes said Russell joined the campaign as an intern. By the summer, she became Holmes’ official campaign manager. “She had never worked on a campaign before, but she handled everything,” Holmes said. Russell attended training sessions and consulted with experienced campaign organizers.

Miller, of Florida 180, also stepped away from the political committee and joined Holmes’ campaign. Part of what excited Miller about the campaign was Holmes’ embrace of younger talent, including Russell. “I loved this idea of training young people to become civically engaged, especially after the last election, when so many of them went in the Charlie Kirk path,” Miller told me. “We’re all getting older, and we want to pass the baton on. We desperately need people like Hannah to do that.”

Russell worked on campaign duties during her study hall period and after school. “It was a grassroots campaign. There was barely any money power to it,” Russell told me. “We had nothing besides people.”

Holmes took an unpaid leave from work to run for office. She knocked on hundreds of doors, sometimes cruising through neighborhoods on a scooter or canvassing under the threat of thunderstorms . She heard stories of families struggling to pay for groceries, gas, or rent. “The cost of living continues to rise and their paychecks are not. And as a public school teacher, I understand that,” she would tell them. She also heard from voters who were upset with Weinberger’s efforts to rename the airport “instead of addressing this crisis that we’re in.”

From the beginning, Holmes said she had a feeling she could win. “We worked really hard and we had a positive message,” she told me. “People are ready for change.”

scraped.title: John Fetterman's first primary challenger is a progressive born in Gaza
scraped.description: “Genocide is just the worst manifestation of what it means for our public policy to be captured by special interests.”
scraped.author: Sophie Hurwitz
scraped.h1: John Fetterman’s First Primary Challenger Is a Progressive Born in Gaza
scraped.body_text:
Ahmed Moor has announced that he will challenge John Fetterman for his seat in the US Senate in 2028. Mother Jones; Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call /ZUMA; Courtesy Ahmed Moor for Senate

It took just days after Democrats’ resounding victory in the midterm elections for a challenger to Donald Trump’s “favorite Democrat”— Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman —to emerge. Ahmed Moor, a Philadelphia foreign policy analyst and writer, is the first candidate to announce his entry into what will likely be a crowded primary field. The 42-year-old Moor was born in Gaza, and has lost family in Israel’s genocide —most recently a 19-year-old cousin killed by an Israeli sniper in Rafah.

That history alone puts Moor at odds with Fetterman, who has become one of the most stridently pro-Israel voices in Congress and has threatened to leave the Democratic Party if it moves against Israel. But without his swing vote , Moor said, Fetterman will be “irrelevant”—and with only 13 percent of Pennsylvania Democrats reporting a favorable opinion of him in an October Quinnipiac poll, exceptionally vulnerable to a primary challenge.

Moor is not alone in eyeing Fetterman’s seat: state legislators Chris Deluzio and Malcolm Kenyatta are both reportedly likely challengers. Former Pennsylvania House Rep. Conor Lamb, who lost a primary to Fetterman in 2022, has also been floated as a candidate, but has so far denied any plans to run.

For now, Moor has a head start on pitching what he calls his “dignity agenda”— Medicare for All, an end to the US war on Iran, universal childcare, and a billionaire wealth tax—to the people of Pennsylvania.

I spoke with Moor via Zoom the day after he launched his campaign. We discussed data centers, his plans to impose sanctions on Israel if elected, and his ongoing lawsuit against the State Department.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

So, you’re new to politics—who exactly am I speaking with today?

I’m a Palestinian American writer, formerly a journalist. I worked in financial services in the past as well. And I’m a foreign policy guy. I just finished up a fellowship at the Foundation for Middle East Peace. I’m running for US Senate here in Pennsylvania, targeting the seat that John Fetterman currently holds.

It would be untruthful to say that I didn’t come to this decision through genocide. I was born in Palestine, I was born in Gaza, and I have family there today. But genocide doesn’t happen overnight. Genocide is just the worst manifestation of what it means for our public policy to be captured by special interests, in this case by the Israel lobby.

I think you can broaden that analysis and say that generally we suffer from a deficit of democratic governance in America. That all of our public policy has been captured by special interests. And you see that in the way that data centers have sprung up across our landscape in Pennsylvania. You see that in the way that AI has begun to intrude into our daily lives unbidden. We didn’t have a conversation about this.

We’re being told today that the equivalent of 9 percent of GDP is being spent on the AI buildout and it’s going to cause massive job losses. Well, let’s have that conversation. I don’t think it’s a good idea—but I’m insisting that we need to have a conversation about it. So that’s who I am, that’s why I’m running.

Why Fetterman’s seat?

Look, Fetterman’s story’s over. I’m not really running against Fetterman. No matter what happens in 2028, that man is irrelevant. I’m running for the future. I’ve got three young girls.

The idea that my kids’ decision set—that in the future, their rights will be more circumscribed than the rights I have, that their mother has—that’s intolerable to me. It makes me angry, and I’m unwilling to accept that.

Thomas Jefferson wrote the words of life liberty and the pursuit of happiness just a few miles away from where I’m sitting now. The idea that people have liberty without having access to everything they need to live a dignified life—I don’t believe that. I think there’s no liberty in poverty.

“Lying awake at 3:00 a.m. on a Sunday worrying about how you’re going to pay for your kids’ dentist bill—that’s not freedom.”

You’ve spoken about a “dignity agenda.” What does that mean in practice?

When you walk down the street and you see somebody who’s unhoused, when you walk around and you see people who are economically insecure or or you drive through rural Pennsylvania and you see communities that are decrepit, where people are generally hopeless, they’re not living dignified lives.

Fundamentally, I think dignity means providing the basics, the material basics—and thereafter, go out and volunteer, or go out and make a million dollars, if that’s what you want, or write a book, or do whatever it is that’s going to make you happy, because that’s what it means to be a free person in a free society. And I have no prescription for what happiness means. I know what happiness means to me. I hope everybody figures it out on their own terms. But I do know that there’s no possibility of self-actualization if you’re lying awake at 3:00 a.m. on a Sunday worrying about how you’re going to pay for your kids’ dentist bill. That’s not freedom.

You’ve also talked about sanctioning Israel, often referencing the Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act of 1986, which levied sanctions against apartheid South Africa. What would that look like?

In 1986, we enacted legislation targeting South African apartheid on the basis of the idea that it’s inconsistent with our values as Americans. We litigated the question of separate and unequal on the battlefield 160 years ago, and we came down pretty firmly on one side of that conversation. We know how we feel about separate and unequal in America. So the idea that Jews have superior rights in Palestine, I’ve never believed in it. I don’t understand. It’s unreasonable to tell me as a Palestinian-American man that somehow Jewish people deserve more rights in the country that I was born in.

So, it’s just the idea of equal rights. Let’s enforce legislation that we enacted 40 years ago in a new context.

You’re one of the plaintiffs in an ongoing lawsuit against the State Department for failing to enforce the Leahy Laws, which should theoretically require that the US stop providing military aid to Israel while it’s being credibly accused of human rights abuses.

Not theoretically—concretely. The law is very clear. The Israelis committed genocide, they’ve committed war crimes, atrocities; they ought to be sanctioned for it in line with existing law. We as Americans lead with our values. I believe that. I believe that cynical people in positions of authority have undermined that argument, and made a lot of people feel that our speech is one thing and our actions another. I’d like to bring those things into coherence.

We are people who value the lives of children. The Israelis have killed 21,000 children in Gaza. They’ve killed 100,000 innocent people . We really don’t know how many people they’ve killed because they won’t allow any journalists into Gaza . And the genocide is ongoing–that bears saying as well.

And so there’s a moment of urgency that isn’t being met by any of our public policy. But about that lawsuit–you know, I’m a rule-of-law guy. I’ve got three little kids, and they’ve got to be able to enjoy Halloween and trick-or-treat in safety.

I believe that should be true for everybody else’s kids. I was talking about the pursuit of happiness earlier. If we don’t have safety, we’re not free people either. I think when the rule of law begins to break down even at the highest levels, that percolates throughout society.

When you see the blatant disregard coming out of the Biden and Trump administrations for the rule of law, for ideas that we’ve articulated and then enacted through legislation that are supposed to govern how we interact with the world, everything else breaks down. So the lawsuit is about enforcing the rule of law. We’ve got laws. Let’s adhere to them. And then we’ve got to hold bad actors to account.

Antony Blinken , Jake Sullivan , Brett McGurk , Jon Finer , and [Samantha Power], who wrote the book on genocide, I think it was a how-to, possibly.

Speaking of all those figures you just named, you wrote a few articles during the 2024 election about why you weren’t voting for Biden that year. I suspect some Democrats might come for you on that front. What would you have to say to them?

I am the best representation today of what it means to engage authentically and enthusiastically with American democracy. I don’t like the leadership in the Democratic Party. I think most Americans in the midterms would say they voted against the war, against the Republicans, rather than for the Democrats. I am not committed to a party as such.

I’m committed to ideas, I’m committed to principles. The Democratic Party can become the party that rejects war and extermination.

But I’m not going to vote for a genocidal leadership. Instead, I’m going to seek to eject that leadership. And there’s a contest now— Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer , these are people who are bought and paid for by AIPAC, which is a pollutant in our political environment.

I represent the future of the Democratic Party. People are fed up with bad behavior across the board. It’s my Democratic Party, not Joe Biden’s Democratic Party.

And you’re running as a DSA member, right?

DSA had me at anti-genocide. Those guys are values-first people. The DSA is the values arm of the Democratic Party. I love those guys.

On the theme of accountability, I wanted to ask you about ICE.

ICE is best understood as a paramilitary militia. It is not a policing force. ICE has to be disbanded. The politicians on both sides who voted to fund ICE need to be held accountable at the ballot box.

We’re talking about rebuilding American institutions. It’s not a small task.

The people who murdered Alex Pretti and Renee Good have to be held accountable for their behavior. We need to drag bad actors into an environment of accountability. And if you’re going to wear a mask and you’re going to go kick down somebody’s door, think twice. We’re going to be in an environment of accountability soon.

You’ve started your campaign quite early. It’s two years out from 2028. How do you plan to spend that time?

This is the bullhorn. This campaign is a vehicle for maintaining pressure on the leadership of the Democratic Party, working for renewal. I’m running for two years because I want to telegraph these arguments into every living room in America and every living room across Pennsylvania. I’m going to go to every one of those 67 counties.

I’m going to meet with people on the left and right—I think Americans are committed to constitutional democracy. And that includes the Second Amendment, you know? You’re not going to convince a man with his origin in Palestine that it’s a good idea for the federal government to seize everybody’s guns.

Alex Pretti was availing himself of the best argument for the Second Amendment. He was confronting a tyrannical regime in an American street, and he was executed. I don’t know what he should have done in that instance.

And I want to have these conversations earnestly and in good faith with every voter in the state and every non-voter too.

Prior to this run, you were best known as a writer, editor, political analyst—you edited the book After Zionism —what from that world do you plan to bring into the Senate?

Principles. In the darkest moments I’ve had, where I’ve felt afloat and unmoored from anything else, a reversion to the principles that mattered to me has helped to guide me.

We’ve got to recommit to our guiding principles, the Bill of Rights, articulated 240 years ago. The Declaration of Independence 250 years ago. Those are good ideas, and the job of US senators to take those ideas and see them rendered in the real world.

That means free speech, which was assailed and undermined by both the Biden and Trump administrations. The IHRA definition of antisemitism is a severe curtailment of speech in America. So let’s keep people safe, yes, but let’s also honor the rights, the civil liberties that make America worth fighting for. There’s this left-right contest, which is real—I’m a man of the left. We can litigate these questions. But what’s inviolable to me is the shape of the sandbox.

And that’s the common thread. I’ve always argued that equal rights should exist in Palestine, Israel. There’s nothing inherently superior about anybody. We’re all just people. That’s the principle that’s always guided me and my work on foreign policy. And it guides me in thinking through the contours of what an American future can look like.
